Śrīḥ.
May there be auspiciousness.
The ritual manual for self-centered worship (*ātmārthapūjāpaddhati*),
the Vāruṇa manual.
I bow to the one with the face of a young elephant, who plays at the sport of bathing in the ocean of ichor flowing from the two surfaces of his temples. 1.

May the dancer in the golden assembly protect us— he who, by means of the tinkling sounds arising from the blossoms of his glorious feet, brings the teachings of grammar into conformity with the actual sounds.

[The fruits] produced from the Jambu, Āmra, Kakubha, Aśoka, Pīlu, and Vakula; and those born from the Plakṣa, Udumbara, Pullāṭa, Aṅghri, Jāti, Campaka, and Śaṅkha.

among these are the eight baths."

Who is the qualified person (adhikārī) for the initiation (dīkṣita)? It is one who is fit for yoga, ritual bathing (snāna), worship (arcana), and so forth. For such a person, at the very beginning, there is the Vāruṇa bath (the bath with water).

For one who has been initiated, bathing in rivers, streams, lakes, ponds, and pools is best; that in canals, lotus-ponds, and the like is middling; and that in wells, oblong ponds, sacrificial pits, and water-cisterns is inferior. Bathing at home is also considered best. As it has been said:
In the venerable Pauṣkara it is said:
"For one who has been initiated, bathing in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, and in marshes or thickets is the most excellent;
bathing in a lotus pond is middling."
(33) They say that bathing in well-water is the best when performed at home; even at home,
the bath should be performed by the initiated on ground that has been smeared [with cow-dung].
In the *Kāmika*:
"Alternatively, in one's own home, on a surface of ground smeared with that [mud], one should perform the bath while seated upon a pedestal, using either warm or cold water."
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"For women, children, kings, those afflicted by disease, and travelers,
bathing with warm water or even a gargle is recommended."
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"Whether at a river, a pond, a large tank, or even a well—four types [of bathing are prescribed]. If a river is not available, one should perform the bath in a well."
Alternatively, in the vicinity of the monastery, one should perform the ritual bath with water drawn from a well using jars,
accompanied by the previously mentioned rites and mantras.
Bathing with a copper vessel compared to an earthen pot yields a hundredfold merit;
silver is a hundredfold more effective than copper, and gold is a hundredfold more than silver.
The fruit at a step-well is ten times that of a well; at a pond, it is more than a hundredfold; and at a river flowing toward the ocean, it is said to yield immediate results.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"The confluence of the ocean, as well as rivers, lakes, and ponds— water touched by the feet of the Noble One is indeed most excellent."

The floating of rafts (*pallavaplavana*) with lotus stalks and the like from ponds and so forth, resembling a tank or a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), is of medium quality; that which is inferior (*kanyasa*) is as follows.
A water-pool, a drinking-trough, or bathing in a pond shall be equal [in merit] if they are located near a temple of Śiva, whether they are small or large.
All sacred fords (tīrthas) are situated therein by virtue of the arrangement of the Śiva-liṅga.
(p. 35) —In the Śaiva Purāṇa—
One should never defile a sacred bathing place situated within a temple;
nor should one who is impure ever perform a ritual bath there.
It is said that at a confluence of rivers, the merit is ten million times ten millionfold compared to a blazing fire;
one should perform a bath in a river, which yields a thousandfold more merit than bathing in a pond.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Bathing at night is not recommended, except when there is a sighting of Rāhu; for rivers constantly flow with the blood of their sons during the night."
Therefore, one should never perform bathing or drinking [with that water]; nor should one take water at night, whether for the sake of the gods or for oneself.
The most excellent preceptor should cause [the disciple] to consume water combined with gold and fire, or else perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
In this manner, the purification of water occurs; thus it is prescribed for bathing at night. Therefore, one should indeed collect water during the day, both for the sake of the gods and for oneself.

Regarding the procedure for bathing therein, it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "Having sipped water, performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), holding *darbha* grass in his hand, and being of serene mind,
he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *saṃhitā* and the *praṇava*."
O Lord, having performed my bath today in this month, on this lunar day, under this weekday, and in this best of rivers,
be gracious to me for the sake of your worship.
Having thus informed Śambhu in his form, one should perform the ritual bathing. First,

having gathered the earth with the Astra-mantra, taken it up with the Heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, and having cast it onto the bank of the water with the Head-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should remove grass, roots, and so forth with the Śikhā-mantra ending in *namaḥ*.
Having sprinkled [the body] with the weapon-mantra ending in *haṃ phaṭ* (p.
37), one should divide it threefold with the armor-mantra ending in *namaḥ*: with one part from below the navel down to the feet;
One should wash it.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Having purified the bank according to the previously stated procedure, one should take earth with the heart-mantra, hold it upon the head,
and remove any pebbles from the crest-lock (*cūḍā*).
Having sprinkled [the water] three times with the Astra-mantra, and again with the Varma-mantra as the cause,
one should wash from the feet up to the navel with one [mantra], and the body with the other.

With the second portion, having sprinkled all his limbs up to the navel with water over which the Astra-mantra has been recited once for the sake of pacifying the impurities residing in the body, and having entered the water for the cessation of mental sins, he—
facing east and having performed the rites such as mounting the vehicle for the Six-faced One— should [honour] the Brahmins.

Having restrained his speech and mental states for the sake of purification, while reciting the *saṃhitā* and meditating in his heart upon the Astra-mantra, which has the brilliance of the sun at the end of time, he should remain submerged in water for as long as possible.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Having touched all the limbs with [the hand] blazing like the sun and consecrated with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), facing east..."
Having entered the water, he stirred it thoroughly with a weapon.
Having restrained his vital breaths and blocked his senses with his two hands, he meditated within upon the fire-weapon,
which was tawny with a mass of radiance.
Having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite, one should remain seated in that water for as long as possible.
According to the Siddhānta:
[one should touch] both ears with the thumbs, and the eyes with the two index fingers.
One should firmly bind the pair of nostrils with the two middle fingers.
One should employ this "six-faced" procedure in the rite of bathing. As stated in the *Sārdhadvishatikā*:
"The knower of mantras, having taken earth with the *astra* mantra recited once, performs the 'bath from impurity' (*malasnāna*)."
One should perform it first by reciting the Saṃhitās just once.
In the Parākhyatantra:
"Having extracted a single portion of earth, one should perform a bath with it that removes impurity, while uttering the Weapon-mantra."
Having taken his own ritual action upon his head in due order,
he who recites it down to the end of the feet and bathes is purified in an instant; he should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), which is the internal restraint of the vital breath.
One should suppress the activity of the mind by means of suppressing the activity of the vital breath; by suppressing the activity of the mind,
one removes that which is evil and mental.
One should meditate on the Astra-mantra, filled with the blazing crests of a greatly radiant fire,
established in the Āgneya-dhāraṇā, and [burning] with the abundant heat arising from its flames.
Water exists as ash all around through its fiery energy; by that [energy], those who are submerged in water perish, whether they are situated within or outside of it.
Those standing on the bank perish, consumed by fire and overwhelmed by fear;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the stainless state of the syllable *Oṃ*, which flows with nectar.
In the *Suprabheda*: "While submerged within the water, one should not show any part of the body except for the eyes;
or else, while submerged up to the face, one may show the upper half."
That which is said to be "immersed at the mouth" (mukhamagna) is equal to fifty hundred [lakhs] in sequence;
when immersed halfway, it is called half a thousand [koṭis], and when fully immersed, it is said to be one koṭi.
Having emerged while engaged in meditation, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in due order; likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Having taken up [the vessel] with water from the midst of the restrained Asuras, [one should rinse] the mouth."
One should mutter the Tāra mantra, "Duḥkhatā," for the destruction of the flood of sins.

Then, among the three castes beginning with the Brahmins, a householder, a student, or anyone else who has been initiated by Śiva should first perform the Brāhmī Sandhyā as prescribed in the Samāsa [text], and immediately thereafter—
Meditating on the Astra-sandhyā: *Oṃ śivāstrāya vidmahe, kālānalāya dhīmahi,
tanno śastraḥ pracodayāt*.

Thus, for the *astra-mantra*: having offered three handfuls of water into the solar orb with the *gāyatrī-mantra*, one should perform recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity. One who is detached from worldly life should perform only the *sandhyā* of the *astra-mantra*, omitting the Vedic *gāyatrī*. A *śūdra*, however, should omit the Vedic *sandhyā* and [perform] the *astra-sandhyā*.

One should worship the twilight (*sandhyā*) itself. For the purpose of meditating upon that, one should sprinkle three drops of water on the head with the *astra-mantra*, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and then, having formed a hollowed palm (*añjali*) with the *astra-mantra* alone, one should recite it with that same mantra according to one's capacity. Alternatively, one should contemplate the *astra-mantra* within the heart.
In the *Mṛgendra*:
"Having bathed up to the head and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), facing north or east,
the twice-born belonging to the two [upper] stages of life (*āśrama*) should perform the twilight devotions (*sandhyā*) according to the Vedic path."
p.
42) Likewise, on the Aṃśumatī river—
at either the eastern or northern [confluence]— the wise man should perform it equally, and also at the southern [confluence].
And in the west, one shall obtain that very fruitlessness.
Regarding the subtle distinction, it is said:
"Having performed the ritual bathing and the libation, one should perform the Vedic rites facing south;
having turned to face north, one should perform the Śaiva conjunction and the sequence."
In the Kāmika:
"Having bathed in water and emerged, the initiate born of the three castes, though previously unrenounced,
should perform the Brahma-sandhyā, O practitioner."
At the conclusion of that, one who has resorted to the concise ritual should worship the Śaiva [deity]; but the other, whose nature is dispassion, should turn away from worldly objects.
One should perform the *brāhmī* [mudrā], or one should certainly perform the *śaivī* [mudrā] under all circumstances— whether in necessity,
in purification, during bathing, or even while reciting mantras.
In Ajita: "At the twilight, or during salutation, or in the rite of libation, or in the act of fire-offering."
Having bathed and emerged [from the water], one who is a householder (bhautika) should first perform the Brahma-sandhyā;
if, however, he is a perpetual celibate (naiṣṭhika), he should proceed with the Sandhyā known exclusively as the Astra.
Whether it be the domestic rites (*gṛhavatya*) and so forth prescribed for the twice-born, or that which is to be done or not to be done— it is considered essential for a Śaiva.
In the *Bṛhatkālottara*:

"Having first performed the Vedic [initiation], one should then enter the Śaiva [initiation]. Likewise, the *bhautika* and *naiṣṭhika* [initiations]; or alternatively, one should perform the *brāhmī* [initiation]."

The Śaivī [initiation], however, must be practiced according to the strict rule; otherwise, there is a fall. The triad beginning with [the initiation] called *vitti* should be performed by the four [initiations] without distinction.
Thus, having performed the twilight worship (*sandhyā*) as prescribed for a *śūdraka*, [it is stated] in the *Rāmanāthapaddhati*: (p. 44) "In this way, O Śvadeva..."?

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should perform the twilight worship (*sandhyā*) while recollecting the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) within the solar disc; having offered the water libation (*arghya*) with the Astra-Gāyatrī, one should mutter it according to one's capacity.
Having likewise performed the bath up to the head and sipped water for purification, facing north and having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
one should recite the Śivāstra mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having turned back three times with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the worship correctly;
this is declared to be the Astra-sandhyā, common to all Śaivas and well-guarded.
Then one should perform the mantra-bath; as stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"This is declared to be the bath for removing impurities; now listen to the mantra-bath. [Regarding] the fish, the frog..."
By serpents and other such aquatic creatures.
Water that is constantly used becomes especially corrupted;
therefore, to pacify those defects, one should designate a sacred bathing place (śivatīrtha).

Thereafter, from a single drop of water at great pilgrimage sites such as the Hāṭakeśvara [Kedāra], [one attains the same]. With "Oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya vauṣaṭ," [one should perform] the previous [rite] with the weapon-mantra recited over the right [hand].
Having performed the recitation of the Brahma-mantra seven times and the recitation of the Śiva-mantra once in succession,

one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the recited Astra-mantra, sprinkle the water while reciting the Śiva-mantra, and touch all limbs while reciting the Brahma-mantra.
Having performed the ritual of making [the self] six-faced and having meditated upon Śiva, one should bathe.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*: "Having drawn [the water] from the great holy sites such as the Ganges with the *aṅkuśamudrā* (hook-gesture),
one should take up the water of consciousness with the heart-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, using the mudrā called *udbhavā*."
One should place [the water] in the heart with the mudrā ending in "namaḥ," and likewise place it in the water with the right hand turned upward and the index finger bent.
The remaining fist is the connection; this is the *mudrā* of the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
In the *Kāmika*:
Having gathered the remaining portion of the water, one should stand in the midst of the water and,
facing north, place a third part in the left hand.
To the east and likewise to the south, and also to the north: the eastern [direction] should be consecrated with the Astra-mantra, while the southern is consecrated with the Brahma-mantra.
One should perform the recitation of the *uttara* [mantra] consecrated by Śiva separately for each; one should then recite the *astra* [mantra] consecrated [by it] in all ten directions in due order.
By means of the application of the Nārāca weapon, one should cast [the body] back into the midst of the water;
then, with the right hand, one should touch one's own body starting from the head.
One should perform a bath in the auspicious water that reaches the end of the body and destroys bodily sins; thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
The preceptor should proceed toward the east or the north for the purpose of bathing;
it is said that bathing while facing the east yields a hundredfold merit.
Even there, the southern bank brings infinite fruit.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"O Six-faced One, by this rite, Śiva-tīrtha shall indeed become the best of all tīrthas."
Merit is auspicious and removes all sins.
Then, having visualized the Moon and Sun, as well as Śakti and Śiva, in the left and right hands respectively,

and having consecrated them with the six-syllable mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should sprinkle [the disciple] three times on the head with the *kumbha-mudrā*. Then, for the purpose of pacifying obstacles, [one should offer] water with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
One should cast [it] into the cardinal and intermediate directions.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Having joined the hands, which consist of the sun and the moon, with the jar-mudrā (*ghaṭamudrā*)."
The consecration should be performed once with each mantra that consists of the root mantra.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:

"With hands in the form of the moon and sun, one should sprinkle with the water-pot mudrā (*kumbhamudrā*), using the six-limbed mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and water repeatedly; the practitioner, having recited the mantras along with the practitioners."
And by the number of new-moon days.
One should perform the consecration daily in due order, while visualizing the nectar-water.
As stated in the *Vīratantra*:
"Having placed the two hands palm-upward, one should join the wrists of the left hand..."
Then one should place the right [hand] above.
One should place the right thumb over the left thumb;
one should make the two middle fingers well-extended and bind the remaining fingers together.
This shall be the *kalaśamudrā*; one should employ it at the time of bathing for the sake of self-protection and for the pacification of all obstacles.
One should sprinkle water consecrated with mantras all around.

If he is a householder, he should bathe according to the protocol for a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), beginning with an oil massage and followed by fragrant *āmalaka* fruit and other such substances.
In the Kāmika:
"One should bathe with fragrant substances such as *āmalaka* according to the royal ritual;
seated upon a golden throne and the like, one should be bathed with golden jars, just like a king."
Having bathed for the purpose of cleansing, one should perform [the rite] with auspicious sounds. In the *Vīratantra*:
"Having anointed the entire body with oil mixed with *āmalaka* and cow dung..."
And having smeared it once more, one should bathe it.

50) Thereafter, having emerged from the water, one should withdraw that sacred site (tattīrtha) by means of the Saṃhāriṇī [mudrā], the Heart [mantra], or the Short Pavilion [mantra]; then, having removed the water clinging to the limbs, one should [proceed] with something pure and dry.

Having wiped himself with a cloth and discarded the wet garment, he should fasten the waist-thread and the loincloth made of fifty-year-old [wool] according to the Vāmadeva [mantra], put on the pure garment as prescribed, and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
In the *Kiraṇa*: "Then, having drawn forth the sacred site (*tīrtha*), it should be placed in the heart by means of the Heart-mantra.
In the *Sārdhatriśatikā*:
One should effect the withdrawal of that sacred site by means of the temple itself.
As stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"Thereafter, having cast off the loincloth and being endowed with the *tāla*-mudrā..."
Covering your private parts with something else, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as prescribed by the injunctions.
p.
51) Does even the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) [wear] the saffron robe or the supreme [white] one?
Having meditated [on it], he should withdraw the Śiva-tīrtha with the saṃhāra-mudrā.
Having worn this and having specially wrapped the loincloth (veṣṭi),
its characteristic measure should be one cubit or even two cubits.
The loincloth (kaupīna) is said to be ten or eight finger-breadths in length and likewise in width;
it may be made of cotton or other such materials.
The girdle consists of fifty threads and hangs down in three parts.
In the *Kāmika*:
"A loincloth is said to be one or two cubits in width and length; the waist-string is twice that [in length]."
It may be constrained by the knot of the two-fold [obstacles].
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"It should be sixteen finger-breadths wide and thirty-six finger-breadths long;
it should be joined, dry, auspicious, fine, and either white or saffron-colored."
The loincloth of the celibate students should consist of thirteen knots,
and they should possess a very firm waist-thread made of muñja grass and a girdle made of palāśa wood.
One should perform [the recitation] for one, two, three, or up to fifty years at most; one should maintain it according to one's capacity with the Vāmadeva [sāman].

In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "A wise person should not perform rituals while wearing only a single garment, nor while naked with only a loincloth, during bathing, worship of the deities, sacrifice, or eating."
Two washed garments should be worn, uncut and not sharpened [at the edges];
there is no fault for lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins) even if they lack a loincloth (kaupīna).
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"Furthermore, it is taught that for a householder, [the garment] may be either saffron-colored or white."
As long as the worship of Śarva continues, one should receive [the offerings]; such shall be the rule.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Every day, one should wash the worn garment or the night-cloth;
the waist-band and loincloth should be washed with alkaline water at the conclusion of purification."
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"I shall now declare the purification of clothing, for by that [purification] one becomes pure;
one whose self is devoid of the purification of clothing becomes impure even if [otherwise] pure."
Daily purification is required for garments used in divine rites;
for other clothes, purification must be performed whenever they become soiled.
One who is pure should construct an arched gateway with three bamboo poles; there, having washed the garments, one should properly hang them out to dry.
On a tree undisturbed by birds, or on a stainless stone surface, or upon a pure cluster of dūrvā grass,
or even on washed blades of grass;
The purification of those defiled by feces, urine, semen, or blood should first be performed with earth and water; thereafter,
purification should be carried out with alkaline substances, cow’s urine, and so forth.
In all cases of purification of substances, one should first take up soft water until the odor and the stain have both been removed from afar.

Silks and woolens [are purified] with coarse substances; linen cloths with white mustard seeds; cotton cloths with bilva fruits; blankets with arishta fruits; garments made of bark-fiber with cow-dung;
and clothes, ropes, cane, feathers, chowries, skins, and bark-garments likewise.
Is there any purification for all those who know?
The purification of vessels made of split bamboo and wood is said to be by means of water; however, their sprinkling with cow-hair [brushes] is proclaimed as a specific rule.
Aṃśumatī:
One should perform the ritual with unwetted cloth without sloth; otherwise, it becomes in vain.
Furthermore, that action is purified by bathing.
In the absence of a full bath including the head, having washed either from the neck down to the navel or below the feet according to one's capacity,
and having wiped the remaining wet limbs with a damp cloth,
one should [purify] with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, using the fire arising from the big toe.
Having visualized the body as burnt, one should drench it with pure water remembered from that agitated power; thus, one becomes bathed.
O Mataṅga, with the word *jyoti* (light) placed at the end of *huṃ phaṭ*, blazing like the fire at the end of an eon,
he respectfully incinerated his body.
Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra should cause his own body to be reached by the water invoked during his personal recitation while uttering the *praṇava*; thus he is undoubtedly bathed.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Nor [should there be] donkeys, crows, vultures, or village pigs; nor [should there be] cocks or ghosts."
By the impurities of the earth, the limbs, the young deer, and the birth-impurity.
If one is touched by Śākyas, Durgaṇḍins, Nirmālyabhojins, Ranyaliṅgins, or others who are censured, one should then perform a bath.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"Those who consume the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*), those who steal the property of the deity, those who misappropriate the property of the Guru, and those who destroy various sacred objects— "
All those who have not been initiated, and especially those touched by such persons, as well as those who have undergone shaving or vomiting, should perform a bath with water.

Regarding the specific rules for bathing when one becomes impure through contact with urine, feces, or putrid matter above the navel— with the exception of the hands— the *Śivadharmottara* provides the following illustration: [text follows].
Having thoroughly cleansed his body three times all over with clay and cow dung,
he should discard the bathing garment and put on a second one.
Having bathed with decoctions and other such substances, he should put on another garment.
Having girded himself with a waistband and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should consecrate the water with mantras.
While meditatively contemplating the peaceful Śiva with devotion, one should slowly perform the bath twenty-one times while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then again perform an ablution upon oneself with the water-pot,
with full handfuls, or with the hollow of both hands.
One should sprinkle oneself with the twelve-fold form of Śiva— either by oneself or by another—
from all sides, for the sake of purifying obstacles and misfortune.
Having sipped water (ācamana), one should sprinkle oneself and the head repeatedly with that same [water];
then, one should perform the bath using a jar over which the mantra has been recited many times.
Thus, having become well-bathed and freed from all sins, one obtains with faith the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas).
In the *Vīratantra*:
"One should perform a bath with a paste made from dogs, cats, donkeys, and so forth."
Whether above or below the navel, one becomes pure by means of seven applications of clay.
Bathing is prescribed in six instances: after vomiting, when the sun has risen, after shaving, after sexual intercourse, following a bad dream, and upon touching a wicked person.
Silence is prescribed in six instances: during bathing, the worship of the deities, meditative absorption, the recitation of mantras, eating, and the performance of fire rituals.
Mataṅga said:
"O best of sages, having thus bathed in water once a day according to one's ability, one becomes qualified for the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) day by day; not otherwise."
Thereafter, the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) should be performed following the water-bath; however, in cases of incapacity, the sin-destroying ash-bath may be performed even without the water-bath.
p. 59) In the *Makuṭa*:
"Having first performed the water-bath, one should afterwards perform the fire-bath (*āgneya*)."
In the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa]:
"The fire-related bath is declared to be another, namely the ash-bath; it is to be performed daily after the water-bath, or else as the unsurpassed [bath]."
In the Kāmika:
"Whoever performs the ash-bath as is appropriate, even just once,
being liberated from all sins, shall accomplish his desired fruit."
Since fire is superior to ashes, why then has he transgressed against it? O sinless one, one who has bathed in ashes is seen to be radiant like fire itself.

Having taken with the left hand the ashes prepared from cow dung and other materials according to the ritual rule and placed within a vessel of elemental substances (*bhūtikośa*), one should deposit them upon the palm of the left hand, purify them through the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, and then take up a small amount of that ash between the tips of the thumb and forefinger.
A lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) or a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), having obtained ash perfected by the *Siddhyakalpa* and other such means,
should consecrate it with the root mantra along with the *Saṃhitā*.
Having purified it from the feet upward with the *Saṃhitā* mantras beginning with "akalpanivṛtti," and so forth;
One should perform the impurity bath (*malasnāna*) with the fierce *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, from the top of the head down to the feet. Likewise,
in the *Suprabheda*:
By the will of Śiva, five cows descended from the city of Śiva to the earth;
they were born from the Kṣīroda, the best of oceans, as it was being churned by the gods and demons— these five cows who are the mothers of all the worlds.
Likewise, in the Śivadharmottara:
"The first bath of Umāpati resembles pure crystal;
there dwells the Blessed Lord Soma, being worshipped by the lords of the Gaṇas."
When the Siddhas, along with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Vāyu, had reached that place,
the illustrious Dharmavṛṣa stood before the Lord’s son.
Where the bull among heroes always resides, there the mothers of the cows dwell;
therefore, Goloka and Śivaloka are remembered as being one and the same.
Whatever qualities belong to the realm of Rudra, those same qualities belong to Goloka as well; [there dwell] Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā.
Thus, the five cow-mothers are established in the world of Śiva; as stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"The tawny, the black, the white, the smoky, and likewise the red."
This description has been proclaimed for those beginning with Nandā and ending with Sumanā.
For the sake of benefiting the entire world and for the gratification of the gods, the Cow-Mothers have indeed stationed themselves upon the earth for the purpose of Śiva’s ritual bathing. (p. 62)
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"Having recited the *gosāvitrī* once, one should offer fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp in the directions of the cows, and having prostrated, one should present them."
One should cause to be given yellow orpiment, ghee, milk, and food; having caused betel to be offered, one should recite the Gosāvitrī mantra one hundred times.
"Let us know Him whose horns are sharp; let us meditate upon Him who is to be known through the Vedas. May He impel our cows.
Having thus worshipped the cow, which is the embodiment of truth, one should likewise take her dung.

In the lineage, there are three types: the pacifying (śāntika), the nourishing (pauṣṭika), and that which grants desires (kāmada). Cow dung is connected to the womb; that which is taken with the hand [is the third].
Having burnt it with Brahma-mantras, that pacification (śāntika) is here described. Furthermore,
whatever has been excreted by a cow or fallen upon the ground, having taken up that which is situated within [the body], one should perform the rite.
Then, one should burn [the object] with the six-limbed [mantra].
That is declared to be nourishing (pauṣṭika); now hear about that which grants desires (kāmada).
It is cow dung that has fallen upon a perfectly pure ground.
Having burned that [offering] with the *prāsāda* mantra, which bestows all desires, one should rise in the morning, O Goddess of Gods,
and be endowed with the vow of silence.
Having gone to a cow-pen and having paid homage to the herd of cows,
one should offer a white cow to a Brāhmaṇa and a red one to a Kṣatriya.
The color of the Vaiśya is said to be yellow, while that of the Śūdra is black; cow dung should be taken in this sequence, for one should not take it otherwise.
On the full moon day, the new moon day, the eighth day, and during the eclipses of both [the sun and the moon]— in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
That ash is said to be of four kinds: the first is called the primary (kalpa), the second the secondary (anukalpa), and the third the tertiary (upakalpaka).
The fourth [type] is indeed unfit; among these, each preceding one is superior to the next. Likewise, those who are barren, aged, diseased, or possessed of inauspicious marks [are unfit].
A young woman who is devoid of ears and hair and rendered witless,
a cow that eats impure food, and a pregnant cow— these must be abandoned.
A brindled cow, a Kapila, a red one, a white one, and a black one—
one should take the dung of these [cows] onto a lotus leaf or likewise on a plantain leaf.
Or one may ward it off with both hands over a *palāśa* leaf, or in the sky; or, having taken cow dung into a vessel, one should hold it while reciting the *Sadyojāta* mantra.
Furthermore, through the reversal [of the process], the knower of mantras should again cast out the middle portion consisting of flesh,
and fashion it into the shape of a ball using the Vāmadeva mantra.
Having dried it with the Aghora mantra, one should burn it again in a pure place; specifically with the Puruṣa mantra, one should then deposit it in a new vessel.
Likewise:
having dried it on a single day, the wise and pure one should burn it with the fire of Śiva, or in the perpetual fire,
while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
In the *Skandakālottara*:
"O Six-faced One, for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the sake of purification,
I have in the past bestowed sacred ash upon my devotees and those who bear the *liṅga*."
66) Or else, the mantra-practitioner [should take] the ashes in a conch shell or a copper vessel;
however, a golden vessel is best, while a silver one would be middling.
A copper vessel is the lowest; in its absence, it may be made of clay. A gourd vessel is inferior, while one made of *paittakī* wood is the lowest of the low.

One should recite the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra once, along with the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva. According to the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*: "With camphor, ushira, hrībera, ketaka, and campaka, as well as madana, [one should perform the rite] with the *Śāna-mantra*."
Therefore, one should perform the recitation with particular care.
And it is said:
"The *ketakī*, *mallikā*, *nāgacampaka*, as well as the *pāṭala*, the lotus, the *palāśa*,
the *tulasī*, the *apāmārga*, and the tips of *kuśa* grass."
Having deposited the lineage there, while the vessels are present and under one's possession,
one should place it in a new earthen jar and protect it with armor.
(67) Take up that ash while recollecting the Śiva-mantra; then, O Nandikeśvara, listen to the secondary procedure as well.
Having taken dried dung from the forest, perform it according to the ritual rules as before; this third preparatory rite consists of dried cow-dung found in the wilderness.
Having powdered it and collected it, make it into a ball with cow's urine;
burnt according to the previously mentioned procedure, it shall become the prepared ash.
Setting aside the previously mentioned ritual procedure, one should perform the purification of the ashes alone as if it were a *piṇḍa*; this is designated as the "unconditional" (*akalpa*) method.
Ash produced by others is proclaimed as "akalpa" (unfit); this [ash] is said to be of four kinds, which destroys all sins.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Taking this very sequence, [one should perform it] with respect to the vessels and the jars."
One should perform the ritual bath at the three junctions of the day, or as often as possible.
It is prescribed at the four, eight, twice-eight, and eight joints; namely,
having performed the bath for removing impurities with ashes characterized by the aforementioned description,
one should perform the ritual bath.
Regarding the cause:

having washed both hands and feet, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and sip water again; then, having recited the mantras once, one should perform the smearing with sacred ash (bhasmoddhūlana).
Having placed the ashes in the left hand, one should consecrate them with the right hand.
As stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Having prepared [the ashes], one should purify them with the root mantra and likewise with the Brahma-aṅga mantras, using the hand."
One should perform the cleansing bath with the right hand, beginning from the head.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"Having taken the ashes of the non-conceptual (*akalpa*), one should then perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*). [This is done with] the five Brahmans."
And it is consecrated with the six limbs and with the mantras beginning with Nivṛtti.
Having purified it with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), one should sprinkle the head and other limbs [with water].
In the *Sārdhatriṃśatikā*:

"O Six-faced One, having first performed the bath for removing impurities (*malasnāna*) with the seed-syllable of the weapon (*astrabīja*), one should thereafter perform the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*)."
The knower of mantras should perform [the rite], beginning from the head.

In the *Suprabheda*: "Alternatively, a wise person should take ashes during the *agnihotra* sacrifice; with that purifying substance, the learned one should bathe according to the previously mentioned procedure."
One should not perform any sacrificial rite (*ādhvara-karma*) without wearing the *tripuṇḍra*.
(p. 70) Now, the ritual bath (*vidhi-snāna*):
Having washed his hands, whether he be a *bhautika*, a religious student (*brahmacārī*), or a householder,

he should apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark on the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet with the mantras of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, and on the two shoulders with the Sadyojāta mantra alone.
On all limbs as well:

the renunciant (saṃnyāsī) or the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) [should apply the ash] by way of the right and left sequence, from the feet to the top of the head in reverse order with the Sadyojāta and other mantras, and likewise on the two shoulders and all limbs with the ash-mudrā.
Or, holding [the ashes] with the thumb, ring finger, and middle fingers,
one should meditate upon the deity of the ashes using the root-mantra of Brahmāṅga and the *kumbha-mudrā*;
having sprinkled [it] on the head, one should perform three *tāla*-claps with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

At the time of bathing, one should withdraw with the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā] the sacred ash that has fallen upon the heart; likewise, on a pure spot, the wise one, with a tranquil mind, should meditate upon the *astra* as before.
Having taken a handful of ashes with his right hand.
Then one should wipe the head, the face, and the neck; thereafter, the chest, the arms, the heart, the back, and the hips.
That which is unreachable by the right hand, one should thoroughly dust off with the left hand,
while both hands touch each other's limbs.
In the Pauṣkara:
"One should always bathe facing north, having merely performed the smearing with ashes.
In the Santāna:
A Brāhmaṇa should shake off all [dust]; a Kṣatriya, however, [should do so] from below the neck; a Vaiśya is to be understood in the same way; but a Śūdra should avoid shaking it off entirely.
For all classes of beings alike, [the ritual] would be devoid of mantra.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*: (p. 72)
For a twice-born man, the ash-bath extends from the feet up to the head;
for kings, however, it is with blood-red ash from the navel upwards.

For a Vaiśya, a vertical streak is prescribed, while for a Śūdra, it is the triple mark (tripuṇḍra); these are made with ashes consecrated by the Brahma-mantra, according to the sequence in the various ritual baths.
In the Kālottara [Tantra]:
"But for Brahmins who are lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), one should perform a bath of all the limbs;
for kings, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, however, there is the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka)."
Likewise, in the Vīratantra:
"One should smear [the ashes] on all limbs, especially for Brahmins;
one should likewise apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) there for kings and Vaiśyas."

In this very manner and sequence for all Śūdras as well; if one is unable even to perform the smearing (uddhūlana) for that reason, one should apply the Tripuṇḍra for the sake of all spiritual accomplishments. The Tripuṇḍra...
Having made [the mark] with moist, white ashes.
p. 73) Regarding the subtle [gifts]:
one *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, two *niṣkas*, and one and a half *niṣkas* for the Brahmins and the other [castes].
And one should perform the ash-bath for all the castes.

Regarding the cause: when joined with water, the middle finger and the thumb [are used]; otherwise, it is devoid of water. This triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra), when properly applied, is the destroyer of all defects.
In the *Kālottara*:
"O child, having placed the two hands palm-upward, the middle fingers, the index fingers, and the ring fingers [of the left and right hands] should indeed be interlaced with one another."
This is the ash-seal (bhasmamudrā) prescribed for the triple marks (tripuṇḍra).
Alternatively:
the form [of the mark] on the forehead is made with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb using ash.
One who is tranquil should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), which destroys even the greatest sins.
p.
74) When ignited, a width of seven finger-breadths is prescribed for Brahmins.
The Tripuṇḍra of Kṣatriyas, however, should have a width of five finger-breadths.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) four finger-breadths wide grants all desires for Vaiśyas;
for Śūdras it should be three finger-breadths, and for women it should be one finger-breadth.

For women of those respective castes, however, that very same [mark] is prescribed. As for the reason: for all those born in the direct order (anuloma), the *tripuṇḍra* is like yellow in color; as it is for others as well.
For all [others], the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be like that of a Śūdra.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Is he a materialist? If he is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), he should face east;
if he is a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*), he should face the directions starting with the northeast."
In some places it is said: "Having smeared [the ashes] over all the limbs, one should apply the *puṇḍra*.
The *santānika*, the seeker of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), and the practitioner (*sādhaka*) [should apply] the triple-mark (*tryāyuṣa*) with ashes.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] on the head with the Brahma-mantras using the water-pot mudrā.
Having shaken off the dust from the ground preceded by three claps of the hands,
one should cast that floral offering (nirmālya) far away and must not step over it.
In this manner, the fire-related bath (āgneyasnāna) should be performed by those practicing celibacy (brahmacārin).
In the *Makuṭa*:
"O Maheśvara, I shall describe specifically the form of the deity of the ashes (bhasmadeva): three-eyed..."
He has three heads, is fierce, possesses three hands, and has qualities as his faces.
Three-legged, three-eyed, with a body smeared with ashes and adorned with kuṣṭha,
he is formidable with the grand display of his tāṇḍava dance and graced by red flowers.
Having meditated upon the Lord, the Sovereign of Protective Mantras, a person shall obtain peace;
one should perform ablutions at the three junctions of the day, or as often as possible. [Santāpa...]
Prior to midday, it should be accompanied by water; after that, it is devoid of water.
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa and the Brahmakaivarta Purāṇa:
It is ordained that for Brahmins, the sacred ash should be maintained with water at all three times of the day;

however, for women and mendicants, it is without water. For forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas), this [practice] applies to every stage. For men who have not undergone initiation, it is accompanied by water, beginning from midday.
Regarding this, other wise and virtuous people say: "There is no rule for you.
The specific locations for wearing the *tripuṇḍra* are stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
One should apply [the mantras] at thirty-two bathing places, or even at sixteen places, as well as at eight places,
and likewise at a single place.
On the head, the forehead, the two ears, and likewise the two eyes, on the nose, the mouth, and the throat— beyond this, there are two *haṃsa*s; [then] on the upper arms,
the wrists, the heart, both sides, the navel, and the two private parts.
And likewise, [the joints] of the pair consisting of the thighs and buttocks, and the knees.
On the two calves and the two feet is the supreme locus consisting of thirty-two [deities]:
the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti), the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa), and the guardians of the directions (dikpāla), together with the Vasus. Dharo... [p. 77]
Dhruva, Soma, Āpas, Anila, and Anala;
Pratyuṣa and Prabhāsa—these are remembered as the eight Vasus. A wise person should wear the Tripuṇḍra with the Vāma mantra dedicated to them.
With a concentrated mind, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* on the sixteen locations of learning, as well as on the head,
the forehead, the throat, and both shoulders.
In the upper arms, the wrists, the heart, the sides of the navel, and likewise in the back and the calves— at each of these locations,
there are presiding deities.
Śakti, Sādākhya, Īśa, [Sadāśiva], and Vidyā;
the nine powers beginning with Vāmā, and the two Aśvins are recorded as the sixteen.
Alternatively, [one should place them] on the head, the forehead, the two ears, and likewise on the throat; on the two arms, the heart, the navel, and likewise on the pair of thighs.
The back of both knees and the two feet [constitute] sixteen [parts].
Listen now to the presiding deities for these locations as they correspond.
Śiva, Skanda, the Moon and Sun, Vighneśa, and Viṣṇu;
Śrī is in the region of the heart, while Prajāpati is in one's own navel.
The Nāgas and Nāga maidens are on the two thighs;
the rivers and oceans are at the feet; and the sacred fords (tīrthas) and weapons are also on the back.
Or thus one should meditate on the sixteen; and the eight locations are now described: the position of the Guru, the forehead, and then the pair of ears.
The two shoulders, the heart, and the navel—this shall be the eighth.
Brahmā and the seven sages are proclaimed as the deities. Alternatively, [the head...]
The arms, the heart, and the navel.
They say these are the five locations and the fivefold forms of the deity; [they are] in the presence of the Guru, the Deity, Fire, and Knowledge,
or when one is about to depart from sight.
Upon seeing those guilty of mortal sins (mahāpātaka) or even an ungrateful person, dusting [oneself] on an impure ground or on a path is not prescribed.
Therefore, being pure and seated on a seat in a clean place, facing north,
one should remain silent and meditate upon Śiva and the Guru.
Just as not even an atom of ash would fall to the ground [if it were held by the power of a planet],
so too should the application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing with ashes be performed.
If one is unable even to perform the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*), one should apply the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) and so forth. Thus,
having performed both the smearing with ashes and the triple mark— what then?
Released from all sins and immediately endowed with purity, one is liberated from all evil merely by the sight of him.
What need is there for much speaking here? O Lord of Gods, all sins whatsoever perish without effort, like [the darkness vanishing at] the sight of the sun.
For one who is devoid of the means for attaining prosperity, there is no attainment; nor is he devoted to knowledge, nor is he fit for meditative absorption, nor for sacrifice, nor even for giving.
Therefore, with every effort, bathing with ashes is supreme;
sprinkling with water using hands touched by ashes is the highest [form of purification].
81) If one touches a twice-born person or someone who has not received initiation, bathing with ashes is prescribed;
as is [bathing] during the three junctions of the day, at midnight, and at the beginning and end of sleep.
Having slept, eaten, drunk water, or performed the necessary bodily functions such as voiding, one should likewise practice the Āgneya rite upon touching a eunuch, a Śūdra, or a woman.
When one has been touched by a parrot, a cat, a mongoose, as well as a cuckoo, a mouse, or others,
one should perform the fire-purification bath (āgneyasnāna).
Then one should perform the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*). It is as follows:

having washed the feet and hands, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), restrained the breaths (*prāṇasaṃyama*), and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should [meditate] with the mind on the Root Mantra upon the Supreme Power residing at the *dvādaśānta*.
Having uttered the final [syllable] and having uttered the end, by means of the nectar-like [stream] issued forth from the partless Śakti...
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"Accompanied by the root mantra and performed mentally, one should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*);
for this mental bath (*mānasasnāna*) is indeed prescribed in all cases."

Thus it is said: "And it has been stated that one should meditate on Him as He returns suddenly from the midst of the nectar-water that has flowed forth from the agitation of the partless power (*niṣkala-śakti*)."
Likewise:
"Enveloped by the root mantra, one should perform a mental bath for oneself, both internally and externally, with a stream of nectar [flowing] from the mouth."
Thus ends the procedure for mental recitation.
Then one should perform the mantra-bath: having washed the feet and hands, sipped water (ācamana),

and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should fill a vessel with water and consecrate it once with the *vyomavyāpin* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) according to the *saṃhitā*.
By reciting the root mantra and touching [the body] three times from the head down to the feet with that water, the destruction of all sins occurs. As it is said in the *Kāraṇa*:
At the conclusion of that, having performed the ritual bath with mantras, having washed his hands and feet,
and having sipped water (ācamana) and performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), he likewise pours the water into a vessel.
Having consecrated that water once with each repetition by means of the *vyomavyāpin* mantras, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the five Brahmans, and the root mantra itself;
One should touch [the body] with that water using the root mantra and the armor mantra;
likewise, one should perform the touching three times from the head down to the feet.
One shall be liberated from all diseases and the destruction of all evils shall occur.
(p. 84) Thereafter, one should perform the divine bath.
For example, having performed the washing of the feet and other preliminary rites, facing eastward and recollecting either the *mūlamantra* or the *Īśāna-mantra*,
with arms raised, by taking seven steps one obtains a divine bath consisting of rain accompanied by the sun's rays.
One should maintain it.
As it has been stated in the *Kāraṇa*: "There,
with rain and sunshine, facing eastward with arms raised, one should recite the root mantra with speech for as long as seven steps."
Then, facing the sun, the wise man should pay homage to it;
when this is done, he is liberated from great sins—of this there is no doubt.
(Māhendra and Divya are synonyms.
One who is proficient in devotion should proceed while reciting the mantra of Īśa.
Thus ends the procedure for the divine bath (divyasnāna).

p. 85) Then, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) either in the forenoon or the afternoon,
he becomes one who is joined by contact with the wind arising from the dust kicked up by the hooves of cows.
Or, by recollecting the armor of Nara while taking seven steps toward the northern direction, the Vāyavya bath is accomplished.

This has been stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*: "The wind-element bath is indeed described as being performed with dust raised by a cow's hoof; while reciting either the *Puruṣasūkta* or the *Kavaca*, one should proceed for a distance of seven steps."
Recalling the mantra from the Mṛgendra-saṃhitā, one becomes wind-born.
This is the procedure for the Vāyavya bath.
(p. 86) Then one should perform the bath of respect (gaurava-snāna)—namely: having washed the feet and hands, sipped water for purification, and become pure;
While reciting the Śiva-mantra, one should bear the feet of the Guru upon one’s head;
by saluting those feet, one obtains the fruit of bathing [in sacred waters].
Likewise, in the Mṛgendra:
"Pure, bearing the feet of the Guru upon his head, he should utter 'Śiva'."
Thus concludes the ritual for the bath of honor.

Then one should perform the royal ablution (*pārthiva-snāna*), as follows: having washed the feet and hands, sipped water (*ācamya*), and performed the ritual self-protection (*sakalīkṛtya*), one should take holy water from the Gaṅgā or another sacred site into the hand, recite the *saṃhitā*, and [anoint] from the head down to the feet with that *saṃhitā*.
One should apply it. In the absence of that [liquid], one should take clay, consecrate it as before, and make the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead and other parts of the body.
As it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Having touched the waters of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sindhu, Sarasvatī, and so forth..."
Or he may take the corpse of one born in that field according to the Saṃhitā.
Likewise, one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the head and other limbs with mantras; thus is described the supreme earthen [mark], which removes all sins.

Thus is the procedure for the royal bath (*pārthiva-snāna*). Among these, the baths pertaining to Varuṇa (*vāruṇa*), Agni (*āgneya*), the mental (*mānasa*), and the mere [recitation] (*mātra*) are obligatory; the others, however, are occasional (*naimittika*) for those who are divine. Regarding each of those...
One should perform the respective baths during the presence of specific signs (*nimitta*). As it is stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
"The group of four beginning with Māhendra is known as the occasional (*naimittika*); the Vāruṇa bath is performed upon the skin, and the Bhasma bath [is performed] with ashes."
And it has been stated that one is constant, while the other is occasional.
In the *Kāmika*:
"For householders, it should be with water; for ascetics, it is made with ashes."
Thus, the occasional [cause] has been illustrated by means of these two examples.
Mataṅga says:
Having been touched by one who is uninitiated, one should perform the fire-purification bath (āgneyasnāna);
due to contact with an outcaste, one should perform the water-bath (vāruṇasnāna).
Having washed his feet (and performed the ritual sipping of water), having bound his matted locks and topknot,
facing north with his head uncovered, and sitting in the *utkukkuṭa* posture with his hands placed between his knees,
[he should perform the rite] with pure waters free from foam, bubbles, moss, mud, and so forth.

For the sake of purifying the thirty-five principles (tattvas), beginning with Earth and ending with Śakti, and for the sake of pleasing deities such as Bhāratī, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule.
Rinsing the Mouth (Ācamana)
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Having tied the topknot on his head and washed his feet and hands externally,
he should sit upon a level seat with a serene face, facing the eastern direction.
With hands placed between his knees, observing silence, not looking at dogs or other such creatures, and becoming single-minded,
[he should perform the rite] with clear and cool water.
One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water that is free from froth and bubbles, strained through a cloth, and drawn up;
one should not do so with water infested by insects or used by those of the lowest castes.
Where a cow does not become free from thirst even by other waters that are turbid,
kept in skins, saline, warm, or contained in the hands or vessels of others.
O Ajitā,
sitting with the topknot tied and the knees raised, with both hands placed upon the knees, without wrapping the head,
and having washed the feet and hands externally.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra* (p.
90): "And one seated in the *utkaṭa* posture should have hands like those of a cow's ear."
Bharata describes the characteristic of the *utkuṭaka* stance:
"The two heels and the two knees are on the ground, and the two feet are level."
At that time, during yoga, meditation, twilight prayers, recitation, and so forth, one should sit in the utkuṭaka posture,
holding water that has soaked a māṣa-bean within the hollow of the left hand.

Having observed [the breath] situated at the base of the thumb, one should drink that [water] with the *brahmatīrtha*. According to the *Ajita*, it is located in the heart for a Brahmin; for a Kṣatriya, it should be the throat; and for a Vaiśya, the palate.
For those of mixed castes, there shall be one hundred [days] of water in successive order.
Having first uttered the syllable *Tāraṃ*, [one should say] "Svadhā to the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*). O Nandikeśvara, through this first drinking, success shall be attained.
(91) The purification of the thirty-one principles, beginning with Earth and ending with Māyā: having first uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), [one says] *hīṃ vidyātattvāya svadhā*.
Thus, by the second drink, the purification of the Śakti-tattva is accomplished;
these three principles are proclaimed as Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadākhya.
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, [one says] *hūṃ śivatattvāya svadhā*.
By this third drinking, there is the purification of the principle of power (*śaktitattva*).
Thus, by means of this sipping of water (ācamana), the purification of the thirty-five principles is accomplished; however, one should repeatedly wash the hands at intervals during the process.
In this regard, the meditation on the *ātmatattva* (the principle of the self) is demonstrated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The *ātmatattva* has four arms and four faces, is square, and is situated upon a lotus."
This indeed possesses the luster of molten gold.
In the left [hand] a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*); in the right, a rosary of lotus seeds.
Resembling blue sandalwood, he is blue, possesses eight faces and eight arms, and holds a wheel, an arrow, and a lotus.
The hands hold the gesture of consciousness (cinmudrā), a conch, a bow, and a lotus calyx.
One should know that the Vidyātattva is proclaimed as having one face with a gentle expression, bestowing fearlessness as appropriate upon the right and left [hands].
Resembling pure crystal, circular, and containing all objects within its womb—
this is indeed remembered as the Śiva-tattva, having five faces and four arms.
Having meditated thus— [the deity] holding a rosary of lotus seeds in the right hand and a trident and water-pot in the left— one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"Having wiped the lower and upper lips twice with the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*,
[one should then touch] the root of the right thumb, the middle finger, and the little finger."
Leaving the middle positions, one should touch those two with the fingers;
furthermore, there is a wiping upward and downward with the three middle fingers.
One should touch from the feet up to the head with water consecrated by the root mantra. (p.
93) As stated in the Kāmika:
Having sprinkled water on his feet, the wise one should touch his head with the thumb and ring finger, and he should touch his eyes with the index finger and thumb.
Having touched both nostrils with the little finger and the thumb,
and having touched the two ears with the middle finger and the thumb while holding water, [one should touch] the two upper arms.
Pressing with the thumb at the navel while all the fingertips are pressed together, one should touch the region of the heart and then the head with the tips of all the fingers.
While reciting the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), one should touch with the palm of the right hand;

or else, using the tips of the thumb and ring finger, [one should touch] the openings of the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears, as well as the two locations of the navel and heart, and the head— these twelve places.
One should touch the heart in succession, starting from the right and the left.
As it is said in the *Parākhyatantra*:
"Then one should touch the limbs: the head, the eyes, together with the nose, and the ears."
The heart, the navel, and the head; from there, the sensation spreads further and further.
The touch of the limbs should be performed with the thumb joined to the ring finger (anāmā).
The thumb shall always be Īśa; the ring finger (anāmā) is the digit of nectar (amṛtā).
By that [practice] consisting of nectar, the gods become satisfied with the nectar of immortality and free from disease;
for the performer of that rite, his actions lead toward the realization of Brahman.
Thus it is said.

(The Sakalīkaraṇa): Then, having taken either the ash produced by the Agnihotra and other rites or that established since the beginning of the Kalpa as previously described, and having first performed the bath for removing impurities according to the previously stated procedure,
one should duly apply the Tripuṇḍra marks on the aforementioned locations.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as before, one should perform the ritual of complete identification (sakalīkaraṇa); that is threefold.
p.
95) || The Ritual of Constituting the Parts (Sakalīkaraṇa) ||
In the Vīra-tantra:

"First is the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭi-nyāsa), the second is the placement of maintenance (sthiti-nyāsa), and the third is the placement of withdrawal (saṃhāra-nyāsa); thus it is said to be threefold. Now [this] is being explained.
The householder is established by way of emanation, and the student by way of persistence;
however, for the forest-dweller and the ascetic, the placement of withdrawal is prescribed.
In this regard, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and the renunciant (sannyāsī) should perform the ritual of withdrawal (saṃhāra-nyāsa):
in the *Santāna-saṃhitā* it is said—
on the little finger is Sadyojāta, on the ring finger Vāmadeva, and on the middle finger Aghora.
Having performed the placement [of the syllables], one should place the Puruṣa upon the index finger.
O Goddess of gods, one should place [the mantra] with Īśāna on the thumb;
this is called the Saṃhāranyāsa, extending from the feet up to the hair.
p.
96) If one dwelling in the forest is without a wife, the *saṃhāra-nyāsa* (dissolution placement) is prescribed;
for the *bhautika* and *naiṣṭhika* celibates, the *sthiti-nyāsa* (maintenance placement) must be performed.
Likewise, in the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
"I shall proclaim the placement of stability (*sthitinyāsa*); listen, O large-eyed one!"
One should place the five Brahmans in sequence from the middle finger to the tip of the index finger.
One should assign Īśāna to the middle finger, Puruṣa to the ring finger, Aghora to the little finger, and Vāma to the thumb.
One should place Sadyojāta here specifically on the index finger;
this placement, starting from the middle [finger] and ending with the index finger, is declared to be the *sthiti-nyāsa*.
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
"The placement of stability (sthitinyāsa) is proclaimed as extending from the heart to the knees; one should place Īśa at the heart and Tatpuruṣa at the mouth."
Having placed Aghora on the head and Vāmadeva in the secret place, one should place Sadyojāta on the feet; this is the supreme [practice] beginning with the placement of stability (sthitinyāsa).
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of creation (sṛṣṭinyāsa).
Reciting "Oṃ haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ," one should purify the palm and back of the left hand twice with the right hand; then, using that same mantra,
one should purify the palm of the right hand once with the left hand, burning [all impurities] up to the wrists by the splendor of the weapon-mantra (astra-tejas).

Having meditated upon those two hands and joined them together [in the *saṃpuṭa* gesture], one should visualize the *śakti*-maṇḍala in the form of nectar between the two thumbs; then, having sprinkled both hands with that nectar while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ śaktaye vauṣaṭ," one should [proceed] with "Oṃ hāṃ śivāsanāya namaḥ."
Thus, having placed the *śivāsana* in the hollowed palms (p. 98), one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva (*śivamūrti*) within that."
Having placed Sadāśiva of subtle form [upon the head], with the thumbs and index fingers: *oṃ hoṃ īśānamūrdhne namaḥ*.
With the thumbs and [fingers] from the index finger to the little finger: *oṃ heṃ*.
Salutation to the one whose face is Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ huṃ, salutation to Aghora, the heart. Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva, the secret organ. Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta, the form.
In the palms of the hands: Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to the body of knowledge (vidyādeha).
Having thus assigned the form of Sadāśiva with the two thumbs,
one should again assign the eye— consisting of vision, action, and will— with the three middle fingers, reciting: *Oṃ hauṃ, namaḥ to the eyes*, by means of the power pervading the entire hand.
In the center, having meditated upon Śiva as pervading the body of Sadāśiva with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ," [one should touch] with the thumb and ring finger.

Having invoked [the deity], one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the fingers of the hands, beginning with the little finger, as follows: *oṃ hāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *oṃ hīṃ* to the head, *namaḥ*; *oṃ hūṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *namaḥ*; *oṃ rhaiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *namaḥ*; and *oṃ haḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*.
Having veiled [the deity] with the mantra ending in *namaḥ* according to the sequence from left to right, and having joined the hands together,
one should consecrate them (*paramīkṛtya*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and then begin the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
With the right thumb and ring finger, one places *Oṃ hāṃ śivāsanāya* at the heart.
Having meditated upon a white lotus provided with a pericarp and sixteen petals,

one should place the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva" there, and having projected the subtle form— which is of the nature of light and extends from the eyebrows to the chin— one should place the Īśāna-mantra on the head.
Having formed a fist and placed it on the face, heart, secret place, and knees,

one should then perform the placement (nyāsa) of the mantras of Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta upon the fingers— beginning with the index finger— in sequence with the thumb joined to each respective finger.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of Sadāśiva— who consists of the five Brahma-kalās— reaching as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) at the heart with the thumb and ring finger while reciting "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge" (vidyādeha),
one should then perform the placement of the Netra-mantra upon those [limbs] with the three middle fingers.
Having recited the root-mantra twelve times at the end of the breath (dvādaśānta) according to the rule as the presiding deity of the specific [deity],
and having invoked the pervasive form with the thumb and ring finger, one should perform the ritual of complete integration (sakalīkaraṇa) in the locations of the heart, head, and crest.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart, head, and crest mantras with the thumbs, little fingers, ring fingers, and middle fingers, [he should place them] as a covering for the throat, extending down to the middle of the breasts.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with the *namo'ntaka* armor-mantra using the two index fingers, and having placed the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) on the palms of the hands with the two ring fingers, one should, for the purpose of expelling obstacles, perform three *tāla*-claps with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* while employing the mudrā in the ten directions.

Having made a binding with a finger-snap and encircled [the body] with the armor-mantra, one should display the Great Mudrā from the feet to the head using the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, for the purpose of inspiring all mantras. Likewise—
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
Having recited the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) twice, one should purify the left hand;
with the right hand alone, one should not [purify] the right [hand], but rather with the left hand.
Having recited [the mantra] up to one repetition, Nandikeśvara should purify his hands, which are endowed with the splendor of the weapon-mantra (astra-tejas),
while focusing his mind on them as far as the wrists.
Having formed a hollowed cup with both hands and joining the two thumbs within that cup,
one should meditate upon the supreme mandala of Śakti by means of the seed-syllable of nectar (amṛta).
Oṃ hauṃ, vauṣaṭ! Having sprinkled those two hands with water, one should contemplate them as a lotus-source joined together; in their center is the seat of Śiva.
Having projected the form by means of the subtle [vibration], one should thereafter recite the mantra;
in this manner, Nandikeśvara should project the form of Sadāśiva.
In the Vīratantra: "Then one should place the five mantras beginning with Īśa on the thumb and the other fingers.
In the Kāmika:
Having meditated upon that supreme body of Vidyā up to the limit of Śakti, and having placed the Eye (the syllable *phaṭ*) on the palm of the hand, one should thereafter recollect the root mantra.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"Thereafter, the rite of sakalīkaraṇa consists of the placement of mantras beginning with the heart-mantra, generated by joining the little fingers and thumbs."
In the *Kālottara*:

"Having performed the placement with the fingers in the center, one should enclose it with the *kavaca* [armor-mantra]. Then, one should perform the placement of the *prāsāda* [temple-mantra] upon all the fingers of the hand."
The placement of the hands (karanyāsa) has been fully explained; after this follows the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
With the right thumb and ring finger, one should perform the placement of the seat (āsana) and the form (mūrti) at the heart.
Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) upon the body according to the rules, one should then perform the placement of the five Brahmans (*pañcabrahmavinyāsa*).
One should place Īśa on the head with the tip of the thumb and the clenched fist;
and Tatpuruṣa on the mouth by joining the forefinger and the thumb.
One should likewise place the Aghora mantra at the heart by joining the middle finger with the thumb;
and one should place the Vāma mantra on the private parts by joining the thumb with the ring finger.
One should place Sadyojāta on the two feet by joining the little finger and the thumb;
one should place Vidyādeha in the heart with the tips of the thumb and the ring finger.

One should place the eye with three middle fingers at a distance of three finger-breadths from the eyes; having placed the *prāsāda* mantra upon the heart, one should thereafter place the limbs (*aṅgas*).
One should place the heart-mantra on the heart by joining the little finger and the thumb;
one should place the head-mantra on the head using the tips of the thumb and the ring finger.
One should place the *śikhā* [mantra] on the crest with the tips of the thumb and middle finger; likewise, one should place the *hṛdaya* and other [limbs], and the *kavaca* between the breasts.
Then, one should place [the mantra] with the two index fingers as a neck-enclosure;
next, one should place the Astra-mantra on the palms with the two ring fingers.
Then, one should perform the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra three times with the clapping of hands;
by means of that, perform the binding of the ten directions with the Acintyaviśvasādākhya-choṭikā-mudrā.
As it is said in the Ajita:
"Striking the palm of the left hand with the fingers of the right hand,
excluding the thumb— that is the tāla-mudrā, which bestows purity."
Then, having formed a very firm fist with the right hand,
one should press [the thumb] properly at its tip with the tip of the index finger.
One should extend the index finger in the act of piercing so that a sound arises;
this mudrā, known as the iron-arrow weapon (*nārācāstra*), is for the rite of binding the directions.
Thus, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Having purified the hands with mantra, one should enclose them with the *kavaca* [armor-mantra]. Then, one should perform the sprinkling, beginning from the feet up to the head."
Having consecrated with the root mantra, one should then perform the Mahāmudrā in due order.
As it is stated in the *Samānatantra*:
"One should touch the feet with both hands and lead them up to the crown of the head; this is the Mudrā."
Mahāmudrā, [attained] from the end through the sequence.
The specific detail regarding the cause has been stated:
"Since one should touch the feet with both hands, starting from 'ka' and ending at the foot [of the alphabet], this mudrā is the Mahāmudrā, following the purification of the hands."
The fruit of this has been set forth in the Pauṣkara:
"If there were a distinct purpose for the constituent parts, which possess an undivided nature, from the possessor of those parts..."
Together with the rite of making [the world] immortal, this is beneficial. Thus it is said.
Contemplate within yourself that very form of Śiva which is described in the *Sarvajñānottara*;
always perform this ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Śiva-mantras upon yourself.

In this way, the practitioner who has extracted the mantra from the body is not summoned by any obstacles for the sake of protecting the body. Thus it is said: "That which is placed upon the head as a protective binding band from the heart... and so forth.
What is the protection for the head? It is the wrapping of the head.
A helmet for the head and crest, armor for the limbs, and a coat of mail; when weapons are grasped in the hand, he stands like a terrifying mountain.
"Like Tārkṣya [is he] to the lowly, being unassailable by those who have eyes and ears. Thus.
108) Now, having restrained the breaths three times with the *mantrasaṃhitā* (or by means of it), and having sipped water again,
one should perform the salutation to the ears.
In the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*:
Having performed the ritual of self-projection (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and established himself through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
the practitioner of mantra should mentally recite the *Śivasaṃhitā* three times.
As before, having sipped water again and performed the salutation to the ears,
[one performs] breath control (prāṇāyāma).

In the Śivadharmottara, the nature of prāṇāyāma is described as follows: "Prāṇa is the vital air residing in the body; its *yāma* is its restraint. It is traditionally taught to be threefold: exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*)."
Pressing one nostril with a finger and [blocking] the other with the other [hand], one should exhale the abdominal air;
because of this exhalation, it is known as *recaka*.
One should fill the body intensely with external air as if piercing it; remaining thus completely filled,
it is known as *pūraṇa* because of that filling.
One neither releases nor grasps the breath situated within or without; when fully filled, one should remain motionless like a water-pot—this is indeed *kumbhaka*.

Thereafter, having applied the divine mudrā to the two eyes with the tips of the thumb and ring finger, one should gaze at the root water while reciting [the mantra] ending in *namaḥ*; then, having sprinkled it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ* using the fire-tirtha (corner), and having struck it with that same [mantra], one should sprinkle it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Oṃ.

Saying "Hāṃ, to the heart, vauṣaṭ," one draws forth the *tīrtha*— such as the Godāvarī or any other sacred stream— from the location of the *bindu* using the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*; then, with the mind focused within,
one brings that *tīrtha* into the water by means of the heart-mantra and the *udbhava-mudrā*.
Having cast [the water] in, having consecrated the Śiva-tīrtha with the root mantra, having protected it with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
and having encased it with the armor mantra ending in *namaḥ* and [consecrated it] with [the one] ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
One should transform [the substance] into nectar by means of the Śakti-mantra and the Dhenu-mudrā.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:

Having purified the water with the [rites of] inspection and so forth, and having drawn the sacred water (*tīrtha*) onto the forehead by means of the *Aṅkuśamudrā*, one recites: *oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya vauṣaṭ*.
Having protected the arrow-tip, O Lord, with the Śakti-mantra,
the knower of mantras should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) to ward off the multitude of obstacles.
In the *Suprabheda*, the nature of the *dhenumudrā* is described as follows:
having formed the two hands into a braid (*veṇībandha*), with the two thumbs joined together, [and] the two index fingers...
The middle fingers are joined together and tucked in, while the little and ring fingers are conjoined.
Thus, these four pairs rain down divine nectar; this is called the Surabhi-mudrā for the purpose of purifying substances.
In the *Kāmika*: "Having performed the ritual identification of the body (*sakalīkṛtadeha*), one should then perform the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*).
Now, the rules for the time of twilight worship are stated in order, beginning with the 'excellent' (*uttama*) and so forth."
One should diligently practice the first Saṃhitā, which contains the Nakṣatras, during the evening twilight;
and some say one should practice the middle Saṃhitā during the midday twilight.
The morning twilight is traditionally said to be threefold: the best is when the stars are visible; the middling is when the stars have disappeared; and the lowest is when the sun has half-risen.
At midday as well, it should be known to be thus conceived as consisting of three *ghaṭikās*;
it is most excellent when the sun is half-set in its orb, and middling when the sun has set.
The youngest [form] is the evening twilight when the stars have appeared; it is considered to consist of three abodes.
For one who is established in the time of the morning twilight and is distinguished, there are two daily rites.
For one who has been initiated into nirvāṇa, the three junctions (sandhyās) are prescribed here; at the fourth junction as well, the supreme teacher [should perform the rite] as before.
That *sandhyā* is considered to be twofold by way of the division between the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*).
In the *Mohaśūrottara*, the definition of *sandhyā* is stated in connection with the [discussion of] the hundred [verses]: "The first is Śakti..."
That which is supreme and eternal possesses the nature of an instrument.
That twilight, when realized through awakening according to the ultimate truth,
