becomes thereafter— resembling a lotus fiber— [utterly] subtle.
Previously, according to the divisions of time and so forth, they were of distinct colors individually: red, white, and likewise dark; the fourth was devoid of qualities.
O Śatakratu, the four [deities] are designated as the seats of meditation located in the heart, Viṣṇu, the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and the supportless [state].
In that regard, the meditation on the totality of powers (*sakalaśakti*) within the context of the *samaya* has been described in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"At the time of the morning twilight, one should [meditate upon] Brāhmī, who is red, in the lotus of the heart."
Adorned with ornaments and garments, red in hue, and wearing red garlands and unguents.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, possessing four faces and four arms,
she stands in the midst of a swan and a lotus, gazing with eight eyes.
The supreme young woman, wearing the sacred thread and resplendent with a garland of lotuses, holds a deer and a rosary in both her arms.
Holding a staff and a water-pot with her two left hands in the same manner,
she is radiant with rows of triple-marks (tripuṇḍra) and adorned with all ornaments.
In a red maṇḍala extending for hundreds of millions of yojanas, the Goddess is well-established in its center as the witness of all actions.
At midday, one should meditate upon the Vaiṣṇavī [form], who is white, radiant with white water-lilies,
seated in the midst of Vainateya and a lotus, possessing one face and in the full bloom of youth.
She wore a forest garland as a sacred thread and was endowed with all auspicious marks; she had lips like the bimba fruit, a beautiful face, a pair of eyes, and fine earrings.
Holding a conch in her left hand and a discus in her right, she bears a mace and the gesture of fearlessness,
with her forehead marked by the triple horizontal line (tripuṇḍra).
Adorned with all ornaments, she is the witness of all actions,
within a white mandala two hundred yojanas in extent.
There, at evening, one should meditate upon the goddess Raudrī, who stands in the center, bestows boons, and brings about stability, residing upon the head and possessing the luster of a blue lotus.
Her matted locks were marked with the crescent moon, her youth was slightly faded, she wore a black antelope skin as a sacred thread,
and she was adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
She is endowed with all auspicious marks, capable of both creation and withdrawal; she is adorned with the triple ash-mark (tripuṇḍra) and holds a trident and a rosary in her right hand.

In her left [hand], she holds the Śakti and the gesture of fearlessness; the Goddess is the witness in all rites, [pervading] the half-set sun [and the world] extending for three hundred million yojanas.
Nandikeśvara should meditate on her situated in the center of the circle of the drop (bindu-maṇḍala);
then he should meditate upon himself as being illuminated by their splendors.

Now, regarding the meditation on the partless (niṣkala) by the sons of [the Lord] and others: for the knowers, the four supreme junctions (sandhyās) now dawn within the heart; though Śiva is one, he attains multiplicity through Śakti and limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"The supreme twilight is excellent, especially at midnight;
having attained oneness through unity, it exists in the form of Śiva and Śakti."
Resembling a spider's thread, subtle, red, white, and black; the fourth is partless, eternal, and meditated upon as the dark one.
That supreme *sandhyā*, which consists of the awakening to Śiva, should become the ultimate *dhātu* (or *yātu*). —
From the *Mohaśūrottara*:

O Hari, what has been told regarding the wise, and what is said concerning the yogins? At the end of the day, for those who practice breath-control, there are two twilights belonging to the sun and the moon.
However, by means of the supreme yoga, that state of the Self belonging to Śacīpati, which is like pure awakening, was described by me otherwise to the wielder of the trident.
Just as one meditates on the twilight naturally according to the sequence of time,

so too, having meditated on the twilight according to one's qualification, one should pour the water of the Śiva-tīrtha previously consecrated with mantras from the right hand into the left hand while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having consecrated [the water] once with the *saṃhitā* in the form of the *praṇava*,
which flows like nectar resembling the moon, one should sprinkle it upon the head using the *kumbha-mudrā* and the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, applied once.
118) Again, having poured water mixed with *kuśa* grass into the joined palms with the left hand,
he should consecrate it with the *saṃhitā-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, using the right hand.
One should sprinkle water flowing from between the middle fingers of the left hand upon the head with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; this is *mārjana* (sprinkling).
Thus, according to the scripture:
"Having bound the *kalaśa-mudrā*, one should contemplate the retention known as *sudhā* (nectar); it consists of the five-syllable *tāraka* mantra and is shaped like a water-pot, facing downwards."
Then, having first formed the *kumbha-mudrā*, one should once more call to mind that [deity] from the *saṃhitā*, who is exceedingly radiant, resembling the moon, and flowing with nectar.
Then, one becomes as if bathed in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist upon the earth;
one shall have authority over all rites, and the fruit of all sacrifices shall be attained.
In the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"The mantra-practitioner, having taken water with his right hand, should pour it into his left hand while reciting the *saṃhitā*."
Having subsequently consecrated it as being of the nature of Śiva.
In the Kāmika: Having placed water in the left hand, one should join the *sruva* ladle to the head with the root,
limb, and *brahma* mantras using the right hand at all times.

Thus. Alternatively, having poured the remaining water into the right hand, one should contemplate pure white water in the form of Dharma entering through the left nostril by means of the *pūraka* breath;
having retained it in the abdomen with *kumbhaka*, one should wash away the sins within the body with that water.
Having visualized that water within as black in color due to the destruction of sins,
one should imagine that water exiting through the right nostril by means of the exhaling breath (recaka), using the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
(120) One should cast [the substance] onto a diamond stone (*vajraśilā*) that has the color of blazing fire, using the right hand in various forms, onto the left side; this is the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
In the Kāmika:
"Having drawn in the remaining white water from the right side with the inhalation (pūraka) through the left nostril..."
And by that moonlight, his sinful body, which was black in luster, was utterly consumed.
One should contemplate the *recaka* breath as it exits through the right nostril; the remainder of that [breath] is the right hand, the knitting of the eyebrows, and the great weapon.
In the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"One should cast water upon the surface of a diamond-stone (*vajraśilā*); that is the *aghamarṣaṇa*."
p.

121) Thereafter, having sipped water (ācamana) either silently or with mantras according to the rule, and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should envelop oneself with the *kavaca* or the *astra* mantra. Thus says the Āgama:
Then, having sipped water twice and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), with a tranquil mind, whenever one sips water,
at that very time one should perform the placement of mantras.
The practitioner should perform this with water from a *karakā* vessel for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the mantra.
One should envelop the body with water consisting of nectar, according to the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*; taking water in the right hand, one should perform the sprinkling.
The weapon-mantra is performed by circumambulation from left to right.

Constantly meditating upon Sadāśiva situated in the center of the solar orb, one should offer the arghya to Śiva by placing three handfuls of flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata) at the level of the heart while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, svāhā! This arghya for Śiva. Thus, one should present the arghya.
In the *Mṛgendra*:
"Having meditated upon the Lord Sadāśiva situated in the center of the orb of the sun."
The mantra-practitioner should offer a handful of water while recollecting with his mind that [the rite] has concluded.
In the *Mohaśūrottara*:

the mantra-practitioner, having offered a handful of water ending with "svāhā" while grasping the *śiva-mantra*, should recite the *gāyatrī* for Śiva; thereafter, [he should proceed] according to his own nature.
Having offered the *arghya* according to the prescribed rite, one should mutter the *gāyatrī* as described below.
In the Kāmika:
"O lords of sages, having stood in the morning and then being seated in the evening,
one should perform the ritual at midday either while seated or while standing."
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Having arisen during the morning twilight, one facing east should offer the arghya water to the Sun; likewise, the recitation (japa) should be performed while standing."
At the time of midday, in the same manner, but with the face turned to the south; having arisen in the evening and offered the *arghya*, one should then sit and perform the recitation (*japa*).
Whether wearing dry or wet clothes, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra while in water;
for it consists eternally of the nature of both the Sun and Fire, and there is no contradiction between water and light.
His body is filled with the rays of the sun through the connection of the channels; having meditated upon the white Gāyatrī in his heart, wearing a white sacred thread.
One should offer abundant sacrificial fees and place [the image] in water on the left;
it has one face and three eyes, and is adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon.
Resplendent with rows of triple-marks (tripuṇḍra), adorned with all ornaments,
wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment, and decorated with white cloth.
Having thus meditated upon Gāyatrī, who holds a rosary in her left hand and is accompanied by Padmālayā in her right, one should then begin the recitation of the mantra as prescribed.
Oṃ, let us know that state which belongs to Maheśa, and then the word "mahādevāya" at the end of the mantra,
followed by "dhīmahi."
Therefore, bestow upon us that auspicious state and impel us toward it; O child, this Gāyatrī has been declared as the giver of the fruit of the four Vedas.
Endowed with devotion, one should recite the Śiva-Gāyatrī at the three junctions of the day; or else, one should recite the three-syllabled Gāyatrī:
"Oṃ Hāṃ Hrīṃ," or the Gāyatrī ending with "Namaḥ," which bestows all desired objects.
By seven revolutions through the city, one reaches heaven by means of ten;
but by twenty revolutions, that goddess leads one to the abode of Īśvara.
"Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one may deliver [others] from the ocean of birth.
125) At the end of the recitation, [one visualizes her] as having come from the solar disc and having re-entered that very same disc.
One should contemplate [this]. And it is said:

"Having recited the Gāyatrī beginning with *oṃ* and ending with the twenty-four syllables, omitting the word of salutation (*namas*), at the conclusion of the *viṣṭi* [period], one should [visualize] 'in the solar orb'."
Having thus recited daily with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and having performed three circumambulations,
one should satisfy the *saṃhitā* ending in *svāhā* for the purpose of illuminating the mantras.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"Endowed with devotion, one should recite the Śiva-gāyatrī at the three junctions of the day;
having thus recited the mantra and offered the arghya, there is immediate dismissal."
Then, having circumambulated three times clockwise, one should mutter the root mantra;
thereafter, for the purpose of illuminating the mantras, one should also perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
In the *Kāmika*:
"Satiating with both hands is taught; satiation is remembered as that which brings delight."
O best of sages, the mantras consisting of the root, the Brahma-mantras, and the limb-mantras are the causes.
Namely: Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva! Oṃ hom, svāhā to Īśāna! Oṃ heṃ, svāhā to Tatpuruṣa! Oṃ hum, svāhā to Aghora! Oṃ hiṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva! Oṃ haṃ, svāhā to Sadyojāta! Oṃ...
Hāṃ, svāhā to the heart! Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the head! Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the crest-lock! Oṃ haiṃ, svāhā to the armor! Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to the eyes! Oṃ haḥ, svāhā to the weapon! Svāhā to all mantras! Oṃ!
"Swāhā to all the gods!"— with these words, one should offer libations using the *devatīrtha* with water mixed with *kuśa* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) from the tips of the fingers.
Wearing the sacred thread around the neck (*kaṇṭhopavītī*), one should satisfy the sages with the formula "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to all the ṛṣis" using the *tīrtha* formed by the joints of the fingers.
With "Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to all humans," one should satisfy the humans using the *manuṣyatīrtha*, which is the form at the base of the little finger.
With "Oṃ hāṃ, vauṣaṭ to all beings (*bhūta*s)," [one should satisfy them] using the form at the wrist, which is the base of the palm.
One should satisfy the beings with the *bhūtatīrtha*.
Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, [he offers] with water mixed with sesame seeds using the tips of the roots of *kuśa* grass:
"Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the Śiva-fathers! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the divine fathers! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the fathers!"
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all mothers; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all kinsmen; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all teachers.
Thus, one should offer libations with the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, which consists of the middle of the thumb and the index finger. Likewise—
In the *Kāmika*:
"For the deities of the mantras, [the name] ends with *svāhā*; for the sages, however, it ends with *namaḥ*; and for humans..."
The word "vaṣaṭ" belongs to the spirits, and that which ends with "vauṣaṭ" [belongs to the gods].
For the ancestors and others, the rite should end with *svadhā*, performed while wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*) in its appropriate manner.
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
"For the gods it is the *upavīta* position; for the sages, it is known as the *kaṇṭha* (neck) position."
With a composed mind, one should offer libations to the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
A wise person should satisfy the gods with kusha grass, flowers, and unhusked rice;
the sages with kusha grass alone; and the ancestors with sesame seeds.
One should satisfy the gods and the sages with water alone; one should always satisfy the ancestors on the bank of the water according to the prescribed rule.
In the *Kāmika*:
"The divine (*daivika*) sacred site (*tīrtha*) is at the tip of the hand; the rishi-related (*ārṣaka*) sacred site is at the junctions of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*). The sacred site...
At the base of the little finger, the Prājāpatya is proclaimed.
The paternal [portion] is at the base of the index finger, and the portion for Brahmā is at the base of the hand; having understood this specifically, perform the libation for the gods and others.
This is the very brief libation (*saṃkṣepatarpaṇa*). Herein lies the qualification for children and others.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
For children, the ignorant, the elderly, women, the sick, and those who enjoy worldly pleasures,
one should perform the libations and other rites by shortening [the procedure] according to the oral instruction of the Guru.

Now, if one is able to perform the extensive libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should do so as follows: one should satisfy the *saṃhitā* mantras ending in *svāhā* using the *devatīrtha*. OṂ HĀṂ, to the hundreds of millions of mantras, SVĀHĀ!
OṂ HĀṂ, to all the Śiva-āgamas, SVĀHĀ! OṂ HĀṂ...
Svāhā to all the auspicious ones. Om (Hāṃ? salutation to Vasiṣṭha. Om Hāṃ salutation to Pulastya.
Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kratu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhāradvāja.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viśvāmitra. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Pracetas. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ṛcīka. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Agastya. Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to Dadhīca. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Durvāsas. Thus [are] the eleven sages [to be worshipped] at the joints of the lunar phases (parvasandhi). Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanaka. Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanatana. Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanatkumāra. Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Kapila.
Vaṣaṭ! Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Pañcaśikhā! Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Ṛṣabha! Thus, with the *mānavatīrtha* at the base of the little finger, one should offer [the oblation] to humans.
p.

131) Oṃ hāṃ, vauṣaṭ to all the elements beginning with space and ending with earth—thus one should offer libations with the palms joined at their roots. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (dakṣaskandhopavītī).

With the tips of *kuśa* grass and water mixed with sesame seeds: *oṃ hāṃ kavyavāhanāya svadhā | oṃ hāṃ analāya svadhā | oṃ hāṃ somāya svadhā | oṃ hāṃ yamāya svadhā | oṃ hāṃ aryamṇebhyaḥ svadhā | oṃ hāṃ*.
Svadhā to Agniṣvātta! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Barhiṣat!
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Ājyapa! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Somapa! Thus [to] the divine ancestors (devapitṛs).
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the ancestors (pitṛs)! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the grandfathers (pitāmahas)! Oṃ...
Hāṃ, svadhā to the maternal grandfathers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the great maternal grandfathers.
Oṃ hāṃ, [p. 132] svadhā to the [great-great] maternal grandfathers.

Svadhā to the maternal grandfathers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the paternal great-grandfathers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the paternal great-great-grandfathers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the ancestors. Thus [are offered) to the deceased ancestors (pretapitṛs).
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all kinsmen. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all teachers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the directions. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the lords of the directions. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the Siddhas. Oṃ hāṃ...

Svadhā to the ancestors to be propitiated! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the Mothers! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the Planets! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the Rākṣasas! Having thus satisfied them, [one recites]: "Oṃ, those living beings in my lineage who have been cremated by fire, and those who have not been cremated..."

"May those who have been satisfied by the water offered upon the ground attain the supreme goal. Having recited this, one should cast the water along with kuśa grass and sesame seeds onto the bank of the water using the Astra mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
(p. 133) Then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, having recited the mantra of the Gaṇa beginning with Ambikā and offered libations,
having discarded the *kuśa* grass, having sipped water (*ācamana*), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the heart-mantra, [he should offer] water...
With the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should withdraw the sacred sites (*tīrtha*), mantras, deities, and so forth. If he is a twice-born (*dvija*),

then after the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* and the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), he should perform the attendance upon the Sun-god Śiva in his *saṃhitā* form, and having recited [the mantra] as much as possible, he should offer it.
If the three junctions (*trisandhyā*) are missed due to the loss of the prescribed time, one should recite the *saṃhitā* once;
as it is said in the *Śrīmṛgendra*:
If the time for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) is missed, one should recite the *Śivaikādaśikā*.

Having thus completed the ritual performance, one should dispel the obstacles standing on the path with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), and [enter] either a cow-pen, a temple, or one's own home within the "cage of weapons" (*astrapañjara*).
Having entered and mentally abandoned the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth,
one reaches the place of worship which pervades up to the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyātattva).

One should enter. Likewise, regarding worship, it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "Having purified the obstacles situated on the path, one should proceed in a celestial chariot consisting of [the five] garments."
Or one may go to a temple or to one's own excellent home.
Mataṅga said:
Having first meditated upon the Lord of the Vimāna, the self-restrained practitioner should then proceed, preceded by the syllable *Aṅgāra*,
with a slight effort toward the irreproachable place of worship.
Thus ends the procedure for purification, sipping water, bathing, and the twilight devotions, according to the *Ātmārthapūjāpaddhati*.
135) One should construct a hall of worship in some delightful location, such as within a house, on a riverbank, or in a forest or grove.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"A hundred and fifty cubits in every direction from the *liṅga* is the sacred field (*śivakṣetra*) of Śiva;
dwelling within that very place is the cause for [attaining] the world of Śiva."
That which is known as the human measure of the field is said to be one thousand [units] when it is self-manifested (svayambhūta),
and half of that in the case of the ārṣa [measure].
All things, both stationary and moving, when propitiated, undoubtedly attain the divine state through the power of the Supreme Lord;
therefore, a dwelling should be constructed in the vicinity of a sacred field of Śiva.
Everyone should worship Śiva for their own sake with offerings; therefore, a wise person [should do so] with leaves, fruits, flowers, and water.
Having made the mind of the nature of Śiva, one should always worship Śiva; except for the abode of the deity,
one should not dwell anywhere else even for a single moment.
Mataṅga said:
Those who have been initiated must reside by taking refuge in a *liṅga* in the southern region; in its absence, they should construct a very beautiful house in a pure place.
Not too far from the sky, a commendable, well-shaded, and auspicious site is recommended.
As stated in the Kāmika:
"One should designate the location for flower gardens, monasteries, and so forth, everywhere."
Aṃśumatī: A wise man should construct a temple for his own sake or for the purpose of sacrifice, as previously described, either in his house,
in a temple of Śiva, or in any other delightful and auspicious location.
And in the *Kiraṇa*:
"On the delightful bank of a great river, or in a grove frequented by people, or on a mountain peak, or at a tree,
or in a house endowed with auspicious characteristics."
(Kālottara, p. 137) Near a temple of the gods, on the bank of a sacred river, or even in a pure house.
One should perform the Śiva-sacrifice.
And in the subtle [practice]:
having washed one's feet in a domestic garden, a temple of Śiva, on a riverbank, in a pond, on a mountain,
or in a royal capital.

One should perform the worship of the mobile liṅga, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; for that purpose, one should construct a shrine room in the northeast corner of the house.
In other locations, such as riverbanks and the like, one may perform it in whichever direction or place one desires.
In the *Kālottara*: "The beautiful hall of worship is situated in the northeastern direction.
And in the *Kiraṇa*:
Garuḍa:
O Blessed One, it has been stated that there should be a temple for the deity in the northeastern direction; tell me its characteristics—what kind of temple is recommended?
(On page 138:
Regarding four-winged houses (*catuśśālā*), another arrangement is considered there:
the eastern wing is called the *śrīgṛha* (glory-house), and the southeast wing should be the kitchen (*mahānasa*).
The bed should be in the south; the armory (or storehouse) in the southwest;
the dining area should be in the west; and the granary for storing grain in the northwest.
In the north should be the storage for goods, and in the northeast the temple of the deities; the house may consist of three wings, two wings, or a single-winged structure.
Regarding the extent of the four *kāṇḍas*: it is recorded thus in the *Mataṅga*:
"Whether it has one hall (*śāla*), two halls, three halls, or auspiciously four halls, it should be constructed according to one's wealth."
Or [he may build] Hiraṇyanābha or Sukṣetra, which is delightful; (Hiraṇyanābha, Sukṣetra, and so forth are the forms of the halls, beautiful in their respective bodies.)
One should always construct an auspicious water-ford, provided with all necessary halls.
To the northeast of the great kitchen, one should construct a sacrificial pavilion; it is always auspicious to establish a granary there, or else on the eastern side.
O tiger among sages, the installation of the vessels representing the waters should be performed according to the rules in the space between the southern and southeastern directions.
For all four-footed creatures, the northern direction is praised;
a wise person should have a house built in such a manner and dwell therein.
Now, the method for its construction: first, having examined the surface of the earth according to its color, fragrance, and taste, one should select a site appropriate for oneself,
clear it, and [prepare] it of stone, baked brick, or pure wood.

Is it made of clay, or is it square? Is it perfectly circular? Is its measurement one, five, seven, nine, thirteen, seventeen, twenty, twenty-one, or thirty-two cubits? Is it a single-storeyed structure?
One should construct a beautiful hall of worship, either two or three stories high, with its entrance on the east, south, or west.

Having divided [the area] into five parts and excluding the central portion for the stone foundation, one should prepare an altar (*vedikā*) made of eight bricks of clay, either provided with four corner pillars or without pillars,
measuring sixteen finger-breadths in height or eight finger-breadths in height.

Above that, on the western side, there is a location serving as the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), one *tāla* in width and depth and five *aṅgulas* in height; to the east of that is a location serving as the half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇḍapa*), possessing the same dimensions in length, width, and height; and to the eastern part of that [is another].
In the five-tāla [measurement], one should arrange four tālas.
Alternatively, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be equal in width and length as previously described; its location should correspond to the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) and other areas,
and it should be provided with a railing (*vedikā*) having a height of eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

One should prepare a local altar-ground marked with cow-dung. If one is unable to construct a worship pavilion, one should designate a pleasing area to the right of the deity in a temple of Śiva or elsewhere for the purpose of worship, and therein construct a hall.
In the Kālottara:
"Having ascertained the color, fragrance, and taste [of the site], one should begin the sacrificial hall,
the place of initiation, the abode of Śiva, and the bathing place."
All these stations of yoga have been proclaimed as her ordinances.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"O Six-faced One, the fire-ritual, recitation, yoga, and the initiation of yoga [should be performed] in a secret,
delightful place on a very pure patch of ground."
p.
142) Regarding that, the procedure for examination is stated in the *Kiraṇa*:

Among those [women] whose complexions range from the color of jasmine, conch, and snow to that of a swarm of bees, starting with the Brāhmaṇa caste and so forth, they should be accepted or rejected according to their scent; those smelling of blood, perfume, or urine and feces are to be avoided in sequence.
And *madhudharā*, *āmra-kṣāyā*, and *kaṭukā*— thus it is said by tradition.
Having recognized [the state] through the characteristics pertaining to color, smell, taste, and flavor, as stated in the *Kālottara*.
One indeed attains all accomplishments and whatever desired siddhis one seeks.
These four are prescribed for a Brahmin; three for a Kshatriya; two for a Vaishya; and one for a Shudra—namely, a wife, a stone slab, and the ground.
In the *Vīratantra*:
"Having dug a pit one cubit deep, one should fill it with that very soil; more [soil than required] is to be known as excellent, while less is said to be inferior."
It should be level and of medium quality; one should therefore avoid that which is inferior.
Having dug at the site of the *mṛtaṅga* (the corpse-peak), one should determine the extent of the channels and cause the extraction of any embedded debris (*śalya*) to be performed.
Hair, ashes, husks, charcoal, gravel, bones, grass, and so forth.
(143) Furthermore, O Great Sage, one should diligently avoid those who are harmful to living beings; serpents, scorpions,
and *yutmāmṛsnā* [spiders] should be shunned.
Turtles, fish, and frogs are considered auspicious among living beings; conch shells, coral, lapis lazuli, and rājāvarta stone are auspicious when found at the bottom [of the water].
And the elements shall be auspicious and bestowers of accomplishment upon the surface of the earth.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should sprinkle with pure water, with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and with the water of Śiva; [and with] the five jewels (*pañcaratna*)."
The preceptor should cast [the substances] there with the root mantra.
One should fill [the vessel] with stones, with intervals of eight finger-breadths of clay,
having collected and taken up the earth from a meritorious field such as Aṃśumatī, on a riverbank, or in a pure and delightful place.
One should fill that pit so that it is level.
Having leveled the ground so that it is even, one should perform the striking with sand to eliminate depressions and elevations,
according to the scripture and the desired requirements for the site.
Endowed with auspiciousness from the noble directions and in accordance with the needs of the patron, [one should prepare] either a stone,
a brick, or even one made of wood or clay.
One should construct the pavilion (maṇḍapa) as square or even oblong; such is the construction of the pavilion, and now the specification of the location is stated.
In the subtle [system], however—
one should construct a pavilion that is square, oblong, or circular as desired. In this context of constructing the pavilion, it depends upon the threefold division of the *mātrā-aṅgula*.

The measure of a cubit (*hastapramāṇa*) and the threefold [measure] corresponding to the killing of a Brahmin should be applied as appropriate, having considered the constraints of the location and other such factors.
It should be contemplated:
on the middle joint of the middle finger in the right hand of the preceptor, the string is said to be of three kinds— equal in length to that joint, and its circumference is likewise of three types.
The measurement of a cubit (*hasta*) is proclaimed to be twenty-four of those finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
In the *Samānatantra*:
"The measurement of a cubit is either thirty-two [finger-breadths] or even twenty."
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"Or nine, thirty, or seventeen cubits; or twenty-one cubits, or even twenty-seven."
In the *Sūkṣma*:
nine cubits, seven cubits, five cubits, or three cubits.
In the *Mohaśūrottara*:
Whether it be on one level, two levels, or three levels, as is convenient;
as stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*: (p. 146)
Having made the length twice that [width], one should make the door one part of the hand-width;
it should be located in the third part and measure one and a half hand-widths.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"One may make the western door, or the southern, or indeed the eastern; in the center, at a distance of one part, there should be twenty-seven finger-breadths."
Then there are thirty-two or thirty-six [units]; the door shall be twenty-five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"One should cause [the deity] to enter through the western door or even the eastern door; thus, in daily worship, the temple is praised as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
The construction of that [shrine], whether on one level or two levels, is described here: having divided the site into five parts, the central portion shall be the altar (vedikā).
Images made of sacrificial wood or clay are superior, never those made of stone or plaster;
they should be sixteen or eight finger-breadths in height and provided with corner pillars and other such features.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"Adorned with various openings, provided with doors and bolts, and possessing a central pillar..."
Or the temple of the deity should be made deficient [in its proportions].
Aṃśumatī—
the womb-chamber is one tāla, and the ardha-maṇḍapa is equal to that; its width is likewise equal to that,
and it is five aṅgulas high.
It should be five *tālas* in length and four *tālas* in width;
it should be raised by one *vidyā-aṅgula* and be free from any unevenness or depressions.
Then, having smeared with cow dung either what is called a circular pavilion (beramaṇḍapa) or a level surface,
the knower of mantras [should act] with the Vāmadeva mantra.
The pavilion above the sanctum should be two *tālas* in measurement;
it should be equal in width and perfectly square.
The pavilion for the deity is said to be five *tālas* in length and four-cornered in width;
one should place a lotus petal in its center.
If the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) is devoid of leaves, it becomes an entrance for the asuras; therefore, having recited the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should place a leaf right there.
Having mentally conceived the temple as well as the dimensions of the altar,

one should, according to the prescribed ritual, place a casket in the area corresponding to the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) upon the pavilion and altar thus constructed; and in the area corresponding to the hall for the image (*beramaṇḍapa*), [one should recite] *oṃ hām ādhāra*.
Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Śakti," in the center of that [space],
one should prepare a firm pedestal (pīṭha) two cubits in length, one cubit in width,
and twelve finger-breadths in height, or else one cubit high.
In the Śrīmayamata: [It is] joined with various colors and adorned with a lotus in the center. (p. 149)
The auspicious [pedestal], measuring six and eight [units] in width, shines forth with feet extended and horses free from trembling;
above that, there should be a lotus petal joined with a pericarp, adorned as beautifully as possible.
Having thus placed the decorated shield (kheṭaka) and stretched out the bow (namanintamāna) upon it,
one should arrange a pedestal (pīṭha) made of ivory or similar materials in the center; and upon that, in the western part,
a lotus-pedestal (padmapīṭha) made of gold or silver, accompanied by a halo (prabhāmaṇḍala).
One should place it facing the east.
As it is said in the *Sūkṣma*:
"Having worshipped the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), one should place the shield (*kheṭaka*) in its center."
Having covered that with food and water, one should place it upon the western upper pedestal.
Above that, there should be a lotus pedestal joined with a circle of light;
likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī*:
And above that, one should likewise place oneself, adorned with variegated garments and ornaments,
upon a lotus-seat on a shield in the western direction.
One should place the support for the garland together with the circle of light,
adorned on the sides of the circle of light with variegated cloths.

Then, one should adorn the worship pavilion with scattered flowers, the fragrance of incense, sandalwood paste, canopies, strings of pearls, banners, flags, camphor powder, mirrors, and other such items.
Likewise, in the Mataṅga: "A place that is well-concealed, secluded, delightful, radiant with scattered flowers,
rich with the fragrance of excellent incense, and anointed with sandalwood and other unguents."
It was covered with a canopy, hung with strings of pearls,
adorned with white cloth banners, and raised with white parasols and flags.
Sprinkled with saffron water, grey with the powder of camphor,
filled with the rays of mirrors for the sake of lamps with unwavering flames.
Thus it is said.
Having entered the worship hall constructed according to the prescribed rules, one should perform the solar worship;
likewise [is] the solar worship.
Aṃśumatī:
Having entered the place of worship and performed the washing of the feet with water from the ritual pitcher, one should discard that remaining water.
Again, having taken water and sipped it according to the rule, the wise man, having entered the interior of the pavilion,
should then commence the worship of the Sun.
"One should worship Śiva in the form of the Sun between Devendra and Anila.
If it is asked what the restriction regarding this [form] is,
they say that it is because the one named Prabhāvatī exists there in the form of the Sun.
(152) But is it not the case that elsewhere it was stated that one should worship Śiva as the solar form alone?
[If so,] why worship the others— the moon and so forth— since they too are forms of Śiva?

"Why is it not performed? "True; however, because it has been stated that the worship of the six supports (ṣaḍādhāraśiva) alone is obligatory, their [other] worship is not performed. And it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
The worship of the Sun, the self-sacrifice, the ritual marks, the Guru, and the sacred book—this is declared to be the constant worship of Śiva through the six supports. Thus it is said.

And because of the identity of Sūrya and Śiva, that very same practice is prescribed in the Vātula: "One should know Āditya to be Śiva, and Śiva to be Āditya indeed; there is no difference between the two, between Āditya and Śiva."
(156) If it is argued that the worship of Śiva alone must come first, even so,
because the Sun is the entirety [of all deities], for that very reason he is to be worshipped first. Thus, in the *Aṃśumatī*:

The wise one, having first worshipped that which resides within the body— the form of the sun as the manifest (sakala) and Śiva himself as the unmanifest (niṣkala)— should thereafter sacrifice to the Lord.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "Now, Nandin and Mahākāla are known as Daṇḍin and Piṅgala; Śiva and Sūrya are the limbs of Śiva, the mantras, the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras), and the planets."
This worship of the Sun is twofold: worship of the maṇḍala (*cakrapūjā*) and worship of the image (*berapūjā*). Likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī*:
"One should worship the Sun in an image, a *bera*, or even in a maṇḍala, or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*)."
Having drawn a lotus according to the method previously described.
And on a small stone slab or even on the ground, one should commence the worship of the Sun.
Having reached the direction facing the east, one should draw the solar disc.
Or, having drawn the *bera* (liṅga), one should draw the mandala as desired upon a wheel;
specifically in a pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), a temple pinnacle (*kūṭa*), or a mandala, using gold.
Or in images made of copper, ruby, or coral.
Regarding the cause—
for this reason, hereafter I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Sūrya; one should daily worship him before sunrise according to the four-fold division of castes.
Circular, triangular, circular, hexagonal, a pair of circles,
octagonal, and nine-sided— this is proclaimed as the solar wheel (sauracakra).

Within a circle, one should draw a triangle and write the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) and [the name of] Aṅgāraka; then one should draw another circle, and outside it, one should place the eight-syllable mantra.
One should place Sudarśana in the six corners along with the six limbs at their junctions; in the pair of circles, one should assign the great Saura-mantra and the Gāyatrī together with the Śiras.

Having assigned the eight-syllable mantra to the eight [sections], one should assign the deities beginning with Indra; then, having spoken of the digits (kalās) and the vowels, one should write them according to the prescribed rule.
One should cause [the syllables] *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *klīṃ* to cry out intensely in the apertures and roam everywhere;

or else, one should write the letters of the alphabet starting from the beginning in the directions of Vāyu, Agni, Śakra, Varuṇa, Īśvara, and Rākṣasa upon the petals, situated in the center of a great pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
The solar wheel is thus proclaimed.
The worship received from one who has mastered the four Vedas and Āgamas shall be the remover of all sins; worship must be performed by a Brāhmaṇa alone—now hear about the worship for a Kṣatriya.
One should draw a circle, a lotus within a circle, a hexagon, a lotus within a hexagon, an octagon, and a square, with the *praṇava* (syllable Om) in their center.
Having placed the Sūrya-mantra on the petal, one should write the auspicious syllables Śrīṃ and Hrīṃ;
one should perform the worship for a Kṣatriya—now hear the worship for Vaiśyas.
A circle, a lotus, likewise a lotus, a hexagon, a circle, and a polygon; having inscribed the *tāra* (OM) in the middle petal, the wise one should write the name of the Sun.
One should write the syllable *hrīṃ* joined with the mantra upon the petal of the Śrī-vajra;
one should perform the worship of Vaiśyas—now listen to the worship of the Śūdra.
The circular [mandala] and the hexagonal one, as well as the circular lotus and the hexagonal one—this is declared to be the central altar; one should write the solar mantra upon its petals.
One should again write "Śrīṃ" and "Hrīṃ" within the hexagon, and then write the syllables "Śrīṃ" and "Hrīṃ" once more.
(157) And *berapūjā* is twofold: for the sake of emanation (*sṛṣṭyartha*) and for the sake of liberation (*muktyartha*). Thus it is said in the *Vātula*:
Worship is of two kinds: for the sake of emanation and for the sake of liberation.
They know that which is joined with Śakti is for the sake of emanation, while that which is solitary is for the sake of liberation.
Then, having sat down facing the east, sipped water for purification (ācamana), performed the ritual placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa),

prepared the offering water (arghya), and presented the arghya for the vision, one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity, gather the materials for worship, and worship Śiva-Sūrya in a mandala or similar locus.
Likewise, having sat upon his seat facing the east, he should begin the worship of the Sun.
Having sipped water according to the rule, one should perform the purification and the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs;
having diligently procured all the materials required for the sacrifice.
In the *Cintyaviśva*,
having personally meditated upon oneself as the essence of the Sun, one should prepare the vessel for the *arghya* offering.

An earthen vessel is declared to be the lowest; one made of copper is middling; and a vessel made of gold is considered the best. Its width should be four finger-breadths, and its height half of that.

Having understood that this is called the *arghyapātra* (the vessel for the guest-offering), one should commence the ritual. One should sprinkle the vessel with water mixed with red sandalwood while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having filled that vessel with water, [one should offer it] with red sandalwood and rice,
or else with red flowers and *kuśa* grass, or with sesame, mustard seeds, and rice.
One should deposit the drop drawn from the forehead, which has the form of nectar;
having worshipped the Sun with the [five] limbs, one should conceal him with the armor-mantra.
Having performed protection with the Astra-mantra, having touched the ground with both knees,
and having brought [the visualization] up to the crown of the head while maintaining the gaze upon the solar disc,
one should offer the *darśanārghya* (offering for vision) with the mantra: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ śivasūryāya namaḥ*.
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity; or else, one should offer the water of honor (*arghya*) with the *Śivagāyatrī* and other mantras—
with the *Śivagāyatrī* mantra, or with the *praṇava*, or with the *hṛdaya* mantra— to Sūrya.
It should always be given once; one should perform worship.
In the *Mṛgendra*:

"Having performed the divine and complete worship preceded by the offering of *arghya*, and having then recited the mantra of Śiva along with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*) and made the formal announcement (*āvedya*), one should begin the subsequent rite. Thus it is said.

Then, having washed the vessel with the Astra-mantra, and having filled it with liquor-like scented water emerging from the Bindu, reciting "Oṃ Khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolkā," one should worship it with the root-mantras of the six limbs.
Having consecrated [the materials] with those very [mantras], protected them with the Astra-mantra, enveloped them with the Kavaca-mantra,
and rendered them nectar-like by means of the Dhenu-mudrā with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having sprinkled the locations where the ritual substances reside with water from that [vessel] while reciting the Astra-mantra,

and having scattered flowers and driven away obstacles with the Astra-mantra, one should worship [the deity] upon a diagram of eight lotuses drawn on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or upon a disc made of copper or other materials, or within an image (bera).
Now, the sequence:
at the western door, on the branch to one's right, [one recites] "Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍin.
Daṇḍin is to the right of the door; he is fair-complexioned, stout, pot-bellied, and possesses a beard.
Holding an ink-pot and two pens in his two hands.
"He is the witness of the actions of living beings and he records those very actions"—having meditated thus, one should then worship him.
Red in color, richly adorned with fine attire, and holding a needle in his hand; and on the left side, Piṅgala, the doorkeeper, bearing a staff.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, [one should worship] in the northeast with: *Oṃ Aṃ Gaṇapataye Namaḥ*.
[One should visualize] the Lord of the Gaṇas, who has the face of an elephant, seated upon a red lotus throne, holding a tusk, a noose, a goad, and a fruit in his four hands.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, [one should offer] in the southeast: *Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to the Gurus*.

[They are visualized as] richly adorned with the beauty of matted hair and crowns, their bodies white with ashes, wearing the yogic belt and the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) over the region of the navel.
One should meditate upon the supreme, peaceful Guru, who bears the mudrā known as Kṛtayoga;
having thus meditated and performed worship, [upon] a pedestal or a sacrificial mound (p.
One should worship the six seats (*ṣaḍutthāsanam*). In the center: *oṃ aṃ prabhūtāya namaḥ*.
In the four corners starting from the southeast: *oṃ aṃ vimalāya namaḥ*, *oṃ aṃ sārāya namaḥ*, *oṃ aṃ ārādhyāya namaḥ*, *oṃ aṃ paramasukhāya namaḥ*.
He has the face of a lion, two eyes, two arms, and two feet;
he wears a garland of scorpions around his neck and is seated upon a cushioned throne.

Having meditated thus, and having visualized and worshipped the white, red, yellow, green, and white forms as facing one another back-to-back in their respective order, [one should visualize] upon that a fresh lotus together with its bulb, seed-syllable, sprout, stalk, petals, filaments, and pericarp.
Having visualized a white lotus and worshipped it, one should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Dīptā, on the petals starting from the east: Oṃ Rāṃ, obeisance to Dīptā.

Oṃ rīṃ, salutation to Sūkṣmā. Oṃ ruṃ, salutation to Rujā. Oṃ rūṃ, salutation to Bhadrā. Oṃ reṃ, salutation to Vibhūti. Oṃ raiṃ, salutation to Vimalā. Oṃ roṃ, salutation to Amoghā. Oṃ rauṃ, salutation to Vidyutā. Thus.
Having performed worship in the pericarp, in the northeast [direction], [one recites]: *oṃ raḥ sarvatomukhyai namaḥ*.
The nine Śaktis should be meditated upon as having the form of blazing lamp-flames;
they hold lotuses in their left hands and fly-whisks in their right.
Facing the sun, adorned with all ornaments, having two eyes and two arms, and red in color— these are to be worshipped in sequence.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should display the *visphurā* mudrā.
Likewise, in the *Sūkṣma*:
[He should worship] Daṇḍin, Piṅgala, Gaṇeśa, and the Guru.
In the *Vijayasaṃhitā*:
"Thereafter, one should prepare a seat—a lotus upon a lion-throne—abundant..."
Having placed [the central element] in the middle, [one should place them] all around in the four directions.
Having worshipped the pure, essential, and adorable primordial bliss, [one should worship] those in the form of lion’s legs in the corners starting from the southeast with the heart-mantra.
In the center of that is a red lotus, adorned with petals in the eight directions; one should visualize the eight radiant Śaktis, beginning with Dīptā, upon the filaments.
From the east to the northeast, in the center is that which faces all directions; its characteristic is described as "the upward-shining" (*visphura*),
with both hands turned upwards and the fingers slightly contracted.
Then, with the two thumbs, one should cause [the fingers] from the little finger onwards to throb in sequence.
She is known as Visphurā, who brings about the presence of the deity.
165) Having meditated upon the seat that pervades from the center of the pericarp up to the end of the Māyātattva, [one recites] *oṃ aṃ*.
Having worshipped the seat with "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Arka," if one desires worldly enjoyment,
one should [visualize] the Sun-god upon it— resembling saffron in color, adorned with all ornaments, two-eyed, with a beautiful face,
and wearing red garlands and unguents.
Endowed with four arms, with two lotus-like hands in the gestures of boon-granting (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*),
and adorned with a halo of light.
Equipped with the sacred thread (upavīta), accompanied by Uṣā and Pratyuṣā; one should place Goddess Uṣā on the right side and Pratyuṣā on the left side.
She has two arms and two eyes, possesses a face like a lotus,
is adorned with all ornaments, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
"One should meditate upon the body of the Sun in this way: as seated upon a lotus, or mounted on a chariot accompanied by Aruṇa, exceedingly gracious, with limbs brilliantly radiant. Thus it is said.
Having meditated upon the God together with His Śakti, one should worship Him.
If one desires liberation— one should [visualize the deity] mounted upon a white lotus, with the luster of a pomegranate flower, radiant red,
possessing great splendor, and situated in the center of a circular mandala.
One should meditate upon the Sun-god as having one face and two eyes, wearing red garments, with his two hands holding a white lotus with a clearly visible stalk resting upon his shoulder.

Having meditated thus, and having uttered "Oṃ aṃ khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolkā, the embodiment of the Sun," while holding a bound handful of flowers (baddhapuṣpāñjali), one should contemplate and install the form that pervades up to the principle of Sadāśiva, reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the two eyes of Bhānu."

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the three eyes upon the [three] eyes, and having filled the hollowed palms (*añjali*) with flowers, one should contemplate the throbbing red drop (*bindu*) drawn from the forehead as pervading the interior of the *śakti-tattva* within the hollowed palms.

Having reflected thus, one should invoke the form consisting of radiant energy with the mantra "Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Śiva-Sūrya," using the *āvāhinī* [mudrā]; then, stabilize it with the *sthāpinī*, bring it into proximity with the *sannidhānī*, and bind it with the *niṣṭhurā*.
O God of gods, Lord of the three worlds, foremost auspiciousness of the universe! O Sūrya, Lord of the world, remain here; you have been installed by me with devotion.
Having thus made this request and offered the *saṃnidhāna-arghya*,
one should display the *bimba-mudrā* for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into presence (*sannidhīkaraṇa*) and for the sake of [inspiring] joy.
As it has been said:
Having joined the right and left hands and extended both palms,
the union of the middle fingers and the thumbs is proclaimed as the Bimba-mudrā.

Thus: having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Sūryahṛdaya-mantra, the head (*śiras*), the crest (*śikhā*), the armor (*kavaca*), and the weapon (*astra*) in their respective locations—the armor in the middle of the breasts, and the other [mantras] on the chest and the weapon on the feet— p. 168) [End of section].
Having worshipped [the deity] with the root mantra, having established oneness, and having performed the protective veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*),
one should display the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā* with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
and offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other substances, as well as flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), incense, and lamps, with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Having offered water for rinsing the mouth and the *arghya* offering, and having bathed [the deity] with the Heart Mantra using oil, curd, milk, honey, turmeric, *āmalaka*, and so forth, and subsequently bathing it again with pure water;
if it is a mobile image (*calabimba*), one should place it upon a pedestal, adorn it with red garments and flowers, and [recite] *oṃ*.
Having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers while reciting "Hrāṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Śiva-Sūrya," and having offered the *arghya*, one should display the *padma-mudrā* and the *bimba-mudrā*.
As it has been said:
"Having placed the two hands palm upwards, one should join the wrists;
the middle fingers and thumbs should be slightly curved, and the remaining fingers likewise kept apart."

This shall be the lotus mudrā; one should place the palms upon each other. As stated in the *Kiraṇa*: "From the joining of the thumbs with the thumbs, and from the union of the two index fingers, the remaining [fingers are joined]."
This is the mudrā called Bimba, belonging to the Sun.

Then, for the purpose of the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga-pūjā*), having requested [permission], one should take the limbs of the deity from the locations such as the heart of the Sun, by means of the *hṛdaya* and other mantras, onto the petals in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest.

One should meditate upon the limbs of the Sun as having gentle forms, two arms, and being radiant, with hands in the boon-granting gesture and holding lotuses; thus, having meditated upon and worshipped the limbs of the Sun, [one should place them] on the western petal.
Having meditated thus on the eye, which resembles a blazing fire, has two eyes, and possesses radiant luster,
one should worship it and then worship the weapon-mantra (*astra*) on the four petals starting from the east.
One should thus contemplate this weapon, which has a mouth made terrifying by fangs and the brilliance of a blazing fire, threatening away the onset of obstacles.
Having meditated thus, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, and having presented the *arghya* with their respective mantras,
one should display the *dhenumudrā* for the heart-mantra and others, the *goviṣāṇamudrā* for the eyes, and the *trāsanīmudrā* for the weapon-mantra (*astra*). Thus says the *Āgama*:

One should display the *dhenumudrā* for the four [mantras], the *trāsanī* and *astra* mantras, and the *locana* mantras; however, one should display the *goviṣāṇā* mudrā for the purpose of bringing about presence (*sannidhīkaraṇa*).
Ajite—
[the mudrā is formed] by joining the index and middle fingers of the right hand.
One should indeed strike once upon the palm of the left hand.
This mudrā is for causing terror; one should employ it in acts of terrifying. Having spread the two index fingers apart, they should be extended like the horns of a cow.
That itself is his eye-mudrā.

Now, for the offering to the deities of the coverings (*āvaraṇapūjā*): at the tips of the petals starting from the east—*oṃ saṃ somāya namaḥ*, *oṃ buṃ budhāya namaḥ*, *oṃ braṃ bṛhaspataye namaḥ*, *oṃ haṃ bhārgavāya namaḥ*. Then, at the tips of the petals starting from the southeast—*oṃ aṃ aṅgārakāya*.
Homage! Oṃ śaṃ, homage to Śanaiścara. Oṃ raṃ, homage to Rāhu.
Oṃ kaṃ, homage to Ketu. Having thus worshipped them... (p. 172)
In the east is Soma, who is gentle, holding a rosary and a water-pot; in the southeast is Maṅgala, red in color, holding a spear and a rosary, with red eyes.
In the south is yellow Budha, holding a rosary and a water-pot; and in the southwest is the aged, fair-complexioned Guru, holding a rosary and a staff in his hands.
In the south is Śukra, white-eyed and with a crooked eye; Kuṇṭhakṣa is in the water, wearing bracelets;
and there is Śanaiścara, who has crooked feet, a cruel gaze, and is fearsome.

In the northwest (Anila), Rāhu is dark-complexioned, holding a rosary and a *khinkharī* staff, with his face turned away and his body erect; in the north (Śāṅkara), Ketu has the head of a female serpent, holds a sword and a shield, and resembles a king.

Or else, one with half the body of a man and half that of a serpent (Nara-nāgārdhadehin), or one who is smoke-colored (Dhūmra), should be worshipped with palms joined in reverence; or alternatively, Soma, Budha, Bṛhaspati,
and Śukra are to be worshipped in the directions starting from the east, while Maṅgala and the others are to be worshipped in the corners starting from the southeast.
All of them assume forms at will, adorned with divine ornaments; their left hands rest upon their thighs,
while their right hands grant the gesture of fearlessness.
Having meditated thus and performed worship accordingly— as stated in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Having offered salutations to Soma and the others, one should meditate upon the planets in their proper order."
As it has been said:
"With both hands constantly joined at the fingers and placed against the region of the heart, the binding of all [the channels] should be performed by pressing with the left thumb."

"One should know this as 'namaskāra' (salutation) and cause it to be performed in all rites. Thus [it is said]. Thereafter, having given water for sipping (ācamanīya), one should satisfy [the deity] with incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), betel leaf, mouth-fresheners, and so forth, while offering water for sipping and water for honor (arghya) at intervals.

Having offered [the oblation] with the root mantra and having recited it as many times as possible, [one should offer] water for the guest-offering (arghyāmbhas) with the root mantra ending in "svāhā.
Having offered water from the crest-vessel to Bhāskara, performed the recitation (*japa*) of the limbs [of the mantra] according to one's ability,
presented the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), prayed for one’s desired object, and offered praise and prostration,
[one should perform the same] for the limbs beginning with the weapon (*astra*) using the *khaṣelkin* mantra ending in *svāhā*.

Having offered the *arghya* with the face turned away and said, "Forgive me," one should raise the mantras residing in the place of enjoyment by means of the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and the *nārāca* mudrā, [reciting]: *oṃ khaṃ khaṣolkāya sūryamūrtaye namaḥ*.
One should visualize those merged into the form by means of the divine mudrā.
Having formed a *añjali* with both hands joined by the thumbs and ring fingers, one should then extend the remaining fingers; this is the mudrā of divine form.
Thus, one should perform the dismissal with dependence upon a physical form (*mūrti*).
However, in the case of a formless [deity] such as in a mandala and so forth, the dismissal is independent; [this is] the heart of the people.
One should visualize [the deity] seated upon a lotus. Having made a mandala with cow dung in the northeastern direction, one should recite:
*oṃ aṃ tejaścaṇḍāsanāya namaḥ*; *oṃ aṃ tejaścaṇḍamūrtaye namaḥ*; *oṃ aṃ tejaścaṇḍāya namaḥ*.
One should meditate upon Caṇḍeśvara, who has a blazing face made terrible by fangs, matted hair, and red garments, and who holds an axe and a lotus, possessing fiery splendor.
Having meditated thus, having worshipped with the heart-mantra and others, having offered the arghya,
having offered the remains of the sun’s garland (sūryanirmālya), and having presented the food offering, water for drinking, and so forth, one should dismiss [the deity].

Alternatively, one may dismiss [the deity] at the conclusion of the Śiva-pūjā. One who desires specific results should perform a special worship for protection, the destruction of fear, and the warding off of missiles and weapons. (p. 176)
It brings the attainment of good fortune and the highest increase of longevity.
Caṇḍamāruta is the savior of all, the nourisher of the earth, the destroyer of epilepsy and consumption,
and the eradicator of leprosy and every ailment.
On this day, that supreme [day] is declared to bestow all spiritual accomplishments.
Having worshipped for six months for the sake of all desired objects, or for a year for the sake of success in all undertakings, one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the procedure for the solar worship at the site of the self-oriented ritual of worship, within the *Ātmārthapūjāpaddhati*.
p.
177) The Ritual for Worship for One’s Own Benefit—Now one should begin the worship of Śiva. The word *yajana* [is derived from] the root *yaja*, meaning "to worship a deity."

In the phrase "saṅgatakaraṇadāneṣu," the word denotes the meaning of the verbal root. Here, "deva" refers to Śiva, and his "pūjā" (worship) is the act of bringing about a complete mutual union between the object of worship and the worshipper. [This is expressed as]: "I worship Śiva; I receive the worship."

The giving of devotion is the bestowing of special grace through the conformity of both [the giver and the recipient], consisting of the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth up to the surrender of one’s own self, as well as the granting of worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). For the fulfillment of this, there is the worship of Śiva; and that [worship] is performed in the *liṅga*, which is the primordial abode of Śiva and consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
This is the task: although the supports (*dhāraṇā*) of Śiva are infinite, the *liṅga* alone is the most excellent.
As it has been said (p.
In the *Bṛhatkālottara*:
"Whatever sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and meritorious shrines exist upon the earth, they all reside at the base of the *liṅga*; therefore, one should worship the *liṅga*."
In the *Suprabheda*:
"All beings indeed go to dissolution during the period of withdrawal; and just as there is creation at the time of creation, for that reason it is called the *liṅga*."
That which is the mark of a person, the cause for the manifestation of a person when [the fire] is blazing— that is the *liṅga* of Sadāśiva;
it is remembered as the *Śivaliṅga*.
The *nāda* is declared to be the *liṅga*, and the *bindu* is remembered as the *pīṭha*.

Here, by the word *liṅga*, the meaning of the verbal root is "to mark" (*citrīkaraṇa*), as it marks [the world] through the processes of emanation, maintenance, and so forth. It is called *liṅga* because it "marks" (*liṅgati*).
That which brings wonder to the world through its creative acts is called the supreme splendor (*pārameśvara-tejas*) of the Lord.
Its locus of manifestation, however— beginning with the *śaiva* [linga] and so forth— is designated by the term "liṅga" through metaphorical usage.
As the teachers have said:
"The *liṅga* is that which is variegated by the five worldly activities;
that *liṅga* is the Śāmbhava light, which shines forth upon the plane of manifestation."
Thus: "In this *liṅga*, worship of Śiva should be performed for one's own welfare.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*:
"He who is established everywhere is always to be worshipped in all substrates (*sarvādhāra*)."
Nevertheless, the Lord Dhūrjaṭi accepts worship in the form of the Liṅga.
Even if worship is rendered incomplete in terms of mantras, substances, rituals, and qualities, nevertheless,
O Six-faced One, that worship becomes complete within the Liṅga.
O son, the worship on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) must not be performed with deficiency or excess;
indeed, worship that is deficient or excessive is proclaimed to be devoid of fruit.
"Or, my child, for these reasons one should begin the worship of the *liṅga*.
Regarding the fixed *liṅga* (*sthiraliṅga*), it should always be performed with effort by those who desire spiritual accomplishment."
The worship of Śiva at a mobile liṅga bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
The etymological definition of *pūjā* is given in the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
"Because all objects of desire are fulfilled and knowledge arises within the self through this fulfillment,
it is therefore called the word *pūjā* here."
This worship is of two kinds: for the sake of others and for one's own sake. As stated in the Kāmika:
"Now I shall describe the procedure for worship, which bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation; [it is] for the sake of others..."
Thus, it is proclaimed to be of two kinds: for one's own sake and so forth.
In a village, a market town, a city, or the like; by a river or even on a mountain;
in the sixty-eight great sacred fields (mahākṣetra) or elsewhere that is pleasing to the mind.
In a temple of Śiva endowed with self-manifested (svayambhu), divine, or sage-ordained (ārṣa) lingas.
Worship for the sake of others is prescribed when the *liṅga* has been installed by human beings,
or when it is a *liṅga*, a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or the like, bestowed by the Guru at the conclusion of the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Sacrificing for one's own sake is declared [to be improper], because it yields fruit only for oneself.
But for one's own sake, it should be performed upon a momentary [maṇḍala] and so forth, or on a mobile liṅga— on the crown,
on the body of the Guru, on an auspicious liṅga, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or within one's own self, or on a momentary maṇḍala.
And in water, sacrifice for one's own sake is prescribed.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"One should commence the worship for one's own sake in a momentary [liṅga], a mobile liṅga, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), in a maṇḍala, or in a painted image on a wall."
p.
182) Regarding the causes: sand, rice, river-clay, cow-dung, and likewise fresh butter.
The rudrākṣa, sacred ash, sandalwood paste, and the kūrca.
A flower garland ground with *gulā* is called the "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) twelfth [type]. In the *Ajita*,
it is said that for momentary lingas, there is no need for a pedestal (*pīṭha*).
In this very context, the specific procedure for worshipping momentary [deities] is stated:
sand, rice, and food should be offered by a twice-born; likewise, river-clay and cow-dung, as well as fresh butter, should be offered by a king.
When worshipped by a Vaiśya, the fruit and ground sandalwood become [the offerings]; when worshipped by a Śūdra, they become a bundle of kusha grass, a garland, and molasses.
p.
183) Regarding momentary [offerings], the fruit is clearly stated in the *Aṃśumatī*:
"Sand is said to grant liberation (*mukti*); rice grants enjoyment (*bhukti*)."
Purification of the self is achieved by bathing in a river; food increases longevity;
cow dung is for the purpose of destroying disease; and fresh butter bestows happiness.
The rudrākṣa bestows the form of Rudra; when ground, it grants nourishment; the fragrant substance produces brilliance, and the kūrca brings good fortune.
In this way, flowers lead to enjoyment, while water leads to union; sacred ash removes all sins, and molasses bestows affection.
The fruit is for the sake of accomplishing one's desired aims, and the sprout bestows excellent qualities;
such is proclaimed to be the fruit of momentary lingas.
One should worship even momentary objects such as sand according to the prescribed ritual; indeed, the bathing, the invocation, and everything else is a mental construction.
After the worship, one should release [the deity]; then, the rudrākṣa is neither subject to measurement nor is it fixed. Its purity comes from washing; one should avoid other [beads].
Thus, the momentary worship is seen according to the path of the Guru; and as an offering for the momentary [rite] and so forth, there should be a large quantity of *gulamudga* beans.
And likewise, the food offering (*naivedya*) consisting of fruits and so forth should be presented in this same sequence;
furthermore, the *citra*, the *ardhacitra*, and the *paṭacitra* should follow in due order.
One should worship the threefold Linga: that made of plaster which may be of various colors, that which is half-painted on a wall, and that which is a painting on cloth.
One obtains the happiness born of palaces through beauty depicted on wall-paintings, and prosperity through a cloth painting; such is the fruit of worshipping a painted liṅga.
Two types of mandalas are taught: either a lotus or a linga. By means of the lotus, one attains prosperity; by means of the linga, it grants all desires.
Thus has the fruit of the distinctions among the moments, signs, and so forth, been proclaimed. Among those various types of signs, the mobile sign (calaliṅga) is preeminent.
The mental [mandala] is superior to the [physical] mandala; from the mandala, the momentary [mandala] arises.
From the momentary, the result is most excellent, and beyond that is the cloth [mandala].
The reflection on the cloth is said to be superior to the [mere] appearance;
the image is superior to the reflection; the *vailiṅga* is superior to the image; and the partless (*niṣkala*) is supreme over the *vailiṅga*.

Because the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and other such sites bestow the accomplishment of mantras, Śiva should be worshipped in the *liṅga* alone for the sake of all accomplishments. Thus it is said:
"One should take refuge in the *liṅga*, which grants success and bestows all accomplishments; for even on the sacrificial ground..."
Because it bestows the swift accomplishment of mantras.
Thus, it is said in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"Listen here to the specific characteristics of the mobile liṅga intended for one's own benefit.
It may be made of stone, metal, or gemstone; thus it is of three kinds.
We shall describe the characteristics of these in the section on the installation of the mobile liṅga (calaliṅga-pratiṣṭhā).
This worship for one’s own sake (ātmārthayajana) is twofold: internal worship (antaryajana) and external worship (bahiryajana). Regarding that—
For those with views of a self, there is only internal sacrifice; for others, however, there is external sacrifice preceded by internal sacrifice.
In the Siddhānta,
I shall fully explain the sacrifice according to the rules and in due order; it should be understood as being of two kinds, corresponding to the respective qualifications [of the practitioner].
For ascetics and yogis whose external powers have ceased, internal sacrifice is prescribed;
for others, external worship is ordained.

O Aṃśumatī, even for those who are impure due to birth or death, for those who weep, and even for one who has assumed the outward marks [of an ascetic] out of theft, mental worship is the highest [form of worship].
Aṃśumatī says:

Even during the impurity caused by childbirth or the impurity following a death, performing worship for one's own sake is prescribed by tradition; the omission of worship must not be committed, even in the midst of birth-impurity or death-impurity.
The rite should be performed with the Śiva-mantra; by mere bathing, one becomes pure. Therein, no impurity remains, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
For the sake of worship, one should specifically disregard both impurity and [periods of] mourning;
thus one should perform the adoration of the Liṅga, free from the performance of optional rites.

At the end of the period of impurity, however, both the obligatory and the optional rites that were previously suspended must be performed. On that day, one should worship [the deity] with double the usual intensity for the sake of compensating for the omission of the optional rites.

Thus, indeed, for the pure Śaivas, such as the Brahmins and others, it is said: during the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (pretaka), one should not perform the worship of the Liṅga oneself.
But for one who has performed his own ritual duties, [the linga] is like ashes devoid of water.
A wise man should worship the mental [linga]; everything is a mental construction—that is the linga.
Having honored him by means of the preceptor or one's own kinsman.

Or one may perform the worship through another; at the conclusion, one should offer three handfuls of flowers. At the end of the period of impurity, the officiating of the sacrifice should be performed according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Tell me, how does a woman who possesses flowers perform worship? She must first perform the internal sacrifice for three days prior.
On the fourth day, having bathed and consumed the products of the cow (gavya), she should perform the sacrifice; if the liṅga has been seized by thieves, she should then worship it mentally.
And one should observe a fast for forty days, subsisting only on coconut water,
milk, or the juice of fruits and the like.
The wise person, devoted to the meditation on Śiva, should protect himself;
therefore, with every effort, one must indeed accept that liṅga.
If it has been obtained, the wise one should take it up with special joy; having performed the purification of the *liṅga* in due order, he should worship it as before.
If one has obtained only the *talliṅga*, one should collect the nine *liṅgas*;
having taken the *liṅga* of one's own guru, one should worship it according to the ancient path.
If the previous signs are seen, one should worship the two in succession;
therefore, with every effort, one should always perform sacrifice until death.
The threefold nature of this sacrifice for one's own self has been explained in detail;
I shall now describe the sacrifice for one's own self, O crusher of [the enemy] Śruntatpra, which bestows health, longevity, fame,
and the fruit of victory.
For the destruction of the sin of killing a Brahmin, for the destruction of the sin of killing a hero, and for the destruction of the sin of killing a cow,
worship is the supreme means of increasing merit.
(191) For the sake of accomplishing all desires and bestowing the fruit of all sacrifices,
there has never been, nor will there ever be, an equality with the sacrifice performed for one's own sake.
It is remembered as being of three kinds for one's own sake: pure, solitary, and mixed;
the pure is devoid of power (śakti), while the solitary is endowed with power.
From Saura up to Caṇḍa, it is proclaimed as the mixed [tradition];
and in the Aṃśumatī, a threefold division is shown by another method.
Worship is of three kinds: exclusive, innate, and mixed. Exclusive worship consists of a single *liṅga*; innate worship consists of five images (*bera*).
That which is accompanied by the images of Maheśvara and the others is called "mixed" (miśra). [This includes] the image of Gaṇeśa, the image of Skanda, Śakti, and likewise the Bull.
That which is joined with the *liṅga* alone is proclaimed as "Sahaja" (the Innate); and that which is joined with Sahaja is Maheśa, whose form is the dance.
p.
191) Those images intended for the fulfillment of specific desires are called "combined" (*sahita*) or "mixed" (*miśra*).
However, regarding these three types, a certain specific rule has been stated, as follows:
Worship is of three kinds: pure, solitary, and mixed. That which is honored by those who have conquered their senses is pure; one should perform the solitary worship dedicated to Śiva.
The teacher should worship both the mixed and the pure, absolute [deity].
Regarding the cause—the fruit of the single *liṅga* and so forth has been described: "The single *liṅga* likewise brings about liberation; the pair [of *liṅgas*] takes the form of disease;
and the three *liṅgas* likewise act as bestowers of both enjoyment and liberation."
Where there is indeed a four-liṅga [shrine], there is a loss of longevity, prosperity, and fame; however, a five-liṅga [shrine] is excellent and destroys the five great sins.
If the sixth [act] is performed, it causes death; the seventh, the destruction of one's abode;
the eighth, however, brings about a great disease or the increase of enemies; and likewise the ninth sign—
One who performs such actions is glorified in the world of Śiva.
And here, there is the qualification for all four castes— beginning with the Śaivas, Mahāśaivas, Anuśaivas, and Antaraśaivas— as well as for their respective women.
The characteristics of the Ādiśaivas and others have been demonstrated in this *Auśaucadīpikā*. In the *Aṃśumatī-ātmarthapūjā*, the qualification [for practice] has been defined:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have received initiation."
One should perform worship for one's own sake, and not for the sake of others.
And there is especially the worship of women born of the four castes.
In the *Makuṭa*:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have been initiated and admitted [to the lineage]..."
One may perform a sacrifice for one's own sake, but one should not perform one for the sake of others.
p.
193) In the subtle [state]—the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and likewise the Śūdra; as well as the mobile [beings].
One should worship daily for one's own sake, especially with devotion.
In the lineage—
for one's own sake there is the mobile liṅga, while the fixed liṅga is for the sake of others; likewise, [this applies to] the Brāhmaṇa,
the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra as well.

One should always worship for one's own sake, whether at the time of the twilight rituals or even at an improper time. As stated in the *Suprabheda*: "For initiated twice-born men of anuloma descent, [worship] may be performed for their own sake."
For those who follow the Ādiśaiva tradition, that which is prescribed for one's own self-interest shall be for the sake of others.
In the subtle [practice],
one should fully worship for one's own sake through both direct and reverse orders; one should always worship for one's own sake, and likewise for all classes of beings.
In the case of one born of yoga (*yogaja*),
through initiation by a Great Śaiva (*mahāśaiva*) or other [initiator] according to the Ādiśaiva [tradition], he becomes a Śaiva.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have been initiated are all worshippers.

One should reflect thus: "For one's own sake, and especially for the sake of the twice-born and other devotees, one should worship [the deity] with what has been given by the Guru; however, one should never worship for the sake of others."
In that regard, worship of both [deities] should be performed according to the Śaiva tradition and so forth.
However, if it is without cause—
if one does not sacrifice for one's own sake, yet sacrifices for the sake of another— that is devoid of self.

Where one performs a sacrifice for the sake of another, how can that sacrifice be [effective]? For the purpose of pacifying its defects, there must be a ceremonial bath, propitiatory rites, and fire offerings.
Having performed [the rites] according to rule, both [types of practitioners] are then engaged in the sacrifice.
In the *Vīratantra*: (p. 195)
If one is truly devoted, one should always perform the prescribed rites and worship Śiva;
