and that [worship], being performed as part of one's own duty, does not result in any fault.

One who has not been initiated, even if he is a knower of the four Vedas, should not touch the Śivaliṅga; nor should a Brahmin who has been initiated fail to worship it for the sake of his livelihood.
One should perform worship for one's own sake, but one should not perform it for the sake of others.
Even a Brahmin who has not received initiation, if he touches Śiva for six months within his lineage, he too—
He is called a *devalaka* and is unfit for the worship of the gods; likewise, even a Brahmin who has been initiated but subsists by wearing the sacred thread for hire [is unfit].
"If one should worship the Lord of Gods [in such a manner], he too becomes a *devalaka*. Thus it is said.
196) Regarding the purpose of service in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*, a certain distinction among these qualified individuals has been shown. It is as follows:
In this regard, my son, there is a certain distinction concerning the worship of mobile lingas; however, for the worship of all [other types], one who is devoted to Śiva-yogins should perform it.
Nor among the three castes, nor among Śūdras or those of the lowest birth.
Those Śūdras who are devoted to the conduct and rituals of Śiva and abstain from meat,
having been initiated by an excellent preceptor who is learned in the higher Tantras and is a Brāhmaṇa— those who are devotees of Śiva—
their worship should be performed just as one's own.
In the *Aṃśumatī-ātmārthapūjā*, worship is declared to be of three kinds— superior, middling, and inferior. Worship performed solely with the mantras of Śiva is the superior form.
Worship with both Vedic and Śiva-mantras would be middling;
worship with Vedic mantras alone would be inferior. Only...
One should perform the supreme sacrifice for one's own benefit with Śaiva mantras.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"Worship is said to be of three kinds—superior, middling, and inferior.
That which is performed with mantras consisting solely of pure Śaiva meanings is called superior."
The middle [level] is considered to consist of the meanings of the Śaiva Vedas, while the lowest consists of Vedic [mantras].
There is no mantra equal to a Śaiva mantra in the three worlds.
Even there, among mantras, that which consists of a seed-syllable (*bīja*) is said to be the best;
this same principle should be understood to apply to the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) as well, due to the equality of the underlying logic. Specifically, regarding that very fire-ritual:
The fire-ritual (agnikārya) is traditionally remembered as being threefold: Vaidika, Miśraka, and Śaiva. That which is performed solely with Vedic mantras is known as Vaidika.
That which is prescribed by Vedic and Śaiva mantras is called "mixed" (miśra); that which is prescribed solely by Śiva-mantras is called "Śaiva."
The Vedic fire is defined as that which is provided with three enclosing stones (paridhis) and fuel-sticks (samidhs) above; the mixed fire (miśrāgni), however, possesses the nature of both.
In this scripture, the Śaiva fire is proclaimed as having four enclosing stones.
One who is joined with the *praṇītā* and the *brahmakūrca* is known as a Vaidika; likewise, one who has [performed] the *miśra* for Agni is a Śaiva, or one who is endowed with both.
In the *Vijayottara*:
"The fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed for Śaiva mantras alone in the Śiva-fire; there is no [oblation] for others there. The Śiva-fire is the fire born of the Self."
If those pure Vedic mantras and the rites enjoined by the Vedas and other scriptures are employed in the fire of Śiva, do they not increase the conviction of the sacrificer?
At this juncture, having bound the Atharva-kānti and other [mantras] upon the ground, Śivā is invoked for the homa;
such is the determination of the meaning of the scriptures.
In the lineage—
Kauśika and Kāśyapa, as well as Bhāradvāja; and Gautama, O Goddess of Gods, and Parāśara, the son of Atri.
One should employ all those born in these families who are skilled in services such as attendance, and who are proficient in both Vedic and Tantric rites, for the purpose of purchase.
But that initiation of Śiva which is performed without a Tantrika is fruitless.
Therefore, one should practice the Śiva-mantras within the Vedic systems; likewise, both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya should practice them in the same manner.
The Śūdra caste, however, should perform the *āyana* as prescribed;
for other Śaivas, the practice is said to be performed silently.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"The Vedic [initiation] is for Brāhmaṇas; that which is both Vedic and Tantric is for the King (Kṣatriya);
the Tantric alone is for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, or indeed, the Tantric may be for all."
In the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*, a specific rule regarding the ritual of worship (*pūjāvidhi*) was stated.

Here, the procedure for worship is also described; listen, O Six-faced One (*Ṣaṇmukha*). The rite of worship for Brahmins and kings is now being proclaimed, along with the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
The placement [of mantras] has been declared; after that follows the placement of the thirty-eight kalās, and after that, Śrīkaṇṭha and the others.
The powers beginning with Vāmā are also called the Śivagāyatrī; the rite of worship is prescribed for Vaiśyas and those born of the feet [of the Lord].
One should perform everything except for the placement of the thirty-eight kalās (aṣṭatriṃśatkalānyāsa), the Śivagāyatrī, and the mantras of the powers beginning with Vāmā.
In the *Suprabheda*,
it is stated that at the time of recitation, [the mantra] should be joined with the *praṇava*; likewise, the six-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as being forbidden for women, Śūdras, and others.
In the Kāmika:
"Even for a Śūdra householder, the performance of daily rites is prescribed; even there, one should worship with mantras alone, though they may be devoid of [specific] reverence."
Aṃśumatī:

"The threefold worship, distinguished as superior and so forth, is most excellent. A wise person should perform worship for their own sake according to their capacity and in accordance with the rules."
The worship beginning from the doors and ending with Caṇḍa shall be the highest;
the worship beginning from the doors and ending with the *nivedya* offering shall be the middling; and likewise, the bath...
And the offering or the sacrifice would be inferior.
Every ritual service should be performed, for there is indeed a specific distinction: the perpetual festival, the constituent part of enjoyment, the evening rite, and the procedure for protection.
One should perform the sacrifice for one's own sake (ātmārthayajana) in due order without the *upasandhi*.

Regarding the worship of the *vala-liṅga*, the *Kāmika* [Tantra] demonstrates a twofold division based on the predominance of either the ancillary (*aṅga*) or the principal (*pradhāna*) elements, as follows:
And the mobile [form] is said to be of two kinds, O limb, namely the primary and the secondary;
for the purpose of worshipping paintings, statues, and so forth, it is placed at their respective front.
It is said that one limb is "worshipped" while another is considered "principal"; furthermore, the manner and the time for the worship of the limbs are as prescribed by the scriptures.
Likewise, for him, it shall be threefold, including the perpetual festivals and so forth;
elsewhere, there is pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*) and likewise the perpetual festivals and so forth.
Having abandoned the other [elements], as previously indicated, that which is intended for one's own self is distinguished.
In this [work], that which is to be performed regarding the ritual services (*upacāra*) in the sacrifice for one's own sake (*ātmārtha-yajana*) is stated after having been determined.
For example, in the *Suprabheda*:
Whether ending with a lamp or ending with an oblation, this is declared to be the general rule for one's own sake; however, for the sake of another, there is a specific distinction.
There should be constant festivals, perpetual fire-sacrifices, worship of the sandals, the waving of lights at night, and songs, dances, and offerings of water for the feet.
One should perform these according to one's capacity in those [shrines], specifically in the Liṅga known as Rathāvara;
in all these aforementioned [shrines], except for the daily festival (nityotsava).
Having set aside the sandals and the sacrificial ground, one should perform the remainder for one's own sake. (p.
204) In the Ajita [Tantra]:
One should not perform the worship of the door, nor the offering to Caṇḍeśa; nor the invocation, the sacrificial oblation, nor the daily festival.
The great bell is not prescribed, nor is the act of veiling (tiraskaraṇī);
the rite of pure dance is not mentioned. Having worshipped the Sun, Vighna, and the Guru, the best of mantra-knowers should perform the sacrifice for the sake of the Self by means of the Self.
In this context, does the prohibition of door-worship also apply to that specific door-worship?
There is no prohibition regarding the mentally conceived door-worship,
because the mentally conceived door-worship is prescribed everywhere.

That which begins with Aṃśumatī and ends with Caṇḍa is proclaimed as the "liberated" (mukta). That which begins with the door and ends with the food offering (nivedya) is celebrated as the "intermediate" (madhyama).
And thus, O Caṇḍeśa, is there not an adaptation even in the case of a prohibition regarding the offering?
In the Vātula [Tantra]:
The forty modes of service (*upacāra*) are set forth as follows:
invocation, the seat, the water of honor (*arghya*), installation, welcome, presence, confinement,
and the visualization of the limbs and minor parts.
With water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering, as well as with scents and flowers, and then with incense and lamps;
thereafter, the bath, the garment, and the sacred thread.
Likewise, incense and flowers, as well as incense-sticks and lamps, collyrium, ornaments,
fans and the like, and even the display of ritual gestures (mudrās).

Worship with these [offerings], as well as food offerings, fire oblations and the like, strength-giving rites, gifts, meditative absorption, recitation, hymns of praise, circumambulation, and prostration.
The offering of water from the hollowed palms, as well as the honoring of the book, the arghya, the ācamana,
and the dismissal (virārjana)— these are recorded [in tradition].
The worship of the deity for one's own sake is performed with forty services (*upacāra*).
Thus, in the *Yogaja*: (206) [text follows]
I shall now declare the ritual service for one's own benefit; listen indeed! [It consists of] invocation, installation, welcome, and confinement.
The ritual for the major and minor limbs, as well as water for the feet, water for sipping, and water for the guest-offering (arghya),
along with fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and likewise the bath.
Garments, the sacred thread, fragrance, flowers, incense, libations, the waving of lights,
ornaments, and likewise songs and dances.
The display of mudrās has been taught, as well as the worship of the enclosure, the food offering, the rite of fire oblation,
meditative absorption, and the recitation of mantras.
Having performed circumambulation and prostration, and offered water for rinsing the mouth and sipping in forty-four ways, one should perform the worship of the deity for one's own sake.
Ajite—
The restriction of time has been established; this worship may be performed for the sake of others.
But for one's own sake, O Janārdana, it is prescribed [to be performed] once, twice, or thrice a day. Likewise, in the *Kāraṇa*:
"One should worship for one's own sake twice or once a day."
One should perform sacrifices for one's own sake, having reconciled them with other [doctrines].

One should prepare the water for the feet and the water for sipping in the same sequence as before. The worship for one's own sake, beginning with the invocation of Ruru and ending with Caṇḍa, has been performed.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"One should perform [this] for one's own sake at either two junctions of the day or three junctions.
In the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
In this manner, worship is prescribed at all four times,
or else at one time, two times, three times, or during the latter part of the night.
Therefore, a householder should likewise worship Śambhu constantly.
However, in the *Kālottara*, it is stated that one should perform worship specifically at the times beginning with dawn.

For one who observes the rules (*niyamavat*), worship should not be performed after three *ghaṭikās* following sunset; rather, the commencement [of worship] should be done while the sun has not yet set. It is stated that even for such a person, there is no fault in performing occasional worship (*naimittika-pūjā*) at night. This is as follows regarding worship at the three times of day:
For whomever [performs] that practice, the worship begun with the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) should continue for three ghaṭikās;
beyond that, one should not perform it during the conjunctions of the planets Jupiter and the Moon. [This applies to] the mantra.
And at the time of sunset, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and other such festival days.
Furthermore, the Śivarātri vow and worship performed at night does not entail any fault;
however, for one seeking liberation (mumukṣu), there is no restriction regarding time. As it was stated by Somaśambhu:
For one desiring liberation, the worship of Śiva is always recommended and is never forbidden.
In the *Kāmika*,
the rule for all [practitioners] has been stated. It is as follows:
Just as it is at the time of origination, so too is the manner of its dissolution; one should perform sacrifices for one's own sake according to one's capacity.
In that very context, the regulation for the water used for bathing, as well as the measurement regulations for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth, have been set forth; namely,
that in the case of self-manifested (*svayambhu*) or Bāṇa-liṅgas and others, one should abandon what has been prescribed [in other sources] and follow one's own desire.
The quantity of water for bathing should be according to the prescribed measure, but for one's own private use, it may be as one desires.

The five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and the water from the ritual jar (kalaśodaka) should be prepared according to the prescribed proportions for the purpose of the ceremonial bath.
Likewise— the worshipper, having meditated in his mind upon the food offering, water, flowers, clothing, cow-products, and scents, should offer them together with the self and the intended purpose.
The food offering (*naivedya*) consists of one *droṇa* of rice; the water is one *droṇa* or half a *droṇa*.
The flower is said to be the three fruits (*triphalā*); the cloth is of the measure of a cubit (*hasta*); [and] the fragrance...
In that context, four palas constitute one prastha, and a prastha is [the measure] of cow's milk.
One should prepare a prastha each of ghee and honey, along with milk-rice and coconut;
one should perform worship for one's own sake.
Perform the sacrifice for your own sake according to the desire of the patron, offering flowers, incense, food-oblations, water, and the service of garments.
Even the transgression of the proper time for this sacrifice performed for one's own sake is said not to be a fault— thus it is stated in the Aṃśumatī.
Just as at the times of conception and as at the time of birth, when the lapse of the proper time has occurred,
one should not cause an expiation to be performed.
The procedure for worship regarding the sick is stated in that very same [text]:
"When mental anguish has been produced, when one is afflicted by diseases, when there is obstruction to the falling of the body and so forth,
and during the onset of illnesses and other calamities..."
Likewise, having performed the washing of the feet even if one has not bathed,
and having smeared oneself with ashes, one should especially perform the worship.
If one is unable to perform worship, one should also perform the act of touching; having placed a flower upon the head while recollecting the root mantra.
Or if one is unable even to touch it, then merely beholding the *liṅga* [is sufficient]. As stated in the *Merutantra*:
"Whether it be the sight of the *liṅga* or the worship of the *liṅga*, if [one performs] this..."
Upon being born, they become lords of the thirty gods.
In the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"O gods, asuras, and others— yakṣas and sages free from envy—
by worshipping the Liṅga, one attains perfection and eternal liberation."
Thus, by relying upon the *liṅga* endowed with ritual action, the practitioner who is devoted to liberation attains his desired perfection and liberation.
Just as water on a lotus leaf is extremely flickering when stirred by the wind, even so,
O Śakra, is the life of living beings upon this earth exceedingly transient.
O Śakra, youth is unstable, and wealth is likewise unstable;
sons, grandsons, and so forth are unstable— thus has the Lord of Splendor declared.
Therefore, having abandoned the nets of delusion— sons, wives, dear friends, and wealth— one should adopt the insignia of renunciation.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"That fool who seeks the essence in the human condition— which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree— is like one seeking substance in a bubble of water."
Since even the ocean, along with its mountains, its thoughts, and its deities, has met its destruction, how could a mortal in this world not go to his end, appearing as fragile as foam?

Now, the sequence of worship: having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), applied the sacred ash (bhasma), and performed the ritual of the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), one should adorn the body with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads; then, having purified the vessel for the general offering (sāmānyārghya) with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and consecrated it by means of inspection and other rites.

On the three parts of this [liṅga], which are its foundation, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara (Śiva), along with their Śaktis, on the middle, the top, and the base-rings respectively, with the heart-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having filled [the vessel] with pure water and consecrated it seven or ten times with the *praṇava*,
and having performed the rites of protection (*rakṣā*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*),
one should sprinkle the western door of this [mandala] with that [water] using the *astra-mantra* and install the door-guardian (*dvārapāla*).
In the *Sahasra*: having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should apply the sacred ash (*bhasma-dhāraṇa*) as before.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
Having adorned his own body with the Śiva-mantras in the proper sequence, and having become one with Śiva with a brilliantly radiant self, he should begin the worship of Śiva.
In the *Kālottara*:
"At the time of grasping [the breath], at the equinoxes, at the solstices, at the transits [of the sun], and also on the new moon day..."
And on the full moon day and on auspicious days.
One should always wear a rudrākṣa during the time of fire oblations as well as on one's own birth day;
thus, the destruction of all sins shall occur.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—
the Rudrākṣa of each of these four castes bestows success upon that respective caste.

Likewise, in the Purāṇa: "Nevertheless, a superior [text] should not be held by the lowly, nor should an inferior [text] be held by the superior; for by not holding it or by holding it, one grants the desired [retribution] of hell."
Ten Rudrākṣas on the region of the neck, twenty on the head, six on each of the two ears, twelve on each of the pair of hands, and one on each of the two upper arms,
strung with a single thread according to the sixteen digits of the moon.
He who wears one hundred and eight [beads] on his crest and on his chest is Nīlakaṇṭha himself.
In the *Kālottara*: "One should cause women to wear rudrākṣas, conjoined with the purificatory rite of initiation (*dīkṣā-saṃskāra*). Just so...
Having initiated him according to the prescribed rite, one should subsequently have him wear [the mark] with the mantra.
It should be worn on the head by Īśāna, and on the neck by Tatpuruṣa; it should be worn on the throat by Aghora, and one should wear it on the heart by Aghora.
One should hold [the rosary] in the hand with the primary seed-syllables or with the Aghora-mantras;
and one should hold the fifty-fold rosary while reciting the Vyomavyāpin-mantra.
Those that are bitten by worms, cut, split, or pierced by thorns, as well as those that have opened by themselves—
especially those that were previously so.
The rudrākṣa alone is indeed the most excellent.
One should avoid those with reversed openings and those with only a single face. O child, a person should wear a rudrākṣa that is free from these six defects.
Briefly stated, each single [bead] should be known to yield the fruit of gifting a single cow; that a Śūdra becomes [elevated] by the gift of Rudrākṣa beads—what wonder is there in this?
Having thoroughly sprinkled [the site] with the thousand-spoked vajra, one performs the fourfold ritual of Brahmā, beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*).
Having worshipped the power (*śakti*) at the base, middle, and tip of the ring of Viṣṇu, Hara, and the other deities,
one should worship it in the heart; having consecrated the water seven times with the *praṇava*, one should display the *dhenumudrā*.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
having displayed the syllable Oṃ, performed the recitation, and prepared the arghya offering, [one should likewise prepare] the Aṃśumatī.

If it is argued that the purpose of introducing the worship of the western door is because the Guru has indeed established the worship of all four doors in the *Kāraṇa*, [we reply: True; for it is stated in the *Makuṭa*: "In the north, one who performs the *nālada*..."
The prohibition of the southern door follows from the statement that "the northern door must not be made," because the northern door is prohibited in the *Cintya* and *Sādākhyā* [Tantras];
therefore, the southern door is used for worship.
Is this intended to establish the superiority of the western gate alone, based on the statement: "One who desires accomplishment, being composed, [should enter] the western gate" (p. 217)?

Furthermore, because of the statement "one should strike the remaining doors starting from the western door," and because of the injunction to strike the doors other than the western one, in the subtle self-oriented worship (ātmārthapūjā), the offering (naivedya) is indeed at the western door.

Since it has been stated [in the scriptures] that "it is in the eastern face," and because all the teachers who composed ritual manuals (*paddhati*) have introduced the worship specifically as being at the western door, the worship of the western door alone should be performed for one's own sake; therefore, that alone is introduced here.
Now, the method for worshipping the gatekeepers:
In the *Sūkṣma-tantra*—one should sprinkle the western door with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and with the water of Śiva. [Worship] Gaṇeśa...
Having worshipped Vāgdevī on the right, [one should worship her] on the left side.
In the center, however, one should worship Mahālakṣmī; on the right, Nandin and Gaṅgā;
and specifically on the left side, Mahākāla and Yamunā.
Having worshipped [the deities] above and below, one should then worship the Śivāstra.
Next, their meditation is as follows, according to the Jñānaratnāvalī:
Dark-complexioned, pot-bellied, stout, with the face of an elephant and four arms;
holding a tusk and a rosary in the right hands, and an axe and a *laḍḍuka* sweetmeat in the left.
One should worship the dwarf, three-eyed [Vighneśvara] above the right door;
and [one should worship] the white, youthful Sarasvatī, adorned with all ornaments,
intent upon playing the lute held in her left and right hands.
One should worship Pustakākṣadhara with two [offerings] in the north; between those two, one should worship Mahālakṣmī, who is golden-colored and adorned.
She holds a bilva fruit and a lotus in her right hands, and a lotus and the gesture of fearlessness in her left;
she is being consecrated by streams of nectar from jars with elephant-trunk spouts.
The god Śrī Nandikeśvara, wearing matted hair and a sacred thread,
holding a trident and a rosary, gentle in appearance, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
On the southern branch, one should worship the three-eyed Lord adorned with the moon,
and the daughter of Jahnu (Gaṅgā), who is white and gentle, seated upon a crocodile,
her arms holding a white chowrie and a vessel of nectar.
To the north of that [Liṅga], one should worship Nandin, adorned with all ornaments, who is dark-complexioned,
has tawny matted hair, is formidable, and possesses a face made terrifying by his fangs.
Terrifying with a frown, wearing a thick snake as a sacred thread,
holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and bearing a serpent and a drum.
One should worship Yauvanā on the northern branch, and then Yama’s daughter, who is dark-complexioned and adorned, standing upon a tortoise on its southern side.
The self-controlled practitioner should worship Him holding a lotus and a jar of nectar; as stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*: (p. 220)
One should worship each [item] in sequence, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the water for the feet (pādya);
[this is done] from the tips of the thumb and ring finger, with the mantra "Oṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva" at the end.
Having placed [the mantra] upon both eyes, one should gaze at the divine obstacles; then, having abandoned those divine obstacles, one should again [use] the nārāca-mudrā.
With the flower held between the index finger and the thumb, saying "Oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ," Nandikeśvara should dispel the obstacles moving through the intermediate space.
By striking the ground three times with the heel of the left foot, obstacles on the earth are destroyed;
by means of the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, the removal of obstacles shall take place.
Then, leaning toward the right, he should enter the threshold-jamb; furthermore, he should enter the temple with his right foot alone.
One should worship the Śivāstra weapon in the middle of the threshold, with the seat and other elements as before;
it has four faces and four arms, and its radiance is like a blazing fire.
O Dakṣa, [he is] facing Śiva, endowed with the trident and the gesture of fearlessness.
Having meditated thus upon [the deity] endowed with a crown of matted locks and having the moon as his crest-jewel, one should worship the Weapon-mantra (astra) while facing west.
Then, having circumambulated Maheśvara, the God of gods, [one should stand] on the south of the threshold.
And likewise, the worship of the deity of the site (Vāstudeva).
The swan saw him— corpulent, fair-complexioned, with a beard and four faces,
holding in his right and left hands a rosary of *akṣa* seeds and a water-pot respectively.
Having thus worshipped [the deity] in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya* [tantra],
one should perform your worship inside the door on the right side [to the image of the Lord], who is red in color,
four-armed, three-eyed, and has the moon as his crest-jewel.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks and joined with the *namas* mudrā,
he is the leader of the Gaṇas, holding an axe and a deer; [he is] the arm.
His right [hand] was equipped with a knife and a cane.
Having placed the eye at the base of the arm and the razor-knife at its end,
[he visualizes himself] adorned with all ornaments, his body smeared with ashes.
He wore a sacred thread made of rudrākṣa beads, was clad in a white sacrificial thread,
and likewise possessed hanging garlands of rudrākṣa as well as rosaries on his hands.

Having uttered "Oṃ Hāṃ Śrīṃ," one should offer salutations to Nandikeśvara. Having thus worshipped Nandin, one should worship his consort Suyaśā on his left— Gaṇanāyikā, who is dark-complexioned, with gracious eyes, and two arms.
Adorned with all ornaments and beautiful with all the primary marks, she has an utpala lotus extended in her right hand, and another [lotus] thereafter.
What is the remainder?
Having uttered the seed-syllable *oṃ hāṃ*, [one should say] "salutation to Suyaśā. Thus, her—
One should worship with devotion for the sake of attaining the goals of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Regarding the rite of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*:

"Whether in the case of a stationary or a moving being, one should worship with these very mantras. Alternatively, having visualized [the deity] as a unified whole, one should worship by means of a single application. Likewise—
Aṃśumatī said:
"Alternatively, one may worship a single door-keeper in the center; the wise person should worship him with the mantra: 'Salutation to all the door-keepers.'"
Having expelled the three obstacles with three strikes of the heel, and having struck three times with the clapping of hands,
one should cast the flower upwards.
Thereafter, having gathered all the materials for worship, such as the water for the ablution and so forth,
one should sit facing north upon the seat of Brahmā and others on the right side of the deity, and [meditate upon] oneself...

One should perform the ritual placement of the substance and the mantra-sign according to the sequence of purification. Thus says the Āgama: "Having taken up the water-pots purified by the weapons [mantras] such as *nirīkṣaṇa* and others, and having obtained permission, one should proceed silently toward the Gaṅgā or other [sacred waters] while reciting the *Śiva-mantra*."
With water purified by a cloth and consecrated by the Brahmāṅga mantra,
one should fill those vessels washed with the Astra mantra, reciting either the Gāyatrī or the Hṛdaya mantra.
In the *Suprabheda*: "Pāṭala, utpala, and padma flowers, as well as karavīra and others, should always be used for bathing water;
they should be unctuous and fragrant."
p. 225) Regarding the cause:
water that is defiled by color, odor, or taste, or is infested with worms, hair, and the like—such water [is unfit].
One should avoid stagnant water from a pond there.
One should carefully avoid a place associated with impurity and devoid of sunlight, but one should diligently select a delightful spot.
One should take water from a river, a pond, or a well,
beginning at sunset until the time of sunrise.
Water used for bathing and likewise water from washing the feet are not to be taken;
as for the nature of other types of substances, we shall explain them in the section on the purification of substances.
p. 226) Regarding the subtle [level]:
the seat consists of *darbha* grass, wood, *sāraṅga*, and likewise animal hide.
Though clad in a tiger skin with its hair intact, he was dressed in garments of precious woolen cloth.
The fruit of the seats made of *aṃśumatī* wood has been described as follows: a square or rectangular wooden seat bestows good fortune; [likewise] a cloth seat.
The destruction of disease is found in the *kambala* [sūtra], and the liberation from suffering in the *duḥkhamocana*.
On a black seat there is the attainment of knowledge; on a tiger skin, the glory of liberation.
According to the *Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva*:
"And for the propitiation of the Lord, [one should sit] to the right side of the deity."
And in the subtle [practice]:
one should arrange a seat as desired on the right side of the deity.
In the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa): "Having seated himself comfortably on a seat arranged to the south of the deity, with his face turned toward the north and his mind disciplined."
And in the *Sahasra*: "Seated upon a beautiful throne on the right side of the Lord.
The definition for that [throne] is stated in the *Kāraṇa*:
Facing north and seated upon a beautiful seat, he should place the tips of his two feet together in a hollowed position between his knees.
With the gaze slightly fixed on the tip of the nose and the body held straight, this is declared to be the beautiful posture (rucirāsana); the wise know it to be worthy of all worship.
And in the *Aṃśumatī* (p.
"Then one should perform the left [hand gesture], known as the *rucirāsana*."
This is declared to be the Rucirāsana, performed while seated upon a seat.
Or as it is stated in the *Śivarahasya*:
"Established in the svastika posture in the southern quarter of the Lord's [abode];
not in front of Śambhu facing east, nor in the north where women reside, nor in the west. For this reason...
Standing behind that, one should worship it.
Likewise, one should not stand before the Lord, nor behind him, nor even near his own side;
for the sake of destroying the flood of sins and attaining liberation, one who is skillful should worship while standing to the right of the skillful one.
One should not be in the presence of women, nor in front of, nor behind one's master;
for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, the Guru should be honored by the capable householder in the right-hand side of the dwelling.
If it is asked, "How can there be the destruction of sin for one who is both terrible and peaceful?"—certainly so;
nevertheless, this is the very nature of reality. As it has been said:
Just as the sun, though mild and cool, utterly consumes the lotus, so too does the Aghora [mantra],
even when peaceful, act as a burner of sins.
Therefore, according to the authoritative word, one should perform the sacrifice facing north.
But is it not the case that the worshipper’s position on the southern side is not appropriate here,
since the worship at the western door is what has been introduced?
Furthermore, it is illogical for the worshipper to remain in that [central] portion while Lord Sadāśiva faces the door;
nor should it be argued that Śiva’s facing the door is unestablished, for it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
One should designate as the east that direction in which the door is located;
however, that door which faces the liṅga is considered the front.

(230) If it is argued that this is not so because it has been stated, "In that regard, the Tatpuruṣa face should be upward and facing forward," [we reply: no, because that statement from the *Kāmika* concerns the perspective of another (the practitioner). This is evident from what follows immediately thereafter.

"Because of the stated injunction that 'the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), the bull, and the trident should face the same direction as the face [of the deity],' since the ritual procedure for worshipping the sacrificial pedestal, the bull, and so forth is prescribed solely for the sake of others (parārtha), [it follows that] the self-purpose (ātmārtha) [is not concerned with this].
Even if the door faces any particular direction, the deity's facing toward the east or other directions [remains fixed].
The practitioner must indeed face north.
In the Śrīmukha image,
during initiation and other rites, the Guru should contemplate the Lord of the Jar (Ghaṭeśa) in the west; [he should contemplate] Īśa,
Tatpuruṣa, Śānta, Nitya, and the eternal Purānana.
In the *Śrībṛhadbhārgava* and other texts:
"One should always meditate upon Sadāśiva, whose face and chest are turned toward the east."
"Having that very one, whose face is turned inward, as the support for the initiation-vessel and so forth"—thus it is said in the *Lakṣmī-Keśava-saṃvāda*:
"In the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, Sadāśiva is always the presiding authority; he faces the east."
Lakṣmī, whose body consists of the digits [of the moon] turned backward.
In the *Śrībṛhatkiraṇodyotikā* and other texts:
Īśa and Puruṣa face east; Aghora faces south; Vāma always has a gentle countenance and faces north; Sadyojāta is remembered as having five faces.
Having entered through the western door as before, one should place a flower with water for the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) in the sky, in a spacious location, while reciting the Astra mantra.

Because the scriptures are manifold, Śambhu is considered to have faces turned in all directions, for he is the presiding authority over all on account of the rites and injunctions of his own tradition; therefore, he is regarded as having an eastern face.

This is the statement of the essence of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Likewise, according to the scripture (*āgama*), let there be a temple for the Lord; however, whether it be a wooden structure or made of stone, it must not abandon its orientation toward the east and other directions, whether it be a *liṅga* or an image.
Or whatever other rite is performed, in each of those the sacrificer worships Śiva while facing north, as is done at Kakubha.

Regarding the subtle section on the worship for one's own purpose (*ātmartha-pūjā*), the author of the *Jñānaratnāvalī* (p. 233) raises an objection, stating that the western door alone [is used] for the offering of food (*naivedya*), while the eastern face [is used for other rites].
The fact that the Lord faces the east has been established by the teachers through many points of consensus.
Now, even though the door is to the west,
since it has been established that one facing the door has for his object the welfare of others, let the deity not face me (who am for my own sake) toward the door, but rather let him face eastward.
We do not agree; rather, we maintain that one must face south. For thus, in all the scriptures, it is established without dispute that the practitioner should face north.
And likewise, on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) and before the mobile liṅga (calaliṅga), Śiva faces the practitioner.

From such statements as these, the fact that [the deity] faces south is indeed established. And this state of being the "Right-facing Form" (dakṣiṇāmūrti) of the God is presented here preceded by a doubt.
If it is argued that this has been established in the *Mṛgendrapaddhativyākhyāna*, we say no.

This is because the statement regarding being "facing the practitioner" (*sādhakābhimukhya*) pertains to the occasional worship (*naimittikapūjā*) within initiation (*dīkṣā*), since it has been established many times that being "facing the practitioner" applies specifically there. It should not be argued that this same principle would apply to the daily worship (*nityārcana*) as well; for here, [the Lord] is not the pervasive one (*vibhu*).

Because of the prohibition beginning with "one should stand in front," etc., the prohibition itself does not apply there in the case of an occasional (naimittika) rite; for that would contradict the statement regarding facing [the deity] in that context. Furthermore, because of the statement "in the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya)," [the deity] is always [present].

It should not be argued that because [the rule] specifies facing eastward, one would not be able to face [the deity] during initiation (*dīkṣā*) by virtue of this very statement; for this statement applies only where...

In occasional rites (*naimittika*), such as the worship of a bridge (*saṃkramapūjā*) and so forth, there is an absence of statements regarding the orientation toward the practitioner (*sādhaka-abhimukhya*), because that [orientation] pertains to that specific context. Otherwise, due to mutual contradiction, both would result in a lack of authority. [This concerns] the orientation toward the practitioner.

In that statement, since Aghora— who is situated on the right side of the face of Tatpuruṣa— would have to move elsewhere, it would follow that the right portion lacks the excellence of being the means to liberation; therefore, even the commentary on the *Mṛgendrapaddhati* [states this].
Because it does not touch upon the fundamental point, it should be disregarded. Furthermore,
even regarding daily worship, there are thousands of statements in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*) concerning the orientation of the practitioner (*sādhaka*).

By stating "not in the east" and so forth, the author of the commentary on the *paddhati*, who is demonstrating his orientation toward the practitioner (*sādhaka*), mocks the very prohibition established in the section on daily worship (*nityārcana*).

Nor should it be said that this prohibition was established by him as referring specifically to a permanent linga located at the eastern gate; for the statement found in the *Aṃśumat-tantra* and other texts within the section on worship for one's own sake (*ātmārtha-pūjā*) actually concerns the subject of worship for the sake of others (*parārtha*).
Because it is impossible to express.
As for the argument that, by the analogy of the Lord of the Pavilion and the Jar, [the deity] faces the practitioner to be protected just as he faces the pavilion to be protected—that is weak.
For in that case, the deity’s facing the pavilion is not for the sake of protecting the pavilion; rather—

Because protection is accomplished by the mere word or by implication; for even in the absence of a primary [deity] facing that direction, the fact that it is to be protected does not cease. Otherwise, [there would be no point in] the deity facing the door for the sake of another.

Because, in the absence of being oriented toward the practitioner (*sādhaka*), there would follow the undesirable consequence that the practitioner could not be protected therein. Protection is established even by a mere atom of a fraction of the deity’s glance.
As for the statement: "The wise one, having entered the place, takes refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti."

The statement from the *Kiraṇatantra* has been cited; however, that too is intended merely to enjoin the placement [of the deity] on the right side, which is in proximity to the face of Aghora denoted by the word "southern form" (*dakṣiṇāmūrti*).
It should not be understood as establishing that the Lord possesses a southern face. This is the correct interpretation.
Because it is not established by those who have studied two hundred thousand [verses].

As for that which, in the *Vīkamudrā-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīmad-raurava-vṛtti* and in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhu-paddhati*, [is described] as being brought face-to-face (*abhimukhībhūta*) by means of the state of being both the one who restrains (*tādin*) and the one who is restrained (*nigrāhya*).
Based on the two statements, "The special proximity" and "the respectful presence before one's face is called *āvāhana* (invocation) here," it is intended that the practitioner faces [the deity];
such is the purpose of that kind of invocation.
Because, even while existing for the sake of another, there would follow the consequence that [the deity] would be oriented toward the practitioner.

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the purpose of this invocation (āvāhana)? it is said: the practitioner's making the Lord of the Kula (Kuleśāna), whose face is turned upward, attentive to receiving the worship is precisely that.
The mounting is the manifestation [of the deity].
This was stated in the *Śuddhākhyā*.
O Six-faced One, there is a certain distinction here regarding the upward-facing [face]: having meditated upon its root, that face is traditionally known as "turned away" (parāṅmukha).
At the time of worship, having meditated upon that [deity] as being present within the face of the ritual action, and having thus made the formal resolve according to the rules,
one should proceed at the conclusion of the worship as previously described.

Nor does this much imply that the Lord is oriented toward the practitioner. However, in the commentary on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*, it is stated that "invocation (*āvāhana*) is the act of manifesting consciousness. That too is contradictory.

As for the statement that "the Lord Īśāna must always look toward the main entrance," by the force of this injunction, those performing worship at the western door face westward, [because] of the Lord Īśa.
It has been stated that [the deity] has arrived; for that too has been established as having the door as its orientation and the external object as its domain.
As for that which pertains to movable lingas in all ritual manuals (*paddhati*s):
Because of the injunction to face the east, the statements cited as indicating that orientation toward that [direction] find their fulfillment by referring to fixed lingas; however,
even that is not elegant, for in all ritual manuals (paddhati),...
Since no injunction for the deity’s facing toward the practitioner is observed in the context of daily worship (*nityārcana*),

it is logical that the statements cited as indicating such facing find their fulfillment only in reference to occasional worship (*naimittikārcana*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the deity] being devoid of desire.

Therefore, this commentary on the hymn of worship, which establishes the orientation toward the practitioner through the arguments set forth in the explanation of this manual (p. 241), [is now presented].
What is to be considered?
Furthermore, does the Lord’s facing south occur by means of his Tatpuruṣa face or his Īśāna face? Not the first.

At that time, it was stated that the efficacy of the seat of Dakṣa— which destroys sins dependent upon it— would be rendered fruitless by Aghora approaching from another direction. Nor is this a desirable consequence, for the attainment of the fruit depends precisely upon facing south.
Then, whatever is prescribed by rule— whether it be food to be chewed, swallowed, drunk, licked, or sucked— should be given repeatedly with the face turned upward.
If it is argued that, according to this statement, the food offering (*naivedya*) should be made facing the face of Īśāna itself—that is, facing the practitioner—it is not so;
for there is the scriptural injunction: "One should offer the food offering with the right hand, and [present] excellent drinking water. (p. 242)

It should not be argued that the *naivedya* (food offering) must be offered with the hand situated in the eastern direction as one's own right hand, because by extending the hand toward the south, its placement becomes possible within the mouth of Īśāna, who faces southward from the *naivedya*.
O practitioner, likewise, by causing distress to the hand during the meal of the deity, one indeed incurs a primary downfall.

Furthermore, the position that the offering of food (naivedya) should be made to the face of Īśāna, because it is the nature of his head, contradicts worldly convention; for people do not eat with their heads, but only with their mouths. However, since Tatpuruṣa’s mouth is directly the form of the [central] face...

And because [the deities] known as the four beginning with Śiva are pervaded by that which is called the essence of karma (*karmasāra*), the offerings (*naivedya*) are likewise [included] in that very place.
It is even better.

In the subtle section concerning the sacrifice for one's own purpose (*ātmārthayajana*), because of the rule regarding the offering of the *naivedya* to the mouth of Tatpuruṣa, therefore, in the daily worship (*nityārcana*),
[the offering] is to be made from the mouth of [the deity] facing toward the practitioner.
Because the arguments presented [in the *Mṛgendra*] cannot be established otherwise, and because it would contradict the offering of the *naivedya*,

the statement made by the authors of the *Paddhati* and the commentary on the *Pūjāstava* regarding the Lord’s facing south must be disregarded; for [this applies only] to the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and the mobile liṅga (*calaliṅga*).

It has been stated that the statement "Śiva faces the practitioner" pertains to the subject matter of the initiation ritual (*dīkṣā-vidhi*), but this is untenable; for in that context, there is no possibility of a mobile liṅga (*cala-liṅga*).
If this is argued, we say no.
In that regard,
since there is no fault in the worship of a mobile *liṅga*, otherwise it would have to be stated:
"By this statement, what [is meant] is the deity’s orientation toward the practitioner?"

It is established either prior to the state of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) or immediately after it. It cannot be the first case, because at that time the practitioner himself does not yet exist, and thus his orientation toward [the deity] would be unestablished. Nor can it be the second case, because immediately following the state of the practitioner, the deity is already oriented toward him.
Furthermore, through re-invocation, there is indeed the manifestation [of the deity], because the fruit is attained.

It should not be argued that the meaning [of "abhimukha"] found in the commentary on the purpose of invocation— which consists of making [the deity] attentive— is entirely different, and not simply the state of facing that direction.
In that case, since it is more appropriate for this statement of "being present" (*abhimukhya*) to have another meaning, one must accept that it has another meaning.
And because it would contradict your own statement. If you argue that this statement regarding invocation (*āvāhana*) and this [present] statement have the same meaning,
and thus both statements together establish the deity's orientation toward the practitioner immediately after the invocation— alas, [then what of the state] prior to that invocation?

It follows that facing east is what we have asserted. Nor should it be argued that this is not my own position either, for I maintain that immediately after the invocation, the deity faces toward the practitioner.

For at the time of beginning the worship, since the deity is already stationed facing the east, it is impossible to turn them toward the practitioner through re-invocation; otherwise, as has been stated, there would be the undesirable consequence that even in the case of worship for the sake of others (*parārtha*), the deity would have to face the practitioner.
And for the sake of others, because others are to be assisted by means of [the deity] alone, there is no facing toward the practitioner through invocation; however, for one's own sake...
It might be argued that [the practitioner] faces that direction because he alone is the one to be graced;
if so, then for the sake of others, there would follow the undesirable consequence that [the practitioner] must face a fixed direction because all those situated in every direction are to be graced.

Furthermore, if one faces east prior to mounting [the vehicle], there is a contradiction with the citation from the *Kiraṇatantra* which establishes that one should face south at the commencement of worship. Now, suppose it is thought: "I shall establish facing south at the commencement of worship by means of the *Kiraṇa* statement."
There is a contradiction with the citation of the words indicating the deity’s orientation toward the practitioner through that invocation (p.
for it would be illogical to effect a turning to the right-facing state by invoking again a deity who is already facing south.
Because of the result.

There is no contradiction with the example; rather, it is the very presentation for the purpose of invocation that is accepted. [Thinking: "By means of the rays of the bodice alone, I shall establish the state of facing south."

If it is argued [that this is not so], we say no; for it has already been stated that its purpose is merely to establish [the deity] in the right-hand portion. Otherwise, later in that very same [text], it would have said:
"Then, having offered the final oblation after the enclosures (*āvaraṇas*), one should worship the Sādhya deities; having marked them with their limbs (*aṅgas*) upon the lotus-seat of the *praṇava*."
One should worship with the *vibhava* [mantra] on the southern side of Śiva;
on the petals of the southern lotus in the *Mṛgendra*, there are the forms of a woman and a man in the eastern and western sections.
The light that liberates from the non-terrible (aghoramocanajyotis) is in the center; it is not elsewhere anywhere.

248) There is a contradiction with the scriptural injunctions prescribing the worship of the mantras to be accomplished (*sādhyamantra*) in the southern direction from the deity; for the practitioner of the mantra (*sādhyamantrī*) [is positioned] in the southern direction from the deity during the worship.
Because the deity’s primary orientation toward the east establishes the presence of the divinity,
therefore, for the daily worship of the deity, there is no scriptural statement establishing an orientation toward the south; rather,
the innate primary orientation toward the east must be accepted by all Śaivas.

And this has been accepted by the venerable teachers (ācāryacaraṇa), the foremost exponents of the ritual manuals (kriyāpaddhati) and founders of the Śaiva tradition, in their commentaries on the *Lakṣya-candra* and other works. Therefore, for the sake of others...
Facing the door of the deity; however, for one's own daily worship (nityārcana), one should face the east during occasional rites (naimittika). (p.
In rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), the general rule is that one faces the east; however, in the case of initiations (*dīkṣā*) and occasional rites (*naimittika*),
facing south and so forth is established by specific scriptural injunctions and is thus beyond reproach— thus all is well.
In the *Viśvasādākhya*, it is stated:

"One should worship the imperishable Śiva by means of the sequence of the five purifications; having first performed the purification of the self, one should thereafter perform the purification of the place."
The purification of substances is the third, the purification of mantras is the fourth, and the purification of the *liṅga* is the fifth; thus has the sequence of purifications been declared, O Lord.
In the Vātula:
"He who knows the five purifications is worthy to perform the worship;
herein [are] the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), and meditation (*dhyāna*)."

Because the purifications of the self are the cause of the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is taught first. [Objection: But was it not already established by initiation (*dīkṣā*) that [the body] contains the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*)?
The elements have indeed been purified. What is accomplished by the purification of the elements? It is true.
Those elements are of two kinds: gross elements and subtle elements.
Among these, at the conclusion of initiation, they are the locations for the experience of karma that is to be experienced.

The forms of the principles (*tattva-rūpa*) that are purified are indeed those consisting of gross external elements, and not those consisting of the subtle elements of the body. As it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*, in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*):
Earth, water, fire, air, and space— these five principles indeed pervade all things.
"The bondage of the body is not established without the five principles;
having understood these through their division into gross and subtle, one should purify them. Thus [it is said]. In this way...
If it is argued that no purpose for initiation (*dīkṣā*) is observed, that is not so. By means of initiation, the karma accumulated over many previous births is burnt by mantras like a seed;
and future karma is blocked like the potency of poison. By which karma this [body]...
Upon the exhaustion of that [residual] karma through experience, liberation occurs at the end of the body;
for there is no immediate destruction of *prārabdha*-karma. It is stated in the *Kiraṇa*:
Just as the wheel continues to spin even after the production of the jar is complete,
being sustained by prior momentum, so too does this body remain.
Karma, which has many births as its fruit, is burnt away by subtle [means] like a seed;
even that which is yet to come is obstructed by him through this enjoyment at the fall of the body.
There may be liberation, or even immediate nirvana.

Thus, it is improper for the self, purified by initiation (*dīkṣā*), to remain in this impure body composed of the five material elements (*pañcabhūta*), which is the locus for the experience of karma impelled by the power of manifestation belonging to *māyā*.
Through the purification by mantra, one's own body must be made to consist of mantra every day and at every moment, because of the lack of stability in the mind. And it has been said by the Teachers:
"Therefore, for one who has been purified by initiation, [the practice is performed] upon the impure body composed of the five elements."
For one whose self is situated in the place where its own karma is experienced.
Then, for one who has been impelled by the powers of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) toward a continuous stream of experience, that state of abiding [in the Self] is improper,
like honey placed in a defiled vessel.
Therefore, the wise person should effect the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) for the body composed of Śakti;
and that [purification] should always be performed, because otherwise there is no stability for the self.
All of this has been clearly stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*. As it says:
"The pure [elements] have already been rendered [so] by the Guru through initiation and mantras;
what is to be accomplished now by purifying these again?"
It is true that the elements are pure, yet they are of two kinds: internal and external; and among these, the internal ones reside within the body.
The external elements situated in the six paths become pure through initiation; however, the elements residing within the body must be purified day by day.
For the self whose bonds have been entirely consumed, who has experienced all that is to be experienced,
and whose accumulated limbs of karma have been burnt away, the pure self remains.

Since it is not appropriate for [the deity] to reside in a body produced from the impurities of a mother and father, one should therefore perform the rite of making [the deity] consist of mantra every day.
When the body has been purified by *dhāraṇā*, Śiva is directly perceived; since he is the cause of that [body] which consists of *māyā* and its effects, he is called Śiva in his direct form.
Internal purity must be established for the elements residing within the body;
that purity depends on concentration (dhāraṇā), and concentration is dependent upon mastery of time.
O being, time is purified here; morning is that which effects purification.

Alternatively— although both types of purification, gross and subtle, have been performed through initiation (*dīkṣā*), because there is no purification of *prārabdha* karma, the bodily, vital, and mental powers— which are of the nature of *māyā*, obstructive, and impelled by that [unpurified karma]— [remain].
For the purpose of obstructing those forms of obstacles which are of the nature of impurity (malasvarūpa), and for the manifestation of Śiva and Śakti within that body, [this is performed] every day.
The purification of the elements must be performed at every moment, because of the lack of stability in the mind.
All of this has been clearly established by the authors of the *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*.
For example:
"Then, having meditated upon a lotus bud submerged in a flood of nectar-water, [one should visualize] that which resides within it..."
One should contemplate the body as being burned, just as before.
The burning by the fire of yoga is said to occur [only] when there is manifestation; it does not occur regarding unmanifest actions.
For those powers of manifestation which are remembered as being accomplished through all mantras—
Those who are hostile take the form of obstacles; their burning away is desired here. Their suppression is not desired, for they are remembered as bestowers of boons.
Because he follows that means (upāya), he is called "by him" (tenānu).
When this has been done, the manifesting powers (vyakti-śaktayaḥ) become restrained; when those [powers] are restrained...
In that very same way, the powers of Śiva belong to him alone.
Then they are projected by means of mantras and installed in their proper sequence; when the ritual is completed, they are withdrawn from their respective places and from the body.
Day by day, through contact with the fire of yoga and being constantly sprinkled with the water of mantra, the powers of Śiva gradually attain increase.
In this way, the individual manifestations and powers are indeed suppressed by those [energies];
he who is pure and whose faults have been destroyed proceeds toward spiritual growth.
Even those who are deficient in limbs become complete; of this there is no doubt.

Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma* three times and having performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should first perform the internal, pure inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*).
Having expelled [the breath] by means of the recaka-primordial breath-control (prāṇāyāma) using the Astra-mantra,
one should fill the abdomen with the external air presided over by Śiva.

Starting from the two big toes up to the crown of the head (*visti*), and from there upwards to the *brahmabila*, it is unified; it is joined with the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and other channels at the heart, throat, and other locations, possesses the form of a hollow tube, and is endowed with downward-facing lotus buds.

Having meditated upon the Suṣumnā, which is known as the abode of Śiva and shines like a streak of lightning within the interior of the body, one should contemplate the stream of nectar flowing from its very interior to its exterior, which has the nature of the supreme ether and belongs to the Supreme Lord.
Having meditated upon the Kuṇḍalinī power, which pervades all that is eternally presided over,

and having contemplated the syllable *HŪṂ* blazing in the center of the Suṣumnā, one should visualize it situated with its face turned downward at the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
p.

258) By means of inhalation (*pūraka*), the cluster of lotuses is made to blossom; by means of retention (*kumbhaka*), it is raised up; and by means of exhalation (*recaka*), having turned it upward, one [perceives] that which resembles the flame of a lamp in the region of the *mūlādhāra*.

Having meditated on the syllable *hūṃ* and having pierced the five knots through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by the continuous recitation of *huṃ phaṭ*, one returns and releases the vital airs through the right channel; then, once again, one places the seed-syllable of the crest (*śikhā-bīja*) in the eastern direction.

Having first recited the mantra of meditation and fixed the mind upon it, one should meditate on the person drawn in by the filling breath as being solitary, free from disease, and like a drop on the tip of a blade of grass; then,
having performed the retention of breath (kumbhaka), one should cause the breath to move upward.

Having taken [the breath] to the end with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should [expel it] with a single expulsion (*ekodghāta*) according to the sequence of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā.
Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the Self.

Thus, one should unite [the self] with Śiva—the supreme cause, free of parts, pure as clear crystal, and of the nature of light—residing in the lotus at the dvādaśānta for the purpose of experiencing the karma that is to be enjoyed. Likewise:
In the *Sūkṣma*: "Having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should carry out the sequence of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). — from the *Kāmikatantrasāra*.
I shall explain breath control (prāṇāyāma) concisely and in detail: the lowest [measure] is known by twelve beats (tāla), and the middle is considered to be double that.
The supreme time consists of three phases for each of the [breath-control techniques] such as exhalation (recaka) and the rest;
these are proclaimed to be the syllables A, U, and M.
One should exhale the impure air residing in the body and situated in the ether;
then, having gradually drawn in pure air by means of inhalation (pūraka), [one should retain it].
One should remain with the breath fully retained like a water-pot, and thereafter exhale it.

Then, having performed the ritual placement (karanyāsa) and visualized the syllable *huṃ* blazing within the hollow center of the body, one should remain motionless, restraining the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
At the end of the syllable *phaṭ*, accompanied by this very exhalation (*recaka*),
one then cuts the five knots and returns from that point.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:

"Having withdrawn [the breath] by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), the knower of mantras should, by means of the heart-mantra, place the life-force (*jīva*)— consisting of the final seed-syllable— upon the top of the syllable *dhūṃ*."
Having meditated upon the Person situated within the crest of the syllable *hūṃ*, whose form is the seed-syllable—
solitary, subtle, become a drop (*bindu*), and free from affliction.
*Kālottara*:
"Thereafter, one should unite oneself with Śiva, the supreme cause, at the tip of the crest-lock (*śikhā*)."
Twelve finger-breadths in length, pure and as stainless as crystal.
One should unite [the soul] with the supreme, subtle Śivatattva, which is of the nature of light and partless, by means of the heart-mantra and the Saṃhāramudrā.
Likewise, in the *Suprabheda*:

"The wise one should, by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, join himself, situated upon a lotus twelve finger-breadths from the tip of his crest, with the ten-syllable mantra according to the prescribed sequence."
Now, since movement is impossible for the Self as well due to its omnipresence, must it not be understood here that movement occurs by means of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body)?
For that [subtle body] too is something to be purified, and because the Self is described as being alone, how could that *puryaṣṭaka* belong to the Self?
In the state of separation, when [the breath] is situated at the dvādaśānta, how could there be union with Śiva?

To this it is replied: the leading forth (*upanayana*) from the subtle body by means of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which is presided over by Śiva and Śakti, has been stated in the *Samānatantra* as follows: "But by means of Śakti..."

"It is led [there]," it is said. But upon the abandonment of the *puryaṣṭaka*, having become a *bindu* through the function of the seed-syllable of the mantra, one should contemplate the entry of the self into the state of Śiva by means of the presiding power (*adhiṣṭhātrī*) of Śiva's energy.
As it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Well-restrained by one hundred thousand [repetitions],
and joined with the state of oneness, one should enter the imperishable Śiva through the seed-syllable in Śiva."
But the knower of reality, by means of the activity of the reality-principle, remains absorbed in it.
One should purify the elements, which resemble the assembly of principles (tattva), from one another;
thus, by means of the function of the seed-syllables, [one should dissolve them] into Śiva in the order of withdrawal for the purification of the subtle body.

One should lead the collection of principles (tattvas), from earth and the others up to the *bindu*, into dissolution within their respective causes. That is to say: earth into smell, water into taste, fire into form, wind into touch, and space into sound.

These subtle elements (tanmātras) reside in the tamasic ego; speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals in the rajasic ego; and those called hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell, along with the mind, in the sattvic ego. That [sattvic ego] resides in the intellect (buddhi); that [intellect] resides in the qualities (guṇas); and the principle of the qualities resides in primordial nature (prakṛti).
That [Māyā], along with rāga and vidyā, is dissolved into kalā; and the principle of puruṣa (puṃstattva), kāla, niyati, and kalā are dissolved into māyā.

Having contemplated the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyātattva), one should contemplate it as dissolved into the principle of Īśvara, that into the principle of Sadāśiva, that into the principle of Śakti, that into the principle of Śiva, and even that into the Bindu, whose nature is unagitated.
The Teachers have also said:

"In the case of smell, the elephant, water, taste, fire, form, wind, touch, and sound, one's own ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) arises; furthermore, these subtle elements (tanmātrās) belong to the tamasic [ego], as do the organs of action and the lords of the senses."

You shine together with the mind, intellect, and senses; that [intellect] dissolves into the sattvic state, and that [sattva] dissolves into the qualities (guṇas), and those qualities dissolve into the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Therein, Māyā, together with Āgama-vidyā, proceeds forward; then the principles (tattva) of Kāla, Niyati, and Kalā follow.
This [sequence] reaches Vidyeśvara within Māyā along with Sadāśiva; she [reaches] Śakti, and this [reaches] Śiva, who is Bindu.
Thus, here by the word *śiva*, the world-level (*bhuvana*) of the *bindu*-principle situated at the summit of the *śakti*-tattva is denoted.
In this manner, the purification of the subtle body should be performed for those who are capable, according to the *vīrasara* method.
For those who have fallen into an untimely situation and for the sick, it should be performed in brief.

For example, one should lead the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka)— consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, smell, intellect, ego, and mind— into dissolution within the fivefold group beginning with Brahmā, the Lord of Causes, which resides in the lotuses of the heart and other locations.
As it is said in the *Sārdhatriṃśatikā*: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— this is the pentad."
Intellect, mind, and ego—these are declared to be the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka).
As long as one is not liberated from these, how could one be released from bondage? One should indeed abandon touch and sound within the Brahman, and taste within Keśava.
One should abandon form and smell in Rudra; intellect and ego in Īśvara; and having abandoned mind and the bindu in Śiva, one who is liberated by these [means] shall go to Śiva.

Thereafter, for the sake of purifying the external body, one should sequentially purify the five elements— earth and the others— beginning with the gross, by means of one another. The earth-maṇḍala is yellow, solid, marked with a thunderbolt, and square.
The seed-syllable *la* is presided over by the Brahmā Sadyojāta and joined with the heart-mantra of the causal Lord Brahmā.
Having contemplated [the self] as pervasive, from the feet up to the crown of the head, conjoined with and endowed with the *nivṛtti* kalā,
one should— preceded by inhalation (*pūraka*)— [direct] the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) through the *suṣumnā* as far as the *dvādaśānta*, reciting: *oṃ hlāṃ nivṛttikalāyai haḥ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Having impelled [the breath] and turned back, one should exhale through the right channel. Thus,

by means of five upward thrusts (*udghāta*), having expelled the qualities of smell, form, touch, and sound, [one purifies] the earth-element by the power of the specific presiding presence of Śiva and Śakti, which is endowed with the power of purification.
One should meditate upon that which has the form of [the syllable] *ta*, being overwhelmed by its own contrary wind.
Herein, the definition of *udghāta* (upward expulsion) is stated:
When the apāna is compressed by the prāṇa as it is being exhaled, and having gone upward,
it returns [downward], this is the characteristic of the udghāta.
And it is said:

"When the suppression is correctly performed, the upward-moving wind proceeds; this is designated as the *udghāta* (upward thrust), while by one's own will [it is performed] as the minor [thrust], known as the *pratyudghāta*."
The three [types of] breath-control (prāṇāyāma), beginning with inhalation (pūraka) and so forth, are indeed established by their very purpose. As it is stated in the venerable *Trayodaśaśatika*:
"Thus, fifteen breath-controls pertaining to the elements have been declared; [this is] of Varuṇa."
And one should purify the wind-element, which consists of twelve [units].
Thus: having abandoned the nature of solidity and so forth, O Wind, what other mandala is there that is white, liquid, and adorned with water?

Having meditated upon the half-moon, the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, presided over by the Brahmā Vāmadeva, joined with Kāreṇeśvara-Viṣṇu, united with the head-mantra, endowed with the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā, and pervading from my feet to my head— *oṃ*.
"Hvīṃ to the Kalā of Pratiṣṭhā, Haḥ Huṃ Phaṭ"—

having thus impelled the vital air (prāṇavāyu) through the Suṣumṇā as far as the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta) by means of inhalation (pūraka), and having returned and exhaled (virecaya) through the right channel (dakṣiṇanāḍī), this is the "upward strike" (udghāta).

Having uttered the fourfold group of qualities beginning with taste (rasa), one should contemplate the water— by virtue of being presided over by Śiva and Śakti— as possessing the power of purification, and as being overwhelmed by its own contrary, fire, so that it takes on the form of that [fire]. Then:
The fire-maṇḍala is red, marked with the svastika, triangular,
with the seed-syllable *raṃ*, presided over by the Aghora-Brahman, and joined with Rudra as its causal source.

Having meditated upon [the deity] as conjoined with the *śikhā* mantra, endowed with the *vidyā-kalā*, and pervading from the feet to the crown of the head, one should perform inhalation (*pūraka*) while reciting: *oṃ hrūṃ vidyākalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ*, [extending] along the *suṣumnā*.
Having impelled the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) to the *dvādaśānta* and then returned, one should exhale through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*). Thus, by means of three upward thrusts (*udghāta*),
having dispelled the triad of qualities beginning with form (*rūpa*), one [should contemplate] the Fire through the power of its being presided over by Śiva and Śakti.
Having purified it, one should meditate on that [element] as being overcome by its opposite, water, which is endowed with power;
thereafter, one should visualize a black wind-maṇḍala, hexagonal and marked with a drop (bindu).
That seed-syllable is joined with the causal principle presided over by the Puruṣa-Brahman-Īśvara and is conjoined with the Kavaca-mantra. (p. 271)

Having visualized [the deity] as endowed with the Śāntikala and pervading from the feet to the crown of the head, one should, preceded by inhalation (*pūraka*), impel the vital air through the *suṣumnā* up to the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*) and then withdraw it, reciting: *oṃ hyaiṃ śāntikalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ*.
One should expel [the breath] through the right channel; by means of two *udghātas*,
having driven away the two qualities beginning with touch, the wind— by virtue of being presided over by Śiva and Śakti—
is joined with the power of purification and [is then countered] by its own opposite, the earth-element (*pṛthivī-tattva*).
One should meditate on the true nature of the elements in that form.
Following that, one should visualize the circular mandala of space, smoke-colored,
marked with a dot (bindu) and the sign of power (śakti), or alternatively, without the mark, as the seed-syllable *haṃ*.
It is conjoined with the mantra of the Eye-weapon, presided over by Īśāna and Brahmā, united with the causal Lord Sadāśiva, and endowed with the Śāntyatīta-kalā.
Having contemplated [the breath] pervading from the feet to the top of the head, by means of a single upward expulsion (*ekodghāta*),

one should cast off the quality of sound; having liberated it into the form of emptiness, which is characterized by eternal purity and so forth, it becomes like pure crystal, overwhelmed by the supreme point (*parabindu*) presided over by Śiva and Śakti.
One should contemplate the nature of the supreme ether (paramākāśa), which is endowed with qualities such as eternity, pervasiveness, and purity;
as it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The earthly mandala is yellow, four-cornered, marked with a thunderbolt, and has the seed-syllable LA."
O Brahman, the Daitya has become possessed of a heart full of longing.
Endowed with the nature of cessation, the five upward thrusts (*udghāta*) consist of the syllable *hlāṃ*;
it is marked by the white lotus of the water-drop (*āpyabindu*), has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity, and possesses *va* as its seed-syllable (*bīja*).
One should know it to be conjoined with the left [side] and lead, and endowed with the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā].
With four upward breaths, preceded by the utterance of "hvīṃ," one visualizes the triangle of fire,
which has seven peaks, is red in luster, and has Rudra as its presiding deity.
The [mantra] called Vidyā is joined with the syllable *rā*, with Aghora-Śiva, and endowed with the Kalās;
it is conjoined with three upward breaths (*udghātas*), preceded by the utterance of "hrūm."
In the southwest corner of the flavor-petals is the dark group of six *bindus*;
it is joined with the face and armor, and is marked by the syllables presided over by Īśa and Adhipati.
One should perform two upward breath-retentions (udghātas) joined with the state of peace (śānti), preceded by the utterance of "Haim," [visualizing] the sky as circular,
devoid of marks, and smoke-colored.

Established in one's own place, accompanied by the *hāmī* mantra and joined with that which transcends the scriptures, one should utter "haum" with a single exhalation (*ekodghāta*), preceded by the movement of breath (*uccāra*).
p.
274) How one should practice meditation:
Having first performed the visualization (*abhidhyāna*), one should immediately burn the body with one's own name. Then...
The mutual purification of the elements.
Thus, when the collection of elements constituting the commenced body has its power exhausted due to the decay of the qualities of the group of elements that sustain it,
[the process of] dessication occurs through [the power] arising from the big toe of the right foot, presided over by the power of Śiva.
Having visualized them as burnt by the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, which is like the fire of time (*kālāgni*),
one should then form them into a mass with the wind [mantra] consisting of the ashes of that [fire] and flood them [with nectar]. As it is said in the *Suprabheda*:
One should contemplate [the fire] burning from the big toe up to the crown of the head like dry wood;
then, having reduced it to ashes, one should gather those ashes together with the wind.
From that [seed-syllable], the previously mentioned nectar should flow forth and emerge as ashes.
Alternatively—for those who are incapable—the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) should be performed in brief. It is as follows:
one's own body consists of the seed-syllables of the five elements, beginning with earth.
It has its sprout produced by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, its root in dharma acquired in the past,
it is protected by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), its essence consists of the principles beginning with Kalā, its branches and sub-branches are the subtle elements and the sense organs,
and its shoots are the perceptions of objects such as sound.
The flower of the manifoldness of existence (*bhāvaprapañca*), which has the intellect as its basis of determination and volition as its fruit,
