is to be enjoyed by the bird-like *puruṣa*; being of the nature of a tree due to its similarity with the banyan tree, it consists solely of the essence of the enjoyer and the enjoyed.

Having visualized the body as having its roots above and branches below, one should, in the morning, first perform the inhalation for six *mātrās* by means of the earth-element concentration (*dhāraṇā*).

Having contemplated [the tree] as rigid and devoid of leaves, flowers, and fruit by means of the fivefold utterance of "hlām," one should visualize it as endowed with glossy leaves, flowers, and fruit by means of the fourfold utterance of "hvīm" through the retention of water during the latter half of the inhalation (*pūraka*).
Having visualized [the body] as dried up and burnt by the fire sustained through twelve *kumbhakas* (retentions) and the threefold utterance of "BHRŪM," and by the Kālāgni rising from the big toes,
one should [proceed] with the first half of the *recaka* (exhalation) and the wind-sustaining [breath] while uttering "HYAIṂ" twice.

Having visualized [the body] as reduced to ashes and dissolved into the ten directions, by means of the supreme *recaka* (exhalation) and the single utterance of "hlauṃ," through the ethereal (*nābhasī*) concentration (*dhāraṇā*), [one should restore it].
One should contemplate [the deity] as having the form of pure crystal, the form of the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*). As it is said in the *Siddhatantra*:
"One's own body, the seed-syllable of the elements, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and their differentiation as sprouts—these are the excellent states of being."

In the *Cintya-viśva-sādākhya*, it is said: "The *kalā* is the essence, conjoined with the moisture of the objects of sense and possessed of the branches of the *tanmātras*; it is to be enjoyed by the bird-like *puruṣa*."
Alternatively, while recollecting one's own body and the banyan tree and so forth,
one should conceive of the tree of saṃsāra as having its roots above and its branches below.
In the *Kāmika*:
"The knower of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted [should] nourish the subtle atom of the earth-element during the first half of the inhalation (*pūraka*);
likewise, it should be nourished from the latter part of the inhalation."
Having cut down that [tree], which is endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruit, and is lush according to the treatises on dispassion (*vairāgya*),
one should then dry it with fire and by means of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*).
Burnt away by the fire of knowledge from the big toe to the end of the body,
the ten directions then become earth through the wind [element] by means of exhalation (recaka).
One should contemplate the pure, stainless sky as dissolved otherwise;
likewise, it has been stated by the teachers in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*:

One's own body is the seed of the elements, with its own sprouts fashioned by Hari and Brahmā; it has karma as its root, is auspicious, has time and other factors as its pith, and possesses sense-objects as its leaves, along with major and minor branches such as the ether and other elements.
It has all states of being as its flowers and is established as the excellent fruit for the bird that is the person.
One should contemplate the Nyagrodha tree as the object of enjoyment, with its roots above and its branches, which possess the flavors of sensory objects, extending downwards.
279) Reciting the mantras beginning with *hlām* and so forth, together with the pairs of half-inhalations (*kumbhāpūraka*) and exhalations (*recaka*),
one should [visualize] the sequential abiding of the qualities located in the earth and other elements, as well as the conjunctions beginning with "son" (*putra*) and so forth.
From the drying up [of the moisture], there is burning and ash; by the removal of that, the river becomes pure through meditative cultivation.
Thus,
thereafter, having meditated upon every object as being slightly distinct from its binding [nature] and as being imagined [as such],
one should [unite it] with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* [and] with the Śiva-power residing at the *dvādaśānta*.

By means of the streams of nectar flowing from the downward-facing lotus, having entered the openings of all the channels from the lower point (apara-bindu) situated at the end of the crest-lock— which is of the nature of the eternally presided-over, of the nature of supreme nectar, and existing as the support of all— according to the sequence of emanation.

Having bathed the entire body, both external and internal, one should then [place it] within the heart of the self— the subtle body consisting of the purified, awakened Self— at the end of the twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta).

For the purpose of ritual placement (vinyāsa), having conceived the Yoga-pīṭha— the seat consisting of Śuddhavidyā— by means of the lotuses of Ādhāra-śakti, Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya, together with the Praṇava joined with the three mātrās beginning with 'A', one should place the Puryaṣṭaka within the pericarp (karṇikā) as that which possesses four kalās.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as having descended by means of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) into that body of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*),
one should [worship] the self as Yama— whose form resides at the *dvādaśānta*, who possesses the seed-syllable with the *sānta* (Ha), and who consists of five parts—
with the *praṇava* during inhalation: Oṃ Hūṃ Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ Hūṃ, obeisance to the Self (*ātmane namaḥ*).

By means of this mantra, having brought [the deity] together with a flower through emanation, the *jīva* residing there is [drawn] from the *brahmarandhra*, which is pierced by streams of flowing nectar, down [into the heart].
One should consecrate [the disciple] with a stream of divine nectar-water from the lunar orb by means of meditating on the *praṇava* at the mouth. Thus, it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The fourfold [powers]—dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya—"
One should install the yoga-pīṭha and the lotus with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Then one should perform the rite of nourishment (svāpyāyana) and meditate on the Praṇava as facing downwards,
flowing with streams of nectar from the base of the spine up to the crown of the head through the Suṣumṇā.

Furthermore, having performed the ritual ablution elsewhere, one should begin the placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs, such as the hands and feet. In this regard, the placement of the specific peaceful form (*śāntamūrti*) should be performed. The sequence therein is as follows: the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*) and the manifest form of Śiva (*vyaktā śivamūrti*).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart with one's own two mantras in sequence, and having performed the placement of the limbs, the gestures of the faces, and the gestures of the digits (*kalā*) by means of the five Brahmans;
One should also perform the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa. It is as follows:
at the tip of the thumb of the clenched fist, "Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna," as in the case of the Mūrti-nyāsa;
with the thumb and forefinger, "Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa," on the face.
With the thumb and middle finger, recite *oṃ huṃ aghorāya namaḥ* at the heart;
with the thumb and ring finger, recite *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ* at the navel;
and with the thumb and little finger, recite *oṃ haṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ* at the feet.
One should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*). As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face; Aghora on the heart."
Having performed the ritual placement on the secret place, one should arrange the left [hand].
One should place Sadyojāta on the feet, accompanied by its respective mudrā.
Thus is the placement of Daṇḍabhaṅginī.
Now, the placement of the facial configurations (*vaktrabhaṅginīnyāsa*):
one should place the *brahmans* themselves, which are the fragments, upon the upper, eastern, southern, northern, and western faces according to the facial configuration,
having formed the *bhadramudrā* fist.
Having first placed [the mantra] "Oṃ Hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna" on the uppermost head with the thumb and forefinger,
one should place "Oṃ Heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa" on the eastern head with the thumb and middle finger, and "Oṃ Huṃ, obeisance to Aghora" [on the southern head].
Thus, on the right head with the thumb and ring finger: *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*; on the left head with the thumb and little finger: [oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ]. (p. 284)
"Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta"—thus one should place [this mantra] on the western head.
And one should place the Brahma-mantras as a garland of fragments [in the following manner]. As stated in the *Kāmika*:
"One should place them starting from Īśāna in the faces—namely the upper, eastern, southern, northern, and western.
This is the placement according to the *Vaktrabhaṅgī*.
Now follows the Kalābhaṅginī-nyāsa.

The ritual application (prayoga) is stated as follows: *Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences, to Śaśinī, on the upper head.* *Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Īśvara, the Lord of all beings, to Aṅgatā, on the eastern head.* *Oṃ hoṃ, [obeisance to] Brahmādhipati, the Lord of Brahman...*
"Brahmā, obeisance to Iṣṭā"—thus on the right head.
285) "Oṃ Hoṃ, may Śiva be mine; obeisance to Marīci"—thus on the left head. Oṃ Hoṃ.
"Sadāśiva to Jvālinī, obeisance"—thus [one worships] on the western head. In this manner is the pentad of the Īśāna-kalās.

*Oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe śāntyai namaḥ*—thus at the eastern face. *Oṃ heṃ mahādevāya dhīmahi vidyāyai namaḥ*—thus at the southern face. *Oṃ heṃ tanno rudraḥ pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ*—thus at the northern face. *Oṃ heṃ*...
"Oṃ *pracodayāt*, obeisance to Nivṛtti"—thus at the western face.
These are the four *kalās* of Tatpuruṣa.
"Oṃ *huṃ*, obeisance to Aghora and Tamā"—thus at the heart. "Oṃ *huṃ*, [obeisance] to the Aghoras..."
"Oṃ *mohāyai* namaḥ"—thus at the throat. "Oṃ *huṃ* Aghora, obeisance to protection (*rakṣāyai* namas)"—thus on the right shoulder. Oṃ...

*Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the most terrible [forms] for the sake of finality*, on the left shoulder; *Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to all-encompassing death*, at the navel; *Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to all [forms] for the sake of Māyā*, in the belly; *Oṃ hūṃ, salutation be to you, O Rudra, for the sake of fear*.
On the back: *Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Rūpa and Jvarā*. On the chest: [same]. Thus ends the eightfold group of Bahurūpā-kalās.

Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, obeisance to Rajā—thus at the secret place. Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭha, obeisance to Rakṣā—thus at the two testicles. Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Rudra, obeisance to Ṛti—thus on the right thigh. Oṃ hiṃ...
"Oṃ *kālāya* pālinyai *namaḥ*" on the left thigh; "Oṃ *hiṃ* kalākāmyai *namaḥ*" on the right knee; "Oṃ *hiṃ* vakaraṇāya saṃyaminyai *namaḥ*" [on the left knee].
At the left knee: *Oṃ hiṃ balakriyāyai namaḥ*. At the right shank:
*Oṃ hiṃ vikaraṇāya namo budhyai namaḥ*. At the left shank: *Oṃ hiṃ balakāryai namaḥ*. At the right buttock: *Oṃ hiṃ prathamāya namaḥ*.
"Oṃ *dhātryai* namaḥ"—thus on the left buttock. "Oṃ *hiṃ* to the Subduer of All Beings, obeisance;

to Brahmāṇī, obeisance"—thus on the hip. "Oṃ *hiṃ* to the Enchantress of the Mind, obeisance"—thus on the right side. "Oṃ *hiṃ* to the Transcendent Mind, obeisance; to Bhavā, obeisance"—thus [on the left side].
On the left side: thus are the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva.
*Oṃ haṃ*, "I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation for the sake of accomplishment," on the right foot. *Oṃ*... [text continues].

"Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta; salutation to Ṛddhi"—thus on the left foot. "Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Bhave; salutation to Druvā"—thus on the right hand. "Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Abhave; salutation to Lakṣmī"—thus on the left hand. "Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Anādibhave; salutation to Medhā"—thus on the nose. Oṃ...
"Oṃ haṃ, homage to Bhajasva Kānti," on the head;
"Oṃ haṃ, homage to Bhava Svadhā," on the right arm; "Oṃ haṃ, homage to Udbhava and homage to Dhṛti," on the left arm. Thus ends the eightfold division of Sadyojāta.
Thus, through the process of sakalīkaraṇa, the deposition of the thirty-eight kalās is performed with their respective mudrās.
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*: five *kalās* of Īśāna and four *kalās* of Puruṣa.
The eight digits (kalās) of Aghora’s face and thirteen of Vāmadeva, as well as the eight digits of Sadyojāta,
should be known and installed according to the sequence beginning with the crown (makuṭa).
Īśāna is the Lord Brahmā, Śiva, and Sadāśiva;
may that Puruṣa Mahādeva, as Rudra, impel us.
Then Aghora, then Ghora, and likewise Ghoratara; and then Sarvatasarva, who is more terrible than the most terrible.
And salutations to you from all; Rudra is remembered as having eight aspects (kalās):
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Rudra, Kāla, and likewise Kalavikaraṇa.
Bala-vikaraṇa, Bala-pramathana, Sarva-bhūta-damana, as well as Mana and Unmana—
these are remembered as the kalās of Vāmadeva.
Sadyojāta, Sadyas, Bhava, and Abhava,
as well as Anādibhava— worship you, O source of all existence!
The thirty-eight *kalās* have been declared; now the *kalā-śaktis* are being described: Śaśinī, Aṅgadā, Ceṣṭā, Marīcī, and likewise Jvālinī.
One should place these five powers of the *kalās* upon the five heads: Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.

Thus, the power consisting of four parts has been described in the face [of the Lord]. [The eight powers] are: Tama, Moha, Kṣaya, Niṣṭhā, Dhṛti, Kṣānti, Smṛti, and Kṣayā; Aghora possesses these eight powers, and thereafter Vāmadeva is spoken of.
Rajā, Rakṣmā, Rati, Pālyā, Māyā, Saṃyaminī, and Kriyā.
[One should perform this preceded by meditation, as stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:]
It has been written here exactly according to the manuscript.
However, it appears that the portion contained herein will occur at the conclusion of the thirty-eight-fold ritual installation (nyāsa).
All forms of the *kalās* have three eyes and four arms; they hold the gestures of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*) and bestowing boons (*varada*),
as well as a trident and a battle-axe.
In all the forms of the *kalās*, the powers (*śaktis*) beginning with Vāmā are traditionally taught;
there are thirty-eight *kalās* for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and likewise thirty-eight powers.
Thus, endowed with power, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) at the time of deposition: [one should conceive of them as] Buddhi, Dhātrī, Bhrāmiṇī, and Mohinī.
Manonmanī is proclaimed as the fourteenth, and Vāmadeva is the fifteenth;
then there are Siddhi, Buddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Dhṛti.
O Nandikeśvara, the power of eight digits (kalās) is said to belong to Sadyojāta; the five digits of Īśāna reside in the five faces beginning with the upper one.
Aghora is in the heart, in the throat, and likewise in the left and right shoulders; it is also in the navel, the belly, the back, and the chest.
And Vāmadeva at the secret place, likewise on the two testicles, on the two thighs,
on the two knees, and likewise on the pair of shanks and calves.
One should place [the mantras] in order on the two buttocks (sphic) at the region of the hips and on the two sides;
likewise, one should place Sadyojāta on the pair of feet and on the pair of hands.

One should place [the mantras] on the nose, the region of the head, and the pair of arms; the Sadyojāta-kalā should be joined, as well as the kalās at the end of the mantras, according to their respective order.
In the *Cintya*,

there is the placement of thirty-eight digits (*kalānyāsa*), endowed with the powers of those digits. There are thirty male digits (*pum-kalā*), and their powers (*kalā-śakti*) shall likewise be thirty.
Śiva and Śakti—of these two, this [Śiva] and that [Śakti] shall become partless (niṣkala).
One should install the thirty-eight kalās and śaktis upon the worshipper and the liṅga.
One should place thirty-one kalās upon the image of Maheśa and others;
among these thirty-eight kalās, twenty-five belong to the goddesses.
Thus, the supreme placement of all [deities] consists of exactly thirty-eight kalās.
In the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*:
"The heads, the five faces, then the heart, throat,
two eyes, navel, belly, back, chest, genitals, penis, the pair of thighs, and the pair of knees."
The two shanks, the two buttocks, the other [two] sides, the feet, the pair of hands, the nose, and the head—
these are the locations of the arms; thus, there are thirty-eight sites for the arrangement of the limbs in the body of Śiva.

Now, the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa: *Oṃ aṃ*, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodaryā—at the end of the eyebrows (*kānta*). *Oṃ āṃ*, obeisance to Ananta and Virajā—at the forehead (*lalāṭa*). *Iṃ*, obeisance to Sūkṣma and Śālī—at the right eye. *Īṃ*, obeisance to Trimūrti—[at the left eye].
Oṃ, salutation to Lolākṣī at the left eye; Oṃ Uṃ, salutation to Maheśvara and Vartulā at the right ear.

Oṃ ūṃ, obeisance to Arghīśa and Dīrghakoṇā on the left hand; Oṃ ṛṃ, obeisance to Bhārabhūti and Dīvatmukhī at the right nostril; Oṃ ṝṃ, obeisance to Tithīśa and Gomukhī at the left nostril; Oṃ ḷṃ, obeisance to Sthāṇu...

*Oṃ* *dīrghajihvāyai* *namaḥ* on the right cheek; *oṃ* *ḷṃ* *bhārāya* *kaṇṭhodaryai* *namaḥ* on the left cheek; *oṃ* *aiṃ* *caṇḍīśāya* *ūrdhvakeśinyai* *namaḥ* on the upper lip; *oṃ* *aiṃ* *bhautikāya*.
*Oṃ*, salutation to Vikṛtamukhī on the lower lip; *Oṃ Oṃ*, salutation to Sadyojāta and Jvālāmukhī on the upper teeth; *Oṃ Auṃ*, salutation to Anugraheśa and Ulkāmukhī on the lower teeth;
*Oṃ Aṃ*, salutation to Akrūra and Śrīmukhī.
At the crown of the head: Oṃ Aḥ, salutation to Mahāsena and Vidyāmukhī. At the mouth: (p. 295) Oṃ Kaṃ, salutation to Krodhīśa and Mahākālī. At the base of the right arm: Oṃ...

*Khaṃ* to Caṇḍīśa and Sarasvatī, salutation to the elbow; *Oṃ Gaṃ* to Pañcāntaka and Sarvasiddhigaurī, salutation to the wrist; *Oṃ Ghaṃ* to Śivottama and Trailokyavidyā, salutation to the palm of the hand; *Oṃ Ḍaṃ*.

Oṃ *ekarudrāya* mantra-śaktyai namaḥ on the tip of the right hand. Oṃ *caṃ* kūrma-ātma-śaktyai namaḥ at the base of the left arm. Oṃ *chaṃ* ekanetrāya bhūta-mātre namaḥ at the elbow. Oṃ *jaṃ* caturmukhāya lambodaryai namaḥ.
At the wrist: Oṃ jhaṃ, salutation to Ajeśāyadrāviṇī on the palm of the hand. Oṃ ñaṃ, salutation to Śarva and Nagarī on the tip of the left hand. Oṃ ṭaṃ, salutation to Someśvara...
Oṃ khecarāya namaḥ at the root of the right thigh; Oṃ ṭhaṃ lāṅgaline mañjaryai namaḥ at the knee; Oṃ ḍaṃ dārukāya virupiṇyai namaḥ at the tip of the shank;
Oṃ ṭaṃ ardhanārīśvarāya viriṇyai namaḥ on the sole of the foot; Oṃ ṇaṃ...

Oṃ, homage to Umākānta and Kākodaryā on the tip of the right foot. Oṃ Taṃ, homage to Āṣāḍha and Pūtanā at the base of the left thigh. Oṃ Thaṃ, homage to Daṇḍin and Bhadrakālī at the knee. Oṃ Daṃ, homage to the third Yoginī.

At the tip of the calf: *Oṃ dhaṃ* to Mīna and Śaṅkhinī, obeisance. At the sole of the foot: *Oṃ naṃ* to Meṣa and Gajinī, obeisance. At the tip of the left foot: *Oṃ paṃ* to Lohita and Kālarātri, obeisance. On the right side: *Oṃ phaṃ* to Śikhin and Kubjinī.
Homage on the left side: Oṃ baṃ, homage to Cchagaraṇḍa and Kapardinī.
On the back: *Oṃ bhaṃ* to Dviraṇḍa and Bhadrā, obeisance; at the region of the navel.
*Oṃ maṃ* to Mahākāla and Jayā, obeisance; at the heart. *Oṃ yaṃ* to the self of the skin, to Bala and Sumukhī-Īśvarī, obeisance; on the skin. *Oṃ raṃ* to the self of blood...

Salutation to Bhujaṅgeśa and Revatī in the blood-vision (rudhiragocara). Oṃ Laṃ, salutation to Pinākin, the essence of flesh, and to Mādhavī in the flesh. Oṃ Vaṃ, salutation to Kharvīśa, who consists of fat, and to Vāruṇī in the fat. Oṃ Śaṃ, salutation to Bakeśa, the essence of bone, and to Vāyavī [in the bone].

*Namaḥ* to the bone. *Oṃ ṣaṃ*, salutation to the marrow-self, the white one, the bearer of the destruction of Rākṣasas, at the place of the marrow. *Oṃ saṃ*, salutation to the semen-self, Bhrukuṭīśā, in the semen.
*Oṃ haṃ*, salutation to Lakulīśa, the self of the *praṇava*, to Lakṣmī, in the heart.
Ardhanārīśvara, Soma, Skanda, Aṣāḍha, Daṇḍin, Atri, Mīna, Meṣa, Lohita, and likewise Śikhin.
Chagaṇḍa and Dviraṇḍa are the two attendants of Mahākāla; alternatively, they are Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākī, and Khaḍgīśa.
Rakṣas, Śuka, Lakulin, Śiva, and Saṃvartaka are remembered [as the male attendants]; Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and the third, Śālmalī, are the female attendants.
Lolākṣī, Vartulā, Dīrghakoṇā, as well as Śākhinī,
Garjinī, Kālarātrī, and Kubjarathā.
Kapardinī, Vajrā, Jayā, Sumukheśvarī, Revatī, Mādhavī,
Vāruṇī, and likewise Vāyavī.
Furthermore, Rakṣovadhāriṇī, Sahajāvadha, Lakṣmī, Vyāpinī,
and Māyā are declared to be the power-phonemes (varṇa-śaktis).
One should place the syllables in sequence together with these powers: having placed the letter *a* on the head, one places the letter *ā* on the circular face.
The letter *i* is in the right eye, the letter *ī* in the left eye; the letter *u* is in the right ear, and the letter *ū* in the left ear.
The letter ṛ is on the right nostril, and the letter ṝ is on the left nostril;
the letter ḷ is on the right cheek, and the letter ḹ is on the left cheek.
Then, one should place the letter *e* on the upper lip and *ai* on the lower lip;
likewise, *o* on the row of upper teeth and *au* on the row of lower teeth.

One should place the syllable *aṃ* at the root of the palate and the syllable *aḥ* in the middle of the palate; in this manner, according to the prescribed rule, one should sequentially assign the sixteen vowels.
The *ka*-group [of consonants] on the right hand, the *ca*-group on the left hand;
the *ṭa*-group on the right foot, and the *ta*-group on the left foot.
The letter *pa* on the right side, the letter *pha* on the left side,
the letter *ba* at the back, and the letter *bha* below the navel.
The letter *ma* is at the navel; above that, the seven letters beginning with *ya* are located in the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) such as skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
Having placed the letter *ha* in the heart and the letter *la* in the region of the anus, one should place the letter *kṣa* in the secret organ,
accompanied by the mantra of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Alternatively, one should perform the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*).
According to the Siddhānta:
"Having first performed the internal sacrifice, one should then commence the external worship of the Jyotirliṅga."
Just as it is worshipped thus within the heart, so too is it worshipped externally.
Therefore, for that reason, the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) is said here to be performed first.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
He who performs an external sacrifice without first performing the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga) exerts himself in vain;
this is the certain conclusion even within the web of the scriptures.
He who, abandoning Śiva who resides within himself, worships Śiva as being outside,
is like one who discards the morsel of food in his own hand and licks his elbow.
In the Kāmika [Tantra]: "One should determine the locations for worship, fire-oblation, and meditative absorption;
the rite of worship is performed in the heart, while one should perform the fire-oblation at the navel."

One should meditate on Īśvara, the bestower of boons, with faces on all sides, upon the forehead; and one should mentally fashion the abode of Īśvara in the heart according to the sequence for invocation.
One should prepare a seat there according to the procedure to be described.
As it is stated in the *Niśvāsa*:
"The heart of all embodied beings resembles the flower of the plantain tree."
In the *Suprabheda*:
"The egg of the earth, consisting of the Skanda [of elements], beginning with water, as well as the stalk and the Pradhāna."
That stalk, extending as far as the ultimate reality (tattva), is covered with thorns.
Regarding the exhalation:
the lotus stalk is proclaimed to surround the nine gates on all sides; one should know the stalk to be eight finger-breadths long, and the knot is designated as "granthi."
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"It should be known as having eight lotus petals, surrounded by the qualities such as *aṇimā*.
In the *Bhīmasaṃhitā*:
On the eight petals of the enclosure, one should sequentially place the eight-syllable mantra from Indra to Īśāna: "Oṃ śivāya namo namaḥ."
In the *Kālottara* (p.
[It is] like the rising sun, adorned with sixteen petals, and measuring one *varta*.
The lotus and its pericarp are four finger-breadths [in size].
The seed-syllable (bīja) is fifty syllables at most; it is the prose that is higher than the highest.
In the *Niśvāsa*:
"The pericarp, equal in size to the joint of the thumb, is joined with filaments."
Mataṅga says:
One should contemplate its pericarp as consisting of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva); and the mantras established within that knowledge shall be the filaments.
In the *Niśvāsa*:
"After a slight interval [from the sun], there is the sun; likewise, from the sun, the moon;
and one should know that above the moon is the supreme orb of fire."
Upon the pericarp there shall be the Sun, and in its center the Moon;
in its center there shall be Fire, and in its center Maheśvara.
In the *Suprabheda*: "Thereafter, one should meditate upon that which consists of Śiva and comprises the thirty-eight kalās."
In the *Niśvāsa*:
"Sadāśiva is [the form] of Maheśa, and beyond him is Śiva.
And it has been said:
The great-souled Sadāśiva, who is even higher than that, beyond the supreme; white, perfectly pure, divine, ungraspable, and the ultimate Śiva.
In the Kāmika:
"In the temple conceived by the mind within the divine *Manokalpa*, one should worship the Supreme Lord with a constant disposition of the mind."
Just as one meditating on the Garuḍas attains the fruit of liberation,
so too here one shall obtain the desired fruit.
In the *Suprabheda* (p. 306):
"All [items] such as the seat, as well as the ornaments, [are to be visualized] in the heart-lotus."
The wise one should perform [the ritual] as prescribed, following the proper sequence.
One should worship by mentally arranging offerings such as perfumes and water for the guest (arghya).
As it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"The [offerings] are those born of water, the lunar, the fiery, the aerial, the earthly, and furthermore, the arboreal."
Furthermore, the sixth is that of Prajāpati, and the seventh is likewise.

Now hear the determination of the eighth, the Śiva-flower: water is to be known as belonging to Varuṇa; ghee, milk, and curd are Saumya (belonging to Soma); incense, lamps, and so forth are Āgneya (belonging to Agni);
and sandalwood and the like are Vāyavya (belonging to Vāyu).
The earthly [offering] consists of bulbs, roots, and so forth; that of the forest trees consists of fruits; the one pertaining to Prajāpati is that which is obtained by effort;
and the flower of Śiva is called faith.
One should always worship Śiva with these eight flowers.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
One should worship the reality known as the "Eight Flowers" of the earthly element in the morning; the earthly element is the whole, fragrance is its essence, and water is its consecration.

These same [offerings] are for the drink and the food offering; the garland of blue lotuses belongs to the fire element (taijasa); the fan and so forth belong to the air element (vāyavya); and song and so forth originate from the ether element (vyoma). Having thus presented these and the other principles (tattvas) according to their correspondence, [one should proceed].
Having meditated on being of one mind with Śiva, one should worship the Śiva-fire situated in the navel-pit by his command. As it is said in the *Kāmika*:

In the navel-cavity, for the sake of the true nature of reality, one should satisfy [the deities] with supreme nectars; having kindled this innate fire and restrained it, one remains free from drinking [ordinary food].
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:

"By means of the movement through the piṅgalā-nāḍī, one should worship the Śiva-fire ignited within one's own heart at the navel-pit there, offering oblations (bali) according to the sequence of the sacrificial ritual."
Having drawn [the breath] through the *iḍā* by means of filling it with nectar and the auspicious *śiva*-syllables,
it is said:
"One should place there the fire of knowledge, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns."
Having visualized the fire from the center of the heart-lotus by way of the suṣumṇā path,
One should join that mass of splendor, glowing like a cluster of fire, at the station of the twelve-finger space;
by the mere act of placing it there, one becomes fit for all ritual actions.
Having offered that according to the prescribed rite to the deity worshipped within, and having worshipped with the eightfold flowers (aṣṭapuṣpikā),
one should then conclude the worship of the [remaining] deities.
In the *Kāmika*:
"One should meditate upon the Liṅga at the place of Sthāṇu as having the luster of crystal and blazing with great splendor;
having meditated on Śiva, whose limbs are that [Liṅga], as one who has resorted to that single state."
Likewise, in the *Cintya-viśvasādākhya*:
"The Great Lord Śiva, whose form is the Bindu, resembling a drop, [is located] on the forehead."
One should always contemplate the conceptual construction situated in the middle of the region.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "Just as a mirror, being constantly polished, becomes stainless,
so too does the intellect of men become stainless through the practice of knowledge."

The internal sacrifice is fully described; it is proclaimed as the purification of the self. He who worships Śaṅkara through the ritual procedures of the internal sacrifice [attains the highest state].

By means of the sacrifice of meditation (dhyānayajña), he constantly attains the supreme goal. Or, as stated in the Vātula: "The stalk arising from the root of the navel is eight finger-breadths long, or even more."
One should visualize a white lotus with a width of twelve finger-breadths.
Likewise, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is not sufficient for detachment; it is the pericarp in the secret place (*guha*),
endowed with the eight petals of sovereignty and joined with the filaments of the pericarp.
In the center of the pericarp of that lotus is the auspicious Liṅga made of jewels.
As stated in the *Skandakālottara*:
"Having abandoned the state of being conditioned by nature (prākṛta), one should contemplate, 'I am Śiva.'"
This is declared to be samādhi; the wise praise it.

Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the place (*sthānaśuddhi*). If it is asked, "What is that purification of the place, and for what purpose?"—it is said: its purpose is the removal of obstacles in the form of fierce *piśācas*. As it has been stated by the Supreme Lord:
May the fierce spirits and piśācas here who strike the earth—
those beings who create obstacles— depart by the command of Śiva.

The sequence for this is as follows: having placed the two hands with palms facing upward at the heart, one should perform the triple clapping of the hands while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ," and then strike the ten directions with the snapping of the fingers.
Having dispelled the obstacles with the Astra-mantra and created a rampart blazing with the color of fire,

one should establish a protective enclosure (khāyikā) outside it on the right by whirling the index finger while reciting "Oṃ hyaiṃ kavacāya namaḥ," and [establish] the net of Śaktis above with the mantra ending in vauṣaṭ.
Having visualized [it], one should display the Mahāmudrā.
In the *Kālottara*:
"For the sake of accomplishing the external sacrifice, one should then perform the purification of the site.
One should expel obstacles with the Astra-mantra and the three-fold sound 'tāla'."
Having performed the binding of the directions with finger-snaps (*choṭikā*), the enclosure with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*),
and the moat with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*)— thus establishing the outer and inner spaces— one should [form] the *śaktimudrā*.
Then, having bound [the mudrā], one should meditate upon this [mantra] proclaimed by Śakti.
Now follows the purification of substances.
Now, one might ask: what is accomplished by the purification of substances? Is it not the case that substances such as water are pure by their very nature?
No, for there are certain classes of substances produced in impure worlds which, due to their inauspicious nature, [require purification].
Because he is unworthy of the enjoyments of Śiva.

Nor should it be argued that his state of being Śiva arises from his connection with the all-pervading Śiva; for Śiva, like the surface of a lotus leaf, is untainted and lacks contact with material substances. Therefore...
Purification must certainly be performed.
As it has been said in the *Kriyāsaṃgraha* (p.
"By abandoning the form consisting of *māyā*, [the soul] assumes its own nature as the power (*śakti*); thus, it becomes an object of enjoyment for Śiva."
That action would be a substance; it is the purification of the substance.
For example:
one who is inauspicious should never perform auspicious rites; however, a substance consecrated by Śiva should be dedicated for the sake of Śiva.
One should sprinkle with that [water] the substances intended for the sacrifice, but not those not so intended; indeed, O Śivā, nothing unsprinkled or unassigned should be offered.
And the materials for the components of worship have been described as follows in the *Suprabheda*:

"One should perform the complete eightfold worship with water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings (*naivedya*)."
One should worship the Supreme Lord with the eightfold [offering].
314) In the Mataṅga:
Vessels or flowers that are not defiled for the sake of sacrifice,
auspicious medicinal herbs, and incenses free from animal products are recommended.
Thus: In the subtle [practice]—
the conch-base and the conch, the foot-base and the bowl,
joined with a vessel for perfumes and provided with a vessel for flowers.
The support for the cloth and the cloth itself, together with the support for the flowers— made of iron,
silver, or gold, and endowed with jewels.
Adorned with rudrākṣas, coral, and strings of pearls, he was beautified by various great ornaments made of the nine precious gems.
Adorned with variegated garments and beautified by colorful ornaments,
it is provided with pieces of cloth and accompanied by the purification of the linga.
Equipped with a water-trough and a vessel for drawing up water, together with a bathing altar,
a footstool, and a vessel for the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Then, a bell, incense, and a lamp, followed by the *ārātrika* rite; thereafter, a stand equipped with a lamp, a vessel for clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
Then there was a cooking vessel, as well as a bowl for condiments, small bowls,
a stand for the bowls, and a water-vessel.
Rice, a hide, a ladle, wood joined with three feet,
and a small knife made of coconut shell for cutting condiments.
The water for the feet (pādya) has already been mentioned; now that which is to be prepared as the substance is being described:
sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and red sandalwood.
Himālaya water, black fragrant substance, gorocana, the two types of madana, the flower, the five flowers,
the eight flowers, and the leaf.
A bracelet, a hanging garland, bilva leaves, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains (akṣata), as well as water-filled [vessels] thus provided with the substances for the water offering.

Combined with substances for the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, and combined with substances for the soup (sūpa) and so forth; tawny clarified butter, pure oil, *śirīṣa* [flowers], and powdered flour.
One should diligently prepare the five products of the cow as an ambrosial offering, along with a coconut,
combined with plantain fruit and all the materials required for the ritual bath.
One should diligently prepare various cloth insignia;
they may consist of five, three, or one circular band, corresponding in number to the Rudras and so forth.
Or one may use nectar (amṛta) in seven stalks, five stalks, or a single stalk;
or cow’s ghee combined with the flame of a lamp, or excellent oil.
Two *prasthas* up to four *droṇas* of pure rice, combined with salt,
*kramaka*, cooked [grains], and various side dishes and relishes.
Marīci salt, cumin, mustard, as well as betel nut,
*supatra*, and white fragrant powder.
Then, the attendants should collect the ashes, the mirror, the parasol, the fly-whisk, the palm-leaf fan,
and the sacrificial materials for Aṃśumatī on the left side.
Having placed a water vessel on the right.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"Now hear the characteristics of excellent vessels, beginning with the foot-stand (*pādya*):
its height and its width should both be five finger-breadths."
The lip is said to be one finger-breadth thick, and the outer portion should be half of that again.

The vessels for water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamana) are prescribed to be made of gold and other precious materials; for the seat, however, one may have it made of half that size, or even half of that again.
And this is said to be the cause of all causes; [as stated] in the Śivadharmottara:

That golden vessel is the best, silver is middling, and copper is inferior; however, in the absence of these, it may be made of clay. When it is made of clay, then a new one should be taken every day. And it has been said:
An earthen vessel should be used every day, and that is desired to be purified by the earth; however, once it has been employed, it becomes like discarded flower-offerings (nirmālya).
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"The merit that one obtains by giving [an offering] with a wooden vessel is proclaimed to be a hundred times greater when given with an earthen vessel."
By the offering of an *arghya* with a copper vessel, the merit is a hundred times greater.
With vessels made of *palāśa* or lotus leaves, it shall be equal to that of a copper vessel. [With] a silver vessel...
The fruit to be known is a hundred thousand times more than the arghya.
The *arghya* placed in a golden vessel is increased ten millionfold [in merit].
Then, one should worship the vessel containing the *arghya* along with the *pādya* and other offerings in a subtle manner; or else—
One vessel for water for the feet, and [separate vessels] for water for sipping and for the arghya offering.
In the *Suprabheda*: "Uśīra combined with sandalwood, joined with dūrvā grass and white mustard seeds—
this mixture of four substances is declared to be the water for washing the feet (*pādya*)."
Cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, jasmine, and mura—these are the six ingredients for the water of sipping (ācamana); now the ingredients for the offering water (arghya) are described.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, rice grains, and well-fermented buttermilk, together with barley and white mustard seeds— this is declared to be the eightfold *arghya*.

The measurement of substances such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth is stated according to the sequence beginning with the highest; this is determined by the substance in the Kāraṇa [Tantra].
Holding each individually is best, while half of that would be middling.
Half of that is known as the "inferior" portion; the substances for the foot-washing (pādya) are said to be threefold.
The units beginning with the *pāda* are proclaimed as being half of each other;
in that very context, the nature of the *dhāraṇās* and so forth is stated:
"Two *bhujas* make one *māṣaka*, twenty *māṣakas* make one *dhāraṇa*, and eight *dhāraṇās* [make one...]".
One pala is indeed called a muṣṭi here.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"But even when vessels are unavailable, [one may use] either a conch shell or mother-of-pearl.

Aṃśumatī said: Its characteristics have been stated—the conch is said to be of three kinds: male, female, and neuter. That which is thick at the base is female; that which is thick at the tip is neuter.
That which is equal at the tip and the base is proclaimed as "Pumān" (the Male); a conchshell originating from copper-colored [clay] is proclaimed as the most excellent.
That of the Gaṅgā is indeed the middling, and that of the Narmadā is the lowest; thus it is said to be of three kinds. Now, the excellence of birth is being described.
A conch shell that spirals to the right is remembered as the most excellent of its kind;
a conch shell with a rightward spiral is prescribed according to its own specific proportions.
The rule regarding the measurement for that purpose is stated:
the best [offering] is a full *prastha*, the middling is two *kuḍupas*, and the smallest is one *kuḍupa*;
this is easily obtained and is called the "conch" (*śaṅkha*).
On the tip of the tail of Aṃśumatī is a conch, adorned with gold and jewels, exceedingly beautiful.
One should wash it with snow; it becomes pure when burnt by [the fire of] the six.
The Śaṅkhapāda [mudrā] is triangular and possesses a ring in the middle. In the Niśvāsa [Tantra]:
"One should perform the Śaṅkha [mudrā], which purifies the interior, externally like a bone; therefore, with every effort..."
It should be fashioned from gold or other such materials.
Regarding the subtle [limbs]:
the base of the conch [the navel] has Earth as its presiding goddess and Viṣṇu as its deity;
one should wear the Aghora-amulet on the belly, which has the Sun as its deity.
There are seven sacred fords (tīrthas) in the mouth, and at the entrance is the deity Candra;
in the three feet is the presiding divinity, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
The Vṛtta and the Ādhāraśakti—these are the presiding deities.
323) Now, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Its proper time is said to be during the subtle solstices,
at the equinoxes, during lunar and solar eclipses, on other auspicious days, and also during the daily and occasional rites.
And for the expiation on one's birth-star, one should perform a bath with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
As stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"Having prepared the *pañcagavya* specifically for the purpose of bathing the Liṅga..."
One should arrange it either in the eastern part or in the northeast.
Then, having smeared the square mandala with cow dung,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring two cubits or one cubit, strewn with darbha grass.
In the Vātula [Tantra]:
One should mark the eastern line, the cross-line (yuga-sūtra), and likewise the northern line;
from one line to another line, or from one square (tāla) to half a square, one should draw [the grid].
The best [quantity] is four *prasthas*, the middling is half of that,
and the lowest is one *prastha* of rice; each of these is to be offered separately.
In the absence of these, one should fashion it with rice or kusha grass; facing north, one should imagine it as being seated.

One should spread the darbha grass on the outside, with the tips pointing eastward and the tips pointing northward; the tip should be adjacent to the tip in the northeast, and the back should be adjacent to the back in the southwest.
One should make the root and the tip equal, as well as the elements of air and fire; the Śiva-tattva is in the middle, while Sadāśiva is in the eastern square.

The principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) is in the south, and likewise the principle of the person (puruṣatattva) in the north; the principle of time (kālatattva) is in the west, while the principle of earth (pṛthvītattva) is in the southeast.
The principle of *aptattva* is in the chamber of Nirṛti, and Marut in the chamber of Vāyu;
Īśa is in the chamber of Prakṛti—thus is the worship of the chambers prescribed.
A golden vessel is called the best, a bell-metal vessel the middling, and an earthen vessel the lowest;
such is what is designated as a "vessel."
One should avoid [a vessel] that is cracked, chipped at the corners, or black in appearance. For the purpose [of the ritual], having taken up the new vessel, one should wash it with scented water.
One should sprinkle it with the Puruṣa mantra and envelop it with the Kavaca mantra.
In the *Vātula*:
"In the center is Supratiṣṭha, and Suśānta is indeed in the east; Tejovat is in the south, and Ratnodaka is in the north."
The vessel of nectar is in the west, and the vessel of Īśa is clearly in the northeast corner;
the vessel of Vyakta is in the southeast, and the vessel of Sūrya is in the southwest.
The vessel for the wind [element] should be a saṃyoga-vessel; the worship of the vessel is thus prescribed.
326) The cow-dung and urine belong to the black [cow], while the ghee belongs to the blue and the tawny [cows].
Having diligently collected the milk from a white cow and a copper-colored cow, [he should proceed].
In the [mandala] called Viśvasāda—milk measuring three kuḍubas is in the center; curd measuring half a prastha is in the east;
and ghee, provided with one kuḍuba, is in the south.
In the north, there should be earth from a mountain slope, cow urine, cow dung, and ghee from a herd of cows; in the west, combined with water—thus it shall consist of five ingredients.
One should fill a single portion with pure water mixed with kusa grass,
either thirty-six or twenty-five blades.
One should fashion either a group of twelve, five, or three [tufts];
the *kūrca* there should be one cubit in length and arranged clockwise.
Two knots, two finger-breadths [in length], and four finger-breadths; or else, a tuft (*kūrca*) of one palm’s measure, *kuśa* grass blades, and *kuśa* water.
In the Vātula [Tantra]:
"The *āmalaka* fruit is said to be the size of a *kapittha* fruit; the *rajanī* is the standard measure of the size of a *kadalī* fruit."
Regarding the causes:
the best of instructors should place rice flour in the southeast;
likewise, *āmalī* and *nirūta* in the northwest, and *rajanī* as well.
Aṃśumatī said:
In the absence of curd, there shall be milk; in the absence of milk, there shall be curd. In the absence of cow dung, there shall be cow urine;
and in the absence of that, there shall be cow dung.

Among the five products of the cow, for whomsoever there may be a lack [of one], that [deficiency] shall be supplied by ghee. In both the superior and the middling [preparations], the cow dung should be the size of a hen's egg.
Alternatively, one may fill [the vessel] with water alone to the measure of the eye; it should be filtered through a cloth and placed according to the prescribed rite.
Having placed milk in the center, curd is said to be in its east;
having placed ghee in the south, one should set down cow dung in the north.
Having placed cow urine in the west according to the sequence of the emanation-arrangement (sṛṣṭinyāsa), one should place ghee in the center; that which is to its east is said to be curd.
To the south one should place cow urine, and likewise cow dung to the north;
and to the north, cow milk, according to the sequence of the placement of the cosmic stations (sthitinyāsa).
One should place cow urine in the center, and place cow dung in the east; likewise, one should place curd in the south and milk in the north.
But in the west, having placed ghee, one should indeed follow the sequence of withdrawal.
One should especially place water with *kuśa* grass in the northeast;
likewise, one should especially provide ground *āmalaka* and turmeric.
From the southeast (Agnikoṣṭha) to the northwest (Vāyavya), one should perform the rites with the Heart mantra and likewise with the Armor mantra.
In the *Kālottara*: "For the sake of conquering the five elements, one should prepare the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) consisting of those [elements];
one should consecrate them in sequence with the mantras of Īśāna and the others, numbering according to their respective qualities."
If a householder is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), [he should prepare the materials] with goats and so forth, and with cow dung and so forth.
In the *Vātula*:
"The milk should be prepared with the *Īśāna* mantra; one should consecrate it five times with the *Puruṣa* [mantra]."
And curd, likewise consecrated with the mantra numbered according to the [desired] result.
Regarding the cause:
with Aghora, one should offer clarified butter; the number of elements has been proclaimed. With Vāmadeva, one should cause cow’s urine and fragrant substances to be offered.
Cow dung, consecrated nine times with the *sadyojāta* mantra,
[is used] for the causal [rite].
One should sprinkle flour on the heart, āmalaka fruit on the head,
and turmeric on the armor-mantra, consecrating each once with water from kuśa grass while reciting the Gāyatrī;
this is the "fivefold Brahma" performed six times.
Regarding that which is born of yoga:

curd is indeed the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*), while ghee is said to be maintenance (*sthiti*). Cow dung and the other [substances] follow the path of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-mārga*), with *kuśa* water at the end.
Regarding the causes: having thrown cow-dung into cow-water, one should pour cow-water and ghee [into it]; then, having mixed ghee with curd, one should pour the curd into milk.
Then, one should sprinkle *kuśa* water there with the heart-mantra and the root-mantra;
and one should recite the Brahma-mantras, the Śiva-aṅgas, and the Gāyatrī once for protection.
Having fashioned it with the weapon-mantra, one should envelop it with the armor-mantra.
Then, having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, one should worship with perfumes and flowers; thereafter, one should offer incense and a lamp while reciting the *astramantra*.

Regarding the matter of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should consecrate [the substance] one hundred and eight times with the root mantra. As it is stated in the *Śivadharmottara*: "Having performed [the rite], one should again recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with Śiva alone, having fasted for a day and night."
Having bathed, he stood white (or purified) before Śiva.
Facing eastward, one should drink slowly with a single mantra beginning with the syllable *oṃ*;
one is thereby liberated from all sins, including the killing of a Brahmin.
Why should it not be performed mentally alone? And it is stated in some places:
"Cow dung, clarified butter, curd, milk, and water infused with *kuśa* grass...

The five products of the cow (pañcagavya), obtained with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and purified by the qualities of the elements, is thus described; the best [measure] is one prastha, while the middling should be three quarters (tripāda).
The lowest [level] is said to have two feet, but one should arrange the *vaibhava* [mandala].
As it is stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"One should especially have [the mandala] made for one's own sake on a *prastha* or similar measure; this is the *pañcagavya*."
The five nectars have been described; now they are further explained.
In front of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), there should be a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) as before;
one should arrange the compartments, the vessels, and the mantras as previously described.
Milk should be placed in the center, curd in the east, ghee in the south, honey in the north, and sugar should be in the west.
One should specifically place the plantain, the breadfruit, and the mango, as well as the scented water,
starting from the southeast (Agni) and extending to the northeast (Īśāna).
Then, having specially prepared the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) for each *prastha* measure, in the absence of sugar, molasses should be used;
and in the absence of honey, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be used.
In the Raurava [tantra],
however, in the absence of sugar-candy (khaṇḍa), sugarcane juice should be used;
and during the consecration (abhiṣeka), the sugar-candy should be dissolved in water.

The consecration (abhiṣeka) is described separately as occurring between each water bath. In the *Sūkṣma-tantra*, it is stated that at the conclusion of the daily, occasional, and optional baths, one should bathe Maheśvara with a thousand streams.
Bathing certainly bestows prosperity and good fortune.
Alternatively, O Destroyer, listen to another way:
that vessel is said to be of three kinds, and the lowest is indeed the third.
Twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) is thus proclaimed as the best;
seven finger-breadths in width is proclaimed as the inferior and middling; five finger-breadths... [is the lowest].
It is proclaimed that the lowest of the low is very extensive.
One should conceive of its base as being three finger-breadths wide; thus, the width of the vessel's wall and its height are described.
An elevation of one finger-breadth is proclaimed as the best; an elevation of half a finger-breadth is proclaimed as the middling.
The wise one should know that the height of the toes is equal to a *pādāṅgula*, while the middle [part] is successively three *yava*s in thickness.
Taking the vessel with both hands, one should consecrate it upon the top of the *liṅga*;
it may be made of gold, silver, or copper, and may be either square or circular.
In a nine-square grid of four rows, one should carefully form a single square that is enclosed and possesses eight openings, with a hollow space in its center.
Outside the square and within the lines, especially in the great directions,
one should fashion the openings for the ears with a measurement of only a single needle’s breadth.
Make twelve other perforations within the intervals between the sections; this is declared to be one hundred and eight, or fifty-one less.
That vessel consists of nine compartments; in the middle compartment, it is surrounded by eight hollows, especially on its exterior.
Within each single word, there are five arrows (five) and nine apertures (nine);
fifty is indeed stated, and twenty-five is also spoken of.
That vessel consists of nine compartments, with a single cavity in the center.
In the middle of other [sections], however, make such a hollow space; this is called "square," or it is also said to be "well-rounded."

As before, the vessel is likewise [drawn] with eight petals and a pericarp (*karṇikā*). In the center of the pericarp is one [deity], and in the directions starting from the east are the eight [deities] of the apertures (*randhra*). Outside of that, in the middle of the petals...
But make the twelfth [finger] hollow.
Within the middle of that outer enclosure, there should be a pair of great spokes;
thus is the hollow described as consisting of one hundred and eight [parts] in sequence.
One should calculate fifty and twenty-five as before; this is declared to be the small measurement, for one's own sake and for the sake of others.

If, out of delusion or ignorance, one should consecrate [a vessel] as a "Bhadra-vessel" for the sake of another while failing to examine it for one's own sake, that is merely a semblance of the auspicious.
In the bright fortnight, it increases one's lifespan, fame, and nourishment like the moon;
one should fill that vessel with water from a conch while reciting the root mantra.
In this very manner, the consecration by streams (dhārābhiṣecana) has been taught in due order in the Kāmika [Tantra]. (p. 337)
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron are called "fragrance. These two, three, or even all four, including camphor, [constitute the fragrant substances].
One should prepare saffron, musk, and camphor with the sandalwoods; of each, one *niṣka*, or half of that, or half of that again.
Likewise—
by anointing Śambhu with gorocanā, saffron, sandalwood, cardamom, camphor, black agallochum, devadāru, musk, and other such substances, one obtains the merit of ten million horse sacrifices.
One should offer incense made of *devadāru* wood to Śiva; one attains the world of Śiva for one kalpa, without a doubt.
By offering incense made from the root of the *bilva* tree to Umāmaheśvara, one attains great sovereignty and,
having given it, shall go to the city of Śiva.
A person who anoints with the fragrance made from *āragvadha* becomes a conqueror of death;
devoted to the Conqueror of Death, he shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
Therefore, among all ritual offerings, the worship with incense is preeminent.
Now, the planting of flowers is described.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"White, red, and black flowers here are designated as belonging to the *sāttvika* [and other] qualities; one should designate yellow-colored flowers as being of a mixed nature."
One should avoid other dark-colored flowers except for the blue lotus; the *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, and white *arkapuṣpa* are beneficial at sunrise.
Karavīra, padma, and droṇapuṣpa are beneficial at midday; mallikā, kṛṣṇa, dhūstūra, and campaka are beneficial in the evening.
Kadambaka, kanaka, jāti, and dvikarṇī at midnight; and droṇa, white lotus, and bahuparṇikā jāti.
The *nandyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, the *mandāra*, the *śatatrikā*, the white *arka*,
the *mālatī*, the *bilva*, the *punnāga*, and likewise the *kurava*.
One should designate flowers such as these as being of the *sāttvika* nature: the red lotus (*raktotpala*), the *padma*, the *dhurdhūra*, and the two types of *bṛhatī*.
One should designate the *pālāśa*, *pāṭala*, and others as belonging to the *rājasa* quality; likewise, the *karṇikāra*, *dhūrdhūra*, *campaka*, *evadha*, and so forth.
One should point out such yellow and mixed flowers as the karañja, vakula,
śākha, śirīṣa, and likewise the ketakī.
Tāṅgalī, pomegranate, āmya, śrīparṇī, and vibhītaka; bandhūka, kunda, yūthikā, cotton, nimba, and kaṇṭaka.
One should avoid the *kiṃśuka*, the *madantī*, and the *kumuda* flowers; one should also avoid fruit that is unripe, overripe, or still in the bud stage.
One should avoid flowers that are infested with hair or insects, covered by spiderwebs, or those that have fallen on their own, even if they are gathered together.
One should discard flowers that have been worn once and those that have been offered [to another deity].
Likewise—
one should not worship Viṣṇu with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), nor Vināyaka with *tulasī*, nor [any deity] with *dūrvā* grass.
One should not worship Maheśānī with a *ketakī* flower, nor Maheśvara [with it].
In the Kālottara:
One should avoid the ketakī flower, the kūśmāṇḍa produced from the nimba tree, that which is born of the śālmalī tree belonging to the piśācas,
and one should also avoid the girikarṇa.
One should avoid flowers that are scentless or foul-smelling; eight types of flowers are to be avoided for Śiva, the Supreme Self.
One should avoid the eight flowers: ketakī, mādhavī, kunda, dhūpikā, madayantikā, śirīṣa, sarja, and bandhūka.
In the *Suprabheda*: "During festivals and the like, on processions, and during the acts of serving food..."
They should always be avoided or accepted according to all the ornaments [of poetic figures].
One should worship the goddess Umā with black-flowered plants, the *mahiṣākṣī* flower, and *śiṃśumāraka* flowers.
One should worship Brahmā with *palāśa* flowers and Keśava indeed with *tulasī*; furthermore, the flowers of *indravallī* are pleasing to Indra.
One should not take flowers grown in a divine garden and offer them to the deity.
According to the *Kāraṇa*:
"One should cause leaves and flowers to be offered for the sake of another [the donor] in due order; as for the remainder..."
One should not perform either occasional rites (naimittika) or rites for specific desires (kāmya).
Worship performed with cuttings of leaves brings about the destruction of the Rākṣasas;
worship performed with cuttings of flowers shall bring about the attainment of all siddhis.
Now, the ritual procedure for incense is described.
One part of agarwood should be taken, with the resinous exudate (niryāsa) being double that amount; sandalwood is said to be three times as much, slightly mixed with camphor.
For fever with chills, incense mixed with honey is recommended;
likewise, guggulu combined with clarified butter, or bilva fruit mixed with sugar.
One should also well-incense kuṣṭha with sandalwood mixed with ghee; likewise, one should apply black iron, resin, and sandalwood in their proper sequence.
This excellent incense is said to consist of one-third of *vyomapakṣa* mixed with a little camphor and saturated with honey.
Uśīra combined with sandalwood, joined with honey and saturated with honey—the portion of that is declared as before; this is called the middling incense.
Guggulu mixed with clarified butter is declared to be the inferior incense.
A lamp is kindled with cow’s ghee or oil and a wick made of camphor.
The flame of the lamp is distinguished by a length of four, three, or two finger-breadths; the lamp should be made with tawny ghee, or with white or red ghee.
In its absence, goat’s ghee or pure oil is beneficial; however, ghee from a tawny cow (kapilā) is best, while ghee produced from other animals is middling.
Clarified butter from a goat and likewise pure oil are considered inferior; they are respectively of the nature of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

One should light a camphor wick, which bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). A flame four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long is excellent; one of three finger-breadths is middling; and a flame of two finger-breadths is declared to be the lowest for a lamp.
One should avoid using oils produced from tree seeds for the Śiva-lamp.
344) Now, the procedure for the food offering (naivedya) is described in the Kāmika:
The grains of *śālī* rice are the best; barley, *vrīhi*, and so forth are equal [to them].
Among the remaining types of *vrīhi* rice, the grain would be the lowest.

And those which are white rice grains are all remembered as being for the Lord; the others are called *vrīhi* rice, and their fruits are each distinct. Likewise, the fruit of the other [white rice] is ten times that of the *śāli* rice.
In the *Kāmika*:
"One should present the food offering with devotion according to one's means; [this includes] leaves, flowers, fruits, water, food, drink, and so forth, as well as medicinal herbs."
One should never eat without having first offered food to the Lord Sadāśiva; indeed, after giving to Śiva whatever edible substance there may be, such as cakes and the like.
His grain, fruits, flowers, and so forth increase;
however, if one consumes it without first giving to Hara— whether the wealth be small or great— that wealth is exhausted.
Is the fruit equal for Ādara and Rudra?
One should perform [the rite] according to one's ability; devotion alone is the cause here. As many grains of rice as there are, so much is prepared as the food offering (naivedya).
For that many thousands of years, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Regarding the Sūkṣma [rite]: one should perform worship for one's own sake using two *prasthas* up to four *droṇas* [of grain].
Aṃśumatī said:
"The best [measure] is declared to be one āḍhaka, while six prasthas would be the middling."
The lowest and the *āḍhaka*—thus the food offering (*naivedya*) is of three kinds;
or else, in another way, the *āḍhaka* may be the highest.
The triad beginning with *uttama* is said to end at the *kuḍuba*;
likewise, half a *phala* of a *prastha* is the same as half a *kuḍuba* of clarified butter.
And one should indeed join half of that half of ghee with a flower alone.
An offering devoid of clarified butter is a gift for the asuras;
therefore, with every effort, one should present an offering accompanied by clarified butter.
Then, for the sake of fulfilling desires, one may offer rice as an oblation according to one's own wish.

Regarding the measures: two *prasthas* are declared to be a *caru*, and one *āḍhaka* is said to be the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). One *prastha* together with a *kuḍuba* is called the food of the *piśācas*.
The food offering for all [the deities] should be more than two *prasthas* in quantity; first, the attendants, having bathed according to the previously mentioned procedure, [should proceed].
Wearing white garments and a white sacred thread, with the *pavitra* grass-grain in hand, he should prepare the cooked sacrificial rice (*caru*) according to the prescribed sequence.
One should fill a water-vat (*jaladroṇa*) with water filtered through cloth; then, having performed the purification of the vessel,
one should wash the rice grains while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having squeezed it repeatedly with water six times, one should perform the washing with the six limbs as stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Having performed the washing with the six limbs, one should pour out the water with the *Sadyojāta* mantra."
Regarding the cause—
the measure of rice— one should purify the water and rice contained in the vessel by means of the primary seed, using a quantity of water equal to or slightly more than half [the measure].
In the *Kāmika*:

"In the great kitchen, which has been smeared with cow dung and the like and sprinkled [with water], one should worship with rice grains— the hearth that consumes both dharma and adharma— using the heart-mantra."
Having extracted [the fire] with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should establish it with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should kindle the fire with the mouth of the Aghora mantra.
Infested with ants and the like, and joined by worms within hollows.
One should also worship the river with wood that is accompanied by sparks;
and in the case of [unfit offerings]: that which is defiled by hair or insects, mixed with gravel or husks, or that which is overcooked or undercooked.
One should avoid offering food as an oblation.
That which is devoid of color and fragrance should be discarded; one should not offer that which is cold.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"Likewise, food offered without a covering, as well as the sight of birds [over it], renders the *naivedya* [unfit]."
Having avoided that, however, the wise man should take what remains.
One should know that in the *santāna* [lineage], poverty accompanied by husks arises from stone, and disease likewise; from hair, death is to be known; therefore, one should especially avoid it.
In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* of the Śaiva [Āgama]:
"The sacrificial oblation (*havis*) to be offered is of six kinds: pure rice, mung-bean rice, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*)."
Curd mixed with sugar and saturated with honey.
Clarified butter mixed with curd, mixed with jaggery, or mixed with honey— any one of these, or several combined, served together with a side dish.
In the *Vīratantra*:
"I shall describe the sequence for milk-rice (*pāyasa*): one should cook milk-rice using half as much mung bean (*mudga*) as rice, with twice as much milk."
O Brahmin, one should cook gulānna with milk equal to half the measure of rice;
half a guḷa of rice is prescribed, along with half a guḷa of clarified butter.
It should be known as *gulānna*; now listen to the description of *kṛsarānna*: sesame should indeed be ground there, with one-fourth the amount of rice.
One should add half a sesame seed to the clarified butter; this is here called *kṛsarānna*. One should likewise add green gram (*mudga*) there, equal to one-fourth part of the rice.
Mudgānna (rice cooked with mung beans) accompanied by coconut fruits is what is described here;
it is superior to a thousand servings of śuddhodana (white rice) and even surpasses milk-rice (pāyasa).
Kṛsarā rice is superior to a thousand servings of milk-rice;
and gulā rice is superior to a thousand servings of kṛsarā rice.
Mudga-rice is superior to a thousand offerings of rice with sugar; in this very manner, the fruit increases a thousandfold at each successive stage.
Now, the method for the preparation of upadaṃśa is described.
In the Vātula [Tantra]:
"Two plantains, as well as two bṛhatīs, likewise two kāravallīs,
and similarly two types of cucumber."
O child, there are likewise two *panasa* fruits, as well as two *kūśmāṇḍa* fruits, two *lābu* gourds,
and similarly two *kośātakī* fruits.
O Guha, one should take the roots of the *śiśu*, the roots of a creeper, the tuberous root (*kanda*), the *sūraṇa*, the mango, and the *tintriṇī*— whichever of these are available.

In the Raurava [Tantra], Śiva has declared that there are two kinds of food for the Kaulas: the *kulmāṣaka* (sour gruel) and the *māṣa* (black gram). One should know that the *māṣa* may be either with its husk or without its husk.
In the *Vīratantra*: "An āḍhaka of black gram (*rājamāṣa*), as well as mudga beans, peas (*śimba*), and *kulattha*.
In the *Kāmika*:
The kūśmāṇḍa, the jackfruit, the ālāmbu, the kālaka, the two types of bṛhatī,
the trapuṣa, and the karkarī— both with husks and without husks.
Each one of the side-dishes (upadaṃśa) shall yield the fruit of one *prastha*; all the side-dishes mentioned are to be seasoned with black pepper and salt.

One should cook [the substances] separately with juices such as cumin and others, according to the appropriate application. In the work titled *Viśvasāda*, it is said: "The width should be one finger-breadth; one should not increase it beyond half that width."
The lip is said to be one finger-breadth in width, and it should be made of gold, silver, or other such materials.
Half of that is to be known as the lowest [size], and half of that again becomes the smallest.
In the *Kāmika*:
"It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even a plantain leaf, or of pure bell-metal."
The wise person should act by taking up the vessel.
In the subtle [rite]:
having smeared with cow-dung, one should place [the deity] in a pavilion before the god.
Having washed the vessel, one should worship the food offering (naivedya),
which is surrounded by side dishes, salt, and cooked condiments.
In the middle [vessel], there should be milk and curd combined with sugar and other fruits;
it should be joined with clarified butter and ghee, and covered with a cloth.
When removing the food offering (*naivedya*), perform the sweeping and sprinkling of the path.

Now the procedure is stated: having washed a special *arghya* vessel made of gold or one of the other materials with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [fill it] with the stream of nectar flowing from the *bindu*.
Having filled [the vessel] with pure water while reciting the heart-mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*, and having placed that substance therein,

one should worship the seat, the form, the five Brahmans, the body of the Vidyā, the eyes, and the primary limbs, and again with the root-mantra; then, having consecrated it with the *saṃhitā* [mantra], [one should protect it] with the weapon-mantra.
Having performed the binding of the directions (digbandhana), one should conceal [the self] with the armor-mantra (kavaca), ending with "vauṣaṭ" and the root-mantra (mūla).
Having rendered [the offering] nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, one should display the *mahāmudrā*.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The foot-washing water (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the *nirodha* [mudrā], in due order..."
A vessel made of gold or any other [precious metal], placed upon the support of the yantrikā.
Then, taking the vessel for the *arghya* offering, one should wash it with the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*. Having resorted to the station of the *bindu*, one should visualize a lotus in the center.
Having filled it with the five Brahmans, the limbs of Śiva, and Śiva himself,
that water is consecrated by mantras and joined with fragrance and flowers.
One should cause drops to be offered at each of the places where they are to be assigned.
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
"First, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to Śiva who has arrived at his feet."
One should offer water for rinsing the mouth in their mouths and present the *arghya* offering upon their heads. — From the *Mṛgendra*:

At the end of the cessation and at the time of emission, the water for the obstructors (rodhārghya) is employed; following the recitation of the name of Śiva, the water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) are used at the conclusion of the worship.

In the Dīpta [state], the water for the feet (pādya) extends up to the Īśvara-tattva; the water for sipping (ācamanīya) includes the Sadeśa [tattva]; the water for the honorific offering to Śiva (śivārghya) extends up to the Śiva-tattva; and the water for the honorific offering to Rodha belongs to the sphere of Śakti.
Having sprinkled oneself on the head with water using the *śakti* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,

one should take the collection of materials for worship, such as perfumes and so forth, between the thumb and ring finger; having looked at them with the eyes while reciting their root mantra, [one should purify them] with the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
Having sprinkled [the object] with the *patākā* [mudrā],
one should strike it with the middle finger using the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*, while employing the upward-pointing *patākā* [mudrā].

One should perform the protection (*rakṣā*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*). As stated in the *Kāmika*: "Protection with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with the weapon mantra (*astramantra*), and striking (*tāḍana*)."
There should be sprinkling with water using the Astra-mantra and the Varma-mantra.
In this regard, the *Pārameśvara* teaches the threefold excellence of observation:
"By means of the eyes of the Sun, Fire, and Moon, which consist of vision (*dṛk*), action (*kriyā*), and the Self (*ātman*), [the object becomes] respectively dry, and likewise..."
It is burnt and joined with immersion in nectar.

Then, for the sake of purification, there is sprinkling, striking with power down to the end of the fiery element, and the ritual application of water; thus the entire collection of rites is to be grasped as being united with the inner disposition.
Likewise, in the Tantrasāra:
"Know that the piercing [of the soul] consists in the distinction between the insentient and the conscious, through the gaze of Śiva."
The attainment of fitness is the striking of an object distinct from the insentient; therein, the manifestation of consciousness is like the striking of a stone,
followed by the sprinkling that results in the production of sparks.
His fame is proclaimed everywhere regarding all things, both conscious and unconscious;
he is present in every substance, from water down to fragrance.

Having thus performed the purification of the substances as proclaimed in the sequence beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), one should cast a drop of the *arghya* water upon one's own head while reciting the mantra,
and then place a flower on the seat with "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Seat of Śiva" (*oṃ hāṃ śivāsanāya namaḥ*).
Having placed a flower on the crown with the *mūrti-mantra*,
having applied a sandalwood tilaka on the forehead, and having offered a flower to the head with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), [one should proceed].
Having said "I am in the state of a bound soul," one should contemplate, "I am pure like Śiva.
Having thus completed the worship of the self and adopted a silence that is not inconsistent with it,
one [should proceed] from the heart and other centers up to the *brahmarandhra* and the *dvādaśānta* by means of the mantra in its short, long, and protracted forms.
Or, as far as possible, having uttered the root mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, the other Brahma-aṅgas ending with the *bindu* (m) are then recited. As it has been said:
"Having thus performed the purification of the materials, one should sprinkle the *arghya* water upon one's own head."

Then, having empowered with the root mantra of the weapon-mantra and placed a flower upon the head, and having applied a tilaka mark on the forehead with fragrant sandalwood, one should perform the worship of the seat and the form by means of the root mantra, as well as the self-worship.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should contemplate within oneself that very form which belongs to Śiva."
Always perform this placement of the Śiva-mantra upon yourself.
Having abandoned one's ordinary state, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva.

This contemplation of the self as Śiva must necessarily be performed at the time of worship, because without the presence of Śiva [within oneself], the status of being a worshiper is untenable. As it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*:

"One who is not Rudra himself should not worship Rudra. Likewise, as long as one has not become equal to Him, one is not capable of propitiating Him. Because of his purity and because of his Śiva-nature, he should contemplate his own body as the body of Śiva.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"In bathing, in recitation, in sacrifice, as well as in eating and worship...
In mounting a vehicle, in the ritual smearing with ashes, in the twilight worship, and in all obligatory duties,
one should always remain silent.
Having uttered the mantra ending with Śivā preceded by Bindunātha, one should purify;
for the mantra, consisting of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), is always presided over by Śiva.
All the remaining [mantras] ending with the *bindu* bring about all prosperity and grant all desires.
In the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
"Having first uttered the syllable *Oṃ*, and likewise ending with the word of salutation (*namas*), [one should utter] the limbs of Brahmā."
Likewise, the palace is the seed-syllable of Śiva.
The eighty-one great mantras, as well as the ten thousand syllables and all other mantras,
are declared to be the purity of mantra.
Is it not the case that, according to the statement, "Mantras are pure by their very nature, granting boons and possessing unfailing power," they are so by their inherent nature?
If it is argued that since those mantras are already pure, performing a purification for them again would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), this is true; however,
their sovereign authority (*aiśvarya-adhikāra*) has been obscured by the veil of impurity (*mala*).
The purification of those powers is indeed intended as the manifestation of their own capacity through contact with the Supreme Power (paraśakti). And it has been said:
"Mantras consist of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), yet they are possessed of the impurity of limited sovereignty (aiśvaryamala)."
All [these deities], possessing the power of blazing energy, are considered to be bestowers of all desired objects.
Having thus performed the purification of the mantra, one should worship the attendant deities, such as Vṛṣeśvara and others, upon the pedestal in their respective locations.
This is stated in the *Aṃśumatī*:
Then, in the south-western direction from the sugarcane [offering], one should worship the seat of Gaṇeśa, and likewise the seat of Sarveśvara in their respective places.
The wise one should separately take the masks of all the images; having covered them with cloth that has slipped down, he should sprinkle them with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra.
Then, having discarded the floral remains (nirmālya), one should perform the mental bath (mānasa-snāna); having placed Gaṇeśa in the southwest (nairṛta) and Skanda in the northwest (vāyu).
One should place Maheśa in the southern region facing east,
and the deities such as Nṛttamūrtti in the north facing south.
To the right of the wheel [is] the ash-vessel and the rosary; in the ash-vessel, however, [one should place] the one called Māyā, and upon the ashes, Lakulīśvara.
One should worship Vāsukī with perfumes and flowers upon the thread; having placed the bull in front of the Liṅga, facing westward.
One should place the power of enjoyment (*bhogaśakti*) on the left side of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
