Likewise, in the *Sūkṣma*: [text continues].
Likewise, one should worship Vṛṣeśvara in the east, Bhāskara to the left of Vṛṣa, Maheśa in the southern region, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti to the south.

One should place Gaṇeśa in the south-western quarter, the Lotus-born (Brahmā) to his left, the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) in the north-western quarter, the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha) to the right, the Dancing Form (Nṛttamūrti) on the left,
and Kṣetrapālaka in the north-eastern quarter.
One should install the Liṅgodbhava [Liṅga] between Kubera and Anila; one should install Bhakta and the others in sequence between Soma and Śaṅkara.
One should place the Ekākṣarī [mantra] on the left side of the devotees,
and one should place Lakulīśa on the left of the Ekākṣarī.
Having placed a flower upon the head, one should subsequently perform meditation;
one should worship [the deities] from Gaṇeśa down to Kṣetrapāla with their respective mantras.
Alternatively, in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"In the south is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, in the north is Nidhaneśvara, and [in the northeast is] Brahmeśvara."
In the southwest and the southeast, [he worships] Mahiṣāntakī.
One should worship the image of Gaṅgeya located in the northwestern direction with a concentrated mind.
Regarding these images, if they are made of stone, a ritual bath (snapana) must be performed every day;
if they are made of metal, a bath should be administered on festival days (parvan). This has been stated in the Pauṣkara:
One should perform the bathing and complete purification of the image according to the prescribed lotus-path; if that image is made of metal, the bathing should be performed on every festival day.
The wise one should invoke the form [of the deity] while recollecting its specific mantra.
One should place clothing, fragrance, garlands, and flowers upon the head.
Regarding that, the manner of invoking the form (*mūrti*) is demonstrated in the *Kāmika*: as follows—
Sadāśiva, Maheśa, and the Rudras—these are considered the threefold [manifestations]. That which is called the body of Śiva is said to be the body of Vidyā.
That stainless power of Śiva which accompanies him is itself his form;
through the differentiation of its functions, it is considered the body of Sadāśiva.
Then there is the form of Māheśvarī, which is peaceful in nature; likewise, she is called Raudrī, but she is fierce in nature.
Among these, the power called Kuṇḍalinī, known as Kriyā, is the cause of the body; [so too are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These are the causal deities who are proclaimed as being born of the field (kṣetraja).
Brahmā and Viṣṇu are the forms, while Māyā is held to be the cause. Rudreśvara...
It is the cause of the body known as action for those possessing a location.
Thus, this twofold [nature] of Sadāśiva is declared to belong to Īśvara; therefore, the body of Śiva is proclaimed to consist of pure knowledge.

For the sake of accomplishing those three bodies, one should first fashion the form. Having thus performed the worship of the retinue preceded by the invocation, one should thereafter perform the purification of the *liṅga*. In that regard:
Now, the nature of the bathing altar (snānavedi) is being demonstrated.
Likewise:
"With gold, silver, copper, or with *madhūka*, tin, and lead—these six substances are prescribed; one should thus prepare the bathing altar."

Having fashioned the *upāna* as the lotus, the *jagatī* as the pillar-base (*kaṃba*), and the *karṇa* as the *kapaka*, one should likewise form the *jagatī* as the horse according to its width and length.
Then, having performed the purification of pride (mānaśuddhi), one should fashion the stalk on the left;
or alternatively, that which is like a stream of milk—thus, it should be a four-cornered square measuring one cubit.
Half of that height is the beautiful [pedestal], provided with a girdle and a cow-mouth (gomukha).
It may be made of *aṃśumatī*,
bell-metal, or wood, circular in shape on all sides, and provided with a tube (*nāla*).
Then, in the middle of that, one should utter [the syllable] together with its foot (pāda).

Taking the *liṅga* for the purpose of bathing, one should place it upon the bathing altar (*snānavedi*). Having established the *saumyanālā* in such a bathing area characterized by these features, having spread a cloth in its center,
and having worshipped it above that with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta," [one recites] "Oṃ hāṃ..."
Thus, in the southeast: *jñānāya namaḥ*; in the southwest: *oṃ hāṃ vairāgyāya namaḥ*; in the northwest: *oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*; in the northeast: [as above]. (p. 368)
Having worshipped Ananta in the north, one should thus conceive of the mobile seat (*calāsana*) consisting of six components with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ*. As it is stated in the *Kāraṇa*:
"In the worship for one's own sake (*ātmārthapūjā*), [one should worship] Ananta, Dharma, Jñāna, and so forth, as the lotus; such is the mobile seat."
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty— this lotus arising from the six is the seat."
I shall now describe the mobile temple, as well as the construction of a temple;
the discourse on temples is concluded, whether they be made of gold or silver.
It may be made of copper, or of wood, or even of an earthenware bowl; likewise, it may be made with a tube or a cord—one should proceed in this manner in due order.
On the *ghṛtavāra* (the ghee-section), outside [the central area], by means of the expansion of the *mānāṅgula* (measuring finger-breadth), it should be circular on all sides or even square.
The pedestal for the *liṅga* should likewise be twice the height of the inner sanctum; one should construct it with very firm walls and endowed with all manner of beauty.
One should indeed increase either the length or the height by two *aṅgulas*;
one should cause the pedestal (*pīṭha*) surrounding the *liṅga* to be fashioned in accordance with the prescribed characteristics.

Beyond this, one must not perform [the construction]; listen now to the procedure for the shoes (upāna) at the end. Having divided that height into eight parts, the surface of the earth (dharātala) is formed by one part.
Dharātala, adhiṣṭhāna, vasudhāra, and masūraga— these are the names for the earth,
as well as its synonyms.
Half of a quarter of the nine-thread [measurement] is proclaimed to be doubled;
that is said to be the *prastāra* for the purpose of the feet, and its equal is called the neck (*gala*).
The pinnacle should have a length equal to the height of the base (caraṇa), and its elevation should be half of that.
One should determine the measurement of the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna) by means of a twelfth part [of the total height].
One should perform the *janma* with one [unit], and the *jagatī* with two; likewise, one should cause the height of the *kumuda* and the *kampaka* to be made with one [unit].
The portion of the wing is said to be the neck; above that, the leaf is one part.
One should fashion the great fillet with two parts and the bamboo-staff with one part.
The Adhiṣṭhāna has been fully described; beyond that is the Pādabarha, which consists of four divisions, each having a single Tāraka.
The length of the base should be divided into four parts, and the pedestal (vedī) shall consist of one part;
it should be merely the pillar itself, devoid of bases (tādi) and other such elements.
A shape with eight sides or six sides is called the *vimāna* form; it should have an upward-facing door, and its northern end is highly praised.
One should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and assign the heart-mantras in their proper sequence; then, one should duly construct the mobile temple in this manner.
Aṃśumatī: Regarding worship for one's own sake, the nature of the casket has been stated:
it is fashioned from gold, silver, copper, or even wood.
It may be square, oblong, or even shaped like a basket.
Alternatively, one should place the *vṛtta* (the circular diagram) likewise within the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*).
Having opened the lid of any one of the boxes for the mobile temple (*calaprāsādapeṭikā*) constructed according to this rite, one should worship Bhīmarudra. This is stated in the *Aṃśumat*:
Then, having entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), he likewise performed the opening and closing of the door; and at the front of the sanctum stood the one of terrifying form, fully present.
One should worship Bhīmarudra, who has four arms, three eyes, and is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; likewise, it is stated in the Kāmika:
Having four arms and three eyes, joined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and accompanied by a peacock-feather whisk,
he is proclaimed as Bhīmarudra.
Aṃśumatī said:
"O God, O Lord of Gods, who brings an end to the night-stalkers, for the purpose of worshipping you, please go to the left of the pure gate;
indeed, be gracious to me."

Having sprinkled [the deity] in this manner, one should address the Lord Maheśvara situated in its center: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the gods, the sole leader of all worlds! Arise for the purpose of the ritual bath and for the sake of self-protection."
Having thus prayed, one should grasp the *liṅga* with both hands, remove the cloth,
and place it upon the bathing altar.
Aṃśumatī: Having taken up the *liṅga*, one who possesses great intelligence should dismiss it with a cloth alone.
In the subtle [rite]: having grasped the *liṅga* with the hand, one should place it upon the bathing altar;
thereafter, having worshipped the previously honored [deity] with the *gāyatrī* and with the general *arghya*.

Having offered the fivefold water for the head (*pañcaśirast-arghya*) with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* according to the sequence of Sadyojāta and so forth, and according to the sequence of the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) and so forth, the enjoyer (*bhogī*) offers incense and a lamp, [worshipping] the five Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta and the five beginning with Īśāna.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from the little finger to the thumb and from the thumb to the little finger,

one should take the flower between the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger; then, at that time, having lowered the worship from the top of the *liṅga* with the thumb and forefinger while reciting the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
Having placed that flower upon the *liṅga* as an offering for the head (*mūrdhni*),
one should deposit the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) in the northeast direction (*īśāna-diś*) with the *hṛdaya-mantra* for the sake of Caṇḍa in a pure vessel.
Having placed the eight *liṅgas* according to the *Pāṇḍura-śāstra*, and having washed the pedestal,
one should consecrate it with the heart-mantra ending in *svāhā* using the general *arghya*.
In the Kāmika: Having performed the worship intended for the time prior to that, which is directed toward the top of the *liṅga*, and having worshipped with the Gāyatrī,
one should then offer the general *arghya*.
And in the subtle [practice]:

having sprinkled with the water for the guest-offering (*arghyodaka*), one should perform the ritual placement of the faces (*vaktranyāsa*). One should place the five Brahma-mantras on the fingers from the thumb to the little finger.

Then, one should perform the sequence of placing the faces starting from Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta; meanwhile, one should collect nine flowers with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger.
One should discard the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) with the thumb and forefinger.
In the *Sūkṣma*—
At the time of dismissal, one should place a flower upon the head.
Regarding the cause:
one should never fashion a linga with a hollow head; one should install it for worship in the northeast, not in the center of the village.
In the Kāmika:
"Without purifying the water with the weapon-mantra, one should perform the general arghya and the worship of Śiva along with His limbs and the altar."
The Consecration.
In the *astrābhiṣeka* (the empowerment of the weapon-mantra), [the procedure is as follows: (375–379;
Having bathed [the deity] with scented water, one should perform the consecration with water from a conch shell; having bathed [him] again with the *arghya* water,
one should place a flower upon the head, as well as fragrant unguents and a sprinkling of cool water.
The consecration by a thousand streams is performed with the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries, through the primary seed-mantra and the Śiva-Gāyatrī mantra.
If bathing substances are not available, one should perform the consecration with ghee alone;
if all such substances are unavailable, the consecration should be performed with pure water.
Having recited the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should place a flower upon the head;
then, recollecting the Śiva-mantra, one should place it upon the lotus-seat (padmapīṭha).
In the *Sūkṣma-ātmārthapūjāpaṭala*:
"Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the nectars (*amṛta*), one should consecrate it with water alone— namely, milk, curd,
ghee, honey, and likewise coconut water."
Having offered sugarcane juice, pure water, and an ablution with scented water, one should then present the mantra-flower and subsequently offer the mantra-food.
Having consecrated [the deity] with a thousand [offerings], one should wrap [the image] in a washed cloth using a special *arghya* offering.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Rāmanāthapaddhati*:
Having wiped [the image] with a cloth and armor, one should establish Śiva upon the pedestal.
A specific procedure for bathing a metal image is shown in the *Suprabheda*:
"Having omitted the seat-covering and without the worship of the door-keepers, [one performs] the daily bath."
Without iron, there shall be a bath on every festival day.

One should perform the appropriate purification by means of sprinkling and other rites for momentary objects such as a linga, a sacrificial ground, a wall, or a painting; likewise for earthenware, walls, paintings, and mirrors.
One should perform the ritual bath for that pedestal. First, in the northwestern direction,

for the purpose of warding off obstacles to the sacrifice, one should meditate upon Gaṇapati facing south as before, and having worshipped him with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati," [one should proceed] for his...
On the left side, facing the southern direction, one should worship Lakṣmī as before with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ. Then, to her left,
one should worship the seven gurus beginning with Sadāśiva with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ to the gurus beginning with Sadāśiva..."

Having worshipped thus and offered the general *arghya*, and having prayed, "I shall fully worship the eight deities with perfumes, flowers, and so forth," he should worship Śiva once permission has been granted.
In the Pauṣkara:
"First, there should be a sacrifice to Gaṇeśa for the sake of ensuring freedom from obstacles.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*, it is stated:
"One should worship Gajānana in the northwest on the Tāmrapīṭha;
having visualized him facing south, one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings."
Having thus worshipped Gaṇeśvara, one should thereafter worship Lakṣmī; and in the northeast, one should worship the lineage of gurus and Nandikeśvara.
One should perform all rites, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), using their respective mantras: Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and then Ambikā.
One should take refuge in Guha, Kṛṣṇa, Dhātṛ, and the seven preceptors;
and having stationed [the deity] in Mṛgendra, one should worship the Grandfather (Brahmā) in his place and among the winds and other elements.
May Gaṇeśa and Kamalā worship your sandals with flowers and other offerings.
Having been authorized today to perform the worship of the Supreme Lord,
one should now perform the worship of the seat (*āsana-pūjā*). An alternative method for this is the *śivāsana*.
The essential nature [of the mantra] is clearly stated in the *Pūjāstava*. It is as follows:

the seed-syllable of the power named Dhārikā, which is dark like a blue lotus; the four syllables in reverse order representing the stages of Dharma, Bodhi, Virāga, and Bhūti; and the two syllables for the body and sandalwood.

"I bow to the seat of Śiva, the lotus with its filaments and pericarp, conjoined with the circle of powers. And this lotus-form seat of Śiva contains the entirety of the paths (*adhvan*). As it is said in that very same [text]: "The earth is the bulbous root..."

"Ending with the reality of time," and so forth. In this way, the sequence of the five seats (pañcāsana) should be conceived upon the seat of Śiva, which is in the form of a lotus composed of parts such as the imagined kanda and nāla, [formed] by earth and the other elements.
And it is said in the *Yogaja*:
"First is the seat called Ananta, after that the Lion-seat (siṃhāsana), and then the Yoga-seat."
But the third is the fourth, which is the lotus posture (padmāsana).
"The fifth is declared to be Vimala; one should arrange them above in sequence. Thus it is said.
And these [mandalas] are to be arranged according to the [appropriate] time.
It is stated in the Śrīmat-Santāna:
For bathing, the lion throne (siṃhāsana) is prescribed; for wrapping with cloth, the infinite seat (anantāsana);
and for incense and flowers, the lotus seat (padmāsana) is declared.
One should offer the oblation into the stainless fire that has ascended through yoga;
having prepared the seats and understood them, one should begin the sacrifice.

Regarding the detailed classification of these five seats (*āsana*), the *Śivāsana* is the supreme limit of realization (*avadhikalpana*). As it is said: "In this context, that which begins with *śakti* and ends with the *nāla* is declared to be the seat of Ananta (*anantāsana*); [the qualities] are virtue, knowledge, and so forth."
They know the posture called Siṃha (the lion).
That is known as the Yogāsana of the Supreme Lord, the best of all; beginning from the lotus-knot and ending with the filaments, this is the lotus-seat.

Above the filaments (kesara) up to the edge of the petals is the pericarp (karṇikā), which is the pure seat (vimalāsana). Having thus prepared the lotus-seat (abjāsana), one should worship it with their respective names.

Thus, upon the seat of Śiva (śivāsana), which consists of all the time-periods (adhvan) and contains the five seats (āsana), one should perform the worship beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti. This is its sequence:
There, first, having worshipped on the pedestal of the Deity with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Yogapīṭha-seat," then, in the center of its lower part,
[one should worship] her who is seated upon the Tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), whose body is white as the Ocean of Milk, and upon whose head...
Having the form of a seed and a sprout, she bestows boons and grants fearlessness.
Having meditated on the Power (Śakti) who holds a noose and a goad, who is Action (Kriyā), and whose form is the Foundation (Ādhāra), one should worship her with:

*Oṃ hām, obeisance to the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti)*. Then, by way of pervading the phenomenal world (prapañca), one should [worship] the Lord of Mantras residing upon the Brahma-stone—the white Ananta, seated upon the Māyā-lotus.
Thinking "I bow down," and having worshipped the seat of Ananta with the mantra "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Seat of Ananta," one should meditate upon Ananta above it— resembling a dark blue sapphire,
adorned with a thousand hoods, joined with palms in the heart-gesture (hṛdañjali), possessing one face and four arms.
Having thus meditated and worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta" (p.
[one should worship] in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners of the pedestal—
The auspicious [deities] have the form of lions and resemble white, sunbeam-yellow, and black;
they are surrounded by many lions gazing at one another.
With faces formidable with fangs, three-eyed and of terrifying form,
they [guarded] the seat and sandals of Śiva in the forms of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages.
Alternatively:
Dharma there has the form of a bull, Jñāna has the nature of a lion, Vairāgya is yellow, and Aiśvarya is a white elephant.
Having meditated thus: *Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dharma; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jñāna;
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vairāgya; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Aiśvarya*. Having worshipped Dharma and the others, who are the embodiments of infinite power, [one worships] Dharma and the rest.
The four limbs of the lion throne are likewise located in the east and the other directions. (p. 389)
Black and white on the eastern side, white and red on the south,
red and yellow on the west, and yellow and black in the northern direction.
Thus, the four limbs possess infinite powers:

non-dharma has its head in the south and its feet in the northeast; ignorance has its head in the east and its feet in the west; non-detachment has its head in the north and its feet in the south; and lack of sovereignty [has its head in the west and its feet in the north].
Having meditated [on the deity] with the head in the west and the feet in the east, one should worship the limbs as follows: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Adharma;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ignorance; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Non-detachment; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Lack of Sovereignty. Thus, having worshipped the limbs, [one proceeds].
Having visualized the lower covering as red in color upon the upper rim of the pedestal (pīṭha), one should worship it in the southwest with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lower covering. (p. 390)

Having visualized a white upper covering above the girdle, one should worship it in the northeast with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the upper covering. Then, in the middle of that, in the upper region, [one should visualize]:
"The *kanda* is like a ruby, the stalk has a luster equal to sapphire, and the *kaṇḍaka*..."

Having meditated thus: "The filaments have the luster of coral, a radiance free from dust, and at their tips they possess the appearance of pearls, shining with the color of gold," one should recite: *oṃ hāṃ kandāya namaḥ* | *oṃ hāṃ bījāya namaḥ* | *oṃ hāṃ aṅkurāya namaḥ* | *oṃ hāṃ nālāya namaḥ*.
Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the thorns. On the mortar-plate: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the petals.
Thus, having meditated upon the petals as being the forms of the eight Vidyeśvaras...

Having worshipped that [lotus], one should worship upon the pedestal in its center with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the filaments" (kesarāḥ). Then, one should worship the pericarp (karṇikā), which has the luster of molten gold and contains fifty seed-syllables, by means of the sixty-four filaments.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the pericarp (karṇikā). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seeds (bīja). Having thus visualized the lotus in its complete form, one should worship the firm seat with "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lotus" (padmāya) and display the lotus mudrā. Likewise, it is stated in the *Kāraṇa*:

The firm seat (sthirāsana) is said to extend from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) up to the lotus. Then, upon the filaments from the east to the northeast, reside the presiding lords of knowledge (vidyeśvara), namely Śiva and Śakti, along with the eight powers beginning with Vāmā.
All [the goddesses] are equal to ten million suns, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon;
they have four arms and three eyes, and hold chowries in their hands.
Having meditated thus in sequence— [the goddesses] with hands granting boons and fearlessness, their lotus-hands joined to Śiva— one should recite: *oṃ hāṃ vāmāyai namaḥ*,
*oṃ hāṃ jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ raudryai namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ kālyai namaḥ*.
Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balavikaraṇī;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balapramathinī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamanī," one [worships] in the pericarp at the northeast (Īśāna).
Manonmanī is the great liberation; she dwells in the void, moves through the void, and is auspicious Śivā.
She has the luster of pure crystal, is beautiful, and holds a rosary.
Having meditated thus on Manonmanī, who is adorned with ornaments such as a crown, possesses beautiful breasts, and is in the full bloom of youth—one should worship her.

Having meditated thus: "Upon the circumference at the tip of the petals is the mandala of Śiva-Sūrya, resembling ten million suns," and having worshipped it with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Sūrya-maṇḍala," [one worships] its presiding deity:
five-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed in each face.
Shining with the luster of molten gold and adorned with every kind of ornament.
Having thus meditated upon Brahmā, who is accompanied by Rudra, who is the cause of the cause of creation,
and who is the very nature of the reality of the Self;

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Solar Mandala," and while meditating on [the deity] at the tip of the filaments within the circle as being endowed with the brilliance of ten million moons and as cool as ten million moons, one worships with "Oṃ hāṃ,
obeisance to the Lunar Mandala."
In the center of that [mandala], one should meditate upon Ādiviṣṇu, who resembles a dark blue cloud,
whose entire body is smeared with ashes, and who is adorned with all ornaments.
Having one face and two eyes, adorned with earrings, four-armed,
bearing the conch and the discus, and accompanied by a gesture of salutation.
One should know Viṣṇu, who wears yellow garments, who is the cause of the cause of maintenance,
who is endowed with a crown and diadem, and whose nature is the essence of knowledge (vidyātattva).

Having reflected thus, and having worshipped with "Obeisance to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Lunar Maṇḍala," one should meditate on the Śaiva fire, which resembles the infinite fire, being fashioned there at the tip of the pericarp;
then, having honored it with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Fire Maṇḍala."
Rudra has the luster of the color of rubies; he is one-faced and three-eyed,
four-armed, with matted hair bound in a topknot, and adorned with a crescent moon and flowers.
[I bow] to the God accompanied by Rudra, whose entire body is smeared with ashes, who shines with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and who is the cause of the cause of dissolution.
Or else: white, bearing the orb of fire, blue-throated, three-eyed,
possessing the serpent-seal and the knowledge of fire, with a trident in hand and four arms.

Meditating thus: "Adorned with serpents, wearing the sacred thread of the Naga kings"— and having worshipped with the mantra "Obeisance to Rudra, the Lord of the Fire-maṇḍala," [one should worship] Gāyatrī-Gaurī, who is of a crooked nature and resembles the ocean of milk, in the center of the pericarp.
Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the Maṇḍala of Power, whose nature consists of the union of desire, knowledge, and action," one should [worship] the Lord who presides over it.
[He visualizes] Īśāna, who possesses the circle of powers, wears a serpent as a sacred thread, has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
is three-eyed, and resembles pure crystal.
The god is endowed with hands holding a sword, a trident, an arrow, and a rosary, while displaying the gesture of fearlessness; he holds a water-pot and bestows boons, bearing a lotus.

Having thus meditated on [the deity] as being clothed in a lion and elephant skin according to the sequence from right to left, one should worship with: *oṃ hāṃ śaktimaṇḍalādhipataye īśvarāya namaḥ*. Above that is the seat (*āsana*), which pervades everything from the element earth up to the edge of the curved [world-system].

Having meditated upon this and worshipped with "Oṃ hāḥ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva," and having placed a handful of flowers at the region of the heart, one should utter "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva" ending with the nasal bindu,
[visualizing] the Form as complete and consisting of the Supreme Light.
Having placed [the deity] upon that image— which has the form of a staff with undivided parts— at the navel of the *liṅga*,
by means of the configuration of a staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgyā*).
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās beginning with Īśāna from the crown of the head down to the feet, one should perform the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa;
then, having thus visualized the Yoga-pīṭha, one should install the Mūrti within it.
The Ritual Procedure for Invocation (Āvāhana-vidhi)
In the *Kāmika*:
"One should install the Mūrti-mantra, ending with the principle (*tattva*) of Īśvara, as the measure of the *liṅga*.
This Mūrti-mantra is declared to be encapsulated by the heart [syllable] and ending with the letter *sa*."
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement of the *kalās*; the procedure for that is stated here.
For the sake of accomplishing the site and the body, thirty-eight *kalās* are recognized.
The deposition of the thirty-eight kalās has already been explained; alternatively, one may perform the deposition of the letters (lipinyāsa), or that which is joined with Śrīkaṇṭha and the others.
Therefore, having invoked the form, one should fashion the body of knowledge (vidyādeha); that which is his stainless power,
inherent in Śiva.
That very [energy], through the differentiation of form and action, is considered the body of Sadāśiva;
it is endowed with the sixth vowel and accompanied by the Bindu and Nāda.
Having meditated upon the peaceful [syllable] joined with the heart [syllable], one should fashion the body of knowledge (vidyādeha);
one should perform this likewise for an image (bera), for Sadāśiva, or even for a linga.
He rests upon a lion-throne of mantras, with the earth and other elements as its curved base;
he resembles pure crystal and is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great being.
Seated in the lotus posture, five-faced, with three eyes in each face,
possessing large eyes of vision, action, and will, and endowed with the digit of the moon of knowledge.
The face of Īśāna is white, the Tatpuruṣa face is yellow,
it is endowed with the black face of Aghora, and the face of Vāmadeva is red.
The western face, which is one and very white, is proclaimed as Sadyojāta; it wears a serpent as a sacred thread,
is peaceful, and is adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial flowers;
his lotus-like hands were busily occupied with a spear, a sword, a trident, and an excellent khaṭvāṅga staff.
With his five hands— two on the right and three on the left— he holds a *ḍamaru* drum, a citron fruit, a snake, a rosary, and a blue lotus.
Having intentionally contemplated the manifestation of pure power (śakti-mātra) above the form,
by means of dissolving the semblance of the *liṅga*, one should abandon the state of being a *liṅga*.
Thus, above the *mūrti*, one recites: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*).

Having thus uttered [the mantra] ending with *nāda* and ending with *śakti*, and having meditated upon that which pervades up to the end of the *sadāśiva-tattva*, appearing like a flash of lightning and possessing the luster of a garland of blue lotuses, [one should meditate] according to the length of the *liṅga*.
Having projected the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*),
[one recites] *oṃ hauṃ netrebhyo namaḥ*; thus, the eye is the seed-syllable of omniscience.
Having assigned the face among the five eyes, and immediately thereafter, with the body held straight and upright,

filling his joined palms with flowers and placing them at the region of the heart, he [visualizes] the Supreme Śiva at the tip of the heart as a mass of splendor consisting of the root mantra, according to the instruction of his own guru.

Having meditated upon Paramaśiva at the *dvādaśānta*— partless, self-luminous, and endowed with all auspicious qualities— one should then, by means of the exhalation (*recaka*), [visualize] the Root Mantra as expressed by the clearly articulated vowels beginning with *a*, *ā*, and so forth.

Having transcended the web of bonds extending from earth up to the Equal One (samāna), and having uttered the Supreme Śiva beyond the Power (unmanā-śaktyatīta), the mantra itself— having become one in essence with Śiva through the relationship of signifier and signified— is the mass of radiant energy (tejaḥ-piṇḍa).

Having brought forth through the *pūraka* breath Śiva— who is endowed with the six limbs beginning with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), who flows with supreme nectar, and whose form is the *bindu*— into the *bindu* between the eyebrows;

Having visualized [the deity] as shining like a thousand autumn moons and having meditated on [him] within the handful of flowers during the exhalation (*recaka*), one should invoke him with the *namas*-mudrā; having brought him near with the root mantra and having invoked and established him in the heart-lotus of the knowledge-body (*vidyā-deha*) with the heart-mantra and the stabilizing (*sthāpanī*) mudrā, one should establish the two forms with the root mantra and the proximity (*sannidhānī*) mudrā.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as having become present by pervading [the space], one should offer the *sannidhāna-arghya*; then,
having restrained [the deity] with the *niṣṭhurā* mantra, one should offer the *nirodha-arghya*, and finally,
having dispelled obstacles with the weapon-mantra ending in *phaṭ*— namely *kālakaṇṭhyā phaṭ*.
Having meditated upon the Liṅga-mudrā with the heart-mantra [Hṛdaya-mantra], [one should pray]: "O Lord, Sovereign of the entire world,
remain present within this Liṅga with a state of great affection until the conclusion of the worship."
Having thus informed [the deity], having offered a welcome and the *arghya* water, having protected [him] with the *kavaca* mantra,

having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the heart and other limb-mantras, and having established oneness by means of the root mantra, [one should perform the rite] with the *dhenumudrā*.
And one should consecrate it with nectar using the Mahāmudrā-śakti mantra.
In the Śrīparākhya:
"Having thus conceived the body as consisting of Śakti, [one should meditate] upon that [body] as the supreme cause—
the supreme, eternal, and true reality whose nature is knowledge, bliss, and happiness."
It is all-pervading among all principles, immeasurable, and incomparable; it is devoid of the signified and the signifier, and its sphere transcends both speech and mind.
One should especially manifest the unmanifest within the self that possesses parts;
this is called the supreme invocation (parāvāhana) due to the constraint of the Śiva-mantra.
Thus: likewise,
having performed the invocation with fire by means of the invocation mudrā, one performs the stabilization with the stabilizing [mudrā].
One should act when there is doubt regarding the destruction of one's power.
Having brought [the deity] close by prostration, one should restrain [the breath] with the *arodha-mudrā*.
One should contemplate the supreme, partless *bindu*, which is joined with *bindu* and *nāda*, ends in the letter *sa*, is endowed with the three measures (*mātrā*),
and reaches the end of the *dhenu* [mantra] above that.
One should mentally meditate upon Śiva as the embodiment of mantra within the creation, between the eyebrows;
having visualized him with a luster equal to the orb of the moon, situated within the handful of flowers.
Having brought [the deity] back by means of the *āvāhinī* [mudrā], one should establish it in the heart by means of the *sthāpinī*;
one should perceive the deity, who has entered into a subtle form, as a body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) on all sides.

One should meditate with a sense of presence upon [the deity] as being embraced by the individual soul (jīva), pervading it through the non-distinction between the body and the embodied one, and turned toward oneself.
In the ritual procedure for worship, one should restrain the Lord there with the [mudrā] called Niṣṭhurā;
then one should offer the *arghya* of restraint to Śambhu for the sake of his presence.
Lifting up a flower with the *hetin* mantra ending in *phaṭ*, [addressed] to Kālakaṇṭhī.
Having removed this [impurity] from the end, one should display the *liṅgamudrā*; having performed the salutation with the heart-mantra and veiled it with the armor-mantra.
The heart-mantra is white at the heart; the head-mantra is yellow on the heads;
the crest-mantra is red in the middle of the crest; and the armor-mantra is white at the heart.
One should place the weapon, resembling a flame of fire, among the groups of missiles; thus, by means of this presence, the ritual of sakalīkṛti is declared.

One should meditate on the limbs, though they possess different colors, as having the single color of Śiva; having offered a flower with the root mantra, that indeed is the act of supreme unification (paramīkaraṇa).
One should perform the nectarification (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) of the mantras with the *dhenumudrā*; having formed the *mahāmudrā* with the heart-mantra, one should effect the illumination (*dīpana*).
Having said, "Welcome to you, O Mahādeva," one should pray to the Lord.
Now, if Śiva is invoked, then there must also be his dismissal.

If it is argued that [if this were so] there would be a loss of [Śiva’s] omnipresence, do not say so. For *āvāhana* (invocation) is said to be the manifestation, through devotion and mantra, of Śiva himself, who is all-pervading. And it has been stated:
"The God of gods, Sadāśiva, who is peaceful and pervades everywhere..."
That which brings about presence is here called "invocation" (āvāhana).
But at the conclusion of the worship, there is no dismissal (*visarjana*) for one who is turned away.
If it is argued that this too is contradictory because [the deity] is omnipresent and thus present everywhere;
In this case, there is no need for such a [physical] presence because it serves no purpose;

rather, here [the grace is bestowed] upon the recipient in accordance with the faith of the practitioner, which is permeated by the relationship between the worshiper and the object of worship. (p. 406)

Invocation is the presence of the characteristic of the subject (the grāhaka). And because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier, through the specific arrangement of the mantra as the signifier, there is also the specific [presence] of Śiva, who is the signified.
It is not contradictory that there will be storage.
If it is asked, "In that case, how can there be manifestation and invocation (*āvāhana*) of the *pitta* (extracted essence) in one place?"—
it is true; nevertheless,
it is logically possible because it is like the manifestation in one place of fire situated from root to tip within a tree.
Just as fire residing within wood requires friction for its manifestation, so too it is logical that the manifestation of this [Śakti] from Śiva requires the act of invocation.
If it is argued that, in that case, repeated invocation would be useless, we say no;
for this is justifiable, like the repeated requirement of air to cause the fire within the hearth to blaze up.
As it is stated in the *Kāmika-tantrasāra*:
"Just as the manifestation of fire residing from the root to the tip occurs within a tree,
so too the manifestation of consciousness in one place does not contradict its omnipresence."
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"Just as fire residing within wood is manifested by means of friction and so forth, so too is Śiva manifested through the power of mantra and devotion."
Or is it that Śiva is without body, being all-creating and all-pervading?
Thus, in the *Suprabheda*: "Just as there may be a blazing of fire contained within a hearth by means of the wind, so it is here with the *liṅga*."
Even the Blessed One is manifested by means of mantra.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Just as one's coming and going here may occur through the door of one's own body, so too [they occur] through the door of the mantra-body."
In the sacrifice to Śiva, there are the going and the returning.
Because he possesses inconceivable power, he is both all-pervading and non-pervading.
If it is asked, "How can Śiva—who is beyond the reach of the self and formless—be visible in one place?
the answer is: True. Nevertheless, [he is seen] in the orbs of the moon and sun, even though Rāhu is invisible.
It is like visibility in a mirror, like fire within wood,
like water at the edge of a body of water, like fire within a sun-crystal, like light within a gem,
like lightning within a cloud, like iron in stone, like clarified butter in milk, and like [the dawn] at the end of night.
For even in the case of Śiva, the status of being visible (*dṛśyatva*) is established just as it is at sunrise.
In reality, however, the invocation (*āvāhana*) of Śiva is his remembrance (*smaraṇa*), and the dismissal (*visarjana*) is... [text ends] p. 409).
This should be understood as its forgetfulness.
As it is said in the Vātula:
"Śiva is indeed of pure nature (śuddhasvarūpa), beyond the sphere of speech and mind;
how can there be his invocation, installation, or dismissal?"
Īśvara said: Just as the indivisible, all-pervading ether, when held within a small vessel,
does not thereby lose its infinity or its capacity for universal pervasion, so it is with the Self.
One should not invoke the formless [deity] associated with the meditations, nor indeed the meditation on form;
rather, one should invoke the deity in its own essential form, which is associated with the formless and the formless-less.
The invisible Rāhu becomes visible within the orbs of the moon and sun; likewise, the all-pervading Self, having pervaded all, is perceived within the intellect.
O Six-faced One, just as one sees one's own self in a stainless mirror made of iron, though it is insentient, so too does the Self see itself within the stainless intellect.
In the very same way, having realized that the form of Śiva indeed resides within the center of the body, just as fire exists within wood or water within the depths of water;

As long as fire remains within the sun-gem (sūryakānta), it is not perceived; likewise, the light exists within the center of the jewel, and the radiance within the clouds. It should be understood as being like iron within stone, or like clarified butter within milk.
O Guha, as long as the rising of the sun is awaited, so long is the rising of the body; through the path of the Guru’s instruction, mindfulness becomes the invocation.
And likewise, the dismissal (visarjana) is said here to be forgotten; in this very manner, one should cause Mahāśiva to abide through [the power of] being (bhāva).
p.
411) This invocation is threefold: with support, without support, and transference.
Likewise,
Invocation is said to be threefold, and likewise dismissal is threefold;
it is threefold as well: with support (sālamba), without support (nirālamba), and transition (saṃkrama).

They know that for the purpose of daily worship, there should be a support [for the deity], beginning with incense; and this applies in all cases of installation, whether on a sacrificial mound, on an eight-petaled lotus, or in water.
In these worship rituals during the month of Ravi (Jyeṣṭha), when the fires are without a support, they know that after lifting and then condensing [the fire],
it is the installation and transference within the image.

Thereafter, having announced, "Welcome, O Blessed One," one should offer a special *arghya* with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya pādyaṃ namaḥ*. Thus, the water for the feet (*pādya*) is offered at the feet;
then the water for sipping (*ācamana*) is offered with the mantra *svadhā* toward the east, south, north, west, and upward directions.

Saying "arghyaṃ svāhā," one offers the *arghya* with the tips of the thumb, ring finger, and middle finger, with the palms facing upward, upon the five heads beginning with Īśāna; then [one offers] a flower.

Saying "Vauṣaṭ," one should offer dūrvā grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth. Regarding the radiant form— whether it be like that [form] or like molten gold— the wise practitioner should offer the arghya water at the time of invocation.
And it is said:
"One should first offer water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, dūrvā grass, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth, along with a formal welcome, according to the ritual procedure."
Likewise:
Holding the vessel containing the specially raised *arghya* water with his left hand,
he should present the *pādya* water with his right hand while facing [the deity] directly.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) at the mouths and the arghya offering at the five heads;
thereafter, one should present dūrvā grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth, according to the worldly custom of worship.
With the heart-mantra joined by the utterances *namas*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*, one should offer these four [substances] there after they have been consecrated.
Then, having offered incense, a lamp, water for sipping (ācamana), and the arghya offering with the root mantra ending in "svāhā" accompanied by the heart-mantra,
and while touching the lower part of the pedestal with the left hand while holding fresh flowers with the right hand, he should remove the previously worshipped flower with that same flower.

Having discarded that flower and washed his right hand, he should mentally contemplate the limbs of the ritual bathing— such as the massage and so forth mentioned for one on a movable seat— even while remaining on a fixed seat; then, with water, [he should perform the rite] using either the Śivagāyatrī or the Hṛdaya-mantra.

Having caused [the vessel] to flow, having bathed it with a drop of *arghya* water, and having worshipped it with mantra-offerings (*mantrapuṣpa*), one should present mantra-food for the purpose of extinguishing the blazing fire.
Likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī*:
"The posture is both moving and stationary, and bathing is likewise of two kinds; on a moving seat, however, bathing consists specifically of anointing with oil and so forth."
Having invoked [the deity] into the steady and dark [forms], one should perform the mental bath; then, one should touch that seat with the left hand while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having taken fresh flowers, one should discard those flowers;
a wise person should avoid flowers that have already been used for worship.
Perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) specifically with the right hand;
at the conclusion of the consecration with the mantra-water, one should cause the mantra-flower to be offered.
Then, having offered the mantra-flower, one should present the mantra-food;
likewise, for the purpose of pacifying the fire, one should offer the oblation that kindles it.
The mantra is called the secret; it is not released from the food of passion.
415) Furthermore, the illumination of the secret is indeed called the food of the mantra.

Then, having recollected the Śiva-mantra and worshipped with perfumes and flowers, and having adorned [the image] with a golden loincloth, girdle, sacred thread, balls, clarified butter, water, a crown, and other ornaments,
and having placed a flower on its head and decorated it with garlands of flowers, [he should consecrate it] with the Astra-mantra.
Sounding the bell, having offered incense, lamps, water for sipping, and the arghya offering,
one should display the *manoratha-mudrā*.
Likewise, O Aṃśumatī, having recollected the Śiva-mantra, one should then place fragrant flowers; one should also apply the *golaka*, the clarified butter-water,
and the crown.
Adorned with all kinds of ornaments, garlands, circular designs, and other decorations;
provided with supports for garlands and embellished with variegated strings.
Likewise, in another place,
one should apply sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and other ointments with the right hand.
Indeed, by two [fingers], it is certainly not from the left.
The two little fingers are intertwined in the middle and rest upon their own palms; the ring fingers and the index fingers have their tips joined together and are made even.
One should place the tips of the thumbs upon the root-joint of that [finger], with the desires [fulfilled];
when the lion has moved, the middle finger and thumb are prescribed for those whose hands are thus positioned in between them.
Then, the two index fingers are joined together on one's own palm.
Placing [the thumb] at the base of those [fingers] and at the tips of the two joints, this mudrā named Manorathā brings about the presence of the Lord.
And in the *Ajita*:
"Having made the two middle fingers extended and joined, one should place them at that location."
Then, having placed the two thumbs upon the joint at the base of the thumbs.
Having joined the backs of the ring fingers, one should perform these delightful [mudrās].
They are to be employed by the worshipper in the rite for the presence of Śiva. [This is] the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā).
Thereafter, having obtained permission from Śiva in the midst of the *āvaraṇapūjā*, one should worship either the fivefold enclosure (*pañcāvaraṇa*) or the single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*).
Now, in the case of the *arthapūjā*, having invoked Śiva into that subtle [space] in its midst—

If it is asked, "Since there is the statement 'one should worship the five-fold enclosure,' how can there be the possibility here of a single enclosure?"—it is true; nevertheless, a single enclosure has been taught.

Because of the statement "in the obligatory and occasional [rites]," and because of the statement regarding the lineage, "the single-enclosure worship is for the sake of the time specifically," the single-enclosure [worship],
which is common to the obligatory, occasional, and optional [rites], is also [performed] in the obligatory [rite].

Because it follows logically from what has been established, it is clearly stated in the *Aṃśumatī-ātmārthapūjā-prakaraṇa* that one should perform either the fivefold enclosure (*pañcāvaraṇa*) or the single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*) according to one's choice. It is as follows:
One should worship the five enclosures in the form of the Lord’s manifestations and so forth; or else, in another manner, one should worship a single enclosure.
In the *Kāmika*, a certain distinction regarding the single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*) is stated:
"The worship of the single enclosure should be performed with the limbs (*aṅga*) and the Brahmās themselves."
Or else, [one may worship] with the limbs alone, or indeed with the Brahmās alone. Thus it is said.
p.
419) There shall be three enclosures consisting of the limbs of Brahmā, the world-protectors, and the weapons.
Among these, there are three seats for the worship of a single enclosure, and [five for] the worship of five enclosures.
Five types of seats are permissible.
It is stated in the *Santāna*:
"In the worship of a single enclosure, one should arrange three seats; one should arrange the three seats as the lion, the lotus, and the stainless [throne]."

Therein, the worship of the first enclosure is at the base of the *liṅga*; the worship of the second enclosure is on the upper part of the pedestal (*pīṭha*); the worship of the third enclosure is on the tips of the lotus petals;
the worship of the fourth enclosure is on the neck of the pedestal; and [the fifth] is on the feet of the pedestal.
The worship of the five veils (pañcāvaraṇa) should be performed upon the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), beginning with the pedestal (pīṭha). It is stated in the Santāna [Tantra] (p.
One should worship the single enclosure of the womb (garbhāvaraṇa) while standing at the base of the liṅga.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"One should worship Ananta and the others on the tips of the petals, and there, upon the neck of the pedestal (pīṭha-kaṇṭhe), one should worship the Vidyeśvaras."
One should worship the Gaṇeśas and the world-protectors (lokeśas) starting from the feet of the pedestal.
Then the weapons [should be worshipped] in the lower region, above the *brahmaśilā*.

In this worship of the mobile liṅga (*calaliṅga*), even in the absence of a foundation stone (*ādhāraśilā*), one should worship upon the lotus pedestal (*padmapīṭha*) which serves as the site for the *brahmaśilā*. Thus, by means of the various modes of the Lord’s pervasion, there is the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).
One should employ [the ritual] as follows: there, having taken the faces from the faces and the limbs from the limbs all around the body of Śiva— like the taking of a lamp from a lamp—
one should draw them forth with their respective mantras, beginning with Īśāna, using the *aṅkuśa* (hook) mudrā, and place them in their respective locations.
One should sacrifice.
It is stated in the *Vijaya*:
"The five Brahmans and their ancillaries [are located] around the God from his faces."
From its limbs, one should draw it forth like a lamp from a lamp.

The procedure here is as follows: having worshipped Śiva with the root mantra, one begins with the first of the five heads, taking Īśāna; thus, "Oṃ Hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the head"—this is on the petal of Īśāna.
[One should meditate on him] as crystal-like, the cause of the universe, three-eyed, moon-crested, and perfectly composed.
He beheld the serene Miśāna, holding a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands.
Having meditated thus, one should perform worship. Taking the face from among the five faces, [one should worship] on the eastern petal with: *Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to the Tatpuruṣa face*.
[One should visualize him as] wearing yellow garments and a sacred thread, three-eyed, and golden in luster.
Holding a citron and a rosary, and bearing the moon upon his crest.
Having meditated thus, one should worship.
Taking the Aghora mantra from the region of the heart, [one recites]: *oṃ huṃ aghorahṛdayāya namaḥ*.
Then, on the southern petal, [one should visualize] the Three-Eyed One, with the moon upon his crown, gentle-hearted, adorned with earrings,
with tawny beard and hair, fanged, and possessing a formidable face.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, decorated with snakes and scorpions, and holding a khaṭvāṅga staff,
a skull-cup, a shield, and a noose.
In the four left hands and the two right hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a sword,
a staff, and the "enemy-crusher" (mace).
One should meditate on the non-terrible (Aghora) form, which resembles a fresh cloud and grants all desires;
having thus meditated, one should worship it.
Taking the secret mandala of Vāmadeva, [one recites]: *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevaguhyāya namaḥ*.
Thus, on the northern petal (p.
the left [hand] is red, with a brilliant red luster, and adorned with a garland, garments, and a sacred thread.
He has a prominent nose and a red uṣṇīṣa, and holds a sword and a shield in his hands.
Having meditated thus, one should expel [the breath].
Taking Sadyojāta from the first limb of the first quarter— namely, "Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta"— [one should worship him] on the western petal as one adorned with garlands,
perfumes, and ornaments, wearing a white turban and white garments, and gentle in appearance.
Adorned with a crescent moon on his crown, having the form of a youth, and possessing three eyes.
One should meditate upon Sadyojāta as white, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
having thus meditated, one should invoke him. Alternatively:
[one should meditate upon] the five [faces], beginning with Īśāna, smiling and possessing gentle eyes.
With very white and golden horns, they were pure-blooded and had faces like those of lords.
Richly adorned with the splendor of matted locks and crowns, decorated with serpents and the crescent moon, [they hold] in their left hands a serpent, a rosary, and a blue lotus.
[She holds] a citron. With her right hands, she holds a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, a boon-granting gesture, and a spear.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the invocation.

Taking the eye from among the eyes, which consists of the seed-syllable of omniscience, [he says]: "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the eyes. Thus, in the northern part of Īśāna, the eye is joined with three eyes, white in color, and facing upward; [it holds] a trident.
And he bears a rosary in his right hand.
In his left [hand], he holds a skull-bowl and a water-pot, adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon;
or else, one should meditate on the Lord’s eye, which is reddish in luster and consists of the nature of vision, action, and will.
Having invoked the form consisting of the three principles (tritattva), which rests upon the triad of mandalas,
with its faces as described for the heart and other limbs, and joined with the [mudrās] held in the hands and so forth;
p.
425) Or, according to the teaching of Yoga-Śiva, one should meditate upon [the deity] as having a single face and holding a trident in hand;
having thus visualized, one should invoke [the deity], taking up the heart which consists of the knowledge of true being.
One should worship with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart" on the southeastern petal.

Taking the head, which is characterized by being the self of all lords, from the region of the head, one should worship with "Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the head" on the northeastern petal, to the north of the eye. [The head] has the nature of sovereignty that is not dependent on anything else.

Having taken the *śikhā* from the *śikhā*, one should worship it on the petal of Nairṛti with: "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the *śikhā*. Having taken the armor (*kavaca*), which is of the nature of splendor and impenetrable by others, from all the limbs, one should worship it on the petal of Vāyu with: "Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the *kavaca*."

Having taken the weapon in the form of *pratāpa* from his hands, one should worship it with the mantra "Oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ" upon the tips of the petals in the four directions starting from the east, and on the left side to Tatpuruṣa and the others.
Likewise:
the heart, situated near the right knee, is located in the direction of fire (the southeast).
The head should be located in the northeast, near the left knee.
One should place the *cūḍāvarman* emerging from the right shoulder in the vicinity of the left shoulder,
and the four formidable weapons in the directions starting with the east.
In the *Kālottara*:
"The heart is like the moon; the head has the luster of gold;
the crest (śikhā) is rich with the color of vermilion; the armor (kavaca) is like a bumblebee and the sun."
The eye is like lightning, and the weapon is equal in radiance to fire.
From the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
[He is] seated in the lotus posture, wearing a crown of matted hair adorned with the crescent moon.
Having three eyes and four arms, and adorned with all ornaments.
And [the goddess] with a skull and a trident in her hands, [the deities] with hands granting boons and fearlessness,
four-faced, and likewise the weapon-deity, fanged and tawny in luster.
In some places, they are described as having four faces, four arms, and three eyes.

In some places, the Nāḍīs are said to be single; or else, they are described as having one face starting from the heart, with four arms, bestowing boons and protection. Or one should visualize them even by the mind as bearing tridents and lotuses, or as having four arms holding a trident and granting fearlessness.
One should meditate thus: "And the weapon [is] blazing with a flaming crest.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"That [mantra], though unmanifest, should make everything manifest in its characteristics."
Furthermore, one should perform worship endowed with color and form.
One should place Īśāna fivefold upon the head; [the other four] upon the four faces;
and for those said to abide in blazing splendor, the fifth is placed with the *praṇava*.
One should apply Aghora with the heart and the [other] limbs in the secret place (guha), and Vāma in the feet;
one should then install Sadyojāta with all the limbs, beginning from the feet.
Having placed the *netra* [mantra] upon the eyes, one should then apply the limbs [of the mantra]. As stated in the *Pauṣkara*:
"The seed-syllable of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is joined with that; the true state (*sadbhāva*) is the heart."
His virtues are loftier than his head.
The state of Śiva is independent, and that crest-lock (śikhā) is situated above;
it is naturally concealed from others, remaining capable even in its concealment.
Because of its similarity to armor (*kavaca*), it is designated by that name; that irresistible majesty (*pratāpa*) of Śambhu is called a weapon (*hetu*).
Just as a king does not shine when he is not supported by his royal officers, even though he remains established [in his position], so too the shadow of Śiva does not shine when it remains alone,
established in itself.
It does not shine. Therefore, for the sake of the Supreme Lord’s splendor, the worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjā*) in the form of veils (*āvṛti*) is indeed appropriate.

For these [limbs], there is invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), confinement (*sannirodha*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), just as with Śiva.
The worship should be performed preceded by the eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras) beginning with the offering of flowers.
The veiling (avakuṇṭhana) and the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) are not to be performed. As it is stated in the Kāmika:
"One should worship these [deities] beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) in due order according to their respective mantras."
For these, there is neither veiling nor the rite of immortalization.
For each of these, the wise have prescribed a set of eight ritual acts; bathing and the attainment of the lamp are not separate limbs by virtue of their nature.
Alternatively—
having remembered [the deities] together with the eightfold ritual refinements (*saṃskāra*) and having offered the *arghya*, for the sake of completing the rite,
[one offers to] Īśāna and the others.
p.

430) One should display the *namaskāra-mudrā* for the purpose of invoking the presence of the Brahmās and the limbs [of the deity] known as the cow, lotus, trident, crocodile, and garland. This has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
Then, for the completion of the ritual procedure, one should display the mudrās:
those of the fire, the makara, the trident, the lotus, and the fragrant [cow], belonging to the Lord of the Brahmas.
The desire of others is not one that brings about proximity.
In the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"When the little fingers are touched together and resting against each other's palms, and so too the ring fingers..."
Having extended the two middle fingers, their tips should be joined together.
When the two index fingers are joined at their tips behind the middle fingers and bent at their ends,
and the two thumbs are likewise joined at their tips with the middle fingers, this mudrā is called the *srag* (garland).
When the two index fingers are bent in front of the two ring fingers,
and the two thumbs are placed behind them, O beloved, it becomes the *makarī* [mudrā], which is like a garland.
Likewise, in the *Śrījayamudrādhikāra*: "In both hands, excluding the thumb (*jyeṣṭhāṅguli*), the index fingers (*tarjanī*) should be bent backward and placed against the face."
The two thumbs should be well-joined and extended in the shape of a mouth;
the two little fingers should be placed between them in the form of fangs.
This is the Makarī-mudrā; it circumambulates all obstacles.
It is formed by placing the two index fingers and the two little fingers behind [the palms].

When the two middle fingers are tucked in, three remain extended; with the palms joined and the fingers anointed, it is the lotus hand gesture (pāṇipadma). The thumbs are held within and the fingers are spread out.
Joining the thumbs with the ring fingers, rubbing the middle and index fingers together, and keeping the little and middle fingers extended—
this is the Dhenu-mudrā, which causes the flow of nectar.

Then, having offered a flower to Śiva with the root mantra, one should perform the act of supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) for the sake of the worship being complete and for the removal of defects.
One should contemplate the single-minded accord of all the limbs— worshipped by way of the limbs of enjoyment— with the possessor of limbs, Śiva, and their being pervaded by the splendor of Śiva;
as it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:

And worship would be *tāmasī* (of the nature of darkness) without the act of supreme identification (*paramīkaraṇa*). Here, by Jñānaśiva, the fruit of both the enjoyment of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) and the desire for enjoyment (*bhogaikṣya*) has been stated, as follows:
"The limbs of enjoyment consist of the worship of various weapons and the self abiding in the lotus, [possessing] the qualities of Śiva."
Oneness of the limbs of the Lord is for the sake of attainment; oneness of the worshipper is for the sake of union with Śiva, [he being] a pure soul.
433) Then, one should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Ananta, situated in the directions starting from the east, in the second enclosure, in their proper order. Therein—
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) have four faces and ten arms like Hara;
they bear crescent moons upon their heads, are gentle, reside upon lotuses, and carry various weapons.
They hold a sword, a shield, a bow, and arrows; they possess a water-pot and a rosary;
they are endowed with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; and they have tridents and lotuses in their hands.
All of them assume forms at will and bestow the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation; they are, respectively, golden, fire-colored, blue, bee-black, moon-white, snow-white, red, and black.
Alternatively:
"With hands granting boons and fearlessness, holding the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*) and a rosary,
having one face and three eyes, they are the Śaivas who bring down divine knowledge."
"Three-eyed, endowed with spears and tridents, having one face or possessed of matted locks"—thus [are described] Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, and Śrīkhaṇḍa. (p. 434)

Having meditated upon the eight Vidyeśvaras named Śikhaṇḍin, one should worship them as follows: with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta," one should worship on the eastern face (or petal); with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣma," on the southern petal; and with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śivottama," on the western (Varuṇa) petal.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ekanetra—thus on the northern petal. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ekarudra—thus on the northeastern petal. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Trimūrti—thus on the southeastern petal. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha—on the southwestern petal. Oṃ hāṃ...

One should worship with "Obeisance to Śikhaṇḍin" on the northwest petal. It is stated in the *Suprabheda*: "Ananta is to be worshipped in the east, Trimūrti in the region of fire (southeast), Sūkṣma in the southern part, and likewise Śrīkaṇṭha in the southwest."
Śivottama is in the west, Śikhaṇḍin in the domain of the wind (the northwest); likewise, Ekanetra is in the north, and Ekarudra is in the northeast.
It is stated likewise in the Kāmika:
"Or else, one should worship from the east up to the northeast. This is said in the Sūkṣma:
The enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśāvaraṇa) has been declared; one should then worship [the deities] starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna.
Thereafter, one should worship the lords of the Gaṇas (gaṇeśvaras) in order on the neck of the pedestal (pīṭhakaṇṭha) in the directions beginning with the East. Among them, in the East—
Red in color, joyful, with four arms, one face, and three eyes, he has matted hair; he holds a rosary and a trident, and his hands are joined in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with: *oṃ hāṃ nandine namaḥ*.
In the southeast [is] Mahākāla, three-eyed, with a stout and dark body, his beard and hair tawny-brown, holding a shaven head, a sword, a shield, and a trident in his hands.
Having meditated thus, [one should recite]: *oṃ hāṃ mahākālāya namaḥ* in the south (*yāmye*).
Nirmāṃsavigraha Bhṛṅgī is white, holding a staff and a rosary, and is eternal.
The three-eyed one, with his crest of flame, was intent upon beholding the gods.
One should worship with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhṛṅgin."
In the southwest is the three-eyed one, dwarf-shaped, with the face of an elephant and a large belly, carrying a noose,
a goad, his own tusk, and a ripe mango fruit.
Having meditated thus: "The leader of obstacles (Vighnanāyaka) has a red body and holds a goad and a left hand [in his two hands]," one should worship him with the mantra:
*oṃ hāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*.
In the western quarter:
Vṛṣa, bull-shaped, three-eyed, with his mind fixed solely on Rudra,
the very embodiment of Dharma, as pure and stainless as clear crystal.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣabhā.
In the northwest—
Skanda, wearing a tiger-skin garment, has eight arms of his own; he has matted hair or is shaven-headed, possesses six faces, and has a dark, non-emaciated, tawny complexion.
Skanda has four arms and the appearance of a child; he possesses a golden luster and is endowed with a spear, a cock, an elephant, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda."
In the north—
[one should visualize] the Goddess standing upon a lion, with two hands holding a trident and a mirror,
adorned with a jeweled casket crown and decorated with pearls and other ornaments.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Goddess. In the northeast:
Caṇḍeśvara has four arms, four faces, and three eyes.
Carrying a water-pot, a trident, a rosary, and an axe.

Adorned with a sacred thread made of great serpents and wearing bracelets fashioned from them, he should be meditated upon as the one who establishes the rules of time, appearing with the luster of a fresh rain cloud.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ caṇḍāya namaḥ*. Among those Gaṇas residing in celestial palaces (*vimāna*), Gajānana resides upon a rat.

If it is argued that the sequence starting from the east is contradicted there— since it has been stated that "Skanda, whose vehicle is a peacock, stands alone as Vṛṣabha; but Gaṇeśvara is indeed third,
starting from Kaubera" in due order— the answer is no, because of the difference in systems (*tantra*) and the resulting difference in ritual procedure (*kriyā*).
Because there is no contradiction. In the *Suprabhedatantra*:
"One should show Kālakaṇṭhī in the assembly of the Vidyeśvaras and Gaṇeśvaras.
Then, on the pedestal-base (pīṭhapāda), one should worship Indra and the others in order, starting from the east and proceeding through the directions."
One should visualize Śakra, mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, golden-hued, wearing a diadem, possessing a thousand eyes, and holding a thunderbolt in his hand.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*.
He is seven-rayed and bears a rosary and a water-pot.
Red, garlanded with flames, holding a spear in hand, and seated upon a corpse.

Having meditated thus upon the Wind, who is the life-force of all beings and who resides within the deer, one should worship him with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ vāyave namaḥ*.
One should meditate upon Kubera, the lord of the northern quarter, seated upon a man, possessing a proud yet dwarfed form, with a complexion like refined gold, and holding a mace in his hand.

Having seen Brahmā— plump, yellow-complexioned, four-armed, four-faced, and riding upon a swan— he, whose eyes were fixed [on him], became agitated with desire.

I perpetually bow my head to the divine trident situated in the northeast direction, which has the form of a person and a dark-complexioned body.

In the northeast is the head, resembling a conch shell, shaped like a lotus bud, and having the form of a human being.
I bow to the divine weapon of Viriñca, which is white in luster and possesses auspicious eyes.

one should place the lamps and other items upon it, sprinkle them with the *astra-mantra*, and [place] a piece [of sugar or fruit] on top of that.
With the best of *vaṭṭuka* [potherbs], the root of *sūrpakaṇḍa*, mixed with *tārakā* and other condiments and side-dishes, sprinkled seven times with milk, along with coconuts,
plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, and other fruits, as well as red rice and so forth.

having separately placed [the offerings] for the images (beras), one should place a leaf upon them, sprinkle them with the visible [mantra],

Having fashioned the food-mudrā and displayed it, first offering water once, three, or five times from a single hand for the purpose of rinsing the mouth with the *astra-mantra*,

and having placed it upon the food, one should perform the *stavana* (eulogy), dismiss [any obstructors] with the *astra-mantra*, sprinkle [the food] all around with the *astra-mantra*, and [worship] with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Having given the *āpośana* water to each [guest] individually, one first bows with flowers in hand using the middle finger and the thumb while reciting the *Gaṇeśa-mantra*; then, having offered that flower, one discards it and performs its re-consecration (*pratyāvana*).

Having offered the food offering (naivedya) to the face of Puruṣa with the root mantra ending in "svāgata" for Śiva, one should offer the food offering either in separate vessels for each of the limbs of Brahmā,
or in a single vessel; likewise, for the forms (bera) of Manonmanī and Maheśa, etc., it may be in separate vessels or in one.
Or, having offered it into the vessel (p.
one should offer it to the forms (bera) of Manonmanī, Maheśa, and the others, using their respective mantras.
One should offer water five times. Likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī*:
having smeared it with cow dung, one should make it generally square; one should place the vessel-base in the center and sprinkle it with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
One should place the food offering (naivedya) and the side dishes (upadaṃśa) in the middle of the stationary vessel;
and in the subtle [vessel],
salt covered with condiments and cooked side dishes.
Milk and curd combined with sugar and other fruits are for the middle [caste].
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"One should abundantly surround that [liṅga] on all sides with well-prepared soups, cakes, side dishes, and various kinds of fruits, both ripe and unripe."
Therefore, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented to the God of gods as before;
with a mind full of devotion, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa) in a small vessel, filling the hands.
Or one should discharge [the weapon] once, three times, or five times, by means of the Astra-mantra.
Having placed many offerings and having covered [the vessels] with a cloth, one should set them upon three-legged stands, each separately for the various images.
Aṃśumatī:
One should not fill [the vessel] while delighting in the arrangement of individual cups; above that, one should place a leaf and sprinkle it with water purified by the *mṛdvī* mantra.
Then, having performed three claps of the hands (*tāla*), the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), and the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*),
one should display the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*) and then dismiss the eastern petal.
In the Kālottara:
"Having placed both hands palm-upward, with the thumb and both index fingers [extended], and having indeed formed a fist with the remaining [fingers], these are proclaimed as the Anta-mudrās."

Having sprinkled [water] with the *astamantra*, one should perform the *āpośana* [rite]; [one] should not give [it] with the middle and ring fingers; one should not say [the word] "first" (*ādya*) regarding the limbs.
One should offer the oblation with the right hand while reciting the root mantra; then, having invoked Tatpuruṣa, one should cause the food offering to be presented.
Having recited that mantra, one should offer it to Gaṇeśa; then, having cast away that flower, perform the washing of the hands.
Thereafter, one should cause the offering of food (naivedya) for the Liṅga to be presented five times, three times, or otherwise,
at least once.
Water?
The wise one should cause water for drinking to be offered, saying, "Wash your hands"; then, with that same mantra, he should present the food offering once.
p.
451) However, one should specifically perform the washing of the hands for each [deity] individually;
one should then join [the offerings] with the *liṅga* alone for Gaṇeśvara and the other deities.

Alternatively, one should not fill a single vessel with rice alone. One should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented to Śambhu with the mantra of his heart. Then, having discarded the remains of the offering (nirmālya), one should perform the purification of the place.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The offerings for the limbs of enjoyment should be given separately; however, in the absence [of these], there should be one [offering]. Likewise, by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:

For that purpose, if possible, his *naivedya* should be placed in separate vessels; otherwise, it should be in one [vessel] that has been purified. Regarding the drinking water (*pānīya*), the *Viśvasārottara* states:
The water was exceedingly cool, enriched with elā, vandana,
and candana, and perfumed with fragrant offerings such as pāṭalī and utpala flowers.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Water, or half a foot [of ground], or even half of that again."
In this context, the threefold division is described according to the sequence beginning with the highest.

Having offered a flower upon the head of the deity with the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*, and having visualized that all incomplete offerings have become complete, one should offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the *arghya* offering with the root mantra ending in *svadhā* or *svāhā*. Then, having presented the food offering (*naivedya*), one should perform the rubbing of the hands with camphor and *takkola*.

Having offered mouth-freshening betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) fragrant with nutmeg (*jātīphala*), one should worship [the deity] with the *arghya* offering using the root mantra ending in "namaḥ. As stated in the *Kāmika*:
Once they are satisfied, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) and then a hand-rubbing powder;
for the purpose of completing the hand-rubbing, sandalwood paste should be given for both hands.
O Lord, one should cause to be offered mouth-perfume and betel-leaves suitable for the deity, combined with cardamom,
cloves, camphor, jasmine, and *takkola* powder.
In honey or sugarcane juice mixed with sugar, it becomes a refreshing mouth-cleanser.

One should offer [the oblation] to the Supreme Lord with the root mantra.
