The Fire Ritual (Agnikārya)
Then, having prepared the necessary implements for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), one should announce, "I shall perform the fire-rite to Śiva," and having received permission, perform the fire-rite.
Who has the authority (*adhikāra*) over the fire? The *putraka*, the *sādhaka*, and the *ācārya*. As it has been said:
In the Kāmika [Tantra]: "Thus, especially in this distinguished initiation of the pledge (samayadīkṣā),
one who is pure becomes fit for the knowledge of the fire-sacrifice and the scriptures."
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"What is the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*)? It is that which follows the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) according to the procedure; by means of that, [one attains] the noble state."
One does not have the qualification for initiation and other such rites.
If the preceptors do not perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) due to negligence,
it must be performed with a hundred-thousand-fold count for every year [of omission].
In this way, the practitioners are liberated from the bondage of birth through auspiciousness.
In this regard, there is no qualification for a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*). Likewise, in the *Devikālottara*:
"O Maheśvarī, one who has renounced [worldly life] has no duty regarding rites such as fire-offerings (*agnikārya*), nor [is there] worship."
Rites for the ancestors, pilgrimages, and religious vows.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:

that of the Parahaṃsa ascetics, and that of the two [others], namely the Asita and the Parasakti."

456) Regarding these two, however, their fitness for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) is prescribed.
This fire-rite is indeed a limb of the *arya* [mantra]; it is for the sake of the self, beginning with the subtle *aṃśumat*.

This is because it is prescribed within the section on worship during the course of worship. Furthermore, even in the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), there is the prescription of a fire-oblation (*homa*) in the navel-pit (*nābhikuṇḍa*). This fire-rite (*agnikārya*) is performed in a pit or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in one of the directions—south, southwest, or northwest.

In the *Kālottara*:
"Then, having supplicated the Lord of Gods, one should proceed from there to the sacrificial hall (*homāgāra*).
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:

In that regard, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); it is described here according to tradition. The rite of fire is to be known as twofold: either in the pit or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Just as a vessel (*kuṇḍa*) of a specific form is the means for accomplishing all desired aims,
so too is the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) proclaimed to be for the sake of all desired aims and for the attainment of success (*siddhi*), in the case of the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).
But for the Vedāśrama, it should be one cubit in size toward the southeast.
One should likewise construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), together with its girdle (mekhalā), extending both in width and height;
it should be made either in the northeast or to the east of the yoga-pīṭha.
Regarding the sacrificial pit (*aiṣṭhika*): one should dig a very firm pit, one finger-breadth deep on the outside;
then, [the altars] are respectively four, three, and two finger-breadths high.
Above that is the girdle (mekhalā), and above that is the womb (yoni) extending twelve finger-breadths;
it is eight finger-breadths in width, and the rim (nemi) is half a finger-breadth in height.

Make the entire [area] around the lips like the thumb, and fashion it like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree; or else, one may conceive of the interior of the womb as having the form of a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Then, at the base of the *yoni*, there should be a slight elevation shaped like a water-pot (*kumbha*);
the *yoni* must be fashioned according to the form of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), and not otherwise.
p. 458) Regarding the cause:
the height is one *pakṣāṅgula*, while the width is one *bhūtāṅgula*; it is in the shape of a lotus.
Likewise, one should fashion the navel in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Two parts shall be the measurement for the petals, and one part for the pericarp;
thus, in the daily rite, fashion the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to its beauty.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) have been declared; now the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) is described.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should indeed sweep it with Darbha grass while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Taking the water for the *arghya* offering and sprinkling it,
one should spread it out pleasantly with sands from a pure place, beginningless [in origin], and measuring one cubit in extent.
It should be three finger-breadths in height, level, and without any depressions or elevations.
As stated in the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
"In the absence of sand, it may be made with dust or even with clay."
p.
459) Regarding the worship for one’s own sake with *Aṃśumatī*, a specific rule for the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) has been stated:
having smeared it with cow dung so that it is perfectly square, one should exclude those *darbha* grasses [from that area].
Then follows the anointing and the touching.
Having prepared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with sand, according to the *Viśvasārottara*:
"In the absence of such a mound, one should instead prepare a circle of cow-dung."
Having performed the preparation, the drawing [of the mandala], and so forth, one should then cause the ritual of the rival (vipakṣaṇa) to be carried out.
Thus, having approached the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the altar-ground (sthaṇḍila), or the mandala,

and having sat down facing either the east or the north, one should, with a blade of kuśa grass, draw three lines starting from the east using the Astra-mantra in the center of the pit and so forth, once they have been purified by the four rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa).
One should bring them together at a single intersection with the northern end;
if facing north, one should [draw] three lines with their northern ends meeting at a single intersection, as well as a line with its eastern end.
One should accomplish it.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:

"O wise one, having first sprinkled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with water empowered by the weapon-mantra (*astra*), O Six-faced One, one who possesses the strength of the weapon-mantra should again perform the drawing [of the lines]."
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*: "The scraping of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is considered to be performed with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), and the sprinkling with the Armor-mantra (*varman*).
And in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
One should draw three lines facing east and one facing north;
thus it was stated by Somaśambhuśivācārya:
"One should draw three lines toward the north and this one [line] sloping toward the east with *kuśa* grass."
Or else, there may be a reversal of those [mantras] by means of the Śiva-mantra.
Then, having sprinkled [the site] with the *kavaca* mantra and visualized the perfection of all consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*),
one should place a seat of darbha-grass bundles in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the *hṛdaya* mantra: Oṃ Hāṃ Vāgīśvarī.

Having offered "Salutation to the seat of Vāgīśvara," one should invoke the Śakti with "Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Vāgīśvarī," visualizing her as dark-complexioned, adorned with all ornaments, and in her menses; having worshipped her, [one should visualize] the red-colored [deity] with three eyes and four arms.
Having meditated upon Vāgīśvara, one should invoke him with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvara" and worship him. Likewise—
afterwards, the knower of the ritual procedure should perform the sprinkling again over the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Or, upon a sacrificial mound, one should place a seat made of darbha grass.
Having specially established Vāgīśvarī in the center of that, [as stated] in the *Mṛgendra*: (p. 462)

The wise man should invoke the Goddess, the Mother of the Universe, according to the prescribed rite; having meditated upon her as dark-complexioned, in her fertile state, and adorned with excellent garments, garlands, and ornaments.
She has a serene face and three eyes with pupils like lotus petals;
or else,
she is Vāgīśī, resembling a lotus flower, four-armed, and possessing full breasts.
One should especially cause a woman who has bathed after her menses and is in the prime of youth to hold a lotus, as well as commentaries and books, against her chest.
The wise one should meditate [on her] as having the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, according to the procedure prescribed for the ritual.
Having thus meditated, [one recites]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī.
Vāgīśvara, however, is red-hued, three-eyed, and four-armed.
Endowed with the boon-granting gesture of fearlessness, and accompanied by the holding of a noose and a trident.
Having thus meditated upon the god Vāgīśvara, worshipped him, and offered the *arghya*,
[one should then take] pure fire produced from a forest or the like, or generated in a pure chamber.

Having placed [the oblation] in a pure vessel, one should cast out the portion for the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) as a fragment of fire toward the southwest corner with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ astrāya svāhā*; then, having gazed at the fire with the root mantra, one should perform sprinkling and striking with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Perform the sprinkling with the *kavaca* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Then, by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vahnimūrti," one should take up the consciousness of fire— which has the form of a shimmering star— and unify it with the *bindu*-fire through the *pūraka* breath.
By means of *kumbhaka*, having unified the two fires— the elemental fire of the navel and the lunar fire—
with this triple fire, one should expel it outward through the *piṅgalā* by means of *recaka*.

By means of the *udbhava-mudrā*, one should cause the fiery seed-consciousness (*bīja-caitanya*), which resembles the flame of a lamp, to enter the fire blazing with garlands of flames— reciting "oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the fiery consciousness" (*vahni-caitanya*)— and having worshipped it with the *saṃhitā* [mantras], one should worship it with the *śakti-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having rendered [the substance] nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, having concealed it with the *kavaca* mantra, having protected it with the *astra* mantra,

having worshipped it with the *hṛdaya* mantra, and having honored it as the supreme power (*vīrya*) of the Lord, one should rotate it three times clockwise above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the purpose of agitating the womb (*yoni*).

Having meditated upon Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī, whose heads are directed toward the various quarters of the compass, one should visualize the embryo being cast by Vāgīśvara into the central channel (*garbhanāḍī*) facing oneself; then, with the right knee touching the ground...
One should cast [it].
As stated in the *Kāmika*: (p. 465) [The *Kāmika* says:]
One should cast into it the fire produced from the churning-sticks by means of the fire of the pure self-principle, or else the fire from a sun-crystal,
or the fire from the house of a twice-born.

One should employ [the substance] purified by mantras according to the procedure for secondary rites; one should purify it in a copper vessel or a clay bowl by means of the rites beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
Having discarded the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters, one should sprinkle it with water from darbha grass;
then, having enveloped it with the Kavaca mantra, one should install the Raudra fire.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Having taken pure fire and joined it to the fire of the *bindu*, and having joined it to the fire of the *jāra*, [the mantra] is not rendered ineffective by the fire of the *tantrī*."
Alternatively—
that consciousness of the fire, having been joined with the fire of the heart-lotus, is raised up by means of the base of the exhalation through the *suṣumnā*.
Having joined [the offering] into that blazing fire conjoined with Paramaśiva, one should perform the oblation (*homa*) in that fire of knowledge (*jñānāgni*). As it has been said:
In the *Kālottara*, one should place there the fire of knowledge, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns;
from the center of the heart-lotus, it flows like a stream of milk through the *suṣumnā*.

One should unite that mass of radiant energy, glowing like a cluster of fire, at the station of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta). By the mere act of placing it there, one becomes fit for all ritual actions.

Rites such as the conception ceremony (garbhādhāna) and even the final expiation (niṣkṛti) do not possess even a sixteenth part of the power of the fire of knowledge. Whether it be a daily, occasional, or optional rite, the worship of the fire of knowledge must be performed.
By merely sprinkling [the vessel] once, it becomes consecrated for the sacrificial ladle (sruk); in this same manner, the clarified butter (ghṛta) should be treated with water from the arghya-vessel.
Endowed with all ritual preparations, one becomes worthy of performing all rites;
or else, O Guha, one should prepare the Śiva-fire in another manner.
One should cause the rite to be completed with those known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva;
by that, [the soul] is born as Śiva, free from all saṃskāras.
Having cast [the offering] with the fire-seed syllable (raṃ), one should then worship the Saṃhitā with the root mantra ending in vauṣaṭ,
accompanied by the dhenu-mudrā.
Having rendered it nectar-like, worshipped it, and enveloped it with the Kavaca mantra, one should then protect it with the Astra mantra and worship it with the Hṛdaya mantra.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Having circumambulated the sacrificial pit three times, he should kneel upon the ground.
In the *Kāmika*:
Having projected one's own self into the central channel of Vāgīśī so that it faces [her], one should contemplate oneself as Śiva by means of the heart-mantra or the root-mantra.

Then, having gathered [the materials], the Goddess herself, having put on [the garment], performed the ritual rinsing for impurity (*āśaucācamana*) and offered water for the *arghya* three times with the *hṛdaya-mantra*; and having worshipped [him] with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras.

Having offered five oblations with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and having given the name "Oṃ Hāṃ, you are Śivāgni, the consumer of oblations," one should visualize the fire as having undergone the five purificatory rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*. Then,
having worshipped the two parents [of the fire] with the heart-mantra and dismissed them, one should [proceed] with the water of the general *arghya* offering.

Having sprinkled the sacrificial pit and its girdles with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should spread ten *darbha* grasses—pointing toward the east and north—upon the four girdles in the four directions using the armor-mantra;
and there, in the eastern, western, southern, and northern directions, [one should worship] with: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ*...
Salutation to Viṣṇu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra;
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ananta—having thus worshipped, [perform] the protection of the fire-vessel (agnyarbha).
One should inform [the disciple].
In the Kāmika:
"Having offered three drops of water and having covered [the fire] with good fuel, one should offer [oblations]."
He performed the purifications and ritual sips with the *śauca-ācamana* mantras, and protected the child with the *astra* mantra.

One should indeed offer five oblations with the *mūla-mantra* preceded by the syllables "sadya" and so forth; one should say, "You are the fire of Śiva," while placing the *mūla-mantra* at the beginning.
One should perform the dismissal of the parents to bring an end to the birth-impurity (sūtaka), having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with water for the guest-offering (arghya),
[laying] blades of grass pointing eastward and northward.
Having strewn darbha grass all around the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the Astra-mantra,
a braid (veṇī) is tied with thirty darbha blades of the size of an arm, using the Mṛgendra-mantra.
It is joined at the front with a Brahma-knot; it is wealth and an auspicious seat.
p.
470) That which has the form of a mass of well-arranged hair is compared to a seat (*viṣṭara*).
In the *Mataṅga*:
Following the previously mentioned procedure, the practitioner, facing north, should place [the lines] with their tips pointing east in the eastern part;
in the southern part, [he should place them] with their tips pointing east; and in the western part, [he should place them] facing north.
In the northern part, the sacrificial grass (viṣṭara) should be placed with its tips pointing eastward, and also in the eastern part.

The enclosing sticks (paridhi) are prescribed to be made from the wood of the king of beasts [the *śamī* tree] or from trees suitable for sacrifice, measuring one cubit in length. The little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*)...
They have thick roots, are green, and are free from wounds.

Having draped these [enclosures] as before, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas). As stated in the Kāmika: "One should worship Indra and the other world-protectors upon the enclosures. [They are to be worshipped] upon seats (viṣṭara).
In due order, [he should worship] Brahmā and Rudra as well.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu and Īśvara in all four directions starting from the east,
[one should then worship] the gods beginning with Brahmā and the world-protectors beginning with Indra.
Having warded off the multitude of obstacles, you shall protect the child;
O Brahmin, the Śaiva fire is now described—listen to it with a concentrated mind.
He is endowed with five faces, red in color, adorned with seven tongues of flame, possessing ten arms and three eyes, and decorated with all ornaments.
Clad in red garments, seated upon a lotus,
sitting in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), and endowed with ten weapons.
Then there were Kanakā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā; likewise Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, and another, Raktā, who was made of gold.
Having meditated on Agni with the visualization: "The three [lines] are situated facing upwards; the remaining ones are in order from the east onwards," one should recite: *Oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*.
Having thus performed the worship, one should offer five oblations of sesame seeds with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ agnaye svāhā*.
As stated in the Kāmika:
O Agni, since you possess divine splendor that is supremely purifying, I therefore establish you in the second lotus of my heart and satisfy you.

Thus, having visualized the desired mouth of the fire according to the measurements of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should worship Śiva— along with his abode, beginning from Ādhāraśakti and ending with Śakti, and including the pavitra up to the end— as eternally present within the heart-lotus of the fire.
In the Kāmika:
"One should fashion the mouth and the measurement of the pit according to one's desire. In the Ajita:
Then, one should fashion a single lotus in the fire with the *śivāsana* (the seat of Śiva),
uttering "to the Lotus-Seat" (*padmāsanāya*) accompanied by a salutation (*namaskāra*). Therein, in the *liṅga*, as follows:
The god Sadāśiva is thus proclaimed.
Then, having meditated upon that deity here, endowed with the five Brahma-limbs,
and having performed all the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).

Then, having joined the mouth of Śiva with one's own mouth, and having offered oblations— either a hundred times, half of that, or according to one's capacity— with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* preceded by *dhṛt* (clarified butter), and having offered oblations for the Brahma-mantras and limbs at one-tenth that amount, [one offers] with the mantra *oṃ hauṃ śivāya vauṣaṭ* into the upward-facing mouth.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* for the food offering (*naivedya*), one should offer three mouthfuls of *caru* with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, then offer one oblation each for the Brahma-mantras and the limbs (*aṅga-mantras*), and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, provide water for sipping (*ācamana*),
sandalwood paste, betel, and so forth.
One should worship with ashes, water for the feet, and the eight flowers.
As stated in the *Kāmika*:
O best of the twice-born, one should satisfy the limbs with a hundred, half of that, half of that again, twenty, or even ten times the tenth part of the [water] offered to Śiva.
For one's own sake or for the sake of others, one should perform the fire oblation (homa) every day; one may perform it once, twice, or thrice a day.
In the Vātula:
"One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) once, twice, or thrice a day. The three-times-a-day performance is declared the best; the twice-a-day performance is middling."
Or, O twice-born Śikhin, he may perform it at least once a day as the minimum;
[he should offer] sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, caru-oblation, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
The "Supreme" has thus been described; now hear about the "Intermediate.
They know that fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*) constitute the intermediate [rite].
The sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and the cooked rice offering are prescribed for the lowest [grade].
With clarified butter or milk, or with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter;
or with barley or rice, or with guggulu resin and clarified butter.
The daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) should be performed according to one's means; for the accomplishment of the rite, clarified butter (ājya) weighing exactly one karṣa should indeed be offered.
One should offer sesame seeds and the like while touching them with the conch mudrā;
however, one should offer parched grains, condiments, and so forth with the banner mudrā.
In the *Kāmika*:
"In the absence of clarified butter, the oblation should be performed with black sesame seeds;
or with rice, or with beans, or even with curd, or with barley."
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with bilva fruits, bilva leaves, or auspicious sacrificial flowers,
or with other [materials], according to one's faith and wealth.
O Ajitā, one should offer ten oblations of *bāhutī* flowers with the root mantra in successive order.

One should perform a fire-oblation (homa) for each of the five Brahmās and the limbs of Śiva. In the *Kiraṇatantra*: "In the oblation, there should be the utterance of 'svāhā' at the beginning and 'vauṣaṭ' at the end."
In the *Kālottara*:
"One should then perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *Prāsāda* mantra.
In the *Catuḥśatikālottara*:
O Mahāsena, when [the fire] faces upward, the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is prescribed therein.
In the Kāmika:
"One should offer sacrificial food (haviṣya) in the measure of a single morsel and present betel."
Or, having performed circumambulation and prostration with devotion thereafter.

Having offered the *arghya* with the face turned away, one should raise Śiva residing in the fire and, having joined him to one's own form according to the rules through the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), one should—without further expectation—unite him with the auspicious Liṅga.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Then, O God, one should dismiss the deity at the conclusion of the ritual of worship. Next, for the three [classes] beginning with the Brahmin, one should offer oblations with the four *vyāhṛtis*."
If it is the fourth [oblation], one should offer it with the root mantra. Afterwards, having presented the bali offering to Brahmā and the other deities, and having paid homage to the fire,
[one should meditate upon it] as possessing seven tongues, red in color, five-faced, and with blazing crests of flame.
I worship Śivāgni, born from the womb of Vāgīśī, who bestows auspiciousness.

Having thus recollected, and having offered the oblation, saying "one should cease," he should unite the fire with his own heart or with the *liṅga* by means of the *niṣṭhura* [mantra]: *oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ śivāgnaye namaḥ*.

Thereafter, one should dismiss Brahmā and the other guardians of the world (lokapālas) in due order. Alternatively, having extracted the fire from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or elsewhere, one should preserve the living fire in a new vessel.
If that fire should go out, one must perform an expiation (prāyaścitta).
In the *Kāmika*:
"Afterwards, having gratified Śiva and the Śiva-fire with the *vyāhṛtis*,
one should restrain it right there and protect it every day."
In the subtle [rite],
having taken fire with a firm [vow], one should offer it into the root-linga; then, having taken the sacrificial seat (viṣṭara) and untied the knot, one should dismiss it.
Having brought the sacrificial grass for strewing, one should sprinkle it with clarified butter; then, taking a single blade of darbha, one should burn the remainder starting from the tips.
Having cast that single [bone] into the fire, make a *tilaka* with its ashes. Wearing those ashes will increase their lifespan, prosperity, and fame.
For the sake of victory and the destruction of diseases, and for bestowing the fruit of all desired objects,
one should apply that *aṃśumatī* ash upon the forehead with the Netra-mantra.
In the *Ṣaṭsahasra*:
"Then, having extracted the Śiva-fire, one should establish it elsewhere and protect it;
there, the suppression (nirodhana) must be performed with the Niṣṭhura-mudrā."
Having paid homage to the remaining fire situated in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should dismiss it.
As stated in the *Vijayottara*:
"One should always protect the fire by means of the oblation of the four vyāhṛtis; or else..."
One should dismiss the fire and then apply the rite of re-consecration.
480) Regarding the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), preceded by the removal of ashes,
the *Kāmika* states:
Alternatively, one may dismiss the fire into the sacrificial pit and preserve it elsewhere; however, if the preserved fire should go out, one should fast and recite the Ghoramantra.
Even though Nirvana is auspicious, one who has fasted for three nights should either recite or offer oblations with the Bahurūpa mantra for the sake of complete tranquility.

In the auspicious southern direction, having prepared a square maṇḍala with cow dung for the sake of the bali offering, one should place [offerings] at the edge of the maṇḍala in the directions from east to north, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Rudras;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Mothers; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Gaṇas; Oṃ..."
Hāṃ, obeisance to the Yakṣas. In the corners beginning with the northeast: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Planets;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Asuras.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the rākṣasas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the nāgas.
In the center of the mandala, in the northeast, southeast, and southwest: *Oṃ hāṃ namas to the constellations*;
*Oṃ hāṃ namas to the zodiac signs*; *Oṃ hāṃ namas to the Viśvedevas*; *Oṃ hāṃ namas to the gods*. Between the northwest and the west: *Oṃ hāṃ namas to Kṣetrapāla*.

Having worshipped with "Namaḥ" and offered the *arghya*, one should present the *bali* to Rudra and the others with their respective mantras ending in "svāhā," using food mixed with water, and then offer water for sipping (*ācamana*). Thus,
it is said in the *Kāmika*:
Or, having prepared a small mandala on the ground, one should offer the bali-oblation right there; one should offer it to the Rudras in the east and likewise to the Mothers in the south.
To the west of the Gaṇas and to the north of the Yakṣas, one should offer the bali;
likewise to the northeast for the Grahas, and to the southeast for the Asuras; [and] to the northwest...
From the nāgas that feed on fat, in the domain of the wind.
To the constellations, the zodiac signs, and the hosts of the Viśvedevas, one should offer a bali sacrifice according to one's desire in the area inside the mandala.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla in the northwestern direction;
this is likewise prescribed for one's own sake in houses, temples, and other such dwellings.
One should offer the *bali* offering separately for each of the retinues beginning with Indra;

according to this statement, one should perform the *bali* mantra-rites for Indra and the others. Likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī* [tantra], it says: "One should offer to the Rudras in the east, and likewise to the Mothers in the south."
One should offer the bali-oblation to the Rakṣasas in the western part and in the north.
The wise man should offer oblations to the planets, the asuras, and likewise to the rākṣasas, and to the nāgas, starting from the southeast (āgneya).
In the center of that mandala, one should offer the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla; having gathered all the mantras, one should then offer the bali once.
Likewise, [one should offer it] to those dwelling in the directions beginning with the east.
One should offer [the oblation] with the words: "Homage to the lords of the directions, the group of Mothers, Rudra, the Kṣetrapālas, and the rest.

Alternatively, at the conclusion of the food offering, as in the case of the ritual for others, one should give the *bali* offering to Rudra and the others upon the mandala in front of that, and then perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*).
Likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī*:
"In front of that, one should offer the bali-oblation and a square mandala; one should worship with water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya-offering, along with perfumes and flowers."
p.
484) However, after the removal of the *baliviṇava* [offerings], one should perform the fire-rite (*agnikārya*).
On the courtyard outside the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), [one should offer] with: *oṃ hāṃ vāyasādidyaṃ samayavedibhyaḥ*.

Having worshipped with "Svāhā" and offered the *bali*, one should offer the *bali* separately for each, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Asyādi and the others; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the deities of the house and the site (*gṛhavāstu*).
Then, one should dismiss them all with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). Thus it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
Having dismissed them and gone outside, one should cast an offering (bali) upon a circle of cow-dung for the dogs, spirits, fallen ones, ghosts, Kāpālikas, and so forth.
Alternatively, one may offer the *bali* with this mantra in brief:
"Oṃ! Those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce abodes, and whoever are gentle and dwell in gentle abodes."
The Mothers who have the form of Rudras, those who are lords of the Gaṇas, and others who are obstacles dwelling in the cardinal and intermediate directions; (p. 485) [all these]...
May all, with well-pleased minds, accept this offering;
may they swiftly grant us success and always protect me from worldly existences.
Having thus offered the oblation (*bali*), one should place the mantras within one's own heart. Thereafter,
having reduced the collection of substances within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to ashes and removed them,
one should smear the interior and exterior of the pit with cow-dung water, and then once again—

At the time of the fire sacrifice (homa), having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and kindled the fire established therein, one should worship Śiva within it as before and offer libations. In this manner, one should perform the rite every day.
As it has been said:
"Every day, the ritual actions prescribed for the *kuṇḍa*, such as its delineation (*ullekhana*) and so forth, should be performed; thereafter, one should cause [the deity] to awaken."
Nor [is there] fire in the case of obligatory and occasional rites.
In this context, it is prescribed that one should perform the occasional rites established by the consecration (*dīkṣā-pratiṣṭhā*). As it is said:
"Once the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) has been consecrated, one should daily deposit the previously consecrated fire into it. Likewise:
"By the command of Śiva, the maintenance of the fire as the fire of Śiva is meritorious for as long as one lives."
Having carefully extracted it from the vessel, one should place it in a firm container.
One should carefully protect the fire with a dense mass of dry husks and small twigs.
Having consecrated the sacrificial pit as before, and circumambulating it daily,
one should place the fire therein and offer libations to Śiva.
At the conclusion of the ritual, the initiates must diligently perform protection as previously described.
Having thus ensured thorough protection, for him who should offer libations until the end of his life— his...
No one here is able to describe the fruit of his merit; therefore, the funeral rites for him must be performed with that very fire.
In other cases, this ritual effect does not apply to ordinary persons;
however, when there is ever a risk of regional distress, the dismissal of the fire may be performed.
Having joined [the deity] within the heart at the *bindu* in the fire of knowledge, one should dismiss it;
then, one should perform the expiation for the seed-syllable that remained stationed there.
When the mind is again composed, one should perform [the rites] as previously described.
Then, having performed hymns of praise, salutations, and so forth, and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
with the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya) in hand, one should go before Śiva, sit upon one's own seat, and proceed.
O Supreme Lord, whatever merit has been performed by me today through acts such as worship and fire-offerings—
that fruit of that merit I offer unto you; please accept it.
Out of my own affection, O Lord, this was not for my own enjoyment.

"O Maheśvara, whatever merit has been gained by me through action, mind, or speech— having spoken thus, [one should offer] the worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth, ending with *svāhā*, along with the root mantra,
together with the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) into the hand of the boon-granting God, using the *udbhava* mudrā, while the knees rest upon the ground."

One who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*) should offer [the fruit]. If one desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), one should recite: "O Lord of Gods, may there be for me that fruit which is the means for achieving both worldly enjoyment and liberation," and thus offer it.
[In the *Aṃśumatī*:]
Alternatively, one should perform the recitation (japa) itself in another manner,
either because of a deficiency in the implements for the fire-oblation (homa) or because one is otherwise unable to do so.
Having recited the mantras ten times the number of oblations offered, one should offer that flower upon the hand of the Bestower of Boons while performing that recitation.
Having offered the *arghya* especially while recollecting the *Śiva-mantra*,
and then having consecrated [the deity] with incense, lamps, inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), and so forth,
and having displayed the incense and lamp mudrās, one should offer the bell mudrā.
Sounding with the bell-mantra and having offered [the oblation] to Śiva,

one should gaze upon Śiva— who is joined by one, three, five, seven, or nine [offerings]— and, having consecrated him through inspection and other rites, display the incense, lamp, and mudrās; then, [reciting] "kṣa," [one offers] to oneself or to Vāṇḍa.
For the sake of liberation arising from mind and body, and for the sake of union with Śiva,
one should take flowers together with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and *kuśa* grass in the hollowed palms (*añjali*) and [recite]: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ ātmā-*

Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the Ātmatattva. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the Vidhātṛtattva. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the Vidyātattva. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the Śivatattva.
Thus, one desiring liberation should offer that which is eternally pure.

If he desires to enjoy [the fruits], he should offer [the gift] after reciting a mantra beginning with the Śiva-tattva; or else, he should offer the purifier (pavitra) with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of all principles.
As it has been said:
One should place the purifier, having become manifest, upon the head; [this serves] daily as a means to counteract [the impurity] produced by the activities of speech, mind, and body.
Because it protects from falling, this is called *pavitraka*.
(Kāraṇa, p. 491)
One should daily offer the sacred thread (pavitra), accompanied by offerings of dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, unbroken rice grains, and sacrificial leaves, while reciting the root mantra.

One who desires the [divine] form should likewise offer [oblations] while reciting and remembering: "Obeisance to Śiva, the sovereign of the reality of the Self," and likewise that which is called Śiva.
Then, the *bhogin* who has attained Śiva should place the purifier upon his head.
Here, by the word *bhogin*, the initiated one is meant.
As it is said in the venerable *Raurava*:
Having become initiated into the maṇḍala of Gaṇapati and Guru, those who have attained perfection through mantras shine with bodies radiant from the splendor of the rising sun;
having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time accompanied by throngs of nectar-like women, their ears droop with delight.
How does one become a master of the supreme sovereignty of the state of Śiva?
492) For one who has become purified, the gift of the *pavitra* destroys the threefold suffering and brings about the accomplishment of all goals.
Thus it has also been stated by the Teachers: "If this is not performed, the worship becomes *rājasa*. Likewise, in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
'Worship without the *pavitra* is proclaimed to be *rājasa*.'"

Having placed the *ārātrika* lamp—consisting of a wick and a lamp—along with camphor in a vessel of nine, five, three, or one [parts], upon a three-legged stand; having offered incense and lamps with the fourfold purification (*catus-saṃskāra*);
having displayed the *dhenu-mudrā*; and having taken [the offering] with the Heart Mantra ending in *svāhā*.
Having rotated each of the iron [vessels] three times in succession and lowered them, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth and the *arghya* offering, mixed with camphor.
Having taken the ashes with the *mṛgamudrā* gesture, having whirled it three times above the *liṅga*,
and having cast it into the *ārātrika* vessel, one should apply the ashes to the image of the God, the Goddess, or the various icons as appropriate, using either the thumb and ring finger. Likewise—
Immediately thereafter, one should illuminate the interior of a vessel filled with smokeless, glowing embers by means of burning incense.
"A lamp is prepared with five, seven, or nine wicks.
In the *Kālottara*:
"One should contract the little finger and the thumb, and extend the remaining fingers; this is the incense mudrā (*dhūpamudrā*)."
This shall be the lamp mudrā; now hear [the description] of that.
One should press the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger with the thumb;
having raised the index fingers, one should display the lamp mudrā.
The single sound (ekanāda) is praised for the sake of liberation by those who are dispassionate;
likewise, the ringing of the bell (ghaṇṭātāḍana) bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
One should produce the sound with the knee, but one should not cause it to be produced otherwise; the striking of the great bell, however, should be performed above the navel.
The highest [voice] has a smooth resonance, the middle is likewise middling, and the lowest has a gurgling resonance; these are the characteristics of sound. —In the Ajita:
Now I shall describe the *ārātrika* for the pacification of all sins: that consisting of nine lamps is the best, while one with five lamps is middling.

The inferior [offering] should be performed with effort using three or one lamp, proceeding according to the sequence of the bowls; then, having lifted it, one should circumambulate it three times above the deity.
In the *Tantrasāra* (p.
Having rotated [the mantra] three times each from the feet up to the head, one should then apply the ashes. Then, the ashes...
Having gathered camphor and other fragrant substances.
Having grasped it with the *mudrā* of sight and rotated it three times over the *liṅga*,
one should then cast it into the lamp-vessel; thereafter, one should place it slightly upon the head of the *liṅga* with the right hand while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
In the Kāmika:
"White, pure, fragrant, and immediately free of grit;
with the thumb and ring finger, one should apply the *tilaka* upon the five faces."
One should sprinkle each individual lamp with the auspicious water (śivāmbhas). Having tied a fragrant flower, one should then display it above the lamp.
If the Goddess is manifest in form, one should apply a tilaka-mark on her forehead; then, by means of the root-mantra of the forehead...
Or else, one should lead it by means of the heart.
p.496) One should apply a *tilaka* on the forehead, the heart, and the region of the arms.
As stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
What is the purpose of protection in the middle of the eye on the forehead?
One should cause the protection to be bestowed upon the god above the forehead-eye.
Immediately thereafter, having performed the ritual touching of water (jalopasparśana), one should present the mirror, umbrella, chowrie, fan,
and palm-leaf fan in sequence with the five Brahmans;
then follow with the hearing of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and the five ancillary sciences (pañcāṅga), as well as hymns, pure dance, and music devoid of vulgar song.
Having gratified Śiva with the sounds [of mantras] and meditated upon the satisfied Śiva together with the limbs of enjoyment,
one should offer three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra and display the Mahāmudrā.
It is stated in the *Aṃśumatī* (p.
"Having performed the ritual touching of water, one should then show a mirror, as well as an umbrella and chowries."
And likewise, a fan made of palm leaves as a condiment.
Having recollected the five Brahmans, one should join them in due order; likewise, with the Vedas and the Purāṇas, there is then the hearing of the five ancillaries (pañcāṅga).

One should offer hymns of praise, dance, song, and the sound of musical instruments before Śiva; as stated in the *Śivadharmottara*: "One should offer a mirror made of clear material before Śiva for ten thousand times ten thousand kalpas."
He is glorified in the world of Śiva.
One should offer a parasol made of jewels or gold, pure as the rays of the autumn moon and adorned with strings of pearls.
He was graced by a parasol, together with a sacred ring, being held over him.
One shall dwell for a long time in the City of Śiva, enjoying hundreds of celestial palaces (*vimāna*).
(From the *Tantrasāra*—p. 498)
One should offer a fly-whisk adorned with a jeweled handle to Śiva, or one with a handle of gold, silver, or other materials; hear now the fruit of that merit:
surrounded by divine splendor, his hand’s fingertips shall be occupied with a fly-whisk.
Abiding in a celestial palace of great enjoyment, one shall dwell steadily in the City of Śiva.
As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"One should fashion a peacock-feather fan and likewise a fly-whisk from the hair of a female yak."
The staff should be made of gold and jewels, or else of silver or copper.
One should especially fashion a staff out of ivory or wood;
according to the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*,
it should be made with the root mantra, and one should place flowers upon the head.
One should bind the mahāmudrā and whirl the hand above it.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Having made a request, the wise one should perform the recitation (*japa*) with a rosary."
This rule is produced for those who are like dice to the dice themselves.
The rosary is so called because it brings about both seen and unseen fruits.

For instance: having taken the prayer-bead garland, one should gaze at it with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) placed upon the hand, sprinkle it with the *īśāna* mantra, bind the directions with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and enclose it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).

Having consecrated it with the *kalāma* mantras, worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra, and having formed the *mālā-mudrā*, the one who knows the ritual procedure should perform self-protection and the protection of the mantra;
then, grasping a flower at the base of the little finger and ring finger, he should cover it with a cloth.
Then one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times, or half of that.
Likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī* [tantra]:
"Having taken up a rosary (*akṣamālā*), one should place it in the left hand; [this is] the *īkṣaṇa*."
The sprinkling is performed with the heart-mantra itself, using the seed-syllable mantra.

The binding of the directions is performed with the Astra-mantra, the veiling with the Kavaca-mantra, and the consecration with the Kalā-mantra; thus it is endowed with the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
In the *Kālottara*:
"Between the two moons, one should contemplate one's own body with effort; by that, the body becomes composed of nectar, such that it cannot be pierced even by those who possess the ten weapons."
Self-protection has been fully explained; now the protection of the mantra is being described. One should place the mantra within the Śakti, and not in the Puruṣa nor likewise in Śiva.
Those who abide in the Puruṣa are powerless, whereas those who abide in Śiva possess tranquil splendor;
therefore, the mantras that have emerged from Śakti bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"One should not join [the disciple] to a reality that is dependent on another" (p.
Likewise—

One should not employ a mantra upon the *puṃs* (the individual soul) nor upon the supreme reality (*para-tattva*). If employed upon the *puṃs*-tattva, it becomes inert; if upon the *bimba*-tattva (the physical form), it is fruitless.

In the supreme reality that is free from conceptual proliferation, a mantra becomes fruitless; a mantra is not accomplished without being recited, nor does an oblation bestow fruit [if it is not accompanied by recitation].
"He who does not worship nor restrain his desire—therefore, one should practice truth.
Thus [it is said].
O Brahmin, the primordial Śakti is supreme and bestows the fruits of Śaivism; she should always be known as non-different from Śiva, like the rays of the sun.

The Mother of Mantras is the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), who is indeed that primordial Kuṇḍalinī. Residing eternally in the region of the heart—[this mark is given in the Mātṛkā manuscript]—she resembles the sun, moon, and fire. She should be known as one-fold, two-fold, or three-fold; she is Iḍā.
From this point, Piṅgalā goes to the south.
Hidden within the Suṣumnā and known only through the mouth of the Guru, it functions by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
From the path of the trident, she goes to the *dvādaśānta* for yogins; through the distinction of going and returning, she proceeds to the state of Śaṅkara.
"Having resorted to the supreme state, which extends from the navel to the limit of the twelve [finger-breadths], one attains the infinite beyond. Thus,
having understood the power and so forth, one becomes capable of protecting the mantra."
In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
"The Lord has proclaimed that one hundred and eight [recitations] is indeed the best; half of that is the middling."
That which is half of that is prescribed as the smallest [measure].
Born from rudrākṣa, it brings great prosperity, grants liberation, and is supremely auspicious—
whether with one face, three faces, four faces, or five.
It should be performed with six faces; therefore, one should avoid those that are mixed. One should place face upon face and join root with root.
This is declared to be the best when the size of an *āmalaka* fruit;
the medium and inferior sizes are the size of a jujube (*badara*) and a chickpea (*caṇaka*), respectively, [measured] with a thread of ninety strands. (p. 503)
The auspicious rite previously described should be performed as before.
One should perform the Nāgapāśa, the Sāvitra, or the knot known as Brahma;
above the knot, one should fashion the Meru known as Meru, which must not be transgressed.
One should wash it with the Sadyojāta mantra, rub it with the Vāmadeva mantra, fumigate it with the Bahurūpa mantra,
and smear it with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should consecrate each [of the other four] with the fifth mantra one hundred times each; likewise, one should consecrate Meru with the fifth and with the Ghora mantra.
Having worshipped Meru with the five [offerings] as before according to the Śiva-rite,
the wise one should take a flower with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger in the *sūkṣma* [mudrā].
Having covered it with a concealed cloth while recollecting the root mantra.
p. 504) Likewise, in the *Cintya-viśvasādākhya*:
"Thereafter, one should mutter the root mantra while employing a rosary; [it should be held] in the left hand."
One should cast the flower with the right hand.
Having placed the book in the right hand, one should perform the recitation, especially that which is mental, whispered, or spoken; among these, the first is the most excellent of the excellent.

The whispered recitation is said to be middling, while the spoken recitation is indeed the lowest; therefore, having abandoned the spoken recitation, one should perform the recitation mentally or in a whisper.
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā it is stated:

"The vocal [recitation] is prescribed for the silent sacrifice (upāṃśu-yajana) and for the act of oblation; the mental [recitation] is declared to be the recitation of mantras, which is the essence of all mantras."
In the Kālottara:
"The wise one should always perform the recitation using the thumb and the ring finger.
The thumb and the ring finger indeed bestow the fruit of all desires;
likewise, in the *Ṣaṭsahasra*: "One should perform mental recitation with the tips of the thumb and the ring finger."
By means of exactly one hundred and eight [recitations], the fruit becomes ten-millionfold.
One who joins the syllables and the non-syllables (vowels) neither too fast nor too slow shall obtain a thousandfold fruit; this word is not false.
For the sake of enjoyment, one should rub [the beads] on the rosary by way of creation; for the sake of liberation, one should rub them slowly by way of the upward path.
The practitioner of mantra should not step over Mount Meru; by stepping over it, he incurs fault. He is purified by reciting the mantra of Bahurūpa one thousand times.
If [the rosary] falls to the ground through negligence, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred times;
for falling in other circumstances as well, no expiation is required.
Alternatively, one should diligently fashion a rosary that is devoid of the Meru bead;
for there is no fault in its transgression when it is bereft of the Meru.
Likewise:
"O Six-faced One, one should not show one's own mantra or rosary even to the guru; at the time of recitation, the prayer beads must be kept secret."
A garland belonging to another’s view would make the recitation fruitless;
thus, having recited the aforementioned one hundred and eight times over the flowers, the practitioner,
having placed those flowers from the palm of his own right hand onto the palm of his left hand, [should perform] the *astra* and *kavaca* [mantras].

Having placed the heart-mantras one above the other, having encapsulated them with the heart, armor, and weapon mantras, and having protected it with the weapon mantra and sealed it with the armor mantra, he should take it in his right hand.

Having placed [the hand] at the region of the heart and meditated upon the recitation (japa) as residing within the power of the sprout of the moonlight of the heart— resembling the full moon— one should,
with the right knee touching the ground, offer the water of the *arghya* with the *udbhava-mudrā* while uttering the *praṇava*.

Having recited the mantra consisting of the three verses together with the *hṛdaya*, one should perform the rite of recitation and, in due order, offer oneself with water from the hollowed palms into the hand of Śiva that grants boons.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
Having placed the left knee upon the ground, one should offer the recitation to Him; it should be consecrated by the Heart-mantra itself and enveloped by the Armor-mantra.
And it is protected by the Astra-mantra and by the mudrā known as Udbhava. Thus [it is said].
Ajita,
I shall describe the ritual of water in the hollowed palms; listen to that, O Janārdana.
The water for the *argha* offering should be placed in the hollowed palms of the right hand.

Having placed that [object], provided with fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, within his heart, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra; listen to that with a concentrated mind.
Oṃ hāṃ! O protector of the secrets and all that is most secret, accept this recitation performed by us;
may accomplishment be mine through your grace, as you preside over it.
Oṃ hāṃ! O Lord Karṇa, whatever good or evil deeds I have ever committed, consume them and destroy them for me, who am established in the state of Śiva—O Śaṃkara!
Oṃ hāṃ! Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire universe. Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; he who is Śiva, I am indeed that very one.
The meaning of this is as follows: you alone are the protector of the secret [mantras] and so forth, such as *śuddhavidyā* and the rest (p.
Therefore, because you are the protector of all, we have composed this [work].

"Accept this recitation (japa). Because, when this recitation is established in the fourth state (turya) through your grace, the accomplishment characterized by worldly enjoyment and liberation will accrue to us; it cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, accept it. O Lord, whatever I have done, whether good or evil—

Karma exists. For one who stands upon the state of Śiva—that is, for one established in the firm conviction and realization "I am Śiva" through absorption in the state of Śiva—[the following applies]. According to Amara, *pada* means "determination," "protection," "place," "mark," "foot," or "object. Therefore, experience that karma.
O Protector, for the sake of the weapon that brings about liberation as its ultimate goal, destroy that which is well-formed;
annihilate that which is ill-formed.
Now, another mantra: "Śiva is the giver; 'śī' is that which stands; the root *yana* is intended here.
Śiva is the enjoyer and the protector; Śiva is this entire universe. The word "rules" (*īṣṭe*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

Or, it means "he presides over. He who, having become pure Śiva through initiation (dīkṣā), performs sacrifice in all places and locations, worships the distinguished Supreme Śiva as the one to be purified, and so forth—he is the worshipper; he is none other than I, Śiva, and you are the object of worship.
By the word "Śiva," one establishes the demonstration of the relationship between master and servant, in that the worshiper shows acceptance by saying to the Lord of the World, "I am yours."
Having thus recited the mantra together with one's own name and the root mantra,

Having enclosed [the offering] with the armor-mantra (*varman*) through repetition, one should present it. As it is stated in the *Kāraṇa*:
"With the right hand in the *añjali* gesture, the four fingers slightly bent, having taken flowers and water, one should cause them to be offered at the base of the feet."
O Prajāpati, at the conclusion of the worship, this is known as the "cupped-water" (culukodaka);

But with three handfuls of fragrant water.

"Then one should cause the recitation of the limbs of Śiva and the recitations themselves to be performed.
Thereafter, the worshipper, together with the mantra, should make a formal request for that purpose."

Having received permission, one should place the forms of Gaurī and the other goddesses in female form on the eastern side— in the left, right, and middle of the southern petal of the lotus that serves as the seat for Śiva, who is worshipped within the center of the Śivaliṅga— for the sake of attaining the excellence of unsurpassed heroic power.
In the western part:
seated upon a white lotus throne situated within a jar of nectar,
four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon.
Clad in a tiger skin, adorned with a lordly serpent and snakes,
he holds a trident and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) above, while holding a vessel of nectar between his two middle [hands].
If he has six arms, he holds a trident and a rosary.
Or [holding] a skull-cup and a pill in the two left hands in the gesture of union (yogamudrā); there is no mantra equal to this for the protection of life.
"This which has been proclaimed is neither non-existent nor real; it is the truth.

Thus, preceded by meditation, one should worship Mṛtyuñjaya and the others in male forms. In the center, one should worship those in both female and male forms: Umā as the left half and Hara as the right half.

His body [is as follows]: the right [face] bears a crown of matted hair marked by the half-moon; the left [face] is endowed with a crest of locks and a jeweled casket-crown; and it is joined on the right side of the forehead with a half-eye.
The ear-ornament (*pattra*) should be on the left ear, even if joined with a lock of hair; one may fashion a serpent-earring (*nāgakuṇḍalaka*) on the right, or otherwise dispense with it.
He was adorned with a garland of *umā* flowers, free from distress, and arrayed in garments of variegated cloth.
She is depicted wearing a tiger-skin garment with her right leg bent,
while her left foot is well-placed and adorned with an anklet.

Thus, preceded by meditation, one should worship the mantras of Umā-Maheśvara, Ardhanārīśvara, and others. Therein, having offered a seat and a form to the deities of the mantras to be accomplished using the *praṇava* (OM),

and having invoked them with their respective mantras enclosed by the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and performed the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), [one should worship] with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings.

Having worshipped [the deity] and recited their respective mantras one thousand, one hundred, or one hundred and eight times according to one's capacity, one should offer them to Śiva, who is colored by the mantra of the specific desire (*kāmyamantra*).
Alternatively, at the end of the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*), the mantras to be accomplished (*sādhyamantra*)—

Nor [should one worship] after having propitiated [the deity]; rather, even on a sacrificial mound (*sthāṇḍila*), the mantra should be meditated upon as a single mantra, joined with all its limbs. Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa*:
Then, having offered the desired *varaṇas*, one should worship the *sādhya*s;
then, having marked them with their respective limbs (*aṅgas*), [one should place them] upon the lotus-seat in the *praṇava*.
One should worship with ritual splendor on the southern side of Śiva;
having thus honored Maheśāna according to the Mṛgendra-tantra, one should worship the mantra to be accomplished for the sake of prosperity.
In every way and at all times, the practitioner should remain concealed as will be described hereafter;
having performed the recitation of the mantra of the object of attainment on the southern lotus petal at the conclusion of the recitation,
he should offer it as previously stated.
As it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara* (p. 516):
"O Maheśāna, having worshipped in that manner before the *liṅga*..."

In the front and rear portions, there are three forms of Indra; [the light] is in the midst of the light of the Aghora-eye, and nowhere else. That ash goes into the middle because it is consumed on the outside.
Its meaning is this: if one worships the mantra to be accomplished in the very center of the lotus-seat of Śiva, then...
It becomes ashes. If one were to worship it on the outside, then it would perish.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should worship the mantras to be accomplished (sādhya-mantras) specifically within the western and central petals of that lotus.
In the *Kiraṇa*: "Garlands made of pearl-jewels or of *rudrākṣa* beads grant excellent accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Those made of conch, crystal, lotus-seeds, or *śakrākṣa* seeds grant middling accomplishments."
Success through inferior materials such as brass, tin, and lead is not desired; a rosary made of *putrajīvaka* seeds is the means for accomplishing all rites and purposes.
One should perform the recitation of that secret mantra one hundred and eight times, or half of that,
or even half of that again.
From the drawing together of the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, the highest accomplishment is attained;
from the joining of the thumb and the index finger, the middling accomplishment is said to occur.

Through the application of the little finger, the lesser accomplishment is said to be attained; and that [accomplishment] should be understood as threefold, corresponding to the three types of success.
Regarding the whispered (*upāṃśu*) recitation performed with the mind, the whispered is praised therein. In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"That which is clearly articulated is said to be *tāmasa*; that which is whispered is called *rājasa*. [The mental recitation is] by means of the mind."
O best among those who know the recitation, one should know that the recitation performed with sattva is the true one.

The wise practitioner should perform recitation that is *tāmasa* for those of cruel deeds, *rājasa* for acts such as subjugation (*vaśya*), and *sāttvika* for divine accomplishments (*divyasiddhi*). One should worship [the deity] accordingly.
In the Pauṣkara:
"A wise person should mutter the mantra mentally for the best [result], inaudibly for the middling, and with audible speech for the lowest."
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should perform *japa* during the day as *āmisa* (fleshly); at night, it is *rājasa*;
and at the junction of day and night (*sandhyā*), *japa* is declared to be *sāttvika*, which accomplishes all goals at all times."

At the time of reciting the mantra to be accomplished (*sādhya-mantra*), one who contemplates the identity of oneself with that particular mantra to be accomplished attains the fruit of the recitation after a long time; however, at that moment, there is no such cultivation [of thought] as "I am that very [mantra]."

519) Since the relationship between the worshipper and the worshipped entails the existence of one who bestows the fruit, one should abandon the position of non-duality (*advaita*) and cultivate [the practice] through a specific mode of contemplation (*bhāvanā*). As it has been said:
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The yogi whose mind is focused on nothing else, having attained absorption in the mantra, quickly achieves success by relying on both non-duality and duality."

But how can there be the presence of pure mantras as the denotable objects (*vācya*) within the impure phonemes (*varṇa*), which are produced from the elements—ether, air, and so forth—and are uttered by the practitioner? It is not, however, directly; rather:
In those [phonemes], which correspond to the place of charcoal, there are those produced by Śiva— manifested and pure in color— which, as their denoters, serve as the cause for their manifestation.

The meaning is that they come into being. One who recites the *kāmya* mantras should, at the time of beginning the mantra, have the instruction for the recitation given by the Guru after ascertaining the favorable lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) of the practitioner-disciple within the squares of the *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth. Thus it has been said:
In the Kāmika:
"That mantra which is favorable to the practitioner bestows accomplishment;
[the mantras] are classified as Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and Sādhaka, ending with the Mākṣara."

Thus, in other cases such as the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) and so forth, the fourth option is accepted; for recitations and the like, success is declared through the *uccā*, *japa*, and *tarpaṇa* rites.
Is the mantra easily accomplished by mere recitation for the destruction of the enemy of the practitioner?
521) A mantra consisting of an abundance of consonants is traditionally held to be destructive. The disciple also...
One who is endowed with moral discipline, or like a son, is devoted to Śiva.

A thousand [gold pieces] should be given to him by the preceptor; the preceptor should then recite that [mantra] a thousand times. When they have arrived, he should secretly accept what was obtained through that pretext, remaining in a most hidden form.

The supreme practitioner of mantras, having accomplished the rites of recitation and other rituals through mantra, cuts asunder— that is, destroys— the obstacles encountered during the practice of recitation by means of another method.
Other mantras grant the accomplishment of all aims through few means; thus, the recitation of the seed-syllable should be performed with two or three times that number.
The number of recitations for a mantra consisting of a garland is prescribed; for a mantra where the number is not stated, it is one thousand and eight hundred.
The fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed at one-tenth the number of recitations (japa); likewise, in the rite of consecration (abhiṣeka), it is considered to be one-tenth of the root mantra.
For the ancillary mantras (aṅga), the worship, oblation, recitation, and so forth, are to be performed at one-tenth the number of the root mantra.
Mantras consisting of more syllables than the *japākṣara* are designated as *mantra*, while those with fewer are called *bīja*.
One should write the syllables of the *pūraka* and so forth in their proper sequence.
One should write the numbers 18, 11, 7, 2, 12, 6, 8,
16, 5, 70, and 1 in the respective compartments;
having thus arranged the remaining syllables accordingly.
And those well-known *mālāmantras* which consist of more than twenty syllables—thus are the fifty *vidyās*. Now follows the sequence of the state of *raṇiraṇi*.
Starting from the first syllable of the name up to the final letter of the mantra and so forth—
whether there be three, six, two, five, one, or four— if these are the mantras for an ascetic (yati), it should be known as "one" or "two" when they are bestowed upon a practitioner (sādhaka).
In this context, due to the limiting adjunct of the mantra to be presided over,
even Śiva— the presider— becomes, by way of metaphorical designation, as if divided despite being non-different. Likewise:
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"For the sake of bestowing grace upon living beings who exist with diverse states of mind, Paraśiva, having arisen through various forms of mantra, stands as the witness of their karmas."
The Soul of the Universe proceeds by observing the place, the action, the disposition, and the pervasion of the deity within the various divisions of the field of results.
Thus. Thereafter, one should worship the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha). Accordingly:
"One should then worship the Seat of Knowledge on the western side of the Deity.
However, in the Kāmika [Tantra] it says:

One should arrange the treasury of knowledge (vijñānakośa) either in the northwest or the south. The Śiva-knowledge, beginning with the Kāmika and other scriptures, is situated in the southern direction. This statement refers specifically to the direct installation in a temple built for the sake of others (parārthālaya).
Likewise, in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"One should fashion a treasury of wisdom (*vijñānakośa*) made of stone, brick, or clay; or [one made] of wood?"
Thus it is made, provided with doors and bolts, and beautified by a surrounding wall.
As stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The school for the sciences (*vidyāśālā*) begins at three cubits and extends up to thirty-three cubits."
It may be a large hall, or a palace, or else a pavilion.
Whether it be a single-hall structure or otherwise, endowed with the appropriate characteristics, the width of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) should be seven finger-breadths in extent.

By increasing the finger-breadths according to the [preceding] knowledge-measure, it should be thirty-one finger-breadths; by that, the length is declared to extend up to fifty cubits. It may be perfectly square or it may be oblong.
