525) One should lead everything according to the path prescribed for other postures (*āsana*). As stated in the *Śivadharmottara*:
The lion-throne of Vidyā was fashioned by Nāga, Māta, Ādi, and others; it was adorned with gold and jewels and provided with a covering of fine silk cloth.
Or a glorious staff-seat (daṇḍāsana), adorned with gold and jewels,
fashioned from the tusks of the king of elephants, or made of red sandalwood.

Having placed [the vessel] inside the flower-house, one should worship it with fragrant flowers. Having worshipped with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat for those who have descended the Śiva-knowledge beginning with Kāmika," one should thereafter place the casket of the treasury of Vidyā upon it.
As it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"He who [offers] a well-filled golden chest, adorned with all kinds of jewels, provided with a lid and a casket, serving as a repository for the treasury of knowledge..."
Or one should have it made of silver or copper, square in shape;
or else of bell-metal, brass, or iron, or constructed from wood, bamboo, and the like.
With a fresh hide dyed with the six impurities, one should clothe the new house that is the abode of knowledge, both inside and out.
One should fashion a casket for the jewel of knowledge, provided with excellent doors and a casing, bound with very firm threads, and equipped with a lock.
Having thus had it constructed according to his means and in a fitting manner, the wise man should wash the treasury-house of the Vidyā with scented water.
Having constructed a divine cloth pavilion, superior even to an inner flower pavilion,
the wise one should duly install [the deity] there upon the Vidyā-siṃhāsana.

In that treasury of knowledge, he should place [the manuscript] with the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha); thereafter, the learned man should worship it with extensive and magnificent offerings.

527) Here, the worship of the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) is twofold: direct (*aparokṣā*) and indirect (*parokṣā*). Among these, the worship concerning the *Kāmika* and other Tantras written down before one's eyes is the indirect [worship].
The objects such as the mandala, the lotus-seat, and so forth, are beyond direct perception. Even in the first [initiation], either the entire *saṃhitā* or one's own *saṃhitā* should be worshipped.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Or, the wise one should worship ten million seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭhas) or his own Saṃhitā with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as food offerings and garlands, just as he would Śiva.
And in the *Mṛgendra*:

"In the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) as well, having thus reflected, one should worship the Lord with garlands, perfumes, incense, and food offerings, performing the ritual according to one's own preference by means of a single utterance."
In the Śiva division, Śiva is to be worshipped; indeed, in the Rudra division, he alone is [to be worshipped],
or rather, in his combined form.

Having worshipped with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ namaḥ sarvebhyaḥ śivajñānebhyaḥ*, and having recollected: *oṃ I worship Śambhu, the bestower of all knowledge, the destroyer of ignorance, who is the refuge of the seat of Vidyā, with body, mind, and speech*, one should say: "Forgive me."
On the lotus within the square mandala, one should worship as follows: at the pericarp (karṇikā), "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśa. Then, on the ten petals starting from the east surrounding that, [one should worship] with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kāmika" in the east.
One who seeks knowledge should worship, upon the nine petals starting with the southeast (vahni), the Śiva-bheda scriptures known as the Yogaja and others; these were [revealed] by Śiva himself,
the Lord manifest, independent of any external substratum.

529) Because the divisions of Śiva have been uttered, the origin of the tantras such as the Vijaya and others indeed occurs within the locus of Rudra and the rest, who are of beginningless form; for it is here [that this happens].

Then, one should worship the eighteen Tantras— known as the divisions of Rudra, beginning with Vijaya and ending with Vātula— on the petals of the eighteen lotuses that cover it, in the order starting from the east, using their respective mantras. Likewise:
In the Vātula [Tantra]:

Having drawn a ten-petalled lotus within a square mandala, one who seeks knowledge [should worship] Śiva together with Vāgīśvarī in the center, and [the deities] in order from the eastern direction onwards.
One should worship the Śiva-knowledges, beginning with the Kāmika, upon the petals; as before, on an eighteen-petaled lotus, starting from the east in due order.
"One should worship the Rudra-knowledges within those very [vessels] during the Guru-yāga" (p.
Thereafter, one should worship the Guru. As it has been said:
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Having thus fully worshipped the knowledge of Śiva, one should thereafter worship the Guru;
one should worship with devotion Śiva, the illuminator of the knowledge of Śiva."

Thus [it is said]. Worship of the Guru is twofold: [direct and] indirect contemplation (*parokṣabhāvanā*). Having gone to the Guru while he is seated upon his own throne, having washed his lotus-feet, and having worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings as if he were Śiva, one should worship him properly by offering three handfuls of flowers.
In the *Ṣaṭsahasra*: "Then, having brought [the disciple] near, one should worship the Guru as before.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
Having performed three circumambulations clockwise, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff; then, rising and resting upon the earth on one's knees, one should make a formal request.
Having joined his palms in reverence and prostrated again before the Guru, [he spoke] to the Lord of Beasts—
A wise person should not salute a Guru who is eating, who is established in meditative absorption, who is intent on the performance of ritual acts, or who is standing nearby.
One should follow behind him when he goes, and enter after him when he enters; one should not act contrary to his will, nor should one wake him while he sleeps.
In the *Kālottara*:
"O Six-faced One, eternal knowledge is obtained through the grace of the Guru from the Lord in the temple."
Wherever the Guru indeed resides, O Six-faced One.

Having first paid homage to the Guru, one should indeed pay homage to the Deity afterwards. There is an expiation for the omission [of worshipping] Śiva, but there is no liberation by resorting to a deficient Guru.
If one should set aside a worthy son of the guru and instead appoint another, his initiation shall indeed be fruitless, and he shall fall downward for a great kalpa.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Having approached a teacher devoid of knowledge, how can one then attain liberation? Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in one who has reached the further shore of knowledge."
Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from one flower to another in the forest,
so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, may go from one teacher to another.
Having received [the teaching], the disciple should release it; otherwise, he certainly falls downward.
In the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"The Guru is to be worshipped like Śiva, and the Preceptor again like the Pavitra."
In the same way, the practitioners (sādhakas) always speak to the spiritual sons (putrakas) as to brothers.
Those who abide by their commitments like friends should be regarded as such by one desiring auspiciousness.
In this context, it should be understood that the *guru* who performs initiation is the *deśika*, the instructor.
Those who revile their guru or the initiates, such as the *samayins* and *putrakas*, should be expelled far from that place; one should then recite the *sadyojāta* mantra a hundred times.
He who, out of delusion, being most wicked, utters a curse against his teacher, and the other evil-minded person who accepts it—
both of them shall go to hell.
Having prostrated, one should diligently worship the guru by the scattering of flowers; by saluting the feet of the guru, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, in the presence of everyone, he should also perform a prostration with devotion as is appropriate toward other well-disciplined ascetics (tapodhana).
Thus it is said in the Mataṅga:
According to the sequence of consecration, he who was initiated first is the eldest;
thus, a *putraka* is senior even to another *putraka*, a *sādhaka* is senior to a *sādhaka*, and a *guru* is senior even to another *guru*. (p. 534)
It has been declared through the illustration of the statement of the rule.
The initiate who abides by the rules is superior to one merely initiated; the adept is superior even to the initiate; and the preceptor is proclaimed to be the eldest of all.
He should pay homage to those superior to himself, as well as to the groups of his preceptors and brothers; furthermore, he should also salute other Śaivas who are purified and rich in asceticism.
One established in a vow (mṛtavratī) should not salute even those who are senior in learning or asceticism if they are settled upon any of the four paths, beginning with the worldly path.

In the teaching of Śiva, among those who observe vows, the elder is he who is superior in spiritual refinement; neither birth nor age constitutes seniority, for true knowledge is the cause of being senior.

In what cases are they considered existing? When the younger brother is consecrated while the elder remains a child; or when the elder is consecrated by the preceptor, or even by some others who were previously waiting.
p.
535) They must show mutual respect toward one another, except for formal prostration.
Likewise—
A younger person must never perform a salutation to an elder, even if that elder is superior in asceticism or learning, provided the elder has already performed initiation and consecration.
Just as an elder brother behaves toward a younger brother, so should one behave toward the son of a teacher; the teacher’s son deserves rising up from one's seat, but not formal salutation.
Thus [it is said].
Now,
the method of meditation: having fashioned a lotus of appropriate size in the south-eastern direction of the deity,
and having conceived within its center that which arises from the six [syllables], there [one should place] the Guru.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the *mukti* (or *mūrti*) mantra, having invoked Śiva into that [image], and having performed the *nyāsa* of the limbs (*aṅga*), one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings;
then, having worshipped the station of Śiva (*śivapada*) with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having meditated upon it—(p.

I take refuge eternally in that very Lord Guru, who out of compassion released all the fetters of my beginningless [bondage] and, at the dissolution of my body, made me a partaker of supreme liberation, and who became the cause for the awakening to the entirety of the Śiva-śāstras. Thus.
One should gratify [the deity] with hymns of praise and other offerings. Then, in the south-eastern quarter, one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha.
According to the *Ṣaṭsahasra*, one should fashion an auspicious lotus measuring exactly one cubit.
One should worship one's own guru in the center of that [mandala], which is provided with a pericarp and petals.
Having prepared the seat there, one should place the image upon it;
one should invoke Śiva there, together with Brahmā and his limbs (aṅgas).
Having diligently worshipped with flowers, incense, and other offerings using the heart-mantra,
this ritual procedure is prescribed for when the Guru has passed away into the state of Śiva.
Having received the command with diligence, one should then commence the ritual action.
Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Having first prepared the seat of yoga as previously described, and having honored the Guru who was previously worshipped..."
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as before, one should place the form (mūrti) ending in the dative case.
Having invoked Śiva into that place, one should assign the limbs as before;
O Bird, having worshipped the excellent Guru with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, [one should worship him] with the heart-mantra.
Thus [it is said].
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Having worshipped Śiva according to the rules, one should then worship His Vidyā; and one should worship the Guru with devotion to Śiva, for these three are equal."
As is Śiva, so is Vidyā; as is Vidyā, so is the Guru. In the worship of Śiva, Vidyā, and the Guru, the fruit is the same.
In this context, as an incidental topic related to the worship of the Teacher (ācārya), the procedure for the worship of Śiva-devotees established in monasteries and similar places is described.
In the *Kāmika*:
Whether they are living or deceased, for those endowed with devotion to Śiva, one should fashion an image,
install it, and worship it.
Likewise, in that very same [text]:
"Then, a person should daily worship the devotee of Prakṛti;
likewise, the necessary purification, bathing, and the salutation during the twilight prayers."
Having performed [the preliminary rites] and entered the palace, he should worship the imperishable Supreme Self in the center of the site and perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having first assumed a body formed by mantra, and then having performed the purification of the site,
one should prepare the special *arghya* water combined with flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and water.

A person should sprinkle the collection of materials previously mentioned according to the prescribed rite; for the purification of the mantras, he should recite the mantra beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ."
Having established [the deity] with the weapon-mantra for the purification of the image by means of the heart-mantra,
one should then provide the seat arising from the six [syllables] according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Having conceived the fourfold [elements] beginning with Dharma at the end of the word *manas* (or *naḥ*) in the seat called Ādhāra, one should fashion the human seat (*mānuṣapīṭha*) with the syllable *praṇava*.
And if the syllables of the name were then the limbs of the foot, what would [the result] be?
Manu says:
"Then, having performed the invocation, one should then place the heart-mantra and the others; [then] the water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamana)."
And one should present the *arghya* with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having bathed [the image] with scented water or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth, and having wiped it with a cloth,
one should offer garments, perfumes, flowers, and incense.
Apart from the daily bath, one should perform a ritual bath for the metal image on every festival day; one should offer an oblation accompanied by a lamp and side dishes.

One should offer betel-leaf at the three junctions of the day, or at two junctions; or else, one should worship according to one's capacity, concluding with the offering of lamps and the final oblation.

Having worshipped Śiva with three handfuls of flowers, one should address him with this hymn. As stated in the venerable *Raurava*: "Having touched the hands, which are full of flowers and radiant, that have been purified by the mantras..."
With his hair standing on end from joy, he said, "Do this now."
Having paid homage to the Lord of the celestial spheres, whose crest is adorned by the moon, I bow forever to the god Sadāśiva, who wears a garland of skulls.
I bow to Sadāśiva, the doer of all, the knower of all, the omniscient, the unconquered,
who abides as the reality of the purpose of all beings.
I bow to that Sadāśiva, the creator of all, who in ancient times created all beings, including the gods beginning with Brahmā.
I bow always to Sadāśiva, the God who is the boon, the most worthy of choice, the giver of boons, the most excellent, whose vehicle is the bull, and who wears the garland of choice.
I bow always to Sadāśiva, who is full of joy, the giver of joy, most beloved, pleasant to behold, the beloved of Umā, and the eternal consort.
I bow to Sadāśiva, the God who consists of both dharma and adharma, who bestows the fruits of pleasure and pain, and who grants both bondage and liberation.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, and the domain of the subtle elements and the senses.
I bow perpetually to Sadāśiva, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa,
whom the high-souled sages of firm vows meditate upon.
I bow forever to Sadāśiva, who is beyond the syllable Om and is most subtle.
I bow to Sadāśiva, the God who is subtle, all-pervading, eternal, the Lord of the lords of all sciences, and the refuge of all principles.
To that supreme deity Sadāśiva— earth, water, fire, air, ether, the self, the moon, and the sun— I bow forever.
He who, having worshipped the Lord of Gods with devotion, recites this hymn before Him,
goes to the supreme state that is tranquil like peace itself.
Having praised the Supreme Lord with these and other verses, one should perform a circumambulation and a prostration with the eight limbs touching the ground.
As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Having praised [the deity] with various kinds of hymns, beginning with those in Sanskrit and Dravidian,
and having prostrated again and again with the most excellent [verses] uttered from the sacrificial pit (*garta*)."
p.
543) If one does not perform circumambulation at the conclusion of the worship, one does not obtain that respective fruit either.
Thus it has been said:
Even after performing worship, he who does not circumambulate Śambhu finds that worship to be fruitless; indeed, his speech is a mockery of worship.
He who performs even a single circumambulation properly with devotion has performed every form of worship;
he is a true worshiper of Śiva.

Thus. Then, having worshipped with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) and presented the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*), one should worship Śiva on the five heads in the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta. On the head, for the purpose of concealment (*tirobhāva*), one should perform the rite with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* while holding the hand face-down over the water-offering of restraint (*nirodhārghya*).

Having requested as before, "Be facing upwards," and having offered the *arghya* for the one facing away, [one should worship] the limbs beginning with the weapon (*astra*) and ending with the heart (*hṛdaya*).
Having performed the worship, one should offer the *arghya* in reverse order of the worship; or else, one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ śivāya sāṅgāya parāṅmukhārghyaṃ svāhā*.
Aṃśumatī: Having performed the worship of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*), the wise one should offer the *arghya* for the averted face;
having worshipped from Sadyojāta to Īśāna, he should then join them in reverse order.
Having worshipped the weapon (astra) in the four directions, from Soma to Indra, one should then worship the eye (netra) in front and the armor (kavaca) in the region of the wind (vāyu).
One should worship the *śikhā* in the southwest (*nairṛta*), the head in the northeast (*īśāna*), and the heart in the southeast (*āgneyī*), as part of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*).
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: "Then, one should offer the *arghya* facing away [from the deity], starting from Sadyojāta up to Śiva,
and from the *astra-mantra* up to the *hṛdaya-mantra*, with perfumes, incense, garlands, and so forth."
(Page number 545 missing; p.
546) One should offer *arghya* to the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadeva*) with the *kāmya-mantras*. Hūṃ.

With the *astra-mantra* ending in *phaṭ*, grasping the thumbs and index fingers of both hands, one should cast the flower upward three times with the *nārāca-mudrā*; then, having raised the limbs [of the deity] and withdrawn them with the *saṃhāriṇī-mudrā*, [one recites]:
*oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ śivamūrtaye namaḥ*.

Thus, having joined [the offering] to the heart and other locations of Śiva with the divine mudrā formed by holding two flowers with the tips of the thumb and ring finger, and having meditated on the dissolution of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadeva*) into the Form (*mūrti*), one should join the optional mantras (*kāmyamantra*) to their respective parts of the path (*svādhvāvayava*) by means of the Mūrti-mantra.
One should join all the mantras within the image.
Alternatively, there is the dissolution of all mantras into the root mantra, the root mantra into the *bindu*, the *bindu* into the *nāda*, and the *nāda* [into the *śakti*].
One should contemplate its dissolution into the supreme power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
According to the *Aṃśumatī*:
"The right wrist and the left hand above it."
One should join the three fingers, beginning with the middle one, in the center of the palm.
One should offer three flowers joined with the thumb and forefinger; having set aside those flowers, one should proceed with the *nirodha* mudrā.
Thus one should perform the *visarjanī-mudrā* with joined palms at the head. As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Having formed the *añjali* with both hands, [one places] the tips of the thumbs and ring fingers [together]."
Then one should extend the remaining fingers; this is the mudrā of divine form.
In the Kāmika:
Having raised the deities situated in the enclosure with the weapon-mantra and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*,
one should unite them with their forms by means of the *mūrti-mantra*.
Aṃśumatī:
One should indeed join the deities of the enclosure worship with the *liṅga* alone.
One should employ the mantras for the seat and worship by means of the *pīṭha* alone.
In the Kālottara:
Having meditated on [the mantras] as having arisen like lightning and then gone to dissolution in their respective places,
one should dissolve the mantras that have reached the place of dissolution into the root mantra.
Then one should meditate on the root mantra as having dissolved into the throbbing point (bindu);
the deities dissolve into the point, the point into the resonance (nāda), and the resonance into the power of pure consciousness (vijñānaśakti).
The power of the self is dissolved in the Supreme, which is established in the space of the heart; from that the mantra is generated, and into that very place it is dissolved.
Thereafter, having worshipped Śiva with the root mantra, offered the *arghya*, protected him with the *astra* mantra, and enveloped him with the *kavaca* mantra;
Having displayed the *dhenumudrā* with the *śaktimantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having sprinkled [the deity] with the *udvāsanamudrā*, [one should say]:
"Thousands of offenses are committed by me day and night; [forgive me], for I am but a servant."
Considering this, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, you should forgive me.
O Lord, you have been troubled by me, a wretched servant of defiled intellect;
yet, being pleased with even a fraction of my devotion, please forgive us.
Thus one should inform [the preceptor].
This dismissal with dependence occurs in the case of a mobile liṅga. On an altar or similar site,

after the formation of the image, one should unite [the deity] with the heart-mantra, by means of the filling and withdrawing breath, into the portion of power within the light-liṅga situated in the center of the heart-lotus.
This is a dismissal that requires no further consideration.
In both cases, one should perform the dismissal without further dependence [on external factors]. Thus, it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
In the case of a mobile linga, the rite is dependent [on external materials], whereas on a consecrated site (sthaṇḍila) and so forth, it is independent;
or rather, it is independent everywhere, since it is prescribed to be performed daily.
In the lineage—
having made the two hands into a *saṃśiṣya* [gesture], O Goddess of Gods, likewise facing each other; having placed the palms together and raised them upward.
This is called *udvāsana* (the rite of dismissal), which accomplishes all desires and goals.
This *udvāsana* is threefold: *nirālamba* (without support), *sālamba* (with support), and *saṃkrama* (transference).
Thus—
The dismissal that occurs at the end of the worship, by means of the sacrificial ground and so forth,
is the supportless withdrawal performed on the day of the removal of the image.
But when it has an object, through being commanded by the teacher and by means of causes such as the "lost touch" (*naṣṭasparśa*) and so forth,
they know its power to effect entry into and transition to another [body].

Then, having worshipped one's own guru, the seven gurus of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), Mahālakṣmī, and the door-keepers Gaṇapati, and having offered them the *arghya* for turning away (*parāṅmukha*),
one should dismiss them into oneself by means of their respective mantras and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. Thus:
In the *Rāmanāthapaddhati*:
"Having taken the general *arghya* water, one should withdraw the *arghya* offerings of the Guru and others, which were facing away, by bringing them into oneself with the *saṃhāramudrā*."

Having offered the *parāṅmukha-arghya* to the images beginning with Gaṇeśvara and ending with the Kṣetrapālas, and having covered each one individually with a cloth while reciting the mantra, he should place them beside the chest using the *astra-mantra*.
p.
552) Likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī*:
having washed one's hands while recollecting the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), [one should do so] for each [limb].
Having taken up the cloth, one should place it with the flower alone.
The arrangement of the garments for Gaṇeśvara and the others should be performed with cloth itself; one should place them at the side of the chest (peṭaka) while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Likewise, regarding the subtle [rite]:
he should cover each of the images separately with flowers and cloth.
But in the case of the causal [image]—
Red cloth such as silk (dukūla) and the like, white garments, black clothing, multicolored cloth, and likewise outer garments and fine silks.
If an image is made for one's own sake, even touching it does not cause fault; likewise, if one crosses a river or an image for one's own sake by means of a boat or the like.
Then, having consecrated [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should subsequently perform the worship in due order.
If there is a crossing of the ocean, one should then perform the purification of the image (beraśuddhi).
"Having performed the ceremonial bathing and the pacifying fire-oblation, the wise one should perform the Satyaga sacrifice.
Thus it is said.

Having recited the Śiva-mantra, one should take the liṅga from the lotus-seat, wrap it in cloth appropriate for that occasion, place it within a casket, and while meditating upon Bhīmarudra and requesting protection, one should close the lid; likewise, in the Aṃśumatī [Tantra]:
Having recollected the Śiva-mantra and taken hold of the liṅga, the preceptor should wrap it in a multicolored cloth and place it within a casket.
Having joined the lid, one should then meditate upon Bhīmarudra; one should hold Śiva at the head, the throat, the two armpits, and the two elbows.
Then one should perform the Caṇḍa-worship.
(p. 554) || Caṇḍa-worship ||

The procedure here is as follows: in the northeast direction of the deity, having prepared a mandala with cow dung, and having drawn there [the symbol] resembling a chisel or a crescent moon with the Caṇḍa-mantra, one should conceive of the sixfold arising seat with the mantra: *oṃ caṇḍāsanāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ*.

Having prepared a seat and, upon it, having projected the form with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍamūrti, Huṃ Phaṇnama," [one should meditate on him] as having a luster like blue collyrium, four faces, and eyes like the sun.
With a serpent as his sacred thread and armlets, why does he have the fierce fire of death in his mouth?
[One should meditate on her] as exceedingly terrifying, with four arms, adorned with flaming matted hair and a crescent moon,
holding a trident and a water-pot in her left hands, and an axe and a rosary of beads in her right hands.
Having meditated upon her as originating from Rudra-Agni, one should invoke the Supreme with the root mantra.
555) [In the case of] Aṃśumatī—
Alternatively—
having invoked Caṇḍa into the mandala, one should then meditate upon his form as having two eyes,
four arms, and being endowed with white garments.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, he has his right foot hanging down and his left foot firmly planted.
With the left hand above the knee and the right hand holding an axe—
or else with hands joined in *añjali*— one should meditate upon the deity in this form.

Having meditated thus, and having performed the rites of invocation, installation, and so forth with the mantra: *oṃ dhvanicaṇḍeśvarāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, [one should offer worship] with: *oṃ cāṃ caṇḍahṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ cīṃ caṇḍaśirase huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ cūṃ*...

Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the limbs [of the mantra]— *caḥ caṇḍāstrāya huṃ phaṇnamaḥ*— and having rendered [the deity] supreme by means of the root mantra, one should consecrate [it] as nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the *dhenumudrā*, and worship [it] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and so forth; or else, [one may worship] solely with the seat (*āsana*) and the root mantras.
Having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra and worshipped him, having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and other articles to the God,

and having presented the *arghya* water, [one should say]: "By the command of Śiva, this food to be licked, sucked, eaten, and drunk, along with betel, garlands, and ointments— the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*)— is given to you as your meal."
Having recited this and offered the remains of the Śiva-offering (śivanirmālya), one should say:
"O Caṇḍa, by your command, all this ritual section has been performed by me; whatever was done deficiently or in excess through delusion, may that become complete."
Having thus informed Caṇḍeśa and offered the *parāṅmukha* (turning away) *arghya*,
one should unite [the deity] within one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* accompanied by the root mantra together with the *pūraka* [breathing technique]. Likewise:
Aṃśumatī—
At the conclusion of the worship for one's own sake, specifically at each junction of the day (saṃdhyā), [one should perform it] in the northeastern quarter of the deity.
On ground smeared with cow dung.
The knower of mantras should draw [the weapon] with the luster of a coin and the shape of a half-moon using the mantra of Caṇḍa:
"Oṃ Caṇḍeśvarāya huṃ phaṭ."

Having meditated upon the center of the lotus, one should offer water for the feet and water for sipping; having offered ointment and a garland with its root mantra, one should likewise cause food offerings and betel leaf to be given with that very same root mantra.
Having offered the *arghya* with the face turned away, one should perform this daily practice.
As stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
He who worships daily is not defiled by sins.
Having offered the *arghya* for the one turned away (*parāṅmukha*) to Aṃśumat, one should then dismiss Caṇḍa. [The rite of] Caṇḍāsana...
And having conceived the form, one should [place] the atoms of Īśa and the others in sequence.

Having performed the placement of the limbs, beginning with the heart, in their respective locations, and having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering to Caṇḍapa with the root mantra and the heart mantra;
This has been declared as equal for one's own sake and for the sake of others; whether performed regularly or otherwise, they are ordained as bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Regarding worship for one's own sake, according to some in the Śaivasiddhānta, there is a rule that Śiva must always and everywhere be worshipped upon the Śivāsana.
And likewise in the *Kālottara*: "Whether it be fixed or moving, red or white, made of stone or fashioned from metal, or consisting of painted [images],"
And Caṇḍa, the restrainer, is stationed in Bāṇa.
In the Siddhānta, and not in other Tantras— neither in the Vāma nor in the Dakṣiṇa— in the unmanifest or manifest Liṅga, in the Maṇḍala, on the sacrificial ground, or in the fire;
Likewise, when the Liṅga is made of Caṇḍa-stone, or red stone, or various jewels and the like, as well as when it is fashioned from wood, earth, ashes, or a wooden plank, fragrance does not arise.
Likewise, in the case of a liṅga made of flowers, the worship of Caṇḍa is mandatory. Thus it is said.

In the Svāyambhuva [Tantra], they are described as "properly engaged. Furthermore: "For those who have acted otherwise, violating the command of Śiva—even though they are initiated—Caṇḍeśvara is their punisher and their sovereign lord."
For those with whom Caṇḍeśvara is pleased, there is no cause for fear;
therefore, those who have taken refuge in the path of Śiva should perform his propitiation.

Thus, because the worship of Caṇḍeśvara by Caṇḍa is specifically taught as the cause for the destruction of all obstacles for the Śaivas, the worship of Caṇḍeśvara must be performed daily at the conclusion of the ritual worship; this is stated in connection with the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) during the occasion of purification (*śodhana*).
*Nirmālya*— according to the *Kāmika*:
"The property of the deity, the substance belonging to the deity, that which has been offered, that which has been presented, and the substance [left over] for Caṇḍa."
Nirmālya is traditionally said to be of six kinds.

A village and the like belong to the deity as his property; cloth and other such items are the deity's substance; that which is prepared as an offering belongs to him, and what is presented is the deity's leavings.
That fierce substance (caṇḍadravya), however, once offered, is discarded as *nirmālya* and cast outside.
Even when the deity has been dismissed (*visarjite*), that which remains on the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is not *nirmālya*; [therefore, its] consumption...
The offering is said to be of two kinds, and otherwise as well.

There, for the God of gods, there is the manifestation of the primordial village of deities and so forth; by means of whatever adjuncts such as rice and the like, there is the eating of food from this day forward.
One who, being utterly deluded and intoxicated by the theft of wealth, seeks intoxicants,
prepares either rice or boiled grain for my sake.
Whether one bestows food upon a devotee or is even called a thief,
if he prepares an offering for Śiva, offers it to me from that very source,
and daily eats the remains with devotion, he is indeed like me.
It has been declared that he who is a consumer of sacrificial oblations (caru) shall likewise become so.
If a man, praised as pure, should eat this with devotion,
his sin is quickly destroyed; he becomes a purified soul, a true Brāhmaṇa.
The rules for that are clearly stated in the *Kāraṇa*:
"If the linga is human, the linga of the learned, it is said to be of two kinds:
the self-manifested (*svayambhū*), the divine (*daivika*), the Bāṇa, the Gāṇapa, and likewise the Ārṣaka."
One should perform worship as before for that which is known as a *śiṣṭaliṅga*.
Indeed, if it is a *śiṣṭaliṅga*, there is a certain distinction:
the *nirmālya* offered there is fit to be eaten by the *śaivas*, and it bestows auspiciousness.
It promotes longevity and increases strength.
One whose self is stainless should accept the floral remains (nirmālya) as stainless and pure;
therefore, the food offering (naivedya) of Śiva is remembered as a substance that is pure.
One should not consume the remains of offerings (nirmālya) from a body that has been smeared with impurities.
One who has been initiated by Śiva is indeed called a Śiva-brāhmaṇa.
For Śiva is pure, formless, and is said to transcend both speech and mind.
Therefore, a twice-born who is devoted to Śiva is called a pure Brāhmaṇa; for him alone is the remains of the offering (nirmālya) appropriate, but it is not suitable for others.
One should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance for those who have accepted [the food] of others.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"For one initiated, the *nirmālya* is that which has attained purity through being enjoyed by the pure Self."
It is not praised to consider the duties of others as one's own.
Regarding the purpose:
the food offering for Vināyaka is for the feeding of Brahmins and others;
the food offering for Subrahmaṇya is for those seeking victory.
Then, after the food offering for the goddess Umā, there is the meal for all;
then, after the food offering for all [the deities], one should feed everyone.
Whoever, such as a pure Brāhmaṇa and others, should feed [others] with the food offered to Viṣṇu (viṣṇunaivedya).
The food offering of Bhāskara, when consumed, leads to the destruction of disease;
however, the food offering of Bhāskara is not to be eaten by those who are not devotees of the Sun.
Likewise, in the Vīratantra:
"The food offering of Divākara shall be the meal for everyone;
it is not to be eaten by devotees of the Sun, nor even by [the goddesses] Jyeṣṭhā and Sarasvatī."
The food offering (naivedya) for Śrīdevī and Bhūdevī shall be their meal.
In the case of Kāraṇa and Durgā, the food offering which is to be eaten promotes health.
On the day of Jyeṣṭhā, whatever food is offered as an oblation increases one's prosperity;
on the day of Mahāmoṭī, the oblation of food increases one's progeny.
The vein, the remains of offerings, the food of women,
the sacrificial food of the Mothers, and that which is unfit to be eaten by Brahmins;
The food offering of Kṣetrapāla is unfit for consumption and increases disease; however, the food offering of Vāgīśvarī is fit for consumption and increases knowledge.
Indeed, that which is fit for Brahmins to eat, as well as what is offered to Brahmā and the food offering (naivedya) presented to the world-protectors (lokapālas),
always brings about health.
That which is offered to Manmatha is said to be edible for all;
however, that which is offered to Sadāśiva is never to be eaten by Brāhmaṇas when it has been consumed by [the fire of] Dīpta.
p. 566) Regarding the cause:
one should then offer the sacrificial food (naivedya) to all, including the retinue and others; [then] the liṅga.
That human form is undoubtedly the remains of an offering (nirmālya).
Having consumed it through negligence, or likewise touched or stepped over it,
one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) along with śamī leaves and the tips of kuśa grass.
Stepping over, giving away, or consuming the remains of offerings (nirmālya) leads one to hell;
where such stepping occurs through negligence, a wise person should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Upon touching [it], wash your hands and feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). Half a sesame seed of its remains is like hell for both the moon and the sun.
Whether it be water, animal products, earth, or even fire— these are the remains of Sadāśiva’s offerings (nirmālya); they are not food for human beings.
And for animals such as elephants and the like, the wise man should either cast them into water, or kill them with fire, or have them buried in the earth.
However, for all [the deities], the food offering (naivedya) is the meal for the attendants;
even then, eating with other people would cause a fault in the meal.
One should understand that through many such statements, the prohibitions apply specifically to human characteristics (mānuṣaliṅga) and not to those of Svāyambhuva and the like.
The nature of the *nirmālya* (remains) intended for oneself is stated as follows in the *Kāmika*:

"That which is offered to one's own chosen *liṅga* is like the *caru* offering; of this there is no doubt. One should cause the *naivedya* (food offering) to be given to one's brothers, sons, and sisters."
And regarding the cause:
that which is for one's own sake and the mobile *liṅga* is called *nirmālya*. (Page 568, unclear)
