569) Now the main subject is being stated: having removed the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings), having purified that place with cow-dung water, having sprinkled it while reciting "Oṃ huṃ astrāya phaṭ," and having dismissed the *arghya* and other offerings;
Having washed his hands and other limbs, sipped water (ācamana), and applied ashes, he recites the *saṃhitā*.
Then, for the purpose of removing all defects of deficiency or excess, or for the sake of attaining the fruit of the worship, he recites the *ghora* mantra once. Likewise...
In the *Kālottara*: "Having offered garments, food, perfumes, drinks, the *arghya* offering, and the most sacred remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*),
one should set aside the *arghya* vessel and, having prostrated, touch [the deity]."
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to one's capacity, the *Śivasaṃhitā* consists of seven chapters.
However, in the *Kāmika*, it is stated: p. 570) In the *Kāmika*—

One should withdraw the worship from the sacrificial ground with three applications of cow-dung; for the sake of purifying what has been dropped or slipped, one should recite the Abhyarcanamala-saṃhitā.
His vessel does not remain [empty]; what is the sequence? Therefore, the *saṃhitā* is well-composed...
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *saṃhitā*; the gift of devotion quickly destroys sins.
Thus [it is said].
In the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*,

it is stated that by reciting [the mantra] twenty-one times at the conclusion of the worship according to the prescribed rule, one attains the fruit of the worship and shall obtain what is taught in the scriptures. There is no mantra superior to the Aghora for the attainment of Kālī.
He who has fixed his mind upon Aghora is the bestower of success; he partakes in liberation, and not otherwise.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always practice the Aghora mantra;
for this very reason, at the conclusion of worship, the mantra must necessarily be recited.
Thus, one should perform the ritual section (kriyākāṇḍa) known as the sacrifice for one's own sake (ātmārthayajana).
And in the *Sūkṣma*:
"In this manner, day by day, one should worship and honor [the deity] according to the previous sequence.
In the *Kālottara*:
However, he who worships with devotion until the end of the body is Śiva himself; having cast off his merit, he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Thus ends the ritual procedure for worship for one's own sake, in the *Ātmārthapūjāpaddhati*,
page 572.
Regarding the worship of Kapilā,
some desire the worship of Kapilā at the conclusion of the worship of Īśa; as it is said in the *Suprabheda*:
Five cows from Śivapura attained Śiva through their devotion to Śiva,
especially from the churning of the Ocean of Milk by the gods and demons.
Five cows were born, the mothers of all the world: Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā.
Kapila, black-and-white, and likewise smoky-red—
these are proclaimed to be the colors for those [cows] beginning with Nandā and ending with Sumanā.
For the sake of benefiting the entire world and for the gratification of the gods, as well as for the bathing of Śiva upon the earth, O Mothers of Cows!
The six products of the cow— cow dung, bile, urine, milk, curd, and ghee— are pure and bring about all spiritual accomplishments.
Through cows the sacrifices proceed; through cows the gods are established;
through cows the Vedas are engraved, together with their six auxiliary limbs and the Pada and Krama recitations.

Having thus observed the cows, he honored them for the sake of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), first offering morsels of food and then worshipping them with their respective names and the *dhruva* mantra.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, sacred grass, and other offerings while preceded by mantras:
Oṃ kapile nande namaḥ | Oṃ kapile bhadre namaḥ | Oṃ kapile suśīle namaḥ | Oṃ kapile surabhe namaḥ | Oṃ kapile samane namaḥ ||
O daughter of Surabhi, Mother of the World, bestower of nectar upon the gods; accept this morsel, O giver of boons, and grant me my desired object.
You have been worshipped by Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Jahnu;
O Kapilā, remove the sin and whatever evil deed has been committed by me.
Cows are always before me; cows are indeed behind me; cows are also in my heart;
I dwell in the midst of cows.
Restrained and pure, one should mutter this mantra with the mind at the three junctions of the day;
liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Śiva.
Alternatively:
"O Surabhi, born from the churning of the nectar of immortality, sustainer of the world! I give you this morsel; please accept it. This is my supreme vow."

Just as between a deity and a bull when both are fed morsels of grass, this fruit is seen to be equal; however, the mantras are distinct. They are the cause for supporting all the worlds, yet they do not grant [mere] life.
"Taking mouthful by mouthful, you shall eat standing; this is my supreme vow.
Having undertaken this difficult vow, one should daily offer water to a cow."
And having praised them with supreme devotion, the wise man, out of fear of terrible danger, should then [offer] to the cows that which destroys sin upon touch.
One should cause them to take the five products of the cow, or, in their absence, one may take those of a single one;
the worship is performed with the previously mentioned *śambaras*.
"In this case as well, among all [cows], the Kapilā is praised.
Thus concludes the procedure for the worship of the Kapilā according to the *Ātmārthapūjāpaddhati*.
p.
576) || The Sequence of Service in the Abode of Śiva ||
Aṃśumatī—
Having entered the abode of Parārtha and beheld the Liṅga,
one should perform circumambulations and prostrations according to the prescribed number of rites.
After observing the linga, one should cause it to enter well into one's own home,
having reflected upon the words of the Puranas and Agamas according to one's understanding.
I shall now clearly describe the procedure for the service of a temple of Śiva.

If one resides near a temple of Śiva, after performing worship according to the prescribed rites, one should regularly go from afar to serve the temple. One should approach from a distance for the sake of service.

Having seen the celestial chariot (vimāna), first pay homage. Having bathed at the holy ford (puṇyatīrtha) where it is visible, wearing clean garments, having performed the daily rites, and observing a fast—(p.
Having offered excellent flowers and other gifts, and having performed the washing of the feet, one should perform service to Śiva;
thus it is said in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
Having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) from his own home for the pilgrimage to Vyāghrapura, and having worshipped the God of gods, he experienced both types of enjoyments.
Having requested permission from them, he departed filled with devotion; the wise man should avoid food provided by others, as well as receiving gifts from them.
One should especially avoid defects such as lust, anger, and the like;
one should observe fasts and other such disciplines, and likewise have the hair shaved.
One should perform the ritual bath according to the rules after meditating upon the three-eyed Lord,
having performed the golden *śrāddha* and offered the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) according to the injunctions.
According to one's capacity, one should indeed give wealth, grain, clothing, and likewise other things—
land, gold, a cow, and a maiden— free from any stinginess regarding one's means.
One should give it to the devotees of Śiva, and especially to the twice-born.
This should be understood to apply to other fields as well.
There too, the sacred sites (tīrthas) situated in the five groups of eight places are supremely meritorious and bestow the state of union with Rudra (rudrasālokya).
O Rudra, there are the eight primary secrets, as well as the eight supreme secrets,
the eight secrets more secret than the secret, and the eight purifiers.
These five [groups], including the eight bathing places (snānāṣṭaka), dwell upon the earth by divine appointment;
they have been established as manifest signs (liṅga) for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
O Six-faced One, whatever water is situated near those very [shrines], that is a supremely meritorious holy ford (tīrtha); having bathed there, one shall go to Śiva.
The meaning is that one attains the world of the gods there.
Having reached that place, [these things] were indeed fashioned for the benefit of human beings in the land of Bhārata.
In ancient times, Hara was ever present during their processions.
Thus it is said.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"That man who, having seen the peak from afar, offers salutation, is liberated from all sins, just as a serpent is freed from its slough."
Likewise, in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "Having bathed at the holy site (tīrtha) where the celestial chariot (vimāna) was seen, and having performed his daily rites, he,
dressed in white garments and bearing offerings, should enter the temple of Śiva."
Wherever one looks around the regions, the palaces and gate-towers of the temples appear;
indeed, the entire ground is Kailāsa.

O faultless Manonmanī, as far as the sound of musical instruments is heard from the abode of Śiva, even that far away, the city of Śiva is directly perceived; there, the sounds of the Sūta’s hymns resound.
As far as the sound of Śambhu’s victory cry reaches.
It is heard that the peak of Mount Rājata is thus described:
having paid homage to the *sthūlaliṅga* in the *Aṃśumat-tantra*, one should enter the temple; [therein is] the *sthūlaliṅga*.
The subtle liṅga is the celestial chariot (vimāna) of Sadāśiva.
The sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), the auspicious liṅga (bhadraliṅga), and the [central] liṅga—these are here called the "three liṅgas.
In the Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva, it is stated that the body is the temple (prāsāda) and the embodied being is known as the liṅga. [This is] the difference between the two.
Therefore, one should meditate in this manner.
One should contemplate the gross liṅga as the celestial chariot (vimāna) and the subtle liṅga as Sadāśiva; within that [subtle liṅga], one should likewise meditate upon Śiva himself.
Alternatively, in another manner, the most excellent of teachers should meditate upon Sadāśiva in the external liṅga and Śiva in the internal liṅga.
The linga alone is the means of measurement by way of its pervasive pervasion;
from the base (hemādi) up to the pinnacle (sthūpī), it is traditionally remembered as the very form of Śiva.
In the Āgneya Purāṇa:
"Śiva is eternally present in a stone image, a liṅga, a celestial chariot (vimāna), a pedestal of elemental beings (bhūtapīṭha), and a temple;
one should always offer salutations there."
Flowers and so forth acquired by oneself are best; those from the forest are said to be middling; those purchased are inferior;
and those obtained through bartering are the lowest of the low.
And the cultivation of a flower garden should be carried out in the region north of Śivāśrama.
Thus it is stated by Nandikeśvara in the Śivadharma:
For all castes who practice the Śiva-āśrama,
the Śiva-dharmas were taught by Śiva for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a woman, or even a Śūdra; or according to one's stage of life—whether a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant.
To the north of his own hermitage, he should establish a very beautiful flower garden,
[to be maintained] with flowers grown in the forest or with leaves produced on the mountains.
One should worship Śiva with flowers that have not been stale, are free from holes, have been sprinkled with water, are devoid of insects, and may even be those grown in one's own garden.

In the *Kāmika*: "One should designate the location for flower gardens, monasteries, and so forth, everywhere. According to this statement, one should perform the consecration (*udbhāvana*) in whatever location is available. Then—
One should resort to the abode of Śiva.
Regarding this, the sequence is as follows:
Having approached the vicinity of the temple, one should first pay obeisance to the *sthūlaliṅga* either outside the gateway (*gopura*) or from the southeast (*āgneya*) direction of the bull.
As it is said in the *Aṃśumat*:
One should pay obeisance to the gross liṅga (sthūlaliṅga) to the east of the gateway (gopura); the prostration to the gross liṅga is performed outside the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha).
Alternatively, having mounted the back of a bull while leaning slightly toward the southeast—
in that very section on worship it is said:
"One should perform prostration to the gross liṅga and enter the circle of the rosary (mālā) all around in front of Śiva."
Having stood at the foremost place of the great seat (mahāpīṭha).
Then, having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, [one performs] the sequence of salutations.
This rule regarding the southeastern quarter pertains to the eastern door.

At the time of prostration, one should not bow while covering one's body with a cloth. One should not perform obeisance in front of Śiva, nor behind him, nor to his left, nor within the inner sanctum. Furthermore, one should avoid oil massages and the like in the temple of Śiva. Likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī*:
That man who bows down to me while covering his body with a garment will be born mute for three lifetimes and destitute for seven lifetimes.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:

"One should never perform recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), or prostrations (*namaskāra*) in front of [the deity], behind it, to the left, or likewise within the inner sanctum (*garbhāgāra*)."
One should perform the salutation to Īśvara and so forth at the northern and western gates exclusively on the left side.
Likewise—
If one stands to the left when [the deity] faces west or north, or otherwise on the opposite side,
and performs the worship and prostrations to Īśāna, will it not lead to fault, or will it not result in the attainment of the fruit?
They would be as follows: in the Raurava [Tantra]—during the time of the concealed cloth (pracchannapaṭa), the viewing of the *liṅga* must not be performed; at that time, the viewing...
From delusion comes the destruction of wife and sons.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: One should avoid anointing with oil, wrapping the head,
and likewise wearing a bodice within the temple of Śiva.
A person should avoid hunger, yawning, hiccups, and other such delusions, as well as spitting, voiding excrement, and so forth, within the temple of Śiva.
Devoid of shoes, a parasol, and so forth, yet endowed with forbearance;
likewise, in the *Rāmāyaṇa*: p. 586) And in the *Rāmāyaṇa* as well—
That man who, having approached the abode of Śiva, defiles it with excrement, urine, or spittle,
shall become a Vetāla.
But he who, having gone to a temple, mounts a vehicle or the like— he too shall not incur that fault,
yet he will become a cripple by birth.
Whoever shall ascend to the temple from the staircase, his foot, together with the wooden slipper, shall encounter suffering.
Or if, desiring honor, he consumes the property of Śiva, he becomes a Brahmarākṣasa and wails in empty forests.
Thereafter, preceded by meditation, one should pay homage to the *balipīṭha*.
O Ajitā, one should pay homage to the *bhūtapīṭha* preceded by the first meditation.
Possessing five faces with five mouths, having ten eyes, ten ears, and ten arms, he holds excellent tridents.
With one throat, one heart, and two feet of deep red color— such is the recipient of the offering upon the sacrificial pedestal of the elements.
Then, one should also pay homage to the flagstaff preceded by meditation. Thus: "One should perform the salutation to the flagpole preceded by meditation [visualizing it as]:
having one face, two feet, two hands, and three eyes, adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass and a line of hair."
His body is white in form, mounted upon his own horse, and he holds a lotus seat and a staff.
The specific meditation during the festival (p.
that which is known as the "pillar" is the Lord; that which is remembered as the "cloth" is the sacrificial animal; and the rope is the noose.
It is said that they are of three kinds.
Having thus petitioned and paid homage to the one with the banner and staff, and having paid homage to the Bull-leader preceded by meditation, one should pray.
As stated in the *Brahmāṇḍopapurāṇa*:
Having prostrated before the Lord, the bull-bannered god who is seated facing him and whose feet have been worshipped with flowers, one should pray as follows.
The Lord, who bestows bliss and auspiciousness upon the worlds,
who is the bull among the eightfold forms, and whose abode is like the sovereign silver mountain (Kailāsa).
May the Lord of the horned ones (or the Lord of the peaked mountain), surrounded by the eightfold divine hosts,
who disperses the clouds with his breath, the King of Dharma consisting of wisdom, being pleased and with a face gracious through his favor, protect us.

O Blessed One, being pleased with me who bows at your lotus feet, grant permission to this embodied soul for the vision of Śiva, for the worship of Śiva, and for the attainment of the perfection that is its fruit within this inner region.

Having thus prayed to Vṛṣanāyaka, one should prostrate like a staff before Śiva. Having likewise prayed to Dharmeśa, who is beyond the bonds of the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), one should prostrate on the ground with all eight limbs like a staff and scatter flowers.
Aṃśumatī:
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground before the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati), all sins fall away;
they do not rise up again with him.
For as many thousands of years as there are particles of dust clinging to the body, for that long one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
p.
590) Regarding this supreme fourfold salutation, it is as follows:
namely, that which consists of eight limbs, five limbs, three limbs, and one limb; [the first being] the crest-lock and the two hands.
And the two ears, the chin, and the pair of arms.
Now hear concerning the eight-limbed and the five-limbed prostration:
having placed the head, the two hands, and the two arms upon the knees.
This has been described as having five limbs; now hear of the three-limbed [mudrā]: having formed the *mukula* (bud) gesture with the hands, one should place them at the region of the head.
And this is the characteristic of the three-limbed salutation by way of its enumeration: the single-limbed salutation is performed with the head alone.
Having performed prostrations before Śiva with devotion, numbering three, five, seven, nine, or twelve times, the man [should then proceed].
One obtains the supreme fruit equal to that of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha),
even if it was performed out of malice or by men devoid of devotion.
Even a single utterance of "namaskāra" shall be a remover of sin; therefore, that man who bows to the Liṅga even once with devotion [attains great merit].
Having attained all desires, he rejoices together with Śiva. Following that, [the state] where the feet are separated by intervals, the hands are motionless, the face is intent on praise,
the mind is fixed in meditation, and the gait is like that of a woman pregnant with a pot of ghee or oil— [This is the *pādāntaritapadaka* meter.]
A man or a woman, having understood it as auspicious, should perform the circumambulation four times in a clockwise direction.
Regarding the cause: by men of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, or even by women, who have bathed well,
whose limbs are smeared with ashes, who observe excellent vows, and who carry rosaries.
p.
592) The ellipsis is that the circumambulation should be performed by those who observe the vow of silence, whose minds are focused on nothing else, and who belong to the lineage of Śiva.
Aṃśumatī said:
"O best of suns, listen as I describe the sequence of circumambulation, which removes all sins and bestows the fruit of every gift."
For the purpose of destroying all diseases, one should then perform a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*).
Regarding that, there is a verse defining *pradakṣiṇa*: "The letter *pra* cuts away all fear; the letter *da* bestows the attainment of liberation."
From the syllable *kṣi*, disease is destroyed; the syllable *ṇa* bestows prosperity.
Because it involves a clockwise conjunction with the food, it is traditionally known as "pradakṣiṇa" (clockwise).
One should move from foot to foot, keeping the hands free from movement.
Praise with speech, meditation in the heart, and circumambulation—these are the four limbs.
(Svāyambhuva, p. 593)
Just as a woman near the time of delivery moves slowly while carrying a jar filled with oil, so too should one perform the circumambulation.
The fruit according to the time for this [practice] is stated in that very same place:
"In the forenoon there shall be the destruction of disease; at midday it grants desired objects;
in the afternoon it destroys all sins; and during the half-watch (ardhayāma) it bestows liberation."
O Ajita, on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth lunar days; during the three births [of the moon];
under the asterism Ārdrā; on a Sunday; and during the Karaṇa known as Vṛṣṭi.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the eclipses of the moon and sun, at the passage of the sun into a new zodiac sign, and during festivals,
one should bathe and perform circumambulation.
He who bows to Śiva with devotion shall attain all his desires and obtain a hundredfold merit; of this there is no doubt.
When these times have been declared, one endowed with devotion and faith [should worship] beginning from sunrise until the sun has set.
By performing circumambulation for that long, one shall obtain all desires;
or likewise, if a man [performs it] for a single day and night during these times.

One who performs circumambulation enjoys infinite fruit. Even one who has come from a long distance, though devoid of hope for reward, should perform circumambulation with devotion and bow to the imperishable Śiva.
O Keśava, whatever state of being arises for him on that path, it certainly grants men the fruit of circumambulation; of this there is no doubt.
A traveler who, while on the road, performs a circumambulation of a Śiva-liṅga and offers salutations,
shall obtain fivefold the fruit mentioned previously.
p.
595) Regarding that which arises from yoga— at the time of a festival or at the time of an offering— by performing circumambulation, one obtains at every step the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
A human being attains the fruit.
O Ajita,
it is taught that for one who has been initiated, circumambulation is prescribed only in the outer [sanctum] of the womb-chamber (garbhageha),
and never within the inner maṇḍala for human beings.
The fruit of a single circumambulation is said to be [the merit of] an *antarhāra* (inner necklace); it is tripled for a *madhyahāra* (middle necklace), and quadrupled at the boundary (*maryādā*).
That which is performed within the great boundary (mahāmaryādika) becomes fivefold; that which is performed outside the limit of the field (kṣetrāvadhi) becomes a hundredfold for men.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"Circumambulating the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*) yields the merit born of ten horse-sacrifices;
the merit in the region of the inner mandala (*antarmaṇḍaladeśaka*) is ten times greater than that."

In the halls containing the *antarhāra* and other structures, the merit shall be tenfold for each respective one. At the conclusion of the worship, one should perform circumambulation by way of both the left and the right paths.
Now, regarding the number of circumambulations:
having performed a single circumambulation of Śiva with devotion and a concentrated mind,
one easily obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).

The supreme circumambulation is said to consist of twenty-one [revolutions]; that of the middling type consists of the number of lunar days (fifteen), and the inferior consists of the number of sages (seven).

That which is performed with a count of five is considered inferior; that which is performed with a count of qualities (guṇas) is called middling; and that which is performed with a count of [further] qualities is said to be the lowest of the low.
Therefore, even a single circumambulation performed with devotion is declared superior;
as stated in the Svāyambhuva: "A single prostration with one staff and even a single circumambulation [are meritorious]. * * * * * * * * * * * *
For the sake of attaining one's desired goal, one should perform a circumambulation a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, or even ten million times.
The specific fruit resulting from the [different] genders is now defined:
the fruit of circumambulating a human linga has been stated; therefore, for one made by a ṛṣi (ārṣaka), it shall indeed be double that amount through prostration.
The fruit at a divine (daivika) liṅga is threefold; that same fruit is declared to be fourfold at a Gāṇeśvara liṅga, and it becomes fivefold.

By thus gently touching the self-manifested *liṅga*, one performs its circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) in four ways: clockwise (*savya*), counter-clockwise (*apasavya*), both clockwise and counter-clockwise (*savyāpasavya*), and limb-by-limb circumambulation (*aṅgapradakṣiṇa*). Thus it is said in the *Aṃśumatī*:
Listen, O observer of noble vows, to the characteristics of the two modes of circumambulation: the first is declared to be clockwise (savya), and the second is counter-clockwise (apasavya).

There is another way, both clockwise and counter-clockwise, performed by oneself with the limbs. The clockwise is said to be *savya*, while the counter-clockwise is *apasavya*. However, [in this context] the *apasavya* is what is called "clockwise."
O Ajitā,
that which is performed by transgressing the thread from left to right and right to left is called *savyāpasavya*; that indeed belongs to those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*).
As for the circumambulation by limb (*aṅgapradakṣiṇa*), which is performed with all the limbs,
its nature as the *somasūtra* is described in the *Aṃśumatī*.
One should apply the width of the temple, its measurement, and the *somasūtra* line to the northern side of the base of the *liṅga*.

This should continue until the end of the sūtra; however, one should avoid circumambulating [the site] if it is too narrow. In a confined space, it should be performed by leaving a gap equal to half the size of the temple.
Or it may be equal to half the height of the temple, because it has been stated that [the measurement] is according to the proportions of the temple.
Regarding the cause: one should perform the circumambulation of Śambhu and not cross over the *somasūtra*;
by crossing it, there would be one [birth] for each [step], whereas by not crossing it, there are thirty million [liberations].

The "unleapable circumambulation" (alaṅghyapradakṣiṇa) consists of moving from left to right and from right to left. The "leapable circumambulation" (vilaṅghyapradakṣiṇa) consists of moving from left to right and from right to left one by one. The meaning is that in the case of the "unleapable circumambulation," there would be three times ten thousand (ayuta) repetitions.

One should not even cross the shadow of [the teacher], just as one does not cross the path of the moon; for it is stated in the *Kāraṇa*: "One should not cross the shadow of the Great Yāma with the thread."
One should perform circumambulation [of the deity] while remaining in the shadow, but in the case of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), one should circumambulate clockwise.
Thus it is stated elsewhere:

When it comes time to step over the shadow, how should one perform the circumambulation? At the end, the wise man should conceal himself within a third part [of the space], starting from the division of the light.
Likewise: "The pedestal, the temple, or the image— whether during a festival, at the time of an offering, or when attended by the Guru— should likewise be situated in the shadow of the *liṅga*."

At the time of performing circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), no defect regarding one's shadow occurs anywhere; however, moving counter-clockwise (*apasavya*) is forbidden wherever there are two *somasūtras* or where there is a temple of Viṣṇu. One must not move counter-clockwise.
One should perform it; indeed, one should simply circumambulate [it] clockwise.

The nature of the "left" (savya) and so forth is clearly stated in the *Aṃśumat-tantra*: "From Indra to Indra [the end of the row], that which is to the right is declared to be 'pradakṣiṇa' (circumambulation to the right).
One should perform the 'apasavya' (leftward movement) in the manner opposite to the 'savya'."
Now hear how one circumambulates by way of the right and left paths: p. 601) as follows—
And [he saw] Caṇḍanātha beginning with Vṛṣa, the bull Soma-sūtraka,
again the bull Caṇḍanātha, and by the side of the region of Nāla.
Again, one should proceed toward the fierce [fire] and likewise to the back of the bull; thus, moving to the left and to the right is here called circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa).
Thus, performing circumambulation by moving to the left and right, one should perform the circumambulation of the bull with the permission of Caṇḍa. And so says the Āgama:
The beginning and end of Vṛṣadeva are declared to have four locations;
it is joined with the three Caṇḍa locations, and on the first day of the fortnight is the Soma-thread.
One should perform circumambulation of oneself according to the specific number of each respective location; likewise, there is a ninefold count, and thus one [method] is prescribed.
The nature of the circumambulation by limb (*aṅgapradakṣiṇa*) has been demonstrated in the *Ajina*:
"Performing the circumambulation by limb, one places one's own body upon the ground."
Having joined his two arms together like a staff, he made a gesture of salutation with palms pressed together.
Having performed a full prostration before Śiva, a person should likewise perform one or even three circumambulations.
Having performed five or seven [prostrations] for the sake of turning away from all evil, one should again perform a respectful salutation before him with devotion.
Having risen and performed prostrations again and again, one should conclude [the rite].
Having bound the fingertips of both hands together, one should perform the *svastika* with the feet; then, one should rotate like a wheel-rim (*nemivat*).
Having likewise done so all around the palace.
The circumambulation limb by limb (aṅgapradakṣiṇa) is declared to be performed in this very manner; thus, each single circumambulation constitutes one thousand circumambulations.
In the same way, other [mudrās] such as the lotus, lion, chain, nāga, and right-turning [nāga], and so forth, are also [to be understood]. Thus, O Śumati.
These are to be seen.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"For ascetics, it is counter-clockwise (*apasavya*); for students (*brahmacārin*), it is clockwise (*savya*);
and for forest-dwellers and householders, it is by way of both clockwise and counter-clockwise."
In the *Svāyambhuva*, even regarding the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*), the procedure for the left and right paths is stated as follows: [text fragment].
However, circumambulation is prescribed for the worshiper even within the inner sanctum; yet even there, one must avoid crossing the shadow or the remains of offerings belonging to the God of gods.
At that time, having avoided the *somasūtra*, one should perform the circumambulation by way of both the left (*apasavya*) and right (*savya*) paths.
In the *Kālottara*, two rules are stated:
"Perform [the practice] within the inner mandala by way of the right and left paths; however, in the region of the outer enclosure..."
The right-hand path is clockwise.
Here, by the first half [of the verse], the rule regarding the right and left positions is stated; by the second half,
the rule for the external position on the right is stated.
In whichever enclosure there is the presence of the sacrificial altar and the bull,
in that very enclosure one should perform the circumambulation, making that the primary focus.

Where there is circumambulation, one should cause the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) to be situated for the bull; having brought it together with those two standing outside, the adept should perform the circumambulation, whether it be of the Lord of Gods and the bull,
or of the Lord of the sacrificial pedestal and the bull.
The wise practitioner should perform an intermediate circumambulation at each respective obstacle.
Having thus completed the circumambulation and returned, he should prostrate before Śiva as before; then, rising up and bowing again and again, he should bring the rite to conclusion.
Ajite—
having again performed obeisance with devotion in that same manner before him, and having stood up...
Having performed prostrations again and again, one should bring [the rite] to completion.
Thereafter, having first meditated upon the two guardians of the second enclosure, one should bow and pray to them.
Likewise, in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "Having bowed to and worshipped the two gatekeepers of the second enclosure, who are leaders of the Gaṇas,
the devotee of Śiva should enter within only after offering praise."
In meditation—
bearing with their own arms the excellent mace and the tarjanī mudrā, and resembling the fierce-rayed sun.

I bow to the two leaders of the hosts, the gatekeepers of Rudra’s abode, who possess crests, armlets, necklaces, anklets, and waist-bands adorned with lordly serpents; who destroy the suffering of those who prostrate before them, and who have attained their status through service to Gaurī’s Lord.
Thereafter, preceded by meditation, one should bow to Nandikeśvara, the lord of the Gaṇas, and offer this prayer:
Bearing an axe and a deer in his palms, with hands folded in salutation to the Lord,
white with the smearing of ashes, radiant with the crescent moon and the Ganges as his topknot—
[I bow] to Tripurāntaka, the foremost among the Pramathas.
I worship Śrī Nandikeśa, who is surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas, whose lotus feet are saluted by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu.

Herein is the prayer: O Blessed One, being gracious, grant permission to me, who am prostrate at your lotus feet, for entry within, for the vision of Śiva, for the worship of Śiva, and for the attainment of the perfection of those fruits.
Having thus petitioned him and subsequently meditated upon the [deity] born of stone and other materials,
and having likewise obtained the permission of Nandikeśvara, one should enter within and first pay homage to Vighnarāja.

One should pay homage to Vighnarāja on the ground while reciting his hymn; scattering flowers at his feet, one should perform a head-blow and a fist-blow, praising him while remaining in the *vahni-sthiti* posture.
One should place the fingers upon the two ears.
Then, having entered the interior of the pavilion and paid homage to the God of gods, one should perform a hymn of praise.
Thus, in the *Aṃśumatī*:
Then, having entered the interior of the pavilion, especially before Śiva, one should pay homage to the God of gods while reciting a hymn of praise.
One should place the *añjali* at both the head and the heart.
This is shown as the *namaskāra-mudrā* in the *Suprabheda*. Likewise, with all fingers joined together, the hands rest upon the region of the heart for all [deities].
The binding should be performed by pressing with the left big toe.
In the *Namaskāra* [chapter], it should be understood that one should cause all rites to be performed;
the hymn appropriate to each respective caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*) is demonstrated in the *Kāmika*.
Whether it be the study of the Vedas, or something else such as the recitation of hymns,
or perhaps the Dravidian languages and so forth, accompanied by song and dance;
One may likewise arrange a song composed in any of the eighteen recognized languages.
The offering of handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Brahmins and others as appropriate has been demonstrated by Aṃsumat.
The preceptor should perform the entry into the inner sanctum; having thus worshipped with a flower, he should recollect the Śiva-mantra.
Upon the entry of the Brahmins, he should enter the half-pavilion; for a Kṣatriya, however, this is done specifically according to the sequence of the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
Having entered the pavilion, one should then stand at the entrance; there, one should worship the principle of the self (ātmatattva) according to the path of the Guru.
The Vaiśyas and Śūdras likewise [should worship] at the front of the bull and on the back of the bull;
having applied a coating of cow dung, it should be made square.
One should worship with the root mantra and perform [the rite] according to the path of the Guru. In the Śaiva tradition:
clothing, wealth, land, female slaves, and divine ornaments.
Incense, lamps, offerings, and so forth, as well as the great sacrificial oblation (mahānivedya).
One should give to the God and the Goddess according to one's capacity; even if it be only a tiny atom, O monkey, whatever little one may have.
One should prostrate only after having made an offering; otherwise, one is not dear to Śambhu. O God, even one devoid of wealth and such may offer leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth to the Lord.
One should indeed bow down to the deity after having offered [the gift], but never otherwise; nor should one ever offer grass, filth, or other impurities found within the temple precincts.
Having purified [the deity], one should bow to the Lord of Gods; never otherwise. Or, in the absence of everything, having even made speech as one's companion, one should bow to Hara.
"The devotee of Śambhu shall not be otherwise"—such is the instruction of the Vedas. Having acted thus according to one's ability, one should behold the Lord with devotion.
In Niḥśvāsa:

[The deity] has five faces resembling the moon and ten hands; he holds a trident, a ṭaṅka, a sword, a vajra, and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya); [the remaining hands hold] a noose, the gesture of granting boons (varada), a goad, a jewel, and fire.
On the left is the form of Sadāśiva, seated upon a white lotus.

They say that the *upānah* (sandals) and the *pādukā* (shoes) are the thighs; the *jagaru* (or *jagaru*) is the hips; the *kumuda* is the belly; and with the two arms and the *kampaka*, they form the [remaining parts].
The throat and the ear should be known [as the locations]; the lower lip is traditionally taught as the lower lip.
611) The forehead, extending from the great fillet to the hairline, should be [anointed] with ghee and water. Thus...
Having meditated upon it and paid homage, one should then discard that flower.
The sight of the *liṅga* at dawn removes [the sins] committed during the night;
at midday, those from birth until that point; and at sunset, those from birth through seven lifetimes.
Thus, the mortal who performs this shall attain *sāyujya* (union) at the end.
And in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"He who, in the morning, beholds the Lord of the gods, whose nature is the Śiva-liṅga..."
He indeed attains a destination that is superior to all others.
By beholding Mahādeva at midday, one obtains the fruit of sacrifice; by beholding him in the evening, having attained the fruit of all sacrifices, one is liberated.
Having seen the sin committed during half a month, one should abandon it on a festival day;
a man should abandon the sin committed during eight days on the eighth lunar day.
Having beheld Śaṅkara at twilight, one is liberated from all sins—
whether mental, verbal, or physical, even those that are most grave.
Likewise, one is completely liberated from minor offenses (upapātaka) as well as major sins (pātaka) by beholding the omnipresent Lord Īśāna in the form of a Liṅga at Saṃkrama.
Having abandoned the sin committed during a month, one goes to the auspicious state;
likewise during the solstices and the half-months of the southern and northern courses.
And by beholding Him during the equinox, one attains the supreme state,
preceded by meditation upon the respective forms of the deities such as the Dancing Form (Nṛttamūrti).
Then, with offerings of various flowers, one should perform prostration;
for in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*,
it is said that [one should worship] Dakṣiṇāmūrti and Śiva as Somāskandeśvara situated there.
One should pay homage to Naṭeśvara, who is mounted upon a bull and has the moon as his crest-jewel.

Likewise—
In the [mudrās] beginning with Apasmāra and those following it, however, he stands firm with his right foot [forward], while his left foot is bent;
likewise, he holds a hand-drum (ḍamaruka) in his right [hand].
On the left is the god Agnidhara with fifteen matted locks;
on the right is the god Gaṅgādhara, endowed with a beautiful form and the moon.
With all his limbs perfectly formed and adorned with every ornament,
his body was like a *japā* flower, engaged in the *tāṇḍava* dance.

O Gaurī, you who possess a single face and four arms, whose form is like coral, who hold a black antelope, an axe, and grant the gestures of boon and fearlessness, who wear an excellent third eye and a garment, and who bear the moon upon your crest.
Together with the slaughterhouse.

Seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), with a red body and two eyes, his two hands holding a white lotus at his shoulder; he is clothed in red garments, adorned with red unguents and garlands, and stands [erect].
I praise Śiva-Sūrya together with his limbs.
In the Rauravottara:
one should worship the fivefold form consisting of Vighneśa, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Viṣṇumūrti, Brahmamūrti, and Durgā.

Seated upon a patch of ground near a banyan tree, I bow to the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the teacher of the three worlds, who is unrivaled among all sages in bestowing knowledge and who is skilled in severing the suffering of birth and death.
Brāhmī, Maheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī,
Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā are the seven Mothers.
These goddesses, who abide as obstacles to heroes, bring about the fear of those who bow down to them;
they behold the one who resembles pure crystal, who has the face of an elephant and four arms.
One should always remember the supreme deity with a protruding belly, three eyes, holding a noose and a goad,
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and with ears constantly flapping.
In the quarter of Vāyu, she is yellow in color, holding in her hands a spear, a bell, a banner, a lotus, a cock, a sword, and a staff;
she grants boons and fearlessness, and holds a bow, an arrow, and a chisel, while possessing six faces.
He has twelve eyes, bears the fear of the fire-crested bird (peacock), holds four arrows in his four hands, possesses a single face, wields two spears, and carries a cock.

One should meditate upon this Kṣetrapāla, who is black in color, endowed with four arms, holding a trident, a ḍuṇḍubha snake, a battle-axe, and a skull-cup; he is adorned with a crown of fire, possesses three eyes, and stands upon a lotus.
In the *Brahmāṇḍopapurāṇa*, a specific instruction is stated:
"At the conclusion of the hymn, one should recite the praise of the Lord’s excellence and [apply] the ashes of the planets."
Having taken up and held [the vessel] for Śambhu, and again likewise at the end of the circumambulation, having indeed uttered "camat"?
Having prostrated and worshipped him while offering praise, and having struck his water-pot with his hand three times,
he prayed for the fruit of service to the Lord, [placing] the Lord’s liṅga between the horns of the bull.
Then Dhvani intended to worship Caṇḍeśvara—
one who has two eyes and two arms, who wears excellent white garments,
who is endowed with a crown of matted hair, and whose crest is formed by the half-moon.
The right leg is extended, while the left leg is bent in a reclining posture; the left knee is raised,
and the left hand holds an axe.
One should perform the service (sevā) in due order, beginning with the sacred seats (pīṭha) and ending with Caṇḍa.
As stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"Even among all the holy fords (tīrtha), [this] protects one from the fear arising from the manifestation of the two cosmic eggs."
"Such are the signs of the Mandri-rite.
Having thus prayed, he sat down beside him facing north,

In this same way, one should also attend upon the temple of the Goddess—as stated in the Kāmika:
"In the temple of the Goddess as well, [the rite] should be performed according to the previously mentioned procedure; or [one may perform it] at a lion[-throne]."
Or even a bull is proclaimed to be his vehicle.
Having prayed to the Lord who faces Īśvara, seated upon the bull-vehicle,
one should thereafter meditate upon the two female gatekeepers.
The two door-keepers of the Goddess, however, hold swords and shields in their hands;
they are adorned with matted hair and crowns, and are decorated in red and dark blue respectively.
Holding swords and shields, they may have either two or four arms;
O Goddess, these gatekeepers grant all desired fruits.
Then, having paid homage to the God and reciting the hymn of praise,
[he beheld her]— richly endowed with beauty, possessing three eyes and dark limbs, holding a lotus, a rosary, and the gesture of granting fearlessness in her hands,
and adorned with a crown, a moon-like face, and matted locks bound in a topknot.
I praise Śiva and Śakti, the glorious Kāmakoṣṭha.
The various forms of the directional deities (digdevas) and the goddesses (sudevis) have been proclaimed; or else, the gods of the abode of Śiva,
or even the host led by the six-faced one (Kārttikeya).
In the southern direction, the presiding deity of the quarter should be established, possessing a form identical to that goddess;
or else, the powers (śaktis) beginning with Vāmā are established as his retinue.
The Goddess Nirmālyadhāriṇī, who is within the range of Yama and Īśa,
has two arms and two eyes for her cause; she is dark-complexioned and auspicious, and in her left hand—
Holding a flower in his left hand above the knee.
Alternatively, one should hold flowers with both hands joined in the añjali gesture; then one should meditate upon Caṇḍeśī and Yamunī according to the prescribed sequence.
In the Kāmika:
"That goddess Śyāmalā, adorned with all ornaments on her two hands, is renowned by the name Yamunī,
holding a supreme blue lotus."

620) Having thus paid homage to [the deities] from the *pīṭhas* up to Caṇḍa, and having established their presence, one should recite the root mantra as much as possible for the removal of transgressions. And upon the entry of the deity—
While the Lord remains present, and again upon his departure, turning one's back toward the two who delight in Śiva is auspicious;
thereafter follow enjoyment, sleep, study, and the performance of malevolent rites.
Likewise, in the case of crossing or touching the shadow of a statue at a gopura.
Stepping over flower offerings, touching them, walking between the seats of the deities,

The measurement of one cubit, a single circumambulation, an untimely visit,
and likewise conversation as it occurs;

Speaking untruths, listening to what is unbearable, causing [the deity] to depart, remaining [in the presence of the deity] while [one is impure], and sitting too close in the vicinity; these are the transgressions.
Laughing in vain, singing in vain, and likewise listening to vain songs; having a mind of attachment toward the property of the gods, as well as touching upon their physical forms.
The speaking of the wicked is like that; likewise, the disparaging of the virtuous is the same.
Both [acts] consist of saluting with one's upper garment and performing circumambulation.
Performing prostrations on the left side of the deity, muttering prayers [inappropriately], and worshipping false deities— these are proclaimed as transgressions.
The treasury of compassion endures these [offenses] committed through ignorance by those who recite the Śatarudrīya while performing the independent ritual (svatantra).
There is no doubt that [the merit of] intentional action is exhausted solely through experience.
In the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"One should not take away even a blade of grass or anything else situated within the temple of the deity, nor what has been offered to the Lord."
And having taken [these], they go into intense darkness.
Leaves, flowers, and so forth that have entered a temple [should be avoided]. Thus it is stated in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*:
One who obstructs the performance of Śiva’s rites and one who misappropriates Śiva’s property goes to the Raurava hell for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
A mortal devoted to the service of Śiva should worship for even a moment or half a moment; he shall bring the fourteen divine worlds under his control and be glorified in the realm of Śiva.
One should offer wealth, whether a *niṣka* or even half a *niṣka*, for the sake of the deity; having obtained the fruit of a thousand cows, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
O Mataṅgī,
those brave men who worship this Liṅga of Māheśvarī with devotion and prostration are themselves perfected ones, lords of the Gaṇas.
They delight in various enjoyments at the departure-place of Umāpati. One would not obtain the station near the Śatarudras, nor the worship of the Liṅga even once, [if one remains] in the abode.
O auspicious one, it is described through devotion to the Śivaliṅga.
Having ascended to the station of Śrīkaṇṭha, one shall obtain most wonderful happiness;
thus, through the division of devotion, one who is always delighted even in the *liṅga*.
In the Śivadharmottara:
"Those who offer salutations to the Lord here and there— even out of association, curiosity, or greed— they attain that celestial chariot."
Whether one recites the name of Śiva even incidentally,
or performs a prostration to him, that shall not be in vain.
Thus have these great destinies been declared for those who perform auspicious deeds;
even by the slightest of means, through the grace of the Lord, they are attained by men.
Indeed, tens of millions of celestial chariots in the form of stars are seen;
specifically, twenty-eight [such chariots] shine brightly above for those of virtuous nature. Thus, [one should perform] service...

Having performed the ritual of extinction (*nirvātya*) and emerged from the abode of Śiva, one should clear away the obstacles situated on the path with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and then proceed to the house located within the lattice of weapons (*astrapañjara*).
In the *Aṃśumattantra*:
"Having emerged from the *ālaya*, one should then enter one's own abode.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*:
One should visit temples, brahmins, and one’s own excellent home;

Until midday, one should engage in such activities as listening to the scriptures of the Śaiva Siddhānta; as it is stated in the Kriyākāṇḍa:

And it should indeed be given on the day measured by the sun’s essence (the twelfth).
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"For as long as the knowledge of Śiva does not become firm for him, for that duration one must especially perform listening [to the scriptures] and other such practices."
Thus [it is said].
In the *Kālottara*:
"When someone, having illuminated an object with a torch in hand, should set it aside,
[he perceives] that which is called the Supreme, the unsurpassed scripture known as the Unmanifest."
The purpose for the arising of this knowledge has been described in the *Svāyambhuva* [Tantra], as follows (p.
For the sake of liberation from the bondage of karma known as the impurity of speech and the impurity of illusion, and for the manifestation of the state of Śiva,
the knowledge of Śiva proceeds.
In the *Kāmika*:
"The Tantra, consisting of Śiva and Rudra, is twenty-eight in number; although there may be but one speaker, it becomes manifold due to the diversity of the listeners."
This supreme [teaching] was brought down upon Mount Meru by the revealers beginning with Praṇava; it is endowed with ritual action and conduct, and is accompanied by yoga and gnosis.
In the *Makuṭa*:
"The listeners of the Śiva-bheda [scriptures] are three times three by way of lineage; those of the Rudra-bheda [scriptures] are two times two, totaling sixty-six."
The number is two hundred and seven; as it is stated in the *Makuṭa* (p.
The Kāmika is said to have three divisions, the Yogaja five divisions, the Cintya tantras six divisions,
and the Kāraṇa seven divisions.
That which is called Ajita has four divisions, Dīpta has nine divisions, Sūkṣma is said to have one division,
and Sahasraka has ten divisions.
Aṃśumat would be Sūryabheda, while Suprabheda is indeed Bhedaka; Vijaya is Aṣṭabheda, and Niśvāsa has eight divisions as well.
The Svāyambhuva has two divisions, while the Āgneya likewise has two divisions; the Vīratantra, in particular, has thirteen divisions.
Raurava is said to have six divisions, while Makuṭa has two; Vimala has one division consisting of Kalā, and Candrajñāna has fourteen.

The division of lunar days (*tithi-bheda*), the *bimba-tantra*, the *prāg-gīta*—these sixteen are traditionally taught; then there is the *lalita*, which is the differentiation of qualities (*guṇa-bheda*), and the *siddha*, which is the differentiation of the ages (*yuga-bheda*).
The *Santāna* in seven divisions, the [tantra] spoken by Śarva in five divisions, the *Pārameśa* in seven divisions,
and the *Kiraṇa* in nine divisions.
The Vātula and the Ravibheda shall be explained separately;
the sequence of their sub-divisions is said to be two hundred and seven.
Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"He whose [name] consists of seven, two, one, six, seven, four,
thirty-two, ten, one, moon, nine, eight, and three."
The divisions of the Āgamas are [calculated] by the eyes of Kāma (2), then by the digits of speech (16), the days of Manu (14),
the fires (3), the oceans (4), the qualities (3), the arrows (5), the worlds (14), the apertures (9), and the sun multiplied by the good qualities (36).
These knowledges each have four quarters through knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*kriyā*), and yoga-practice (*yogacaryā*).
Among these, however, the nature of the Supreme Lord is [found] in the quarter of knowledge (*jñānapāda*).
Furthermore, the nature of the *kalā*, *pralayākala*, and *sakala* [souls], as well as the nature of the bonds (*pāśas*) consisting of the *āṇava*, *kārmika*, *māyīya*, *bindu*, and *rodha-śakti*,
and the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) beginning from the *śiva-tattva* down to the *pṛthivī-tattva*, [are explained].

And [he describes] the manner of creation by means of these, as well as the nature of the worlds and the lords of the worlds— which must exist as the instruments for the experience of the selves— and the dimensions and transformations of the worlds at the first dissolution.

The nature of the intermediate dissolution (*madhyamapralaya*) and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the manner of creation following those dissolutions, the dress of the Pāśupata, Mahāvrata, and Kāpāla scriptures,
their essential reality (*tattva*), the meaning declared therein, the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), the immeasurables (*aprameya*), and the restrictive rules (*niyama*).
They are proclaimed.
By means of the Yoga-pāda, however, these thirty-six principles (tattvas), the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras), the Self (ātman),
the Supreme Lord (parameśvara), Śakti, and Māyā— which is the cause of the universe— along with Mahāmāyā, [are explained].

The power [of yoga] consists in the non-perception of the reality of sense objects, the attainment of supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, and the methods of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), meditation (*dhyāna*),
concentration (*dhāraṇā*), recitation (*japa*), and absorption (*samādhi*), including the various types of *dhāraṇā* such as that of the root-center (*mūladhāra*) and others.
And its non-abiding is proclaimed.

In the Caryāpāda, however, [the topics include] expiation (prāyaścitta), the investiture of the purifying thread (pavitrāropaṇa), consecration (pratiṣṭhā), the characteristics of the Śiva-liṅga, the characteristics of manifest and unmanifest liṅgas such as Umāmaheśvara,
and the characteristics of the lords of the Gaṇas such as Skanda and Nandin.
The characteristics of the rosary, the yogic belt, the staff, the water-pot, and so forth, as well as the funeral rites,
the Śiva-śrāddha, and other such matters, are explained on page 632.

By the *kriyāpāda*, however, are explained the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), liberation (*nirvāṇa*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and the initiation that serves as the means for enjoyment and liberation for those who have entered the Tantra;

as well as the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*), ritual bathing (*snāna*), twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*), worship (*pūjā*), recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), adoration (*arcana*), and the [sacred] ground (*bhūmi*).
These [factors] are equal and distinguished with respect to their appropriation.

Then, having prepared books containing the Śiva-knowledges— characterized by the appropriate marks and produced on leaves made of copper and so forth, or on birch bark, or on sacred palm leaves, according to their availability— one should [place] them therein.
They should be written and recited by means of a stylus, or with ink and so forth, using scripts such as Nāgarī; as it is said in the *Santāna*:
Now I shall describe the book; listen briefly, O observer of noble vows. One should have it made twenty-two finger-breadths in length according to the measurement-finger (mānāṅgula).
The width of that book is said to be four finger-breadths; endowed with these characteristics, it is known as the Lakṣmī-leaf.
One should know that the Śrīkara [measure] has a width of twenty-one finger-breadths and a depth of three finger-breadths; it is the best when combined with the middle [proportions].
It should be twenty finger-breadths long, diminished by three finger-breadths [to become seventeen];
this is known as *candrakānta*, and it is considered either superior or inferior.
I shall describe the superior [measurement] for the medium [type]; listen, O Sarvāṅgasundarī!
It is eighteen aṅgulas in length, and likewise one and a half aṅgulas in width.
Now the middle [type], known as Nalina, shall be described;
it measures seventeen aṅgulas in length and two [units] of five and three aṅgulas [in width]. It is to be known as Śrīnivāsa, and now Śrībhadra is being discussed.
The length is sixteen finger-breadths, with two [parts] of five finger-breadths each;
the middle three have been described— now listen further.
Fifteen finger-breadths in length and two finger-breadths with a spout— this is called the "Abode of Lakṣmī," and it is said to be the lowest of the superior types.
Fourteen finger-breadths in length and two finger-breadths in width, it is known as Umābhadra;
this is the middling among the middling [types].
Thirteen finger-breadths in length and two finger-breadths at the base of the fire-altars—this is to be known as the Śacībhadra; it is now described in nine ways.
Endowed with these characteristics, it brings all prosperity to men; [it is worshipped by] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śarva as well.
Kālarudra, Nīlarudra, Pralayānala, and Sarvabhakṣa-Śiva are declared to be the presiding deities; now their Śaktis are also described.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikāriṇī, Balavikāriṇī,
Balapramathanī, and Sarvabhūtamanonmanī.
Then Viśvāmitra, Vālmīki, Kāśyapa, Aṅgiras, Gautama,
Gālava, Gārgya, Vasiṣṭha, and Śaunaka likewise.

A wise person should collect a manuscript endowed with these characteristics;
it should be made of birch bark or even of *meru* leaves.
Alternatively, one should especially take a palm leaf;
as it is stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"It should be made according to one's own proportions using a palm leaf or the like, or else with copper."
It should be fashioned as being joined with two hollows.
The leaf-measure is divided fourfold; that [measure] is again threefold. By means of the fourth and third parts, there should be a middle section, and the central part should be hollow.
Having divided the length into five parts, it may be [constructed] with two of those parts, or with three parts, or even with one part;
this should be done according to the logic previously stated.
In the lineage [of the ritual],
having prepared the *jāti*, *kramuka*, *uśīra*, and coconut in equal proportions upon a leaf, it should be made to whatever thickness is required.
On the two sides, however, it should be fashioned like the surface of a mirror;
one should decorate it with the characteristics [of the deity], dark as a blue lotus or the color of a Jāti flower.
One should take cotton thread and especially make it into a rope;
with twenty-seven threads, the rope is said to be of the highest quality.
The middle cord is said to consist of eighteen threads; that which is joined with nine threads is called the inferior cord.

Regarding *sulupya*, however, there is the *nārāca* and the *santāra* combined.

Alternatively:
the pedestal should be two finger-breadths [high] with four finger-breadths for the wings;

The seat of Śiva-jñāna is demonstrated in the Dīptatantra; for that seat, the length of the staff is eighteen finger-breadths.
It should be two finger-breadths in circumference, entirely circular or square,
and made of gold, silver, copper, or even iron.
One should fashion a bud at the tip of the staff, adorned with lotus petals; one should divide the staff into five parts and discard one part at the top.
One should release that measurement as one quarter; the *rajju-muṇḍana* (the cord-cutting) consists of three parts, joined with two apertures and the exit of the cord through the doors.
Joined with various threads and joined with various knots—thus is the seat described there; one should arrange the remainder according to the proper method.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"The book should be worshipped in the center [of the mandala], seated upon a seat consisting of a reed-fiber mat; thus it should be written."
Having performed the worship twice or even once, day after day.
With horns that are symmetrical, neither too thick nor too thin,
with well-developed and glossy limbs, and neither too widely spaced nor too closely joined.
Have this book written in the Nandināgarī script using characters distinguished by their vowel quantities (mātrās), svarita accents, conjuncts, short and long vowels, and so forth.
In the Kāmika:
"The preceptor or even the disciple should write it or cause it to be written on an auspicious day,

This Śivajñāna has been diligently inscribed by Paśu using characters originating from various regions that are endowed with beauty.

Having worshipped Śiva with perfumes and other offerings, one should [worship] the Mātṛkā, who is the very form of Śiva.

The knowledge of Śiva, which had been lost over time due to negligence,
was written down with missing or extra syllables by those who were careless;
it was taught through oversight and destroyed by those of small intellect, and even after being corrected by teachers possessed of limited knowledge.
[One should avoid] that which is endowed with useless words, that which is redundant despite having a good meaning,
that which lacks consistency between its preceding and succeeding parts, and that which contradicts one's own established doctrine.
For one who has lost the light through metrical license, for whom the meaning of the words is obscured,
and who is occasionally beset by such and other faults;
The wise preceptor who correctly performs the consecration,
being a knower of the true meaning of the Śiva-tattva, is that supreme Lord of Knowledge.
Relying upon this knowledge, the fivefold sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*) proceeds.
Thus, it is stated in the *Śivadharmottara*:
What are the signs of study, exposition, and hearing? Thus, this fivefold sacrifice of knowledge has been proclaimed.
Of all sacrifices, the sacrifice of knowledge is the giver of liberation.

In this regard, first there is the desire to know the meaning; then, when the time comes to engage with the meaning of the scripture, there is hearing it in its entirety and reflecting upon it through reasoning; after the ascertainment of the meaning, there is meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*). When these three are present, knowledge arises at the time of completion.
One should state the conclusion.
