Now, the sequence of the exposition:

on a ground purified by smearing with cow-dung and the like, free from defects such as indigestion (ajīrṇa) and so forth, avoided by those who have not received initiation, and cleansed; [one should place] that which resides within the path of the Self in the center.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord, the Guru, and Gaṇeśvara, and having prepared the thread and other materials required for the ritual— ensuring the secret,
authentic thread is placed upon something [elevated] facing east— one should say, "O limb, here before you," and, having accomplished the purpose, one facing east should begin.
The Guru gave the explanation, beginning with the statement of the relationship [between the topics].
p.643) Following the sequence of the streams (*srotas*) according to their divisions, there is indeed a reckoning [of them]. For the sake of practice,
he whose [teachings] have been proclaimed [takes] his own Guru and the streams starting from the *Kāmika* upwards.
Having circumambulated Sitāṅga and the others,
and having joyfully reached the extensive [teachings] such as Uttara and Prācya, as well as Trotalādi, one attains the Āpya [tradition],
the Caṇḍādhisārāsida, the domain of Caṇḍanātha, and the Lord of Mantras of Śiva.
The wise know the eight currents (srotas) to be the divine, the rishi, the guhyaka, the yoginī, the siddha, and the kaula.
One who travels against the current should state these [matters] individually;
having been authorized by him, one should recite them in the Mataṅga at a pure place, on a clean spot, in a secluded and solitary location.
With a delighted and purified inner self.
A wise person should not perform teaching in the proximity of those who are superior.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
In a secluded, solitary, delightful, and venerable place, one who has conquered the senses and bathed in purity should cause the Guru, the Vidyādhara, to proclaim the knowledge of Śiva.

And it should be heard by those who are such [as described], who are disciplined and devoted to that; and having joined the Guru at the beginning and the end, by those endowed with true devotion. Thus, in the *Kiraṇa*:

Having bowed down according to the prescribed rule, one should thereafter recite or listen to the Śiva-śāstra, or else another general scripture that includes the Lord; this is the duty toward the Guru’s seat of yoga (yogapīṭha),
which should be thirty-six aṅgulas in length and four aṅgulas [in width].
It was broad and variegated with rows of petals.
Having made a square measuring one cubit, place three *śaṅkus* at its two corners;
outside, it should have the elevated surface of three lotuses, adorned with majesty.
(645) One understands [the teaching] as it truly is; even one who is learned should listen with a single-minded focus when [the teacher] is present. When doubt arises, one should inquire with wisdom.
There is no obstruction...
[as stated] in the Mṛgendra-tantra.
For the Śaivas, the first is the Kāmika; then the Aghora, the Acintyaka, the Kāraṇa, the Jñāna, the Ajita, the one called Dīpta, the Sūkṣma, and the Parama.
The thousand-rayed [sun] [revealed] the *Saṃjñā* [tantra] in the *Suprabheda*;
[he revealed] the *Vijaya* among the *Raudra* [tantras], and first the *Niśvāsa-pārameśvara*.
The Svāyambhuva, the Āgneya, the Vīrabhadra with its Raurava, the one called Makuṭa-vimala,
and that which is known as Candrabhāsa.
Mukha, Bimbaka, Udgīta, Lalita, Siddha, as well as Santāna,
Nārasiṃha, and the supreme Kiraṇa.

From that time forward, one should not explain [the text] extensively for a long period on the first day; even though the commencement has been reached, it is understood as being excessively premature.
Having established three, two, or even one root-sutra,
he should cease thereafter, until he is obstructed by obstacles.
p.
647) That wherein the tree of the meaning of the Great Mantra is mounted as if upon a seed—
that is the Root Sūtra, adorned with the word "atha" and the rest.
Is there another indicator for that? It may be a word expressing a numerical designation;
the statement of its defining characteristics and essential nature constitutes the summary of the commentary (*bhāṣyasaṃgraha*) on that which is other than it.
Dhoyī spoke thus: "O mother, now that we two have had our sins destroyed, let us attain radiant fame in the world and uphold the teachings of Dharma."

On the days following that, he who upholds the Kṣatra [lineage], free from support on the path, [attained] a state of heedlessness; he [performed] the inference of the Pālakālavas and the Pauras, as well as the fire-offering (pāvaka);
furthermore, he [established] the form named Ācārya, well-guarded and beautiful, upon the previously mentioned seat (pīṭha).
Having placed [the object] upon the machine, the preceptor himself, facing eastward, should draw [the thread] for the purpose of cutting.
Having placed [the disciple] face-to-face, having addressed him with "Bho," and having instructed him to recite and so forth,
[the teacher] [should proceed] with sentences suited to the respective local dialects such as Sanskrit or Prakrit, or according to the capacity of the disciple.

Having commenced the commentary by describing the relationship, subject matter, and purpose— consisting of six aspects— of the divine and super-divine forms within my own interior, [I shall explain] the eight streams of the *Kāmika* and other [Tantras] in the upper current (*ūrdhvasrotas*), the white-limbed [Tantras] in the southern current (*dakṣiṇasrotas*), and the great [Tantras] in the northern [current].

The five currents consist of the eastern currents such as Srauta and Ālāpa, and the western currents in the form of Caṇḍa, Apidhara, and so forth; furthermore, there are the eightfold counter-currents known as Mantreśvaragaṇa,
Vyāṣa, Gūhya, Yoginī, and Kālakā, as well as the forward current, which is the lineage of the gurus.
One should state the reason for the composition of this treatise.
As it is said in the *Kāmika*:
On a portion of ground smeared with cow dung and marked with colored lines,
which has been perfumed with scattered heaps of flowers and fine incense;
A wise man should not engage in study near those who possess a burning lamp, nor in the presence of pure Śaivas, nor indeed in the vicinity of bound souls (paśus).
One should teach the disciples gradually and awaken them to devotion to Śiva;
that which is given according to the Śiva-vidyā is called the gift of knowledge (vidyādāna). Herein, he who [teaches] the disciple appropriately by means of worldly words—
And by means of local dialects and the like, as well as through the traditional scriptures (āgamas) concerning such beings.
The wise man should awaken that which resides in all places by means of those residing in a single location;
as it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
With your mind fixed upon that purpose, you should explain it to the devotees of Śiva,
while protecting the lineage of gurus by ensuring they abide in the right conduct.
One should not [recite] when there is indigestion, nor during the belching of undigested food, nor during the pressure of urine or feces;

nor during vomiting, nor during diarrhea; nor while one has not bathed, nor after having engaged in sexual intercourse. Standing on pure ground that is free from the hearing of animals [or the sound of livestock], [one should recite].
Having performed worship for the sake of attaining the ultimate state, one should honor Śiva, whose form is the Praṇava, as well as Gaṇādhyakṣa, the Guru, the agent, and the locus of action.
Having placed a book containing a secret sacred thread upon something, one who has achieved his purpose, facing east or north, should say: "O dear one, read this."
The teacher should begin the exposition preceded by the words of Ambarārya.
Regarding this, the definition of the connection (*saṃbandha*) is found in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*:
p.

651) Furthermore, O Lord, the connection between Śiva and Śivā is the Great Bliss (Ānanda). From Soma comes the divine [revelation] known as the *Antarāla*, which is the divine scripture (*āgama*) residing within the *amāni*.
Elsewhere, a fifth type has been mentioned,
as follows: "The hairless, the divine, the semi-divine, and likewise the non-divine— these five types of relationships have been proclaimed."

Having thoroughly understood the thirteen types of disciples, beginning with the *adhvālaṃka*, one should instruct them according to the specific disposition of each Buddha's secret [teaching], avoiding days when study is prohibited.
Thus it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
Adhvālaka, Nirādhāra, Pramādī, Tamasopara, Kṣatradhṛk, Cyāvaka, Pālaka, and likewise Gālava.
Paura, Anumanu, Pāvaka, and Pu are proclaimed; Vicāradhī is also to be known— these are the thirteen disciples.
Having entered and plunged into this path, which is the meaning of all tantras, and because of the connection with these [teachings], even amidst statements that appear unrelated;
That which is called *adālaka* upon entering is the infant *adhvālaka*.
Furthermore, for an object that has been grasped, there exists no other support for its persistence.

O great sage, although spoken, it would remain without support due to the weakness of its foundation; therefore, you should not be negligent, both because of your own indolence and because of the certainty of the listener.
In the Tantra, a disciple who is negligent is considered unworthy of the cause; even when engaged with effort, he remains constantly under the sway of sleep.
Even a student who has mastered [the teachings] is considered tamasic if he is clever only at the beginning and at the end,
having merely understood the divine scripture.
Having reached the "Lord's Umbrella" (īśchatra) and having performed [the rite] above, he acts; that disciple, whose vision is wounded, is to be known as the fifth in the lineage of disciples.
One whose mind, like that at the end of a vow, has previously wavered from its own object toward something else,
and who asks [questions], is declared a *śrāvaka* on the path of a *śrāvaka*, and is called a *śiṣya*.
Always knowing [the truth] in silence, he does not even entertain doubt; he would not inquire about even the slightest matter, for he guards his own status as a speaker.
He is called Pālaka because he protects his own path, having correctly understood the scripture through the instruction of the Guru and by observing the traditional teachings.
Out of pride, Gālava, though but a child, would not have sought anything at all from him;
yet here he is, exerting himself before us at the time of the exposition, moving restlessly to and fro.
One who speaks excellently and is well-composed is a *paureyaka* toward the teacher;
he is so even when questioned or not questioned by both the questioner and the teacher.
Even if one does not know, one should nevertheless always speak as authorized, having thoroughly reflected upon everything exactly as it was taught by the Guru, like fire.
That disciple who grasps [the truth] by means of the straight path is considered pure;
he is led by that very path wherever it leads upon investigation.
With a joyful countenance, he proceeds like water flowing into water; with the intent to serve, he always properly grasps all matters.
The one whose intellect is characterized by discernment is declared to be the most excellent among the lineage of disciples; these are proclaimed here as the disciples of the high-souled Guru.
All these seekers of liberation, who are experts in the scriptures of Śiva, are capable of determining [the truth] by whatever means they may be able.
The teacher must always provide an explanation for one who is permitted to proceed, as seen from the rule regarding the utterance of words.

Having performed the word-segmentation (padaccheda) for that [text] and immediately thereafter the analysis of compounds (samāsa), the intended meaning should be explained with careful consideration according to the proper rules.

It is not because of the observation of a contradiction between the meanings of the preceding and following words; rather, it occurs where a specific object follows the sequence of two alternative positions (*koṭi*).
Since it is seen here that the meaning proceeds toward similarity with the actual object,
by that path either that *pada* or the *sūtra* should be supplied.

O best of sages, where the determination of a matter is not seen through direct perception, it is established by means of speech; for even one standing nearby does not perceive the reality through mere words.
In that regard, one who possesses [the necessary qualities] must reach a definitive conclusion regarding the requests for composition.
As stated in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
"My word may be contradictory, doubtful, unequal, or equal; it may be a treatise..."
One should act according to reason; one should not direct oneself according to one's own personal whim.

When [the word] *apeta* is used in conjunction with the grammatical factors (*kāraka*s), then the object of the verbal action (*svādya-uddeśa*) must be indicated by the most excellent teachers for those who have been divided [into their respective case roles].

The seventh case is to be employed in the sense of the sixth, and the sixth in turn in the sense of the seventh; by this sequential application, one should practice the transposition [of cases]. The seven factors of action (kārakas) are to be joined with their respective objects according to the requirements of the meaning.

O domestic priests, even though it has been heard and approved, the exposition of the text must always be performed with diligent effort, word by word and sentence by sentence, according to the manner of the food [offered].
Thus.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should not teach for the purpose of receiving Śiva-knowledge on the full moon, the new moon, the fourteenth, or the eighth [lunar days], nor during the junctions (*saṃdhi*)."
In this regard, there is a transition of the junction (*sandhi*).
Thus, it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
One should not teach on the fourteenth day, on the eighth day of either fortnight, nor on the first day,
the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, or during the sun's transit (saṅkrānti).
There was thunder, forest fires, and an earthquake, followed by the drawing of bows; at twilight there was thunder and the quarters of the sky were obscured, and a halo appeared around the armies.
A rainbow appearing in the sky from mist; these [omens] are seen in cities.
An unobstructed sound from the atmosphere. A meteor is a form of fiery light shaped like a staff.
An earthquake is the shaking of the earth. And finally, a bow in the western direction, the quarter of Varuṇa.
Regarding these, the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) lasts for one day; however, when a *kīlaka* occurs during a solar or lunar eclipse, it lasts for three days.
Such portents (*utpāta*) take the form of a *kīlaka* appearing within the disks of the moon and sun.
Upon seeing that [eclipse], and when Rāhu causes defilement, there is a suspension of study for three days;
for five nights following the mouth of Hari, and during the purification of the enemy of Makha (the sacrifice).
In the case of the death of a person in the presence of Hari, or at the awakening of Hari (the festival of Janmāṣṭamī), or during the Parameśvara-pavitrārohaṇa ceremony,
the impurity lasts for five days; however, if a cat, a snake, or a frog passes through the interior [of the house], it lasts for one day.
If three hooded serpents are seen, it lasts for three days; if two hooded serpents are seen, it lasts for two days.

On the day one hears rumors of an end, hears of a burning, smells the odor of a corpse, or encounters a harsh wind; on the day such things cease, or on the day of one's birth or death—these days are excluded.

If the Guru has become Śiva, [one should observe impurity] for one month; if it is a brother, a disciple, or the like, for three days; if it is a king who is a Śaiva, for seven days; and if he follows the dharma of the bound (paśu), for three nights.
In the *Ṣaṭsahasra*:
the full moon, the empty eighth, the new moon, the sixth, and the two first days (of the lunar fortnight).
During the Vyatīpāta yoga, at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), and during the three Aṣṭakā festivals.
Especially on the day following the completion of a vow at twilight, when a sage has died,
when a perfected being (siddha) has died, or when a great king has passed away.
When there is the falling of meteors and firebrands, the appearance of a comet, mist, an affliction of the army,
or untimely rain;
If a lizard, a frog, or a cat intervenes [between the teacher and student], or if a snake enters [the space] while the *anaddha* rite is being performed,
there shall be offerings and worship for three nights.
In battle, near a corpse, upon the wailing of women, likewise when a cruel king is seen, or when executioners are in sight;
When one has traveled a great distance, during physical exertion, in a cow-pen, at a royal festival,
during the introductory song of a courtesan, and likewise between vomiting and exhaustion— on all these occasions, there is a complete suspension of Vedic study.
It is to be known in the two types of worship—that which is to be awakened and that which is to be realized.
Thus [it is said].

O great sage, [one should perform this] on the fifteenth, the eighth, and the fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, on the sacred festival days (parvan), during all great festivals, and at the twilights.

On all the junctions of the lunar phases (parvan), those whose nature is that of a practitioner (sādhaka) should not study; likewise, upon seeing their teacher or a brother in a state of disrespect anywhere.
One endowed with devotion should not study this supreme knowledge of causes during auspicious times, nor, O observer of noble vows, when misfortunes have arisen.
In times of adversity for devotees of Śiva, or for kings of great soul,
this study must be performed by the practitioner as declared by me.
In the *Mṛgendra*:
"Listen, [that which is] performed according to the rules taught by the independent [tradition] during non-study periods is false; it is Śaiva."
Knowing this, one who is short-lived here undergoes the state of a dead ghost.
This knowledge of Śiva, like the scriptures of the bound souls (paśu-śāstra), should not be led astray by various disputants.

It should not be illustrated to those who associate with impure people. It must be given only to a disciple endowed with devotion and faith, who has been purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta). Thus:
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should never engage in verbal discussion of the Śiva scriptures, nor should one recite them in an assembly of impure people."

O Six-faced One, for one who possesses supreme devotion toward the God and constant devotion toward the Guru, and whose power does not lie in other scriptures, one should apply knowledge to that [Guru].
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Those who study or write the knowledge of Śiva without having first worshipped it, or in an improper manner..."
They bestow [it], they hear it, and they recite it.
And being deluded by greed or by the discipline of false knowledge, they establish themselves at will in the unconditioned realms.
Having neglected the discourse on the knowledge of Śiva, he speaks of other things; though capable, he does not study, and instead indulges in pleasure.
"Or he who hears of the engagement with the impure in an impure place—
in brief, knowledge regarding all limbs is considered equal to censure."
Regarding the Three Jewels—
the established doctrine is practiced by the virtuous who have been purified by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
As stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
O Guha, the meaning of the Śiva-śāstra is the most excellent among all scriptures;
it is more secret than the secret, and must be guarded with great effort from those who are not fit to receive it.
It must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who lacks devotion, nor to an atheist; nor to one who hates the guru, nor to one who delights in other scriptures.
Entirely nihilistic, cruel, deceitful, fond of quarreling, and practitioners of sorcery who employ trickery, they ask questions with sweet words, or else provoke anger.
A wise person who desires their own success should not place trust in them.
Likewise, in the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"O fair-faced one, this knowledge of the manifest stream should be protected from my devotees."
Just as one would protect wealth from thieves with great effort.
At the conclusion [of the Mataṅga], the wise one, having prostrated at the feet of the Guru, should cease, having performed [the ritual].
And indeed, the service of the limbs is properly completed by the feet.
Thus, he who always provides this exposition with a serene countenance shall rescue his disciples from this ocean of saṃsāra.
And whoever, being devoted and with a mind always dedicated to Śiva, should hear this, he is fit to proclaim here the path of the lineage of Gurus.
In the Śivadharmottara:
"The supreme sin of that person of deluded intellect who, having studied the knowledge of Śiva, abandons it, should be known as equal to the drinking of liquor."

He who hears the Śiva-knowledge according to the proper method and acts accordingly shall attain Śiva-knowledge; in the opposite case, he goes to hell. Even he who recites a single verse or half a verse of the Śiva-knowledge [attains the same].
Listen to the fruit of his merit compared to other Śrāvakas: the merit that results from giving the entire earth filled with all kinds of jewels for three eons— [that is surpassed by this].
"O Lord, by reciting the meaning of the verses through the knowledge [of them], one shall obtain that fruit. Thus it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"As long as there is the cognition of the syllables in the book of the knowledge of Śiva..."
For that many thousands of kalpas, the donor shall dwell in the city of Śiva.

Having rescued ten ancestors and brought ten future descendants under his control, he shall establish them in heaven and himself go to the great, divine city of Śiva, together with his mother, father, sister, son,
dharma, friends, and kinsmen.
Accompanied by his entire retinue of servants and the inhabitants of the city.
By the power of the gift of knowledge, one shall go to the divine city of Śiva,
provided that one offers this most excellent and venerable manuscript, which is not to be defaced, to one who is devoted to the knowledge of Śiva.
Listen to the fruit of his merit.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are leaves in that most beautiful heap,
for so long is he honored in the world of Śiva.
He who provides the leaf, the first sūtra, the ink, the ink-pot, and the pen, as well as the arrow, the bow, and other such implements, is entitled to a share of the wages for that work.
Whatever else there is of this kind, such as that which is used for half [the measure], whether it be large or small,
it becomes destroyed.
Having offered even that single limb of knowledge according to the extent of his wealth of faith,
he is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments.
It is also shown in the Sūtasamhitā:
"The transcription of the Śiva-vidyā and the gift of its manuscript is declared by those proficient in the Śiva-scriptures to be devotion to Śiva."
The depositing of Śiva’s scriptures, bathing, and the construction [of temples] by those who possess faith— these are declared as "devotion to Śiva" by those expert in the vision of Śiva.
And it is said in the *Puṇḍarīkapuramāhātmya*:
"He who provides leaves for the transcription of the Śiva-śāstra to a twice-born devotee of Śiva shall attain this world."
By giving a Śiva-scripture, a thread, ink, or a pen, or by providing protection for a scripture, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
He who, having preserved another's Śiva scripture during a national upheaval,
returns it later, shall attain union with Śiva.
Thus ends the procedure for hearing the Siddhānta within the ritual manual for worship for one's own benefit.
May the Lord of Śrīśālīvāṭī protect [us].
(p. 668) || The Ritual Procedure for the Midday Worship ||

Then, at the time of midday, having performed the bath and other rites, one should worship Śiva in detail as before. If one is unable, one should worship the Lord with the "eight-flower offering" (aṣṭapuṣpikā). Thus says the Āgama:
Having performed the midday ritual with five sacrifices during five muhūrtas,
one should worship with supreme devotion at six thousand [recitations] during the morning, at midday, and likewise when the sun has set.
With devotion, according to the ritual of the eight flowers.

For the poor, the protectorless, children, women, and the simple-minded; for those who enjoy worldly pleasures, those afflicted by disease, and those whose souls are distressed by study; for those devoted to the Śiva scriptures and those whose nature is benevolent—does not the accomplishment of their welfare come through food?
p.
669) The "Eight Flowers" (aṣṭapuṣpikā) has been taught for those who are both attached and detached.
Herein is the sequence: having sipped water (ācamya), performed the ritual of the limbs (sakalīkṛtya), offered the water-offerings (arghyāṇi), and bathed the deity;

Having placed [the deity] upon the pedestal, one should arrange the seat with one flower and the form (mūrti) with another; then, having fashioned the five limbs— excluding the eyes— with five flowers, one should worship with the root mantra and perform special offerings according to one's capacity.
On that very seat, one should first offer a flower with a pure mind;
the offering of the form (mūrtidāna) should be performed with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), while the other [offerings] are made with a flower.
By the offering of five flowers, one should arrange the five limbs; likewise, by the eighth, Śiva [is worshipped], and thus the "Eight-Flower Rite" (aṣṭapuṣpikā) is described.
p.
670) Likewise, the eight flowers consist of the seat, the image, the root mantra, the limbs, the eyes, and [the remaining] four;
these eight flowers are common to all [practices].
She bestows all accomplishments here, as well as in all stages of life (āśramas).
Alternatively, one should worship the deity seated upon the previously honored pedestal with the eightfold offering of flowers (aṣṭapuṣpikā).
Thus, in the Kriyākāṇḍa:
One should worship the Supreme Lord after performing the bath and other rites as before;
or else, one should offer the eightfold flower-offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā) to the deity already previously worshipped.

Alternatively, when the deity has been worshipped at dawn, one should perform the worship with an eight-flower offering according to the number of that specific time, and then perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
In the *Rāmanāthapaddhati*:

"If one is unable to perform the morning twilight worship (*sandhyā*), one may perform the midday worship as well; having performed even the 'eight-flower' (*aṣṭapuṣpa*) worship, one should then conclude with the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*)."
If,
due to some deficiency or by any means whatsoever, the daily rite is performed at a Linga worshipped by others,
then the final result is equal; however, this is not the case if the rite is performed in an abbreviated form.
Indeed, a mixed ritual should never be performed.
And it is said:
"One who is not in a hurry should always perform [the rite] using the liṅga and other implements consecrated by another."
Or they may have equal conclusions. One should conclude the ritual procedure with the *puṣpikā* (colophon).

Those who know the ritual procedures should perform the rite as prescribed in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), and not otherwise. That person of deluded intellect who performs a mixed rite according to both [Tantras] incurs a *śara* [obstacle].
"Its sin is declared to be equal to the drinking of liquor.
672) Now, in the case of the common *liṅga*, worship should be performed using only common mantras.
Likewise: the Praṇava, the Mātṛkā, the Madhya (or Vyomavyāpin) with its six syllables, the Prāsāda,
and the Ghoramantra— these are considered the seven common [mantras].
With these, the wise one should worship Śiva, who is common to all.
Having thus completed the midday ritual, one should partake of food.
Thus, having performed the midday rite, one should eat; not otherwise.
For those two who have not desisted, [there is] the sound of Saturn, which is honored by the gods.
"The mantras do not preside over that [which is devoid of yoga], for they are established upon the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha).
Thus ends the procedure for the midday worship in the *Ātmārthapūjāpaddhati*.
p. 673) || The Rule for Eating ||

[The Procedure for Eating Alms-food from a Continuous Line] Now follows the procedure for eating. There are two kinds of eating alms-food: eating alms-food from a continuous line (*sāntānika*) and [ordinary] eating alms-food. Of these, this is the procedure for eating alms-food from a continuous line.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"The lineage beginning with the disciple is the Śaiva succession (*santāna*); that which is offered to the Guru as a substance is known as the alms of the lineage (*sāntāniki-bhikṣā*)."
Likewise, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The wealth, grain, villages, and other such things that have been given by gurus and accepted with devotion by disciples, or [given] by pure devotees such as the twice-born and others."

That which is given with devotion should always be accepted, but not from others such as those who drink liquor; one should avoid the property of the gods, the property of the guru, and the property of outcastes.
He who cooks for his own sake alone is called a slayer of a Brahmin;
[but he who cooks] for the sake of the gods, the teacher, the fire-ritual, and likewise for the honoring of guests, [is not].
It is said that the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is cooked by oneself using dry fuel-wood,
free from insects and other impurities, in a clean and smeared kitchen.
The cooking should be performed by oneself, or it is considered acceptable that it be done by others who are pure.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Having offered the best of all cooked food to Śiva, one should offer it into the fire and then distribute it."
"The portion for the Guru"—this is the rule that must be observed constantly.
He who daily eats the first portion of all cooked food after having offered it to Śiva, Agni, and the Guru, is Rudra himself;
of this there is no doubt.
But that man who eats without having first offered [the food] eats only sin,
accumulated through agriculture, usury, trade, anger, falsehood, and the acquisition of wealth by such means.
In these [occupations], sins increase through the five defects of the slaughterhouse:
sweeping, anointing, water, fire, and grinding.
There are five slaughterhouses for householders that constantly increase their sins;
one is not tainted by these sins through the worship of Śiva, the sacred fire, and the guru.
Therefore, because of these terrible transgressions, one should worship the triad of Śiva, the fire,
and the guru for as many days as the number of those who have attained siddhi.
For that many thousands of years, the donor shall dwell in the city of Śiva.
According to the *Śivadharmottara*:
"One should cook for the sake of the gods, the sacred fire, guests, and mendicants, and never for one's own sake; [one should not cook] for oneself..."
He who, out of delusion, would cook for the sake of hell, truly lives [in vain].
For those whose cooking is for the sake of the gods, whose sexual union is for the sake of progeny,
and whose life is for the sake of heaven— for them, the opposite leads to hell.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"When the cooking is finished and the house has been smeared [with cow dung], and the cooked food has been brought [inside], the pure preceptor, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*),"
One should sprinkle water from jars over the cooked food in due order.
Having extracted the finest portion of that cooked food, one should offer half to Śiva; then, having gone with the remaining half and having thoroughly cleansed that hearth, [one should proceed].
There, having kindled the fire of knowledge and worshipped it with the heart-mantra,
one begins the procedure for the rite of offering into the hearth (*cullikā-homa*) according to the *Kriyākāṇḍa*. Herein is the sequence:
Having purified the fire-chamber according to the ritual, having drawn that fire into the heart with the *pūraka* breath,
and having unified it with the primordial fire, one should then [proceed] with the *recaka* breath.

Having taken up the seed-syllable of fire (raṃ) by transcending the positions of the head and the heart, and having meditated with the thought, "You are the fire of Śiva," one should place the fire of the hearth.

The meaning is: by means of the sequence of abandoning the locations of the letters beginning with *ka*, which brings about the manifestation of Sadyojāta and the other [faces] that preside over them.
And in the *Brahmaśambhupāda*:
"With their respective seed-syllables, one should further cause Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, and Nareśvara to enter [the fire] in sequence," and so forth;
then [one installs] Śivāgni and Cullikā.
Thus [it is said].
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Soma. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sūrya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bṛhaspati. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Prajāpati.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to all the gods. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

Having performed the worship beginning with "Namas" and ending with the offerings, one should give oblations with these [mantras] ending in "svāhā," ask for forgiveness, and then dismiss [the deities].
Then: *oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ*—thus on the right arm of the hearth;
*oṃ hāṃ adharmāya namaḥ*—thus on the left arm; *oṃ hāṃ sarvaparivartāya*.
"Namaḥ" [is used] in the case of vessels for gold and other materials. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa, the dweller in water," [is used] in the case of water-vessels.
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahāvighnarāja; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hāṃ..."

"Salutation to Mahālakṣmī"—thus [at] the upper *udumbara* beam of the main door of that house, on the door-jamb (*dvāraśākhā*). "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Subhagā"—thus at the grinding-stone (*peṣiṇī*). [Note: Here, the text appears to be incomplete or corrupted. ... [at] Raudrakoṭṭagirika.

"Namaḥ" [is used] for the *vyūla* (or *ulūkhala*) pestle. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the weapon dear to Balabhadra," [is used] for the *musala* club. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Death," [is used] for the *p.* (679).
"Obeisance to Devacodita"—thus [he should offer] to the broom. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kūrmāyudha"—thus at the head of the bed. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda;
obeisance to the Lord of the House"—thus beneath the central pillar of the house.
Thus one should perform the *vāstubali* offering.
Likewise:
"The body of dharma and adharma, the hearth, the architectural form, the vessels, and the water..."
Likewise, the pitcher, together with the machine, the mace, and the pestle.
One should likewise place the mortar together with the broom, as well as the female owl and the female tortoise; and at the main door of the house, one should place Vighneśa and Sarasvatī.
One should worship Lakṣmī on the door-jamb and Maheśvara in the middle of the door;
and at the two door-posts (dumbara) of the house, one should worship the deity known as Śaktimayārā.

Below the central pillar is Skanda; below him is the Lord of the Site (Vāstunāyaka). Kāma is at the head of his own bed, and likewise, the sword is on the sword-throne, as is the vehicle of the vehicle.
And likewise, the maiden [should perform] the kindling of the lamp with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, water, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth.
"And those dwelling in the hermitages worship [it] for the sake of bringing about all prosperity. Thus [it is said].

Then, having washed his feet, sipped water, and performed the ritual placement of mantras (*nyāsa*), he enters the dining area— which has been smeared with cow dung, purified, adorned with flour-dust, provided with a canopy and lamps—
and offers the guest-water (*arghya*) and other offerings, marking the ground with four, three, two, or one line according to the sequence.
Seated upon the pedestal of the aforementioned means of valid cognition,

[the practitioners] should all face east, west, north, and south within square mandalas measuring one cubit each, located in front of themselves, and enclosed by four, three, two, or one line drawn with ash.
p.
681) Prior to the meal, the guide and others sit in a single row together with those of equal caste who purify the row, as far as possible.

Having assumed the vīrāsana posture with hands bound between the knees, [one should perform the rite] in vessels of gold, silver, copper, or iron; or in kāṃsya vessels purified seven times with ash and consecrated by the Aghora mantra; or in vessels such as those made of plantain wood, which are free from prohibitions.
Or they should eat food that is free from what is prohibited or unsuitable for consumption.
As stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Having washed one's feet, sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), performed the ritual placement of mantras (*nyāsa*), and become composed, one should take up a seat."
One should proceed with the aforementioned [ritual] for the purpose of eating.
Regarding the six thousand [hairs]:
is the wearing of hair or its removal praised? According to one's own wish. But as for the wearer of matted locks, he is one whose body is marked with ashes.
One should wrap the matted locks (*jaṭā*), but one should not wrap the shaven head. Thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
Having specially cleansed that place by smearing it with cow dung,
and having adorned it with flour-dust, one should prepare a nearby canopy.
Aṃśumatī:
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung and made it square, one should arrange a seat provided with a lid and accompanied by a lamp.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"One should eat in the place prescribed, having prepared a seat (*pīṭha*) in the temple; that seat for the teachers (*deśikās*) must be constructed according to the proper characteristics."
The seat for the Guru should be thirty-six finger-breadths, or thirty finger-breadths;
for the Sādhaka it is eight finger-breadths, and for the Putraka it is twenty.
p.
683) One should perform the rite of the *samaya* day, which consists of twenty-four finger-breadths;
it contains four, three, two, and one lines, extending from the Guru down to the end of the *samaya*.
One should not make the outer face [of the mandala] faceless; it should have a face like the *yogapīṭha*.
According to the *Ṣaṭsahasra*, the mandala should be one cubit in measure, square, and possess four lines.
But for the sake of providing food, one must always perform service for the teacher.
It is taught that for the practitioner and others, [the mandala] is diminished by one line for each;
in the section on ritual action (Kriyākāṇḍa), having performed the refinement in front, the Guru, facing east, [should surround it] with a line of ash.
Having stood facing west, the son.
The practitioner faces south, and the initiate faces north.
(From the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, p. 684)
The practitioner should have a gentle face; the others should be situated facing west. Or, even one of these [faces] may be used, but one should not eat while facing south.
If he eats out of negligence, he is tormented by diseases. As stated in the *Kāmika*:
"He who eats with his head covered, and he who eats facing south—he [is afflicted]."
"And on the two beds; he eats that which has been eaten by a Rākṣasa. Thus it is said.
In the section on ritual action (Kriyākāṇḍa):
[It was inhabited] by Śiva-devotees who were pure in their conduct, Śaivas whose wealth was their asceticism,
who were mutually unmixed, most excellent, and free from agitation.
The sage, with a focused mind, should eat in a single row with those who are pure from birth, disciplined, devoted to their gurus, and of noble character; thus it is said in the *Kiraṇa*.
The vessel for the Guru should be made of gold; that of the Sādhaka, however, should be silver;
for the Putraka, it is said to be copper; and for the Samayin, it should be made of iron.
In the absence of these, one should certainly not cause [the vessel] to be made of copper or bell-metal;
for it is said that in the absence of bell-metal, [a vessel] made of iron is prescribed, which is equal to that [copper] when recited with the *ghora* mantra.
In the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa):

Facing the four directions and observing silence, [the practitioner should use] a copper vessel in the absence of [another], or else a common bell-metal vessel that has been purified seven times with ash.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"With leaves of plantain, lotus, palāśa, mango, and madhūka; with jackfruit leaves; and with those abounding from the kumbhī, campaka, punnāga, kuṭaja, and other [trees]."
By these and other well-known [plants] belonging to the same genus—
such as the *aśvattha*, *bhairaṇḍa*, *mallāta*, *nyagrodha*, *arka*, and *vibhītaka*— [one should proceed].
A vessel for food becomes auspicious through the application of Śāka, Udumbara, Sarja, and other such substances as nasal drops.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
One should not eat from castor, holy fig, bottle gourd, banyan, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, or *ketaka* leaves when they are full; furthermore, eating directly upon the ground is sometimes recommended.
Or else, with hands between the knees, or in the bound hero’s posture (baddhavīrāsana),
the practitioner and the other two [disciples] should eat while observing silence. They should eat.
Just as it was spoken by the Lord and the Teacher according to their will.
Herein is the definition of the *vīrāsana* posture—
according to the *Suprabheda*, p. 687):
With the left foot fallen upon the right, it is called *vīrāsana*; this is especially prescribed for the time of eating.
Then, having washed the vessel, spread ghee over it, and filled it with pure food along with side dishes,

sprinkle the food with the Astra-mantra; then, consecrating it seven times with "Oṃ juṃ saḥ mṛtyuñjayāya vauṣaṭ," and sprinkling it again with water using the Astra-mantra together with the [deity's] name.

Having sprinkled [the area] with the *kavaca* mantra, one should offer a *bali* to the Nāgas and others—namely to Nāga, Kūrma, Cakraka, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—on a maṇḍala smeared with cow dung in the left portion using food measuring about half a mouthful, saying: "Svāhā to the secondary vital airs (*upaprāṇavāyu*)! and having thus given it.
Having offered water that has flowed from the ring finger and the tip of the left hand,
[one should offer] the remaining water submerged in black gram with the silent mantra: *māṣamagnam oṃ amṛtopastaraṇam asi svāhā*.

Then, having consumed [the food], one should perform the Prāṇāgnihotra. It is as follows: Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Prāṇa; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Apāna; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Vyāna; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Udāna; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Samāna.
Thus, holding the vessel with the left hand using the thumb, middle finger, and tip of the ring finger,

one should satisfy the vital breaths (prāṇa) and others, and then offer the remaining food as an oblation into the fire of Śiva residing in the digestive fire of the stomach while reciting the root mantra.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"When the [mantra] has been recited seven times with intensity, having meditated upon the nectar of Mṛtyuñjaya,
one should sprinkle the devotee and others who are to be consecrated there with the Mṛtyuñjaya-mantras and so forth."
Having divided this into seven parts, one should offer water as well.
In the *Kāmika*: p. 689) [End of citation]
"Oṃ juṃ saḥ"—this is the mantra of the god Mṛtyuñjaya. Thus, one who has [the syllable] "amṛte" at the beginning, joined with the *kuṭa* (the letter *k*) below it...
Then, one should take food that has been rendered nectar-like by means of the three milks; by that, it quickly becomes nectar, and when consumed, it shall conquer death.
Having carefully collected water with the Lord Amṛteśa, one should drink that water after reciting [the mantra] a hundred times; one certainly becomes immortal.
Thus it is said in the *Aṃśumatī*:
"Having washed the vessel, one should pour clarified butter into it;
having filled it with pure food, one should then sprinkle the clarified butter over it."
Having sprinkled that food, which is provided with condiments, one should place it on a mandala smeared with cow dung to the left of oneself.
On the ground, one should scatter an offering (*bali*) the size of half a mouthful for the *nāgas* and others;
the wise person should offer a handful of water, pouring it out for the *nāgas* and others.
Then, having performed the sprinkling, one should touch the food with the *prāṇa* breath;
likewise, one should perform the *amṛtopastaraṇa*, and thereafter the *āpośana*.
Likewise, the sources of all beings are established in the apāna within the self; the gods are established in the udāna, and the ancestors reside in the samāna.
The serpents dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla) are established through the vyāna breath;
[they are reached] by the tips of the thumbs and middle fingers of the right hand, with the tips of the fingers directed downward.
One should satisfy these [deities], situated within the midst of the flames of the fire located inside this sacrificial pit,
with individual oblations, taking care not to touch their teeth.
One should offer the remainder, mixed with ghee and condiments, to Īśa;
this is called the Prāṇāgnihotra, which is superior to a hundred Agnihotras.
One should especially touch the vessel with the left hand;
remaining silent, one should eat until the mind reaches complete satisfaction.
In the *Suprabheda*: "Having offered five oblations of breath with the five life-force mantras (*prāṇamantra*),
and having touched that vessel, the wise one should thereafter eat."
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:

"Then, having offered the oblation of breath (*prāṇāhuti*), one should again perform the fire-sacrifice to Śiva (*śivahoma*) in due order. For this [rite], the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the wife (*patnī*), the altar (*vedī*), and the strewn grass (*paristaraṇa*) take the form of the breaths."
These are explained in the *Suprabheda*:
"The self is the sacrificer, and the intellect is known as his wife."
And one should worship well within the fire situated inside the lotus of the heart.
Having strewn darbha grass from the hair-roots [of the sacrificer], and having uttered the syllable *oṃ* joined with the word *śiras*,
he should then sprinkle water around [the fire] and consecrate the vessel with the mantra.

One should drink water from the hollowed palm with the *amṛtīpeta* mantra. Having offered the first portion to the *prāṇāgnihotra*, one should avoid garlic, mushrooms, and the like, which are prohibited by other scriptures. While eating, one should consume [the food] with salt and clarified butter.
One should not eat by means of another's hand. One should not drink what remains after being drunk.

If food is defiled by flies or similar insects, one should remove a minute portion, sprinkle the remainder with water, and then—whether with ash, ghee, or even over ghee itself—thoroughly purify it before eating.
At that time, one should not look at an impure Śūdra, a dog, a monkey, a woman in her menses, and so forth; nor should one follow their speech.

And one should not hear [the sound of] belching. O Avalokiteśvara, if one should vomit what has been eaten due to negligence, one should immerse oneself in water. If it is half-remaining as food when the sight [of the person] occurs, one should simply perform a bath.
Upon hearing those words, having released what was in the mouth, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should eat food that is moderate in quantity and well-prepared with oil, silently, using the right hand.
Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Having abandoned garlic, mushrooms, and the like, as well as fish, meat, and so forth, for those of the first-born [caste]..."
And also for the sake of food and sustenance...?
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Likewise, garlic, meat from a crow, *gañjana*, honey, fish,
or even visible salt do not yield immediate results."
And garlic mixed with ravaka, chatrāka, and red-stalked palāṇḍu;
likewise garlic, śve... [and] kṣādra, as well as that which is upon leavings.
Likewise, one should not take clarified butter produced from the sea.
One should not eat food cooked in oil that has been kept overnight, except for other [specific] items; nor should one drink water with hands washed with water alone.

One should place water in the bowl [and eat with it]; one should not eat with the mouth wide open, nor should one eat from the hand of another. One must not consume water left over after drinking, nor while yawning, sneezing, speaking, or laughing. [One should avoid food] containing fish-bones, frogs, nails, hair, or cowrie shells.
If [the food] has been seen by flies or the like due to negligence, one should remove that portion.
Having sprinkled the remainder with water and ashes, one should purify it with hands washed by the person to be purified;
[one must avoid] impure Śūdras, outcastes, dogs, flowers, women, donkeys, and pigs.
At that time, one should not look upon outcastes, leather-workers, and the like;
hearing their speech is also not desired.
Likewise, if one perceives the sound of that fourth caste (*turyajāti*) through negligence, one should plunge into water;
when one sees it while half of the food remains unconsumed, then that is considered bathing. Having heard...
Having discarded that speech from his mouth, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Taking up such [food] as this and avoiding other types, he remains present; taking only a small amount of his own food, which is oily, he eats it silently with his hand.
In the Śivadharmottara:
"One should not eat food that has been touched by flies or hair, trodden upon by a foot,
mixed with dust or ants, or which one has spat upon."
All reptiles, flies, bugs, lice, bedbugs,
and gadflies found in food are purified by the remaining ash.
Curd, milk, ghee, oil, honey, and likewise molasses, coconut, water, and *udaka*— this is the group of six.
For food that is defiled by hair and other such things, as well as that which consists of those [defiling substances],
is purified by removing just that much and sprinkling ashes over it.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "During the purificatory rites such as conception and so forth, one should never eat in a cremation ground;
a devotee of Śiva should avoid anything touched by a woman in her menses or others [impure persons]."
Mataṅga said:
"The sacraments beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the tonsure (cūḍā) have been proclaimed;
O best of Brahmins, one must never eat at those sacraments."
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"When cooking is accomplished. In the *Kiraṇa*:
That effect, like the remains of another's meal, one should discard from its existence.
In the *Ṣaṭsahasra*:
"One should not eat the leftovers of others; by eating what is given by one's husband, one incurs no fault."
In the *Kālottara*:
"If one eats by oneself without first feeding the gurus, that entire meal is indeed excrement;
such is the nature of that eating."
An army falls instantly, and likewise one who goes alone; therefore, with every effort, one should eat what has been offered to the Guru.

The remainder of the guru’s [food] is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be nectar; having offered it in his absence, one should eat it along with those established in the four stages of life (āśramas).

Having eaten in this manner, taking a small portion of the leftover food and offering it on the ground with the words "Svāhā to those dwelling in the realms of pretas and hells," he should then wash his hands and take a handful of water (cūluka).
Having taken [the water] with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ amṛtāpidhānam asi svāhā" and having sipped it,
one should take the remaining water with the little finger,
purify the hands and other limbs with the powder and other substances placed in the hollow of the palms, and wash the feet.
Leaving aside the water remaining from that, and having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) with other water,
one should [offer] water poured from the tip of the thumb of the right hand with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Kālāgnirudra," for the sake of purifying the fault of eating.

Having consecrated Kālāgnirudra located at the tip of the big toe of the right foot, bathed with ashes, performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, formed the parigha-mudrā, churned the navel with the vāmadeva mantra,
recited the ghora mantra seven times, and released his silence;

One should cleanse the mouth with betel leaf and other such items. Likewise, having uttered "Svāhā to those dwelling in the realm of the departed and in hell," one should cast a small amount of the leavings upon the ground while reciting the *kama-mantra*.
With hands thoroughly washed,
O Aṃśumatī,
one should release the remnants of the *āpośana* rite onto the ground, as well as from the mouth.
And a water vessel filled with water from a conch shell.
Having washed the hands and likewise cleansed the mouth,
[one should use] powder made of *kuli* mixed with *sthacūrṇa*, or else powdered mung beans.
Having washed one's feet, one should discard the remaining water.
Furthermore, having taken water again and sipped it according to the rule, the wise man remains defiled by sin for as long as he continues to eat the funeral balls (piṇḍas).
Then, for the sake of purifying that sin, one should eat only a very small amount— just enough to sustain life— at the tip of the nail of Dakṣa’s right foot.
The practitioner of the heart-mantra of Kālāgnirudra should sprinkle with the thumb of the right hand;
this water from the hollowed palms should be applied starting from the base of one's own feet.
Having placed [the ring finger] of the left hand at the navel region,
one should join it with the thumb of the right hand, which represents the Sāmaveda.
Having extended both hands, one should place the mouth upon the right thumb;
this is declared to be the *parigha* [mudrā], which destroys evil food.
Thus is the Prāṇāgnihotra eternally proclaimed; having recollected the Śiva-mantra, one should touch [the mouth] with the left hand at the heart.
Having set aside food obtained from another's house, one should eat after first reciting the Śivagāyatrī;
thereafter, one should engage in the proclamation of Dharma and the hearing of the Purāṇas.
Or else—
One should sprinkle with water from the tip of the big toe of the left foot while reciting: "Oṃ, obeisance to the reality of the self (ātmatattva)."
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"Having thus eaten [the offering] situated on the left foot, one should bathe the big toe with water."
With the thumb of the right hand, however, turned downwards.
One should sprinkle the reality of the self with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Regarding the *bhadrapāla*, some say that according to the rule for binding mudrās, one should bind the *parigha* (crossed-arms) mudrā with the right hand alone.
Then, having performed the ritual dusting (uddhūlana) and made the ritual assignments (nyāsa), and having bowed to the Guru-deity and recited the Aghora mantra seven times,
one should thereafter release the vow of silence.
Thus.
Thus ends the procedure for the meal consisting of alms for the sake of peace, according to the *Ātmārthapūjāpaddhati*,
page 702.
The Procedure for Alms-food:
Now, for the sake of the livelihood of those who have reached the final stage (*naiṣṭhika*) or practitioners (*sādhaka*), one should perform the wandering for alms (*bhikṣāṭana*).
In that regard, there are four kinds of alms-food: that obtained from a lineage (*sāntānika*), that which is unasked for (*ayācita*), and that which is [obtained] spontaneously (*svayaṃ*...).
"Alms-food (bhakta) is that which is given by honey-makers. This has been stated in the *Pauṣkara*:
"Four kinds of alms-food (*bhaikṣa*) are proclaimed for the high-souled practitioners (*sādhaka*):

that gathered like honey (*mādhūkara*), that which is offered spontaneously (*svayaṃdatta*), that obtained from a household where a marriage is being performed (*sāntānika*), and that which is unasked (*ayācita*)."

In that regard, the nature of alms received from a lineage-holder has been previously described as supreme. The nature of what is given unasked and spontaneously is explained in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
When pure food is respectfully presented without being asked for—
ranging from food up to land— that is called *ayācita* (unasked) alms.
One should avoid accepting what is given unasked from Kirātas, actors, fishermen, cowherds, executioners, and others who are outcasts or accused of grievous sins.
Whether he has entered for alms or wanders about by himself,
the alms brought forward or given by himself are free from possessiveness.
In the Pauṣkara:
"The alms given spontaneously by others that fill the mendicant's bowl,
as he wanders from house to house, is known as *mādhūkara*."
In the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"Just as a bee, even while taking nectar, does not harm the flower,
so too should one who is patient take alms from the master of the house."
That which is endowed with these characteristics is always considered a proper fast;
indeed, O Nandikeśvara, alms-food is the best form of perpetual fasting.
In the rule for alms-gathering, the *mādhūkaraka* method is especially unsurpassed. One should wander for alms among the four castes, avoiding those who are accused of crimes.
One should never eat food from a single source, even if it comes from the family of Bṛhaspati;
however, if one accepts alms due to the pressure of a request, no fault is incurred.
"Even in the house of an ignorant person, honey-gathering alms (mādhūkarā) are considered pure.
Thus it is said.
This practice of *mādhūkarī* is of two kinds: begging for grains (*kaṇabhikṣā*) and begging for cooked food (*annabhikṣā*). Among these, begging for grains refers to begging for rice;
it should be performed only in the forenoon, directed toward those who are hungry and desirous of liberation.

The second [type], however, concerns those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*); it should be performed when the sun is situated in the west (*pratyak*). In that case, [the materials] consist of leaves made of copper, iron, *brahmavṛkṣa*, and so forth.
The begging bowls for those seeking worldly enjoyment (bhogin) are made of gourd and the like; those for those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) are the vessels of the seeker of liberation.
These should be made twelve finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths in height.
Every day, after sipping water and observing silence, begging for alms is the highest [duty].
By the final quarter [of the verse], that alms-food is thus indicated;
or rather, should alms consisting of grains be sought from many teachers, or not?
Then the cooking should be performed by oneself, or [the rite] should be divided into three parts if [the disciple] is pure.
As stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"But when one is endowed with wealth and is constantly devoted to the quarters..."
Deprived of wealth, he should wander for alms, subsisting on gleaned grains or food cooked from such scraps.
In the commentary on this [verse], it is stated in the *Mataṅga* (p. 706): "The meaning is 'the begging of atoms' (*kaṇabhikṣā*) or the begging of cooked food (*pakvānnabhikṣā*)."
Now I shall describe the wandering for alms as it is performed by ascetics for the sake of liberation;
having completed all their duties, they should do so when the sun has reached its western course.
In the construction of the altar from the center:
the alms-bowl must necessarily be made of copper or even iron;
it should be known to be eight finger-breadths in height and twelve finger-breadths in width.
Likewise:

For one desiring food, an alms-bowl made of copper, iron, or the leaves of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree and so forth is prescribed; for one desiring liberation, a gourd vessel (*tumbaka*) and the like are prescribed.
The alms-bowl should be made of copper or fashioned from leaves;
the *brahmavṛkṣa* is the *palāśa*. Likewise, in the *Kālottara*:
One should use the leaves of *palāśa* and *madhuka*, as well as the leaves of *kadamba* and *āmra*; however, one should avoid the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *piśāca*, *akṣa*, and *kesara*.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"In the absence [of other vessels], a gourd vessel is beneficial for one who possesses desire."
For one desiring liberation, the *tumbaka* vessel is best, or else that which was previously mentioned is beneficial.

Then, having washed his feet and sipped water, bathed with ashes, changed his loincloth, and put on an upper garment; having bound his matted hair and sipped water again, he performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and,
holding his own prescribed vessel with his heart-mantra, washed it with the weapon-mantra.

Having consecrated [the items] with the gaze and other rites, having empowered them with the Kavaca mantra, and having covered the saffron robes and so forth with a pure cloth, one should contemplate within that [cloth] the Īśāna face along with the Astra and Gāyatrī mantras;
then, having placed the Gāyatrī upon the staff and the umbrella, [one should place them] in the right hand.
Wearing his sandals, having saluted the auspicious Guru, and having requested, "May I eat even a morsel? he received permission and maintained silence.

Visualizing the vessel as blazing with a flaming weapon, one should take up the great weapons and so forth; like one who has seized the wealth of Śiva from those fallen, accused, or brought forward, one should consume it as if it were clarified butter.

One should wander for alms among the four castes in pure households. At that time, one should not spit, show contempt, or display anger. Having reached the courtyard of a house for the sake of alms, one should look at the tips of one's own big toes while saying, "Give alms."

Having remained for the duration of time it takes a cow to return, he should go to another house. While going, if called back, he should not return; remaining right there, he should accept alms, and he should not accept what is offered by means of wood or similar objects.
One should give alms-food to a mendicant who is wandering for alms. In this way, one should accept alms while avoiding those things that are mutually prohibited.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"What is the use of the fault of accepting gifts, or what is the use of the fruit of giving?
What need is there for the labor of cooking, which is the locus of many defects?"
If one is detached from these [worlds] and desires to attain great merit,
one should build a hut made of grass and leaves at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) that does not possess feminine characteristics, and [dwell there].
Let there be such an abundance of attendants as long as one proceeds with the mantra.
Waiting for the imperishable foot that is separated from the body and the path,
and constantly bringing about awakening, may those who take refuge in Śrī Śiva be auspicious.
Having bathed with pure ashes and put on a loincloth and upper garment, having sipped water for purification and observed silence, he should meditate upon Śiva as his Guru.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The wise practitioner, observing the vows, should always take hold of the vessel."
Having washed it with the seed-syllable of the weapon, one should encircle it with the armor-mantra.
The knower of mantras should meditate on Īśāna in the center and on the Gāyatrī and Astra;
he should constantly recite the Astra mantra and, remaining pure, go about for alms.
Having placed the Astra-mantra upon his staff and the Gāyatrī itself upon his umbrella,
he should then constantly wander for alms, avoiding those who are outcastes or censured.
Those such as village hunters and the like are censured.
In the *Mataṅga*: "Physicians, barbers, cowherds, Maṇḍas, liquor-sellers, and fishermen..."
One who subsists on alms should always avoid the house of a village headman.
One should avoid usurers and those who deal in small weights;
likewise, the husbands of Śūdra women, those of immoral conduct, and village leaders. And so forth.
And those who are temple-attendants (devalakas), as well as other men who have fallen away from purity.
All those who live by unjust means must always be avoided when seeking alms;
one should diligently avoid that house which abounds in the pleasures of liquor and meat.
O Sage, one should not enter that house where there is the keeping of cocks, dogs, donkeys, or camels, nor that which is defiled by women.
Seeking alms, the supreme practitioner should wander for alms among the four castes;
he should avoid the company of the wicked and never abandon his own tradition.

O Sage, when the worship of gods, fire, and guests, as well as the purification of the recipient, is observed, alms should be accepted from that person by one of great intelligence; this is known as the *avicārya* (unhesitating) gift.
Alms from a woman who has anointed herself with oil, or one who is barren, or one who is despicable, should always be avoided; furthermore, [alms] should not be accepted by hand.
In the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa):
It should not be offered with a ladle, nor with the hand, nor with a bronze vessel, nor even by me [directly].
Or by one who is pregnant with a low-caste woman, or by one whose mouth is ablaze, or by one who brings about the end [of others].
At that time, one should not spit upon a person of authority, nor touch one who has gone astray, nor bite the lip of a serpent;
one should also avoid reviling others and shun a place crowded with dogs and the like.
Neither in Nangastya nor in Brāhma did those who subsist upon the gods and goddesses approach the courtyard of the house, having encountered the four castes of pure lineage.
Having spoken the words "Give alms," with his gaze fixed on the tips of his big toes,
he should wait for that length of time until the cow has joined her calf.
The sage should reach the place where the water flows and then proceed elsewhere;
even while traveling, he should not come from that region if summoned.
One should take the alms brought by the sacrificers right there;
one should not give alms to one who wanders for alms, nor should those who are censured be given alms.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"If one should discard alms that have fallen into a vessel or those that have fallen upon the ground..."
Having taken alms sufficient to fill his bowl or merely for his own satisfaction, he should enter his hermitage while recollecting the merit of the village-dwellers.
If the bowl has been defiled by discarded offerings (*nirmālya*) or other such things, he should bathe along with the alms-bowl.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"Having begged for as much as fills his bowl or just enough for his own satisfaction, and having recognized the auspicious nature of the worlds, he should proceed to his own excellent hermitage."
Having placed the alms-bowl in a clean spot, washed one's feet,
sprinkled [the body] with ash, performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, sprinkled the alms-food with water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and consecrated it with the *mṛtyuñjaya-mantra*.

Having mentally divided [the food] into three parts and offered it to the deity and the guru, one should set aside one part of the remaining measured morsel for water and one part for the movement of air.
One should fill one part and consume it with water and so forth, as previously described. As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
Afterwards, with measured morsels of food mixed with incense and ghee,
one should fill half of the empty stomach, and that half with water.
One should not fill [the stomach] beyond what is necessary for the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and its remaining functions.
For one who observes the rule of eating alms-food, one should never eat food from a single source.
Having washed the hands externally...

Having cleansed the teeth with a tooth-stick and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, one should sprinkle oneself with ashes, meditate upon Śiva, and then cleanse the mouth with leaves or other materials.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"Having brought that alms-food and placed it on a clean,
level spot, having washed one's hands, feet, and so forth, one should again perform the *vāva* [mantra] as before, sprinkling it with water from the heart-mantra."

One should then give food to one's own preceptor, Śiva; thereafter, having consecrated it with the *kṣura* mantra, one should eat. By that [consecration], it quickly becomes nectar (*amṛta*), and by eating it, one becomes a conqueror of death.
One should eat while observing silence, and one should not do anything that causes extreme opposition.
In the Mataṅga:
"Whatever has been requested in one's own home with devotion, as well as those things brought from elsewhere— all that which was previously mentioned."
Having performed [the ritual], one should eat; never otherwise. Thus it is said.
In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
"Thus has the wandering for alms been described as the universal characteristic. There is no merit equal to alms; there is no austerity equal to alms."
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, whatever merit is found in all acts of giving, as well as in the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances;
A man who subsists on alms would obtain that fruit multiplied ten millionfold [if he were to do so] at a place where a guest turns away with his face averted once the cooking has been completed.
The gods and all the ancestors turn their faces away from him; however,
when the proper time has arrived, that gift which is given with diligence and without hesitation indeed uplifts his entire lineage.
Ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Of all worthy recipients, the guest is the most excellent;
whether he be deficient in limb or complete in limb, impure or pure.
He who avoids begging when the time for it has arrived is worthy of worship without hesitation; he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Taking all of his merit as its fruit, that guest departs; yet, when he rises up in extreme anger at the improper time without reflection, [the host suffers].
He is indeed called a slayer of a Brahmin, for he is always impure in many ways; knowing this, one should always diligently engage in the practice of begging for alms.
The perfections of one who subsists on alms and has conquered his senses are accomplished;
O Śikhidhvaja, all other forms of receiving gifts are said to be excluded except for alms.
Likewise:
"The giving of alms is a great gift; alms are not a recipient at all."
The fruit of both is equal for the giver as well as for the recipient.
Therefore, having taken hold of faith, the observer of the vow should always practice begging for alms.
As stated in the Śivadharmottara:
"One should avoid the *mādhūkara* method of begging, food obtained by chance (*sikthānna*), and fasting."
That which is known as alms-food for householders is food from a single source.
In this regard, however:
at midday or else at night, one should eat without wandering; householders should eat twice a day for the sake of increasing virility.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Having sipped water and emerged, one should indeed consume the tooth-stick.
One should perform the cleansing of the mouth with *pathyā* and other such substances; one should never consume betel leaf, which is merely a cause for coloration.
Thus ends the procedure for eating alms-food within the ritual manual for worship for one's own benefit.
Hari Om!
May there be auspiciousness!
May Śālīvāṭīśvara protect [us].
The virtuous ought to forgive the offense committed by me.
In the year named Bahudhānya, during the month of Kṛttikā, [of] the illustrious Śivasahāya...
He has five faces resembling the moon, ten arms, and holds a trident, a chisel, a sword, a vajra, and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands;
in his left hands he holds a noose, the gesture of granting boons, a goad, a jewel, fire, and a white lotus, and he is seated upon a white lotus.
The very nature of Sadāśiva.
O Lord, [I salute you] who bear an axe and a deer in your palms, who offer a salutation with joined hands,
who are white from being smeared with ashes, who shine with the crescent moon, the Ganges, and your matted locks,
who are the destroyer of Tripura in turn, the foremost among the Pramathas, and surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas.
I worship the venerable Nandikeśa, whose lotus feet are honored by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu.
Salutation to Śiva.
May there be auspiciousness. Hariḥ Om.
